There's no "neutral" button for reviews. I'm on the fence about Firewatch, but don't want to discourage people from buying it. What you'll get out of it depends on how you value games - It's not bad and there's a lot it does right, it tells a story that can leave an impact, but be aware that it's only about 3-4 hours long, linear, and with few gameplay elements.

Firewatch is more like an interactive movie than a game, with beautiful visuals and decent voice acting - Although despite that, after getting halfway through I realised I wasn't really enjoying playing it. I bought it blindly on release without finding out more about it first - I was hoping it'd be a survival timesink with a story. Instead it turned out to be a very short walking simulator, which isn't want I wanted from a game. After refunding (and swapping it for Subnautica) I watched other people play it - The story was good enough for me to want to see how it ended, at least.

Short game as it is, you actually get out of it what you put into it - Although many of the plot points are only explained if the player throughly explores some rooms. It's also dependant on how the player responds to the dialogue, despite that not changing where the player goes or the plot's events - And IMO this makes the plot fall a bit short. Also, the game seemed as if it should've been longer and wraps up far to quickly at the end, almost as if the devs ran out of budget or something. 

If you don't mind that then go ahead and get it - Just don't expect it to charm your socks off. IMO, there are many other games out there which tell better stories while actually being fun to play at the same time. This makes me think that perhaps Firewatch should've been an animation or a film instead, especially considering the linearity of its plot. It'd work better as a game if the player's actions had more consequences.

I got into this for a few hours and will be going back shortly, but just wanted to get an early review in noting that the experience has definitely been worth the money already.

Firewatch is a 'walking simulator' to an extent, in that you explore an area and find clues with very little in the way of problem-solving, but the thing that sets it aside from others in the genre is that it's less about being a puzzle-solving archaeologist, picking over the aftermath of something more interesting that's already happened, and is more about being some guy going about his job while the excitement kind of happens in close proximity - all with some company who you can interact with.

The dialogue (and its delivery) is fantastic and would be great even if you weren't offered options on how to respond.  But there are options and that increased level of involvement had me fully-engaged for hours, hunting down any excuse to get those two kids talking again.  Choosing different options to see how it changes their conversations is probably something that will have me doing another playthrough or two.

In a similar way to how I felt like conversations with your ship-mates were the best parts of the Mass Effect games, I felt like the character-driven dialogue is the best of this game (impressive visuals and authentic-feeling sound aside).  And it slathers that special sauce all over its otherwise pretty-but-simple walking/exploring base game.

A few hours of exploring and I'm hearing that I might be either at the mid-point or even close to the end, and it doesn't really feel like it... but knowing that I might almost be done really just leaves me hungry for anything else these guys might do in the walk-and-talk genre.  The talky... I need more.

This game is...confusing.

In a good way.

I don't mean that the storyline is confusing or that the gameplay is perplexing. The game itself, as a piece of art or literature or just as a game, is enigmatic. Hard to pin down. After finishing it in a little over twice the time it takes most folks, I am sad, vexed, upset, and still in awe. 

It's a rail shooter without any shooting, a mystery without any distinguishable question, and a bit of an open world game, but in a very strict environment. It looks like a choose-your-own-adventure, and it certainly behaves like one for most of the runtime. But it's not quite that either. 

Many reviews have been playing up the mystery angle. Saying it's similar to Myst or the Witness. I'd say it's closer to Twin Peaks: the mystery is there, and yet it's somehow beside the point. 

Firewatch is about the relationship two people can form in the face of loneliness. The intro starts you out filling in the blanks of how the protagonist, Henry, got to his current place in life. He's got a rocky past filled with love and heartbreak, and his journey to the park is the culmination of growing anger, fear, and uncertainty. This place is an escape. Letting you mold that path is a good way to both introduce players to Henry and allow them some tinkering to make him more their style. The reasoning is that you'll identify more with a character if you've made some important choices [i]with[/i] them rather than in place of them. The choices you can pick from are still Henry's, you're just sharing the responsibility.

After the lengthy but not unenjoyable intro sequence, Henry gets to his watchtower, a place you won't spend much time in despite the typical nature of the job. Over the radio, you'll meet your co-star, Delilah, supervisor and fellow firewatcher. 

Now, the game let's you continue making some choices. Most significantly, when Delilah speaks to you over the radio, you decide which responses (if any) you throw back at her. I've played by myself, and I've played with a friend. For the most part, these choices only affect the remainder of the conversation. I had a feeling that they made some vague impact on later convos or minor actions you can take, but that's not the point. The conversations are the point. The whole game is about talking to this person, or not talking to them. Every day spent wandering the vallery was more about her mood, her personality, her questions than it was about the valley itself. There are two things that I know will stick the most in my memory of Firewatch: the gorgeous vistas of the Wyoming wilderness, and the sound of Delilah's voice when I've actually gotten her to laugh at one of my dumb jokes or when I've pissed her off for inexplicable reasons. That very human connection, and the uber complex emotions surrounding it, are a triumph and the true centerpiece of Firewatch.

While the rest of the game has some issues (glitches, mostly - some miniscule, some glaring), it'll be hard to forget my trip to Wyoming that I took with Henry and Delilah. Thank you for that, Campo Santo.

Firewatch is a gorgeous experience set in a mountain ranged forest with a highly enganging story to follow. Opening with an emotional scene and the ability to go on this retreat to firewatch in the forest, was a humbling moment. You are constantly kept on edge of your seat, except for a few puzzles and points when key checkpoints don't register right away, but I must say, there were many points when I had chills. For real, the hairs on my arms were standing up from the wonderful soundscape.

 Being a landscape photographer, I thoroughly enjoyed the ability to use the Steam screenshot feature to capture the stunning landscapes at vary times of the day and even using the built in game camera to capture some fun polaroid type snaps.

This is going to be very brief: I do NOT recommend. I think this game should be $9.99 at the MOST based on total game time available. You'd be hard-pressed to put 6 hours into one playthrough (I played essentially nothing but the main plot and finished in about 3.7 hours). That is, unless you'd be willing to play again, which I'm decidedly not. And here's why:

First,
Graphics: 8/10 
They're gorgeous, albeit a tad cartoony on the character (you). Exploration is really nice on the eyes; there is a lot to take in visually and it's enjoyable.

Characters: 7/10
It'd be higher. I actually liked both characters and their backgrounds. However, as I've said, I finished the game in 3.7 hours. Certainly not enough time for me to fully engage with the characters and their lives.

Story: 3/10
Man. It started out great, as most people say. It reallllly builds a lot of tension, and then, that tension is just...gone. There's no other way to explain it. They had every opportunity to make something insane out of the plot and they just didn't. They JUST didn't. Not to mention, given that it's such an abominably short game for the cost of it (I even got it on sale and I'm still pissed I paid as much as I did), I don't think I would have been satisfied even if they utilized a neat plot-twist as the ending. Just...very underwhelming.

Gameplay/Controls: 6/10
It handles well enough. Gotta say, there were a couple irritating aspects to the control. First, you can get stuck in areas. If you try to travel outside the bounds of the map on seemingly flat land and get yourself stuck somewhere, you may have a hay-day getting yourself out. It's honestly a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ design flaw. It's also irritating to not be able to run while holding the map, and a few other tidbits here and there that irk me.

That average probably comes out to like a 5 or 6. But I still wouldn't play it. If you can get it for like 5 bucks or less, then go ahead, but wow, I'm so utterly underwhelmed, it's just not worth it. I'm not even going to rate the music - it was fine for what it was, pretty nice to listen to and fits the setting of the game, but it doesn't change my mind about any of this. Buyer beware.

Firewatch is a game that should be played casually while lying back in ones chair. It is short and sports very beautiful graphics while telling a nice down to earth storyline with amazing voice actors to boot. With no real danger to the player and non-existent combat the game focuses on exploration as a primary means to drive its narrative. I would recommend it to anyone looking for a unique experience.

This reminded me a lot of Gone Home - a fairly open environment that tells a fairly direct story by funneling players through a story in a beautiful environment while seeming to give them more freedom than they truly have. It's opening follows the pages of the first few minutes of Up, but it then develops into a strong story of its own, as the player Henry and his radio companion Delilah work as fire wardens and pass a summer. It teases several things but ends up providing a fairly straightforward story that I found myself truly invested in. The environment itself is a huge part of the game - even though you are wandering through areas of a fairly constant world, it always looks new and different through the use of time of day and environmental impacts. I spent about 4 hours in the game, and I kind of wish they offered an opportunity after you finish to go back and explore the environment without any constraints. It has a little bit of Metroidvania-gating, but it works well. Actually, everything about this works well.

My favorite part of video games is that they let you escape reality for a little bit. This is exactly what Firewatch is.

Firewatch A Story of Escape and Reflection

Sometimes life feels so heavy that you want to leave everything behind and go somewhere where no one else is. Just to walk, to breathe, and to turn down the volume of your thoughts... Firewatch is the digital equivalent of this exact feeling.

The sweet graphics of the Forest and the beautiful music drifting in the background give you a deep sense of peace from the very first moment. Henry's retreat to that tower is actually a reflection of the desire to escape from feelings and life that lies within us all. That tower feels like a safe haven, isolated from the rest of the world.

However, the silence of the forest eventually makes the voices you ran away from clearer. Firewatch gently but firmly reminds us that no matter how far you go, you cannot escape yourself. The solitude spent in that tower turns into a bittersweet yet healing experience, teaching you that you must eventually face your feelings.

Now this is an interesting game, and one that's made me experience something I'd never seen before. Because when I played it, I was left with a bittersweet feeling. Maybe I was expecting something greater, bigger, with more impact, or maybe I just wasn't blown away by what it told me. After finishing the game, I went on an evening stroll, and everything clicked: it was never about a story with plot twists, or about a mind-bending ending... it was all about human characters, with human fates and human stories to tell. Nothing more, nothing less. It's a game that, despite its distinct art style, manages to feel realistic, and convey emotions such as solitude, and holding on to a silver lining (named Delilah, in this case), all accompanied by a fantastic soundtrack.

Regarding the gameplay, it's a walking simulator where you've got nothing but a map and a compass to figure out how to reach your objectives. Despite the more than often long hikes, it feels more like a nice time to relax than a hassle. This, however, causes some paths or mandatory items to be unclear, and the geometry feels weird at times. The story is definitely unique, and really good, but not a masterpiece (the dialogues and acting are indeed stellar, though). I encountered a few bugs along the way, and the geometry was sometimes weird, but nothing that ruined my experience. If you want a different kind of narrative game, definitely try Firewatch out.

This game was a great experience, fantastic story, very engaging characters and certianly pulled me in emotionally. Exactly what you want in a game like this. Because of this, I have no choice but to recommend this game. HOWEVER, I want to list here the reasons I DONT think the game is worth the current price, or more than $5 or $6 in my opinion (given comparable games on Steam) - 

-The game lasts a MAX of around 5 hours. I can't say that I explored everything possible, but I certainly uncovered most all dialouge lines and secrets in this game in around 4 and 1/2 hours, left the game running for around an hour while not playing which accounts for the extra hour. I simply can't recommend a game with that few hours of play at $12 - the price I bought it at ON SALE.
-The ending was quite disappointing. I'm sure it was a great artistic statement, but for me it felt unfufilling and was a shock when I realized the game was really ending - I assumed I was simply triggering another plot of the storyline, one that would extend the game for another 10-15 hours.
-I have seen the graphics noted as a major selling point for the game, and I certainly liked the graphics, and the feel of the game was done masterfully, especially with the intermittent soundtrack. However, the "motion blur" (which I set to low) was somewhat of an annoying mechanic, and the game lagged and was slow to respond at several points during my playthrough.

This being said, I loved this game, and while the ending doesn't sit well with me and left me unfufilled, anyone who is looking for a game that plays out with a good, intriguing story, has a powerful envirnoment and mood that sucks you in, and character development at an emotional level unheard of in such a short span of time and with the level of interaction you actually have. 
At a minimum, I would expect to at least get an equal amount of hours out of a game as that at which I paid for it, but I enjoyed Firewatch enough to give it a positive rating regardless. I hope this review is helpful to any of you considering this game.

As a rule I see a walkie talkie and am like how the hell are they talking in a canyon and then i start to not care. Listening to the voice over the radio sets the mood. 

Without the voice acting the game would be ruined. The actors are just spot on, the art style is refreshing. I can play an hour of squad and it just feels like another game trying to make realistic graphics. The cell shading is a refreshing style much like The Long Dark. Don't let this fool you though, it is not that. It is sadly very short and it makes you want to play the whole way through as it tells the story much like a movie does. The color, music, actors all make the mood. There are no tricks here, if you look real hard you see the truth but at first the adrinaline is pumping and you see what you saw and take if for what it is.

Firewatch isn't a bad game; this is more of a mixed review than a negative one. 

There is genuine effort to be seen at every moment, be it the charming art style, the soundtrack, or the surprisingly impressive voice acting. The work invested into this game is apparent and recognised, but despite that effort and care, and a sound setup for an intriguing story, Firewatch falls short in its execution.

To keep it brief, the game's story sets various pieces in motion, only for most of them to fizzle out into nothing substantial; the primary mystery, once revealed, doesn't live up to the anticipation that is otherwise competently built up during the game's events. The banter between the two primary characters is fun and at most times convincing in its delivery, but for all of their development - and much like the mystery - there isn't a particularly satisfying ending; everything is left very open-ended, which might be intentional.

At its full price, I wouldn't recommend Firewatch, but for a decent discount it will reliably provide a few hours of intriguing story telling.

The camera pauses on his hand, showing his bare ring finger for a few seconds before he looks out at the place he's leaving behind. Henry has left his ring behind, just as he's left his heart. [h1]So simple, yet so beautiful[/h1]
My first encounter with Firewatch was while I was in bed with the flu, suffering from a massive headache. Because I am a person that never can do nothing, I was looking for something to watch. Firewatch seemed to be the perfect game. Not too bright, wonderful nice colours and no loud noises. What I got while watching a Let's Play, was an experience that hooked me all day long. And although I already knew the story then, I chose to play it for myself afterwards. 

[b]Characters[/b]
You play Henry, who, for the first time in his life is a lookout inside the National Park in Wyoming. Not really because his heart burns for Mother Nature, but because he suffered a personal tragedy. To flee from it, he took a job, in which he only has to sit on top of a tower, watch the vast forest beneath him and do nothing. At least that was his perception of the job. The reality is quite different.

With Henry, the (at some points) quite naive, trustful, but also impulsive man, you get a main character who is just as likeable as Ezio from Assassin’s Creed II. Not because you are playing him while major things are happening in his life, nor because you condone his decision to become a fire lookout, but because you feel his helplessness. You sympathise with him and you both grow during your stay in the Shoshone National Forest.
Next to Henry, the only “main” character is not even physically present. Delilah, his lookout boss/colleague, is only contacting him via walkie-talkie. These contacts, these witty jokes and these serious conversations make a larger portion of why you like Henry. Delilah acts as a moral compass, guiding Henry (and you; as the player can determine the answers Henry gives) through Henry’s feelings of guilt and slowly opening up to Delilah.

The chemistry between Delilah and Henry is instantly there, hooking you as a player, leaving you longing for the next transmission of Delilah! The link between Henry and Delilah is astonishing. These conversations are so much fun to listen, for instance when you find the underwear of two teens near Jonsey Lake and report that to her, she playfully tells Henry to pick up his tongue of the ground and get his job done. Wonderful! The whole game continues through with these beautiful conversations!

[b]Environmental Story Telling[/b]
As because the only source of information is Deliah, the game relies heavily on environmental storytelling. You go to explore the wilderness and stumble upon stuff. A fence, a locked gate in a cave, stuff like that. Everything you see will come back at a later point. Two teenagers drink beer, you’ll find the beercans everywhere at the site of the *SPOILERS AHEAD* [spoiler]cut telephone wire[/spoiler]. Or your [spoiler]bedsheets[/spoiler] were stolen and you’ll find them in the [spoiler]destroyed camp of the teenagers[/spoiler]. Everything that happens is not explained by the game, but you as a player are motivated to explain it to yourself, getting creative in terms of what could be going on.

[b]Dialogue[/b]
As explained above, the only dialogue is between Henry and Delilah, taking place while on the walkie-talkie. You, as the player, are given three options of what to answer, having only a limited amount of time to decide. The dialogue is one of the best features in the game!

[b]Exploration[/b]
As this is a walking simulator, you’ll walk a lot. And surprisingly, the game is not an open world that has 5000 ways to one objective. Somehow there is only a straight way to your next objective, although the straight way is, in fact, a twisted, beautiful path.
And as a walking simulator, it doesn’t really give you the freedom of Skyrim or the combat system of the Arkham Series but instead gives you a map, that compares to a level of Call of Duty, with many areas being locked off or inaccessible until you get the right tool to do it and a story comparable to the likes of an Assassin’s Creed. And it works. It is no bad thing that a lot of areas are not accessible until you find, for instance, an axe. Because the story allows it. It grips you, you want to know what is going on, and that, compared with the environmental storytelling, really hits the nail on the head. Yes, you want to explore, but the game manages it to give you so much and so little to explore at the same time that you, as a player, are not even bothered by the fact that you cannot go into that cave right now, or possibly ever. (Losing the keys, honestly…)

[b]Graphics[/b]
The games’ graphics are not realistic, but so beautiful! As you are a ranger, you’ll walk a lot outside and see a lot of sunrises and sunsets. And boy, they are beautiful. You can see that for yourself in my screenshots.
A bright yellow afternoon, going into a nice orange-red sunset. That describes a lot of this game’s scenic moments. As for I am colourblind, I am not the one to tell you about colours and stuff, just that it is very, very beautiful. For me, this game looks a lot like Borderlands, just toned down a lot, but with the beauty of a Witcher 3. 

[b]Sound/Music[/b]
The music is so beautiful, I do not even have words for it. It is very relaxing and surprisingly turned down to a minimum. It only starts at certain points, for instance when *SPOILER* your tower is broken into. Or when nobody talks and you can just enjoy a hike through the forest, listening to a gloomy guitar playing in the background, catching yourself humming along and having such a good time, in this beautiful game.

[b]Controls[/b]
The controls are pretty straight forward, there is literally nothing fancy to it, no double bindings. It is, at the end of the day, a walking simulator.
The only thing I have to criticize is the weird animation when, for instance, climbing rocks. Henry doesn’t touch the rock, but his hands float a centimetre above said rock.

[b]Recommendation:
Completionist[/b]
Obtaining all achievements is fairly easy, as long as you explore everything you’ll see. Seeing as the game only contains 10 achievements and 5 are definitely unmissable, you’ll have not really the need of a second playthrough to get all achievements.

[b]Expectations[/b]
As explained at the beginning, my first encounter with Firewatch was while suffering from the flu, not wanting to watch anything with bright, flashing lights. Judging by the thumbnails of my favourite YouTube-channels, Firewatch was the game for me. And it was really a gem! I already knew the story when I began playing, but that did not diminish my experience at all. Seeing something is one thing, but experiencing that same thing, feeling immersed as Henry, seeing his story and the story of the game through his eyes, is just great and I can fully recommend it!

Firewatch is a game that brings itself to the forefront among the recently abundant 'Walking Simulations'. I say 'walking simulation' because first of all it's not a survival game or a game with a lot of mechanics and a lot of things to do. Those who have played Dear Eshter or Gone Home will understand what I mean, and even though they are similar, Firewatch stands out in many ways.

First of all, Firewatch is a story-driven game. But it doesn't do this with cutscenes or anything like that. You will be in dialog with the person on the other end of your radio throughout the game. With very well written dialogs, the game draws you in comfortably and you find yourself wondering what will happen next as a result of the developing events.

One of the most important things you have to do is to find your direction. With map and compass in hand, you try to find your way to your mission and you get lost a lot. The map is covered with lots of trees and hillsides, so you can get lost a lot, but the environment looks so beautiful that you can find yourself looking around. Since it's mostly an open world game, you have the opportunity to walk around before your mission. However, you cannot reach some areas immediately because you need the necessary tools. Apart from that, there are material boxes left for the fire lookouts, which is the job you do in the environment. In each box you can find some unnecessary items and you can also find new map information for you to explore.

You will be in contact with the person in the other watchtower with the radio that has been with you since you first started working as a fire lookout. You can get information or chat with your radio for many important or unimportant things in the game. Some of your answers are in multiple options and you can say whatever you want. This adds a very different flavor to the story because some of the things you talk about can be brought up again. Apart from that, every once in a while you can talk about your personal life or the mission over the radio to keep the story going. This is the part that sets it apart from other walking simulators because it draws you in as you talk and makes you like the characters.

Apart from walking and exploring, you use some equipment, so it doesn't feel like a game left completely unattended. The reason I say this is because some walking simulations lack a lot of mechanics, so there are a lot of things that are missing. This game, on the other hand, has some platforming elements. Crossing the street, going up and down ropes or clearing your path with an axe.

Graphically, it is very satisfying. There is a lot of detail in the environment. We never see Henry, the main character, but we can see his hands and body all the time. The animations are very fluid, like a Pixar movie. The day-night cycle changes according to the story, but you don't realize that the transitions are pre-written, they are very smooth.

The music comes out very rarely, but again, it's crafted according to the story and when it does, it hits the spot and focuses you on the story.

The gameplay may seem short compared to other games. I finished it in 5 hours, but I can say that it is enough for other games of this genre I have played. You experience the story a lot, but the ending may not satisfy everyone. I think it was written very realistically. If you say that this is a game and it should be written in a crazy way, I can't say otherwise, but this game shows that storytelling can be done in a great way without being too fantastic.

In conclusion, Firewatch is not a game that everyone can play and enjoy. It's not a game with tons of game mechanics, puzzles or shooting. But it is a very pleasant experience. And when I say experience, it's definitely not a “Dear Eshter” style game that tells a story as you walk. It has mystery, humor, and sometimes it gives you goosebumps. I definitely recommend it to those who like this genre.

I've seen so many reviews and recommendations about this game, which thrilled me a lot. As a guy who loves fast paced games and shooting, I always have space for a lovely, slow and peaceful story based game. 

Now, games like these, like Firewatch, are the ones that some people call "walk simulators", and it's understandable if you're not the type of person who doesn't care about listening to people, which is another aspect about Firewatch. 
No there isn't much to say about the gameplay, although I do agree with some saying that it's not that engaging, unique or revolutionary.

But let's just make this review done. 
Firewatch it's a story about people, they make decisions, mistakes and think. These are not characters built for the plot, they are built to experience stuff after experiencing a lot in their lives, just like you.
The gameplay is focused on your decision to what to say in a conversation, which was amazing, I was very engaged in Henry's conversations. You climb, find stuff and use some equipment for your tasks.


One tip I should give you is, don't feel like you have much right to judge or review the human characters in this game because they feel very real and if you think they're unrealistic or generic, is because you didn't meet every person in this world and you know how to talk to ONLY a certain type of people. 

No, I can't relate to these characters (cuz I'm a 23 old guy who's still "trying" in life), but I can feel their connections and emotions, their way to show struggles, doubts, happiness. There are bits where I felt myself nervous or just anxious for the characters, and it's not only because the game makes me care for them after some time, but because they show emotions that I felt myself too, and for others too.

Overall, the game is already 10 years old, and it aged pretty well in terms of visual looking and standards (no AI back then, just pure natural art).

The ending, NO SPOILER, at first kinda disappointed me, but then I realised that life sometimes is just like that. The ending of a chapter of your life might be more different than you expect. Life is still going, we are going to experience more, and there is no guarantee that we are going to end a story the way we wished. Things happen just like that, we can't go back and we can't always fix everything in our lives. We only get to choose what to do and how to handle things, how we grow through them and not how it's going to end.

Firewatch taught me some things to remember: we're all experiencing different lives, we all love in different ways. It taught me to remember, without being stuck in the past.

People will tell you that this game has a bad ending, or that it's unsatisfying. 
It's definitely not what you thought was going to happen, that's for sure.

How else could it have ended? Is there another version of this game that has an ending that would make you absolutely satisfied? Would the decision that character made in the end not make sense in the real world? Would it be true to the game you just spent hours involving yourself in?

[b]Buy this game[/b] (preferably on sale) and do your best to sit down and complete it in one or two sittings.

Firewatch is a great concept that does not go far enough. The game is about a guy named Henry, who meets a girl and gets married, only to realize down the line that she has dementia. Henry starts drinking and then gets a DUI and has his wife taken from him by her family. In an effort to find an escape, he takes a job as a Firewatch Volunteer at Shoshone National Forest. During his time there he notices many strange happennings in his territory, which turns into a suspenseful mystery that many will find must be played until the end. 

One playthrough will last you about 4 hours, which for $20 bucks seems worthwhile since it is more than just a movie, it's an interactive experience where you really get to be engrossed in the details. Let’s start with what is great about this game, the graphics are absolutely gorgeous. Early on you are given a camera where you can take pictures of the game. I knew where this was going the moment they gave it to you. And it’s cool that they allow you to do this. As I was playing the game I thought the camera would become a central gameplay mechanic, where you needed to take pictures of things that you saw as evidence to defend yourself later, sadly this is not the case. 

As I continued playing, I kept on wanting this to be one of those fluid choose-your-own adventure books, where you could play and make decisions and things would end in a very different way, much like the Stanley Parable or Who is Oscar Lake or even Myst. Nope… And here in lies the absolute disappointment with this game. Rather than this game being a linear narrative, it really could have gone one step further and create random encounters with different outcomes. 

Do I regret spending $20 on this game? No. Considering that an IMAX movie in my area costs $18.59 for a single IMAX ticket, I think that this game definitely pays for itself. This game offers way more value than an IMAX experience as it is more interactive, where you can take pictures and it takes place in a first person perspective, where you, the player has the ability to look around and really take in the environment.

The sound design in this game is excellent. The voice acting makes you believe you are there in the moment. The interactions between Henry and Delilah are amazing and feel completely real. As you explore the game you hear your footsteps through the wilderness and the sound of the stream. I guess the only thing that took me out of it were the slightly repetitive noises when Henry would jump down long casms. But this is forgiven because of all the radio chatter and excellent storytelling of the game. In a way it is what I wanted Alan Wake to be. 

Honestly, there is not to much gameplay, and the visuals, sound, and the way you interact with your environment really lend themselves well to that escapism feeling you get from a book or movie, and considering you play Henry from a first person perspective, I think this game would be the perfect way to showcase VR done right.

If you are really into narrative experiences, you should definitely check this game out, however, if you want more puzzles, and exploration gameplay, this game may not be for you.

Up until that point I was quite absorbed in it all and looking forward to the ending, so it was a bit disappointing to see how it played out. 

If you can overlook that annoyance, the game can be very atmospheric and generally does a great job at giving you natural looking environments to wander around in - it reminds me a lot of "The Long Dark" in some respects, giving you the sense of being alone (or mostly alone...) in a vast wilderness. The voice acting is superb throughout, absolutely no complaints there. Graphics and sound in general were excellent, particularly some of the weather/lighting effects. 

I'd recommend this game, but it's definitely not going to be for everyone. If you enjoyed games like "Dear Esther" or "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter", you will very probably enjoy Firewatch too. If you think of those games simply as "walking simulators", don't buy this!

A very exciting and engaging game from the onset. The prologue is clever in that it repeatedly flips between the backstroy of the main character, Henry, and the beginnings of his journey in the present day. The choices at the beginning are not game changing but are reflected in certain dialogues further in the game (for example the name of the dog you choose to adopt) which is a nice touch.
The main story itself is very well written and cleverly builds up from the humorous adventure at the beginning to the mystery that eventually defines the game. 
Certain strange events that occur begin to play on your mind and you find yourself consistently intrigued to go on further and uncover the truth behind the happennings. I honestly found myself on edge with my heart racing as I became a little creeped out by the eerie development of the plot - the humorous banter shared between the two main characters is a welcome relief at times. I do believe that a lot of the suspense comes from being on your own for the entire game with nothing but a voice on a radio to keep you comforted. The world is wonderfully designed and the way the player must navigate with a physical map and compass adds more realism and appreciation for the world as you really have to 'discover' it as you go and find your own way around. I really liked the whole setting of it too, the role of a lookout in a forest/wilderness was well thought of and was perfect for this genre of mystery/adventure.
I only have one criticism for the game - Despite the brilliant storyline and building of suspence, I feel like such a strong development was let down by what happened to be a pretty 'nothing' ending. By the end I felt like all the effort and time had not been rewarded enough. The great mystery behind it all was disappointing. I hoped for a last minute plot twist or maybe a cliffhanger for a follow-up game but unfortunately it never happened and the ending felt very final - I understand many would like this but I personally appreciate a good cliffhanger to finish.
However, this criticism does not outweigh the many positives of an outstanding product (and at under £10 it was well worth the money!). I would love to see more games like this in the future and I would happily recommend it to others.

I've played this for the first time over the last couple of days and I think the label of "disappointing" it sometimes gets is a bit strong. I think I'd go for "unfulfilling". The setup of the story opens up lots of intriguing possibilities to weave a story that will haunt your thoughts for some time (like What Remains of Edith Finch does), but a lot of the roads it could go down turn out to be dead-end streets, and the mystery fizzles out in exactly the way they're hoping the forest fire will, without ever really burning bright.
The device of each warden being in their own tower, out of reach, is on the one hand a smart metaphor for their emotional isolation, but on the other a real barrier to caring about them as much as I'd have liked, and the way the characters act (or don't act) is somewhere between criminally lackadaisical and frustratingly solipsistic.
I'd rate the whole game as pretty good, but not a "must play". If you're in the right frame of mind, and it's on sale, then you can get things out of it - but I can't bring myself to give it an unqualified recommendation. Which is a shame, because I think these people have a great game in them.

I don't really know what to say about Firewatch. Having played it through recently I feel a bit shell-shocked. As the end credits went up I felt like an emotional wreck and had to use quite a bit of British stiff-upper-lip not to cry. I have been playing video games since the days of the ZX81 and don't ever remember a game reducing me to tears before. Apart from Big Rigs and that was for entirely different reasons.

I understand the criticisms of this game. It isn't long - but I thought the story was perfect and the length of the game fits it exactly. Often the dialogue options may not fit what you want to say - this is a story driven game and you shouldn't try to express yourself through the character (Henry), but rather advance the story through his character. It took me a while to latch on to this. Your actions influence the game progression in small (but very satisfying) ways. The story won't break and change dramatically based on your choices.

I'm sure that by now you will have looked through some of the screenshots for this game. Pretty isn't it? Would you also agree that it is simply the most beautiful game you have ever seen? No, I guess not. The graphics are good and suit the game perfectly, with the use of light being especially atmospheric. But the beauty of the game is more than that - it's the voice acting, the story, the animation, the music, the ideas - all the components are indeed beautiful. But the beauty of the product as a whole is far greater than the sum of it's parts. By the end I was in something of a state of shock. I talked about it to my friends until they all thought I was odd(er). I made them watch the credits and explained to them the significance of the final photos while I choked back tears. I ranted and rambled like a guy you meet in an underground railway station at 2:00 AM. 

This game really got to me in a way that no other game ever has. I want to meet the developers and buy them a pint of beer. I want to go outside and hug random strangers then live in the wilderness for exactly 79 days. I want to sit in a darkened room listening to Etta James. I want to play Big Rigs from start to finish. All of the above (apart from one) are true and a direct result of spending 5 or so hours playing Firewatch.

I absolutely loved this game. In this jaded 47 year old gamer's opinion Firewatch is something very close to perfection.

This game is beautiful. 

I could leave the review at that and that would almost be enough - the star player is the environment (of course, as you barely see another human for the duration of the game) with its crisp colours, sunset-illuminated vistas, and its unforgiving paths. That said, there's beauty in the script too, with an introduction that crushes your feelings to a pulp before you do anything but click a few times and a warm dialogue between the protaganist and the co-worker in the neighbouring tower. 

I felt the pacing was perfect - any time it was getting a little dull or samey, you'd get a wisecrack over the radio. Walking around and exploring never felt overwhelming but never felt too constricted either. This was helped by the map (THE MAP!). I really love this game's map - it feels like part of the game in ways that other game maps just can't seem to grasp. Whereas most games have either a tiny always-present minimap or a map you can only access via a pause menu, Firewatch gives you a physical map that your character scribbles all over. This gives it a personality that other game maps lack, avoiding the grim sameness that a computer generated map with a key just can't avoid. I also liked that it didn't hold your hand - to work out which way to go always required a few moments' thought and occasionally checking the compass.

Overall, I'd highly recommend this game. Despite its reasonably short playtime (I got four hours out of it, according to Steam's stats), it's an immersive experience that really packs an emotional punch.

I think it's utterly unfair that this beautiful game receives so many bad reviews lately only because one of the devs wants to show off as the big holy Sheriff for political correctness. In my opinion, both the "OMG he used the n-word" hystery as well as the political negative reviews for this game are stupid and childish. So what I'm going to do now is write a review for this GAME for people who might consider playing this.

Alright, what we have here is a classic walking simulator. It's the narrative story of a man who had to face serious downers in his life, and therefore decided to apply for a firewatch-job in the wilderness of Wyoming, far away from everything and everyone. He moves into his watch tower to spend months in almost total loneliness. Only with his radio he keeps brief contact to other members of the firewatch. 

Our boss on the other end of the radio sends us out to "missions". Like early in the game, we have to find a few hiker teens that left their trash eveywhere and started fireworks, which in the dry woods is far from a good idea, of course. A routine mission, as it seems, but while we are out there surrounded by nature, strange and mysterious things happen, and we got to find out what's going on. I'm not going to spoiler any more of the story, as it's a relatively short story of roughly 5-6 hours.  The game lacks any kind of "action". Pretty much like "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter", we walk around, discover and explore locations and follow the narratively told story. Sounds a bit boring, and well, for players who seek action, it probably will be boring, but for story fans it's a really nice little gem. A lovely game for a long, rainy weekends day. Besides the story and dialogs, I really liked the graphics. Firewatch uses a graphics style that is almost comic-like. The setting is really beautiful, with warm and lovely light moods, and still many objects, like rocks and clouds, are lacking details. Still walking through this simulated nature somehow feels right and natural. Hard to describe. I hope you get what I mean. Anyway, I've had a good time playing this game, and can clearly recommend it to fans of story-driven walking simulators.

[h2] THE GOOD [/h2]
[list]

[list]
    [*] Not enough gameplay mechanics, it's a walking simulator, and the main thing that keeps you going as you walk is the Radio and Delilah, without that you're just left bored at times, and although the game is relatively short, you still feel VERY slow with everything you do, every jog, every animation to jump down, rappel, it is all slow even after doing the same mechanic 50 times, the duration of the animations continue to feel sluggish and slow.

Firewatch is a very short, calming game that I would say I ended up enjoying. While not an amazing, glowing recommendation, there are things I enjoyed and I could see a very specific audience loving.

The game is more of a story than anything, and that's perfectly fine for the creators telling a story that they wanted to tell, but I can't say there is much gameplay behind anything. It's mostly just walking, while trying to be immersive and atmospheric. It begs the question that, of all mediums, why does this need to be a game? Honestly, it could have been a very long independent film, or a short series, but I can't really pinpoint what made them want to make a game out of this other than a rather pretty map to explore. It lives up to it's definition of a "walking simulator". I can see that being most people's biggest complaint with this, and that is completely fair. I can see a ton of people finding this boring. The game even begins in a different style that lacks gameplay, where you just click text on a screen, it was even a little jarring compared to what I thought I was buying into. However, I can't say I disliked my time with it.

In terms of things I liked, the world you're set in looks and sounds gorgeous. There are many moments in the main story, and definitely in the free roam mode, where you can travel and reflect in silence, with subtle hints of naturistic sounds. It had successfully immersed me. It compliments the built-in photo mode very well. The ambience was very calming and sedative in a way that I can't really describe. While I think this may be the wrong entertainment medium for this story, the plot itself seemed to feel genuine, as well as the voice acting. I could feel the heart and soul that they were pouring into this. The theme of isolationism and long distance communication was sold to me as what the creators wanted you to experience.

I feel like the developers accomplished what they wanted, and it definitely isn't for everybody. If you're super into slow, atmospheric, methodical experiences, you'll probably really enjoy this. Even just hiking around in free mode without looking at my map felt like a nice day out on my own. It just felt sweet and non-confrontational, and I was mellowed by the whole act. However if you want a more exciting and eventful way to spend a few hours, stay far away.

I try to remember the summer (it's getting into a rainy British autumn now), and the first thing I think of is Firewatch. It has a gorgeous, memorable palette, that just gets more and more beautiful as the summer in the game wears on.

Players take on the role of a park ranger, during the heat of an American summer. They have a tower, a map, and that's about it. All around, a gorgeously laid out national park, to explore at your leisure.

There's a plot and a decent mystery to it too, which you will have to solve piece by piece, but the main draws are by far and away the experience of navigating this forest wilderness, which isn't dangerous at all, but just has this look that sears into you heart, particularly towards the end of the story. Some entertaining dialogue crops up throughout between the player character and the major NPC, one watchtower away, and keeps the pacing of the game flowing well.

In terms of negatives, asides from choosing dialogue options, and also navigating (as best you can) the park itself, which is possibly one of the most appealing mazes ever constructed, there's not much else to do, but that's not really what Firewatch is about - it's all about the peeling back of a mystery, both concerning the park, and the people you encounter. And above all, it's about exploring the forest itself, which has the same kind of unique character as a location as Dunwall did in Dishonoured, or Rapture in Bioshock. It's just that memorable.

This game is amazing, but only if you fully know what you're buying.

[h2]📝 Quick Thoughts[/h2]
Won't include spoilers but reading this review might give away something you might want to know or experience for yourself. This is mostly how I feel about the game, not about what this game is.

[h3]📖 Story (Main plot + Narrative)[/h3]
The main story has a powerful base to it. It makes sense, and it's very well written. You can feel that a lot of thought was put behind each section of the story or each incident that happens in the game. The presentation of the main story is perfect.

[h3]📚 Side Content/Side Stories[/h3]
I didn't see any side content or side story, it's just the main plotline and everyone is a part of it. You can finish the game and walk around in free roam, that's mostly it.

[h3]🎭 Characters (Main + Side)[/h3]
A substantial amount of thought is put behind every character in the game. Just like visual novels where you choose one option out of many, you talk to Delilah the same way, except, she remembers everything, not just for the next response but for the entirety of the game. There are other characters which at first feel like background mobs, but surely you're going to think about them once you're AFK.

[h3]🎶 Sound & Music[/h3]
Music is immersive. When I say immersive, I mean, it changes with what's happening and it fits right. That, and the selection of the music tracks, very nice. Whether it's a beautiful morning, a suspenseful corner, a dark cave, or a shocking reveal. You'll feel it. The noise that MC makes, the sound of items you interact with, even the walkie-talkie static, it fits right, it's not annoying.

[h3]🎤 Voice Acting[/h3]
Voice acting is REALLY well done, you can feel the emotions if you have ears for it. I loved it!

[h3]🎨 Visuals (Graphics + Art Style)[/h3]
Since I played it on a good PC, it looked fantastic. I often stopped playing and just ... looked at my screen. This is the type of art style I won't mind using as a wallpaper. It's not realistic at all, it doesn't try to be, and still, it's gorgeous.

[h3]🎮 Gameplay Experience[/h3]
To me, it's a cozy game. There are no stressful game-sequences or timed challenges. Controls are basic and simple. No complex puzzle solving or spending your night finding clues to open a box. It feels like a restricted open world game which you can play linearly. The game doesn't let you run off of a cliff, which is a good thing.

[h3]🌍 World Building & Level Design[/h3]
The forest is beautiful. The terrain is believable. The map sections and region locking is really well done. The day-night cycle never felt intrusive. When the atmosphere of the game changes, you will clearly feel it. I sure did.

[h3]⚙️ Game Performance (Loading, Bugs, Framerate)[/h3]
There are no intrusive loading screens, once you start the game, you'll play all of it. However, there are some bugs when you switch apps (Alt + Tab), it won't register achievements and sometimes audio goes bye-bye. There's also a minor bug where you walk off when you interact with an item in front of you. Apart from this, I didn't face any crash. I personally didn't notice any frame drops or screen tearing.

[h3]🏆 Extras (Achievements, Grind, Replayability)[/h3]
Most people will consider this game a single playthrough game. There are, however, different choices you can make to experience different interactions and conversations. There is virtually no grinding in this game. You can choose to find trash and pick it up (clean it) but there's no reward for it. Achievements are relatively easy to 100%. You can play the entire game without any outside help, and then 100% it within a couple of hours (or minutes) on your second playthrough.

Firewatch was a pure pleasure for the eyes to play. The visuals are stunningly beautiful and can easily join the ranks of gorgeous games like Eastshade or the Witness.


[b]Plot[/b]

We play as Henry who came to work for the summer as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness while trying to escape from the troubles in his life. Our boss Delilah is the only contact we have with the human world. And we spend our days chatting with her about life or any questions we may have through a radio while roaming through the park.

There is one aspect in the plot that I found questionable, or maybe it was an oversight from the devs. At some point in the story, the park is covered by fire smoke, but at no time is it mentionned that Henry wears a breathing mask that would have helped him survived that part. I found that kind of strange.


[b]Exploration[/b]

Firewatch has been labeled a walking sim, but it has so much to offer that I would qualifiy it more to be an exploration game such as Infra but without the puzzles.

I found the exploration aspect in the game really interesting. While we will in any case uncover the very emotional game story, we don't have to follow the given path. We can in fact freely deviate from it, go the opposite way and explore every nook and cranny of the available game map. There are tons of objects and places to discover. I recommend reading all documents as they reveal more details about the plot and the game world.


[b]Dialogues[/b]

We are free to ask Delilah about anything we find, and are given several choices to answer her questions or we can just ignore them. I do not know how much our choices affect the game ending, but they do affect some of the later dialogues content.
Of course, there are still some mandatory dialogues to complete if we want to progress in the game.


[b]Screenshots & Camera[/b]

I took hundreds of screenshots while playing. And my favorites were the different possible views with the background sun, especially at sunset. 
Let's note that we can remove the central round pointer by selecting 'hide Interface' from the 'Settings' menu.
The game also has an in-game camera that allows us to take 18 pictures. I had no idea what it was for so I used it to take pictures of places (vista points, waterfall...) that had some unremovable in-game floating description. And we can actually find the photos inside the saved files folder or get a link by clicking on 'Camera Roll Upload' in 'Special Features' that allows us to download the pictures and optionally order a paid print of them.


[b]Free roam mode[/b]

The game offers a free roam mode where we can freely explore the whole game world.
There is a treasure hunt we can do in this mode which consists of finding 5 audio tapes of the game soundtrack (4 tracks per tape). We can then listen to them while exploring (not available in storymode).
Strangely, as soon as we pick up one of the cassettes, a music icon will appear on the right side of the screen which cannot be removed, so all screenshots taken afterwards in that mode will show the icon. So if we want to take nice screenshots in this mode, we must not pick up any cassettes and cannot do the treasure hunt.


So anyway, I have been amazed by the high quality of this game and all what it offers. This is a perfect explorer dream and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys exploration games and hiking sceneries.

I mean, who knew pine-scented body wash could pair so well with a folk-inspired score? But now, the story. It's like a rollercoaster that promises twists and turns but leaves you craving a little more loop-de-loop action. It's good, don't get me wrong, but it's like ordering a pizza and realizing they forgot the cheese – still delicious, but something's missing. So, in summary, Firewatch is the game you never knew you needed, with a view that could make a mountain jealous, tunes that stick with you like a catchy jingle, and a story that's good but could use a sprinkle of storytelling magic. Seven out of ten – would hike and hum again. (8.5/10)

Firewatch is a single-player first-person mystery set in the Wyoming wilderness, where your only emotional lifeline is the person on the other end of a handheld radio. Yes, it's a walking sim.

So let's get the obvious out of the way first. Firewatch is a walking sim. No running and gunning, no arcade elements, some dialogue choices. I have to say I luv me a walking sim. And this is one of the best. Dealing with some personal troubles you take a job far away from civilisation, summer spent in the middle of nowhere, to clear your head and deal with current worries.

The game is short, at around 4 hours, during which you'll travel around the beautiful environments, deal with your traumas and uncover new mysteries while having only one other human to talk to, a fellow ranger - Delilah. I read a lot about this game, and I expected a good game and a poor ending. I got excellent game and ok ending. I understand how some poeple might feel everything is leading to a climax and then nothing happens, but to me the ending was in line with all of the game.

Anyhow, if you like walking simulators or adventure games in general this is one of the best walking sims I experienced. If you like the genre even a little bit and/or like slowly told human stories just play this. You will not be disappointed.

Firewatch is just one of those games. It's quite short but it has some weight to it. The storytelling is excellent at leading you down one path while setting up another. There is some setup, but for the most part, significant events blindside you, leaving a lasting impact. Unfortunately I watched a YouTuber play through the whole thing when it came out so I knew about the big stuff going in. But now as an adult, I picked up on so many other details that I missed before. 

Firewatch is a game about many things. It's a game about forgetting, a game about running away from your hardships. It's a game about coping in some of the best and worst possible ways. And above all, it's a game about self reflection. Firewatch is a story game more than anything else. Don't go in expecting riveting gameplay because most of this is a walking sim. Pay attention to the nature, to what is being said on the radio, to what Henry is thinking throughout the game. If you can get past excessive swearing, then you should pay attention to Delilah as well. It was nice to have a male character dealing with emotional stuff. Not for that alone, but for the ability to make him be open about it. Henry doesn't have to be closed off, you can let him open up about his issues and he'll do it. Rare healthy protagonist moment.

A lot of the story of Firewatch is told to you directly, but a good chunk is through environmental details. Being out in the open nature starts off as pretty nice. It's relaxing and beautiful being out there. Later on though, you begin to feel vulnerable. It's too open, too normal. I love how that simple change in vibe was executed in the story and how much weight it put on the closing act. For a game that only lasted just shy of 5 hours for me, that was some grade A execution. 

I really don't have much else to say without delving into spoiler territory and my comments on the audio design are just "good." For it being a 2016 game, there are a surprising amount of bugs still in the game. Many of which were pretty blatant and didn't take much looking to find. There are animation issues, lighting problems, and I could sometimes see object ID text through solid objects. Those aren't game ruining but the animation stuff could mess with your immersion which I didn't care for. 

All in all, I really enjoyed Firewatch. If you haven't played it and are interested, then definitely give it a shot. Firewatch is an experience you'll play once, but you'll likely not forget it.

My first and most likely only review ever. Hopefully you take something out of this. I was first interested in this game once I saw the trailers. It was intriguing, mysterious, and I don't think I have ever played a game like this before. With that said I decided to go ahead and purchase it. Lately, there has been a lot of hype surrounding the game as many streamers have been playing, youtubers have been playing it, and people in general have been playing it and there has been several consistent good reviews of the game. I can vouch for it.

The game starts off with an interesting text based scenario where you (the player) get to decide how exactly you want to start your story. Then you get put into the forest. I can describe how beautiful the scenery is and you start to believe that everything is real. The sounds, the dialogue, and movement is so realistic I actually feel like I'm not playing a game, but rather living the protagonist's story. The dialogue used in the story is mostly between you and a person named Delilah. She's basically the only source of communication through out the game and the conversations you are able to have with her are rich and sometimes quite intense. You have choices to pick to see what to specifically say to her and no matter what you decide to choose, they are all great. I kept looking towards my radio as I always wanted to see what was next. I constantly wanted to speak to Delilah.

The story is captivating and gripping. I found myself getting paranoid (at best) being in the middle of the forest and occasionally looking back and around me to see if any monster/freak/pervert was following me. Although the story can be easily decrypted and you can predict the outcomes, it was still suspenseful and I kept on wondering what was going to happen next. The only real downfall for me was the ending. I wish it had a little more of a bang. It felt unsatisfying and I just sat in my chair wondering "that's it?" Regardless of the ending and how short of the story is, I still felt like they did a great job at retaining the player's attention.

Please do yourself a favor and play this game.

[h1] SYNOPSIS (Spoiler-Free) [/h1]

A game about Love& Loss, and a Mystery 'Who-Done-it?'.

Firewatch is a hiking simulator, that puts you in the shoes of a heartbroken man who takes a job as a Firewatch Ranger to escape the crushing thoughts and responsibilities of an old lover.  It's firstly a game about love and loss, but also a game with mystery, tension, and paranoia.

In Firewatch, you reside in a watch tower in the middle of a national park alone for 3 months.  You're only means of communication is a walkie-talkie that's used to communicate to a woman (Delilah) in another watch tower positioned across from yours in perfect view.

Throughout the game you're handed daily tasks from Delilah on the other side of your walkie-talkie, with the game also giving you dialogue choices that you can pick to further the story.  You're usually given 3 dialogues on how you can respond to her on the other side- Do you stay closed off?   Do you open up about your past relationship?  Or do you reciprocate as she attempts to flirt with you?  As the days go on, you two soon begin to develop a relationship which plays for most of the story.  

The back and forth between you and the main character turns varies from Sarcasm, flirtation, etc, with you being able to choose how to respond to your only lifeline of sanity.

[h1] MY THOUGHTS (Possible Spoilers) [/h1]

I actually cried playing this game.  
Firewatch is one of the most engaging stories I've ever played.  You really feel connected to the characters you encounter; and as if you exist in this games park as actual 'firewatcher'.  It's one of the games where I literally couldn't wait to play it again.  

The dialogue choices has me laughing out loud at times, with a huge grin on my face as the characters talked.
Your character also has to face the morality of deciding whether to move on from his wife or to stay with her, as she has fallen extremely ill and cannot take care of herself anymore.

It's a game about love and loss with a huge emphasis on mystery, tension, and dread.  The game is a hiking simulator, but at no point in the game, did it feel like a hiking simulator, or like a chore.. as the game always has something new for you to see and do. [h1][b]Full Review at [url=https://gamedragons.net/viewtopic.php?f=6&t=244]GameDragons.Net[/url][/b][/h1]

[b]Presentation[/b]
Firewatch is one of those games that manage to tell more in a few hours than most games do in a few dozen hours, it's a believable story full of intrigue, unknown and natural interactions between people, all wrapped with a positive message about life and finding the enjoyable parts in each sad story. The story follows Henry, a fire lookout in the Shoshone National Forest, hired following the Yellowstone fires of 1988 in order to increase the security and report any potential fire threat so it can be prevented before it's too late. Trying to escape the tragic recent events in his life, Henry decides to take the job for the summer in hopes that the silence and loneliness would help him reflect on life and move forward, but that silence only lasts for a little while, as the Shoshone National Forest seems to be a place where a lot of strange things happen. 

Joining him on the journey is his lookout boss, Delilah, to whom he is supposed to report any suspicious activity around his lookout as well as perform any tasks given to him by her, but as the summer goes by their relationship grows closer and the interaction between Henry and Delilah takes center stage in the game. Campo Santo's biggest achievement with Firewatch is presenting the story in a way that feels natural and believable, as if it came straight out of a classic novel, with the conversations taking a more relaxed and natural dialogue, instead of something that feels scripted; part of that can be attributed to the fact that Henry can answer Delilah's questions and interact with her in a bunch of different ways, either by being serious, funny or even flirting sometimes, but no matter which dialogue option you choose their conversation will always feel natural and that can be heard in the voices of the actors. 

Even if it starts in a more relaxed open manner, the story does get spookier as the days go by, but Firewatch is not a horror game and it doesn't even attempt to be one, because that's not what this story is about, instead the game uses the loneliness of the woods and the missing pieces of the bigger puzzle to always keep you on your toes and look twice behind your back, even if there will be nothing else behind you, except more forest. A few days in the game reaches its peek of mystery as you'll try to make up scenarios about what is going on before the game tells you and because that suspense is so high it does feel like a disappointment when the game does reach its conclusion, but that is something that I would rather not spoil for you, so you can find out what Firewatch is all about on your own, because truly the story is one of the game's highest points.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
Although it may seem like another walking simulator at first, Firewatch blends the lonely walking though the woods with suspenseful moments as well as freedom of exploration, as aside from the main objectives you can often stray from the path to find different supply caches, collectibles and even adopt a turtle. Even if at first your movement options will be limited, you will eventually find gear that will naturally unlock new areas of the map, as ropes will allow you to descent steep hills and the axe will allow you to chop through any trees blocking your way, and although those are your main and only traversal options, finding each gear piece as the time passes by makes it feel like you're never doing the same thing for too long and always finding something that may aid your adventure onward. 

Another thing that you will do a lot of is talk to Delilah on the walkie-talkie, as your conversations are seamlessly incorporated into the gameplay, allowing you to report any findings to her, ask for advice or just hear a familiar voice when you're out in the wild and feeling lonely. The way in which you respond to Delilah will also affect your relationship to her, as if you crack a joke she will remember to return the joke the next time the opportunity pops up, making the whole conversation feel tailored to the way you respond as Henry. 

[b]Graphics[/b]
Considering the fact that there isn't a lot of variety when it comes to the map and the locations you visit, since most of it is just forest with the objective locations being pretty obvious even on the map, it's quite surprising how drastically the map changes according to the time of day and the weather, as the forest will spark up with nuances of orange, bright red or clear sky blue depending on the day, the location and the time. The only missing thing that seems to have been overlooked is the lack of wildlife and plants variety, even if the area in which the game takes place is just a forest, it's disappointing to see that most trees look similar and animals or birds are nowhere to be found, except for your pet turtle. 

[b]Audio[/b]
Even if there are a couple of tunes that will play during key moments of the game, for most parts you'll be stuck with the sounds of nature, which isn't necessarily a bad thing since the silence of the wind blowing through the trees adds to the atmosphere, but once again it feels weird to hear the sounds of the forest without any birds chirping in the distance. On the other hand the dialogue is excellent, with the actors genuinely feeling like they're having an actual conversation, as both Henry and Delilah's dialogue feels natural, with occasional laughs, pauses and even angry outrages. 

[b]Extras[/b]
Firewatch is a quality, but short game, as the entire experience takes around 4 hours to complete, and since there are no additional modes or a reason to replay the game, that's pretty much all you get, so you either liked the story and the message enough to justify the purchase or you don't, but if you like environmental exploration games with the focus on storytelling you most likely will like Firewatch.

[b]Verdict[/b]
Firewatch tells an intriguing story full of mystery, suspense and wonder, the like of which you may only see in some more toned down Stephen King novels, but adding on that with great voice acting, superb, although sometimes repetitive, landscapes and gameplay elements that feel simple enough to allow anyone to play through this game.

First off, I would like to start off by saying that I had an amazing time playing this game. Throughout the entire game I was interested, drawn in, and hooked on every line. I was focused on every little detail, trying to figure out the mystery behind it all. I knew for sure that there was something bigger going on, some twist at the end, that just when I would think I have it figured out, it would soon turn it all around and blow my mind. I was excited, thrilled, and totally immersed in anticipation of this grand revealing of the unbelievable truth. 

Except it never came. All the build up, all the suspense, all the mystery was thrown away and the plot was revealed to be much smaller than anticipated. Even up to the very end, I was convinced that something would turn around, that there was no way it could end like this. But it did. And after a fairly disappointing final dialogue with your supposed "friend", it ends. No epilogue, no cliffhanger, nothing. 

At the end of this riviting and exciting journey, I experienced an ending that made all the mystery and wonder vanish as quick as it came, and made me feel like the only other character who I actually was able to become attached to didn't give a sh*t about our hero in the end at all. I faced the credits feeling as if I failed. That maybe I screwed something up. That somehow there was more than the disappointment I had experienced. But there was nothing. That's all there was.

So to conclude my review, I will say this: the journey was amazing. I have never played a game that drew me in this much and made me care about all my little actions like this game did. So in that regard, it was a success. But the ending was a failure. No other way to describe it. I'm not saying I need a happy ending, or one with a bowtie that makes everyone happy in the end. I just want an ending that lives up to the hype the gameplay created. You cant have an ending that disappoints the players. I want a ending that makes me feel as much excitement and thrill as the gameplay did. But it simply did not deliver.

So after careful thought, I would recommend this game to anyone who knows nothing about the story. But keep this in mind: enjoy the journey. Don't fantasize and ponder about how all this could add up. Just enjoy the moment, enjoy the character development, enjoy the scenery, put yourself in the characters shoes and live the ride. And when the ending comes, don't expect a grand ending to it all. Just look back on the story and remember the parts that made you laugh, made you sad, or made you just happy. Thats all I can say. Just enjoy the ride.

I bought this game out of impulse because it was on sale and it wasn't what I expected at all. I thought it was going to be more of a roleplaying-survival game, but I suppose I was content with the game. 

To be honest, I do enjoy narrative games that are casual and this was a good game to an extent. Graphically, the game is stunning and has loads of varying colour palettes that are visually impressive and suited to the moods of the game. 

The overall gameplay is very interactive and immersive. Sometimes I hated Delilah and other times the conversations were funny and entertaining. At times conversation and gameplay would be downright sinister, making you feel uneasy and threatened. I suppose that's why the game's ending upset me. Lots of plot and other questions were left unanswered; it felt a bit rushed in my opinion. 

Both the voice acting and music was incredible, and I'm a sucker for high quality audio so it really gave life into the lonely world of Firewatch. 

If the developers made another game using the same engine, where you played perhaps as a firefighter, I believe it would be a superb survival game similar to The Long Dark or Kona. 

Overall, it's an alright game. Not very long, very easy and intriguing at times. But not worth the full price.

Firewatch puts you in the shoes of Henry, a man who recently joined the Wyoming Firewatch as a way to escape his personal problems. You are introduced to Delilah, another Firewatch and your supervisor at another tower. The interaction and dialogue between Henry and Delilah feels authentic and reactive based on the choices in the conversations you made. The voice acting for both Henry and Delilah are superb. The developers had put a lot of thought into how conversations branch and accounts for what the player did or didn't do in the game. 

Another thing that stands out with Firewatch is how the natural scenery is absoultely gorgeous. The lighting, environmental effects, and ambience sound effects come together make the forest truly immersive. 

There are some reviewers who despised the ending of this game, which is understandable from a gamer's perspective on expectation and reward. Personally, I think the game ended perfectly based on the narrative and the story that the developers are trying to tell. 

There's a neat commentary playthrough that is unlocked once the game is completed once. There are various audio tapes in the game world in each game day that offers more insight on the developer's development process and game design choices as you play the game. One gripe that I have with the commentary playthrough is that it's easy to miss certain tapes and there's no way to go back to them once the game moves on to the next day. 

Overall I would recommend this game if you are interested in narrative games with interesting characters set in a unique wilderness setting and don't mind the relatively short game time (I clocked in at 18.4 hours because I played the game twice: second time I was listening to the commentary; one can finish the game in ~3-4 hours if exploration is kept to a minimum).
