I was so excited for Firewatch. I'm a forest firefighter, and seeing a game in this setting was unusual, and really got me interested. I watched every gameplay video and trailer that came out, which got me insanely hyped for it. I even preordered it, which served as a healthy reminder for me to go back to my personal policy of not preordering games.

I'm pretty disappointed, to be honest. 

The trailers gave the impression of a creepy thriller set in the wilderness, and probably the first hour and a half (if that) lived up to that hype. I was on the edge of my seat, blood pumping, jumping at loud noises. The plot had grabbed me, it was creepy and interesting, I was suspicious of everyone, even Henry himself. 

And then it just fell apart. It's like they were writing the plot outline on a friday arvo, thought "♥♥♥♥ it, let's wrap it up so we can head to the pub for beers," and hastily wrapped it up into a very tidy package. No mystery, no puzzles, nothing to solve. Once it started to wrap up, i lost interest. I wasn't scared, I wasn't curious. I finished it in like two and a half hours, and that's reading every document, taking it slowly. 


Don't get me wrong, it's got good points. The design and aesthetic is awesome, great setting. very basic gameplay, but that's not a bad thing in every case. in this game though, it feels like a tool so you can wander through the bush and collect items. 
You can adopt a tortoise. Dialog is witty, well written and well voiced. Too bad it seemed like the options had no impact on the outcome of the game, which honestly in hindsight makes the dialogue seem so useless.

I wish I was defending this game, because i waited so long for this to come out. If the plot was deeper, or choices had impact on the outcome of the game, or the game was longer, then maybe I would be recommending it. But for 20 USD (more in AUD), I can't. that's like 10 dollars an hour! If it was 10 bucks or less, maybe I'd recommend it. Wait for a sale or something if you want to play it.

tl;dr:  buy when cheaper
cons: Shallow gameplay, short unfulfilling plot, choices have no impact on outcome of game, too expensive, conclusion was weak and disappointing. 
pros: witty clever dialogue, great setting, nice aesthetic, you can adopt a turtle, first hour and a half is gripping and thrilling

Firewatch is the perfect game for those who want to experience the thrill of being a park ranger without actually having to go outside. I mean, who needs fresh air and beautiful scenery when you have a computer screen and a controller, am I right?

The game is really relaxing - I mean, what's more calming than wandering through a serene forest, listening to the sound of birds chirping and leaves rustling? It's like a virtual spa day, but without the awkward massages.

The game also has a gripping story that will keep you on the edge of your seat (or couch, or beanbag, or whatever you choose to sit on). I won't spoil anything, but let's just say that there's some mystery, some intrigue, and a healthy dose of suspense.

Overall, Firewatch is a great game that will give you both a relaxing and exciting experience. So put on your ranger hat, grab your trusty map, and get ready to explore the great outdoors - without ever leaving your house.

Without being negative, Firewatch probably deserves the title of "Walking Simulator" more than any other game I've played. None of your actions actually change how the story unfolds (so far as I can tell) and while the scenery is thankfully pretty enough to be a pleasant stroll it's really just an slightly interactive walk on rails. Don't get me wrong, it's a compelling story despite a somewhat weak ending, but you won't be solving anything especially. You're just along for the ride.

This is probably all quite deliberate on the dev's part, as where your choices DO make a differences is how you choose to speak to, and build a relationship with, Delilah - the woman on the other end of your radio and this is where the real meat of the game is. There's no real replayability in the game, but on my first run-through (which took a little under four hours altogether) I kept Delilah at something of a distance, behaving as I probably would in real life. I'll probably have a go at some point at seeing what happens if I reciprocate her advances or just attempt to annoy her as much as possible.

I find music in these kind of games more effective when used sparingly and Firewatch certainly hits the mark there, dropping in some very atmospheric music at key points. It's the first time I've played a game where I've actually been tempted to buy the soundtrack DLC.

All in all recommended, as it's a very lovely game. Can't help but feel its short length and almost zero replay value doesn't quite justify it at full-price however, so maybe wait for a sale.

I have not played a game like this before. Firewatch is mostly about exploring the wilderness and occasionally chatting over a walkie talkie with Delilah, your boss who's stationed at a nearby watchtower you can just make out in the distance.

It works because the landscapes are stunning, the dialogue is well acted and well written, making me curious about these characters, and the story reacts in subtle and mostly effective ways to your choices, making me feel that I'm actually influencing this world. I did not replay the whole game to find out how much difference choices actually make on the overall story, but it's fairluy obvious that your choices leave small marks in the world: a place on the map is marked with the name you jokingly give it, and so is a fire. A sketch of yourself is based on the description you chose to give, and the choices you make about your character's past in the intro leave little ripples throughout the story.

There were a couple moments when the fiction broke down because of small timing issues (like a piece of dialogue triggering before I had actually seen whatever it was about), but mostly the game manages to uphold the illusion, and in some moments managed to actually surprise me and move me. It's immersive in a way, because there are lots of little realistic details in the world, but at the same time the character I played as was not me: from his physical appearence to his way of talking to his background, Henry is a distinct person, like a character in a movie that I happened to be moving around as.

The issue of the playing character's physical appearance is also interesting: though you often see Henry's hands and legs you never see your own face, except in sketches or photographs, and the first one of these instances was suprising both because of Henry's distinct physique and because I'd read about that sketch in the introductory section, before I acutally saw it. It was a queer moment of disconnect, because at the same time it made the prologue "real" it pushed me away from identifying with Henry.

From a practical perspective, it took me 7 hours to finish the game. I had to play on medium settings because my laptop could not keep up, and even so there was some stuttering so I didn't get the best experience of the visuals, but I don't recommend playing on low settings as without some of the effects the landscape then becomes "flat" and loses the sense of magic that it has even on medium.

Finally I'll finish with a little spoiler to describe what was for me the most memorable moment in the game. In the middle of the night you get a call on the walkie talkie, and Delilah passes you over to your wife, Julie, who is on the phone. She has an australian accent, and we just exchanged a few words, and I suddenly found out Henry's nickname for her, nothing much happened but it made the whole situation between Henry and her real all of a sudden... and it felt like a dream, as it must have for Henry, I just had to search for this moment in somebody's playthrough on youtube to be sure I had not imagined it.

Firewatch is a story-driven game based around a man's job as a fire look-out in the Wyoming forest. There is very little interaction with any other characters, except for Delilah, your supervisor. The game isn't so much about watching for fires, rather the discovery of two human beings trying to understand each other. It mainly focuses on character as quirky comments are thrown back and forth over a little hand-held radio. The gameplay is really straight forward and linear. You uncover bits and pieces of a mystery throughout your tasks.

The game is very short. Do I like the game for what it is? Yes. The visuals and art style is amazing. I would, however, not pay $19.99 ($17 for the sale I got it for) for the 4 hours of gameplay again, and that's with me moderately pausing every now and then. You can easily finish this game in one session, such as I did. It should be priced more at the $5-10 range for the amount of content present in the game.  Movement is a little funky at times and there were multiple occasions where I would get stuck between trees or on a rock that was a few inches off the ground. There were also times where it was confusing as to where the game wanted you to go, but it's nothing that can't be figured out eventually. The voice acting is amazing though and the dialogue makes it seem like they were actually humans.

Quick as this is on sale at a price which I believe is commensurate with its value.  The pros are that for those of us watching with wonder the evolution of video games, this is definitely a step towards interactive novels.  In this case you are playing a first person (named Henry) who is unraveling a mystery while on a respite from the world in the mountains of Wyoming.  His backstory is nicely told in the first few minutes.  Other pros are the gameplay ease and little Easter eggs such as the camera (which you should use and use the entire roll, no spoilers but just do that) and the implied recommended reading list based on all the paperback novels (alot of Richard Sturgeon books) strewn around the cabins and supply drops.  Henry's only human interaction is with Deliah, his supervisor whom he communicates with through a radio.  Ostensibly, he's in a remote firewatch looking for, well, what else fires but also keeping tabs on park visitors and wildlife but soon they find they are being watched and they uncover things that don't make sense until the area is fully explored.  The negatives about this game is that it ends all too shortly and there's a bit of "is that all there is?" but it does fully emcompass a story line - however, you can play the game again (and get slightly different dialogue based on your responses to Deliah) with the game-maker's dialogue and someday I believe I will do that.  At any rate, if you like to see the evolving possibilities of this video game medium and it's potential to strive towards great works (and yeah, I'll say it - ART), this is one to check out.

Firewatch is one of those story-driven games that sticks with you long after the credits roll. You play as Henry, a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness, communicating almost entirely with your supervisor, Delilah, over the radio. What starts as a quiet summer job quickly turns into a mystery that had me hooked until the very end. The atmosphere is top-notch: stunning visuals that make every sunset screenshot-worthy, paired with a soundtrack that knows exactly when to kick in. The writing is sharp, natural, and genuinely funny at times, while also carrying real emotional weight. The voice acting between Henry and Delilah brings the whole experience to life, it honestly felt like eavesdropping on two real people. Gameplay is pretty minimal (lots of walking, some light exploration and decision-making), but that’s not a flaw here. It keeps you focused on the story, the environment, and the choices you make in conversations. If you’re looking for an action-packed adventure, this isn’t it. But if you enjoy narrative-driven games, strong character writing, and a beautiful setting, Firewatch is absolutely worth your time. And hey, the 100% achievements were satisfying but not frustrating, which made the completion really enjoyable.

UPDATE:
Alright, I've played through multiple times at this point, only 1.5ish days into its release and I've seen only one alternate ending, no spoilers there, just got curious as to what would happen and was pleasantly surprised.  I saved and reloaded at what I saw as key plot changing points in the game after playing through to the end so that I could cover more ground at a faster rate; however, it seems that the ultimate ending is unavoidable.  This game is more about the journey than the destination.  There are a lot of different experiences to be had for everyone in many playthroughs, but I am a bit sad about some things and how it seems to be much more of a narrative than I had thought.  I expected a more decision-based, cause and effect game with so many endings that my head would spin.  I still love it though.  It is a beautiful game and the dialogue is amazing.  I understand that this game might not be for everybody, but don't let a (mostly) inelastic ending ruin your opinion of the game.  Sometimes in life endings are unavoidable, the ultimate of which being death; our lives are defined by how we live them, the mere fact that we ultimately die is unimpressive.  Sorry to get metaphorical, but it really is a deep game and maybe saying something like this will give those that are bothered by the way the story ends or its lack of elasticity, or help somebody that is holding back on purchase because of all of the harsh reviews.

Set your expectations and you will be fine.

* The dev team was 12 people, this is an indie game
* There is a shallow, but complete feature set
* There is no gameplay, in the traditional sense of the word
* Yes it is short, more like an interactive movie than a FPS
* There are no guns, no monsters, no aliens and no video game cliches
* Often choices are made for you; days end when the story dictates, dialogue happens and the main character does things on his own every once in a while that you cannot influence (some of these are in the trailer btw)

One thing this game does really well, is it puts you in a specific mood at the end or it did for me.  Like some of my favorite movies that I watch over and over.  If you are looking for a reason to replay it, don't expect achievements or unlocks.  Play it again because you enjoyed the story and how it made you feel.

Take it for what it is, not what you want it to be.

Firewatch is a short but deeply atmospheric narrative adventure that left me both satisfied and curious for more. Set in the Wyoming wilderness, you play as Henry, a fire lookout spending the summer in isolation, at least until your radio crackles to life with the voice of Delilah, your supervisor, and a slow-burn mystery begins.

The writing is sharp and natural, and the dialogue between Henry and Delilah is the emotional core of the experience. While the mystery is engaging, it ultimately resolves more quietly than I expected, which left me with mixed feelings.  It was realistic, yes, but maybe a touch anticlimactic.  I also felt as though the game were a bit too short.  Another two or three hours of story content would've clinched this for me.  As for the story itself, it was beautiful.  (8/10)

The controls are flawless. Everything from walking the trails to climbing rocks feels smooth and intuitive, and the minimalist HUD keeps you immersed without distraction.  I played the game exclusively on my Deck, and I ran into no issues whatsoever.  (10/10)

The visual beauty is where Firewatch truly shines. The art style is stunning in warm, painterly landscapes that shift beautifully with the time of day and weather. Every view feels like a postcard you want to frame. (10/10)

The audio design is solid, with subtle environmental sounds that make you feel like you’re really out in the woods. However, aside from a few well-timed music cues, the soundscape sometimes felt a little sparse, which occasionally undercut the tension or atmosphere. (6/10)

Firewatch is a visual and emotional journey worth taking. It’s a game you don’t play for action, but for the experience of inhabiting a place, listening to a story unfold, and feeling just a little less alone until the credits roll.  (8/10)

IMPORTANT: 
Although the game takes around 3 hours the finish "fast", I would really recommend taking it slow and reading all the small details as if this would be happening to you in real time in real life.
Sometimes they are a bit hidden or seemingly unimportant at first: just keep them in mind and use your brain to connect the dots as you go on.

If you do so, the game will reward you with a deeper ending that will make much more sense.
You could argue/ criticize that the ending is anticlimactic (like I read in some reviews), but it didn't bother me at all.

In retrospect, putting all the info together, the meaning of the story was well worth it.
Sure it's not stated as a fact and thus open to interpretation but you can make a pretty accurate/ provable guesses  as to what happened and why with continous obervations and logical thinking.

This game can be beat in a short amount of time. But as I was going, I thought of it like this, translate this game into a novel and you will probably reach the full length required for something to be considered a novel. Compare to the price which is about $20 and it is incredibly worth it. Firewatch is stunningly beautiful with a plot that is thick with undertones and moments of true suspense. Though I don't know if decision making plays a huge part of the game, dialogue feels dynamic and real. 

However, since it's a strong narrative game, it's very linear. There isn't much to explore apart from when the game lets you go on a new path, but on the first trip through any area it's pretty awe inspiring. 

However, I wish I could've been more immersed but it's to be expected that the game isn't about you right from the get go. A succinct character is introduced with a dynamic backstory. There's no reason for you, as the player, to think that you are in any way Henry. The only thing you are is a choice for his dialog and the engine that drives him. I think that if you go into the game thinking this, you'll have an awesome experience of being a part of a great visual story with a thrilling conclusion. The best part is, I don't think anyone's story is necessarily the same. Maybe your desicions give you better outcomes, but maybe they don't. 

For some, this can be a very introspective game, making you look at yourself and your own relationships.

If you're looking for a great narrative game, then I highly reccomend this, but if you're looking for something with cool gameplay or skill based gameplay, look elsewhere. Firewatch is a visual story, so just let yourself enjoy it and get caught up in the emotions.

The game's graphics are stunning, with a distinctive art style that makes the forest and its surroundings feel both beautiful and dangerous. The soundtrack is also noteworthy, featuring a hauntingly atmospheric score that perfectly captures the mood of the game.

One of the most impressive aspects of Firewatch is its storytelling. The game's plot is intriguing and unfolds slowly, with the player discovering new clues and plot twists as they progress. The game also features some excellent voice acting from the two main characters, Henry and his supervisor Delilah, who communicate through a handheld radio throughout the game.

As Henry explores the park and its surroundings, he must navigate treacherous terrain, search for clues, and make choices that affect the outcome of the story. The choices the player makes throughout the game can have a significant impact on the ending, making for a highly replayable experience.

The game's themes are also compelling, exploring loneliness, loss, and the human need for connection. Through Henry's interactions with Delilah, the player is forced to confront the complexities of relationships and the difficulties of forming meaningful connections.

However, while Firewatch is an excellent game, it's not without its flaws. The game is relatively short, taking only around four to six hours to complete, which may be a disappointment for players looking for a longer experience. Additionally, some players have criticized the game's ending as unsatisfying or abrupt.

Overall, Firewatch is a beautifully crafted game that tells an engaging story and explores complex themes. Its stunning visuals, haunting soundtrack, and excellent voice acting make for a compelling gaming experience that is sure to leave a lasting impression on players.

Firewatch is a game I expected more out of, but perhaps that is intentional. 

The game begins with a very beautifully written and presents an example of a real life issue that instantly made me reflect on my own life and loved ones. Throughout the game, you're taken on this emotional journey with compelling, genuine characters that were brought to life with the help of incredible voice acting. Exploring the forests of Wyoming was simply beautiful (albeit frustrating at times since I lost my sense of direction frequently) furthering the themes of the game and greatly enhancing immersion. The story builds up nicely, but ultimately, Firewatch emphasizes the journey over the destination, and I believe it's important to approach the game with this perspective to avoid the disappointment that some players experienced.

[h2] Mystery? [/h2]
Firewatch is marketed as a "mystery game," but the actual mysteries within it feel quite insignificant. If your sole focus is on uncovering the truth and reaching the ending, then you might not enjoy yourself. That was how I personally felt when I finished it myself and found myself saying "that's it?" out loud. However, if you immerse yourself in Firewatch and really take the time to savor the beautiful scenery, engage in the conversations, and think about how you feel in the shoes of the protagonist, then I definitely think you'll find an emotional journey that is quite special.

[h2] Verdict [/h2]
While I don't believe Firewatch to be the most revolutionary or unique game in its genre, it offers about 4 hours of intriguing story, wonderful characters, and easy 100% completion. If the game's concept interests you, I would recommend giving it a try.

If you want a short and dirty review, a wonderfully written game that doesn't offer anything to someone expecting more than a story.

Longform review:

Firewatch easily reminds me the most of Gone Home if you approach it purely from a technical aspect. The entirety of the game consists of moving place to place, examining objects and easily runs less than 3.5 hours if you're trying your hardest to speed throught it. The idea isn't that it's a game, but a story you minorly shape. Through literal choices in the opening to dialogue between Henry and Delilah, you affect who Henry is as a person, and what type of relationship he forms with Delilah. But this isn't a roleplaying game, you don't choose branching paths, and some people might take issue with this if they're expecting something more. If you want a well written story about adults dealing with adult problems, you'll enjoy the game and most likely get your money's worth. For everyone else, just avoid it.

On a technical aspect there's some minor framehitching, shadow resolutions are horribly low in quite a few areas (even on Ultra) and you'll need a decent rig to play above 60 FPS on all the max settings. If you need frames desperately, SSAO should be the first thing you disable. Personally I turned it off even though I could afford it, mostly because I'm not a fan of the effect anyway. There are a LOT of issues regarding keybinding, you cannot bind a key already bound (so customizing them is a chore) and there's no confirmation upon selecting them making it more cumbersome than it needed to be. Other than these issues the game ran perfectly fine with no crashes.

If you like story games, buy it. If you don't, pass.

VERY MINOR SPOILERS BELOW

[spoiler]There is one thing to note, I've seen a LOT of complaints about the ending and while I don't think they're entirely unfounded do NOT go into this expecting a huge payoff. Part of the game's story is revolved around this, so if you're expecting something groundbreaking, don't. I found it a perfectly fitting ending, and while implausable (like, really implausible) the payoff was more than enough to satisfy me, but I can see people getting dissapointed because of how well the game builds up tension.[/spoiler]

Firewatch clocks in at around 4 hours of gameplay (or 6 if you're directionally and navigationally dysfunctional, like I am), and it's worth it. It's an incredibly well-done game - albiet small - but it relies more on character and story than anything else.

The one complaint I've heard others voice is that there are plot holes and the ending is a disappointment, but I don't quite see it that way. There were unanswered questions, and a few points that straight-up should have been explained FAR better than they were (which was not at all), but many of the "holes" people talk about are really "fill in the blanks." For example, Delilah's character never reveals a particularly rich history, but it's about what she doesn't say, and what the player interprets that that makes Delilah especially interesting: she can be a very different character for each player.

I personally liked that the plot of the game was open-ended in a lot of aspects, because when in life is everything really wrapped up so neatly?

If you're looking for something with twists and turns that ends with everything wrapped up - this is NOT the game for you.

If you're looking for a great experience with character depth, fantastic voice acting. a mystery, and a beautiful little world to explore, then this game is absolutely for you.

Firewatch is more of an experience than a classic game, as the story is quite linear and failing is impossible. It may belong to the adventure genre best.

You play as Henry, a decent guy, who seeks out the loneliness of being a look-out in the wilderness of Wyoming in order to escape his adverse situation at home. For the first half of the game, this works out somewhat as it seems to be an enjoyable experience. I actually felt like being in the woods, enjoying the great light effects and the mellow sounds of mother nature, including this ever-liberating wind sound.

However, things take a mystical turn, but the resolution of the plot isn't mystic at all - it reveals Firewatch as an anti-game. Sort of like Spec Ops: The Line, the game doesn't serve diversion or escapism; no, it made me come back to reality in quite a harsh way. Turns out that the end is quite realistic, depressing and mature in a sense that it's not your usual hero-antihero-story, and neither a story of survival nor extraordinary events after all.

Firewatch left me with a lasting impression, which is basically the most important thing what art can do. A game you'd just forget can easily be regarded as a waste of time. However, it makes me feel quite blue.


And now a bit more profane:

Pro:
-unique, at least in my experience
-good voice acting
-very lovely graphical design, especially the light effects
-an adult story

considerable:
-if you play super-slow like I do, you're finished in 8 hours, but most people probably need no more than 4-5 hours. I wouldn't spend more than 6$ on this.
-your expectations regarding the story may be hurt. If you don't like surprises (the real unexpected ones), you will probably get angry.
-Gameplay is reduced to the minimum, it's basically walking, talking and navigating (no fighting, crafting, real puzzle solving etc.)

As someone who is relatively new to video games (I only started playing seriously about a year and a half ago) and who's majority of experience with video games was from watching let's plays, I wasn't sure what to expect from this game. I remember soon after the game came out, watching my favourite youtuber at the time play through the introduction of the game and wishing that I could play myself, but not knowing how. 

Right from the start, I could tell that it would contain a very personal feel with little choices that are brought up later, and a unique sense of humour and personality between the characters. I found myself radioing in to Delilah about every little thing, eager to hear more of the conversation between the two characters and to watch their friendship grow more over the course of the game.

The game isn't too heavy with music, and most of the time you will be listening to the sounds of the grass or the birds, which is nice, but can lead to the player losing interest as it can get a bit boring (however, this is a walking sim, so I'm not sure what I was expecting.) When the music does play, It is beautiful and simple and lets you know that you are going in the right direction, which can help if you're a bit lost. Similarly, The dialogue between Delilah and Henry is also a good indicator that you are heading in the right direction, which really helped when the game asks you to hike across the map.

Unfortunately, I was running the game off of a laptop, so I started off with about 7 fps (no joke) but after fiddling with the settings, the game seemed to run fine. The world is stunning, with a gorgeous colour palette of warm and cool tones that change over the course of the day, meaning that trails that you might walk often, never seem to get boring. I would have to say that at some parts where there is mist or smoke, it is very hard to see, and I found myself relying heavily on my map in the last chapter of the game, and still being lost for some time, however, this could be due to my inexperience as a player.

Overall, I found the ending to be slightly lack lustre, with the storylines being wrapped up pretty quickly in the last chapter of the game. I found the conspiracy storyline to be engaging and found myself at the edge of my seat when entering the fenced off area, (although, to my knowlege, this area was never explained- how could someone living in secret in the forest get all of that expensive equipment?)  What happened to Brian Goodwin was heartbreaking, and seeing his body in the cave caused me to mentally take a step back and I genuinely felt impacted, especially when remembering his play fort nearby and seeing his selfies in the credits. 
My main issue with the game is that I felt disappointed that you never see Delilah, although it is a very unique experience seeing all the easter-eggs from the plot in her watch tower (eg: Her drawing of Henry, and the Pork pond sign), which made me happy.

This game... It’s hard to put into words how I feel about this game.  I bought it shortly after I watched [url=https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLMBYlcH3smRzvljKjxfsPCM6ibjr6ox-0]JackSepticEye's[/url] whole play through of it.  The game really stuck with me after I had watched the entire play through from start to finish.  I found myself contemplating it quite a bit and so I had to experience it for myself to know for sure.  Quite honestly, I'm glad I did.

Having watched the ending over the lets play I originally felt the ending was lack luster and anticlimactic, however now having experienced it for myself and having to make some of the tougher choices I find that the ending is actually very apropos.  I found myself feeling for the 'antagonist' of the game (I put that in quotes because he's not really an antagonist but I lack a better word for him).  I understood how his character was written and why he did what he did.  Even though I knew the ending of her story, [spoiler]I found myself whispering "Please wait for me, Delilah" as I rushed Henry to the cable car in the final sequence and actually felt hurt and disappointed that she didn't.[/spoiler]

I've seen a lot of complaints about the length of the game, that it’s "too short".  True, they could have padded the game out by sending you on other random tasks that took place during the time when the game skipped several days, however the game [i]really[/i] doesn't need it.  The story alone keeps this game engaging and makes the game really stand out for its genre.  Granted it’s very "walking simulator"-like but it’s by no means boring.  Yes, it's only about three to four hours but I feel that it’s honestly as long as it needs to be, any longer would have made the game have less of an impact in my opinion.  And yes, the game has a very linear story, but in this age of games that are bursting at the seams with survival mechanics and multiple endings its actually rather refreshing to find a game where the plot has a definitive end and where the developers focused more on the journey than the destination.

The music in the game is beautiful but used sparingly which I feel adds just the right amount of tension, relief or effect when it needed to.  The rest of the time you are left with the ambiance of the forest which adds a nice peaceful contrast to the tension the story starts building upon.

The art style for the game is truly fantastic.  Every single frame feels like a painting, be it looking out over some of the games beautiful vistas or focusing in on specific objects.  A lot of care went into building a world where everything is unique and fascinating.  The world is full of vibrant colors that draw you in and really help with immersing you in the rich story the writers built.

Far and away the best thing about the game is the writing.  The interaction between the main characters, Henry (your character) and Delilah, is very beautifully crafted.  From witty banter between them to the serious and frantic moments the dialogue feels very natural and unscripted no matter which option you choose.  I found myself reloading my save file from time to time because I either wanted to relive one of these interactions and listen to them again or to choose a different option to see how the characters responded.  Both characters are incredibly three dimensional with their own goals and flaws which makes them both relatable and believable.  They undergo what I consider is some of the best character development ever put forth by a game.  It’s very easy to find yourself invested in these characters, wanting to know what happens next in their story.

Despite the shorter story than what modern gamers are used to and despite not having multiple endings I really must recommend this game.  Honestly I'm glad I bought it at full price to help support the developers, testers, artists, writers, musicians, and voice talent that put a lot of heart and soul into building this game.  It's very obvious that the team at Campo Santo were dedicated and passionate about putting out an amazing game with a fantastic story and superb dialogue.

If you are looking for a game with a rich story with three dimensional characters backed by amazing art then look no further and get this game.  It will be worth every penny.

At first, I honestly thought Firewatch was going to be another calm, walking-simulator type of game. But as soon as I started playing, I got completely hooked. It’s calm, relaxing, and atmospheric... yet at the same time, it carries this quiet, lonely, uneasy feeling that makes it unique. I was so glad I decided to play it.

The story is easily the main strength of the game, right alongside the atmosphere, art style, and the amazing character interactions. It genuinely felt like watching a movie ... it starts slow, funny, and lighthearted. The banter between Henry and Delilah had me smiling, and I actually enjoyed doing all the little tasks she gave me. But as the story begins to unfold, you start to feel that something isn’t right. You don’t know what it is, but that mystery pulls you in deeper and deeper. I loved every bit of it. And the voice acting ... man, both of them absolutely nailed it. Every line sounded natural, emotional, and real.

The atmosphere and music are another highlight. You might be walking somewhere for a task, or just exploring, and the world is quiet ... all you hear are the sounds of wind, insects, and birds. Then suddenly, the music fades in... and uff, it’s magical. I also loved interacting with random things during exploration. Like when I found that cute little turtle, or that weird abandoned cabin on a hill , small moments like those made the world feel alive and mysterious at the same time.

And that ending... well, let’s just say it was bittersweet but realistic. I personally loved it. I won’t say too much about it, but it made me emotional. It felt like a reflection of real life.. how we used to spend time with friends, laughing, playing, making memories... and then life gets busy, people drift apart. Sometimes someone enters your life, you share something special, and then they’re gone. That’s what Firewatch made me feel... nostalgic, a little heavy, but grateful

Firewatch is a game about a man named Henry who took on a summer job to watch for fires in a national forest in Wyoming to temporarily leave behind some frustrations of life back home, who's only emotional and human lifeline is a female called Delilah on the other end of a radio.

Wow. Besides the flora rich environment, and the great pacing, this game packed some serious punch in the three hours of gameplay in its storyline. Henry is trying to escape some trouble back home with his wife who was diagnosed with a form of dementia, and he was no longer able to take care of her. His boss Delilah is the only other person who he has contact with throughout the game constantly. Feelings begin to fly and the two form a great relationship and friendship. Frelationship? I don't know. I digress.

What makes this game so great is the storyline. Many people were upset and could not get over the end (myself included) because it did not feel proper. It felt cut off, short, and very anticlimactic. However if you sit back and think about the process of the game and how Henry and Delilah progressed together and put two and two together about events that occurred ([spoiler]H and D were paranoid about the potential Government employees spying on them, tapping into their radios frequency, listening to their conversations, which apparently was solidified when they thought the biologists camp was a monitoring station spying on them, but once H found out Ned was simply covering his end because of the death of his son, and making up everything as he thought they were out to get him, H and D suddenly realized everything they had done was out of human feelings of paranoia, and ultimately, for nothing.[/spoiler]) you realize that it was simply basic human gut reactions. The final knife in the heart so to speak. We see ourselves in Henrys shoes, doing the exact same thing, and when everything we worked for was taken away ([spoiler] Delilah leaving us and not staying, never meeting up like she wanted when she told you over the radio when she was flirting[/spoiler]) we feel hurt, and betrayed, and confused. Almost like a "Real life simulator 2016". 

Campo Santo really drew into human feelings and interaction in this game and really hit the nail on the head. I'm still not over it and I feel an emotional pull to this game, which is very hard to come by these days. I absolutely recommend this game. It will put you on the feel train even if you didn't buy the ticket.

The Cons:

Firewatch напоминает Death Stranding в миниатюре, где основное занятие – исследование живописных локаций и выполнение рутинных задач. И хотя хайп вокруг Firewatch вполне понятен, лично для меня она оказалась проектом, скорее, средним по качеству.

Firewatch по сути, "симулятор ходьбы" с неплохой графикой, в котором вы исследуете лесные тропы, чтобы разобраться с различными происшествиями. Однако, несмотря на приятный визуальный стиль, игра не поражает ни выдающимся сюжетом, ни "захватывающей" атмосферой. Если бомбить прям принципиально, то игра нередко бесит микрофризами, пропадающими обьектами, а также моментами, когда главного героя отбрасывает с сторону, при взаимодействии с каким нибудь вентилем или замочной скважиной.

Прохождение Firewatch занимает немного времени, и одним из ее ключевых, в плохом смысле слова элементов является иллюзия выбора. В начале игры вам предоставляется возможность сформировать историю знакомства главного героя, Генри, с его девушкой. В дальнейшем ваши решения немного влияют на реплики в диалогах по рации с вашим наставником, Делайлой. Тем не менее, эти изменения не добавляют истории глубины или нелинейности. И как бы вы не хотели - собираете вы улики, мусор или открываете все или не все ящики с припасами, конец будет один, как и развитие истории после пролога, с МИЗЕРНЫМИ изменениями.

Стоит ли играть в Firewatch? Если вы ищете расслабляющую и атмосферную игру, в которой можно просто бродить по красивым локациям и наслаждаться неспешным повествованием, то Firewatch может вам понравиться. Firewatch – это игра для тех, кто умеет расслабляться и получать удовольствие от простых вещей. Конечно, разработчики могли бы постараться над историей лучше, но, имеем что имеем.

[h1] THE FIERY WYOMING INCIDENT [/h1]

Firewatch resembles Death Stranding in miniature, where the main activity is exploring scenic locations and performing routine tasks. And although the hype around Firewatch is quite understandable, for me personally it turned out to be a project of rather average quality.

Firewatch is essentially a "walking simulator" with good graphics, in which you explore forest trails to deal with various incidents. However, despite the pleasant visual style, the game does not impress with either an outstanding plot or an "exciting" atmosphere. If you make a joke out of principle, then the game often infuriates with microfreezes, missing objects, as well as moments when the main character is thrown aside when interacting with some valve or keyhole.

Firewatch takes a little time to complete, and one of its key elements, in the bad sense of the word, is the illusion of choice. At the beginning of the game, you are given the opportunity to form the story of the acquaintance of the main character, Henry, with his girlfriend. In the future, your decisions will have a bit of an impact on your conversations over the radio with your mentor, Delilah. However, these changes do not add depth or non-linearity to the story. And no matter how much you want to, whether you collect evidence, trash, or open all or not all of the supply crates, the end will be the same, as will the development of the story after the prologue, with SCANTY changes.

Is it worth playing Firewatch? If you are looking for a relaxing and atmospheric game where you can just wander through beautiful locations and enjoy a leisurely narrative, then Firewatch may appeal to you. Firewatch is a game for those who know how to relax and enjoy simple things. Of course, the developers could have tried to work on the story better, but we have what we have.

Be serenaded by a girl in a watchtower a few miles over while you try and figure out who is trying to kill you both. Or is she in on it too? High immersion rating, good voice acting, enjoying the plot.

Let's avoid spoilers here and get right to the meat of it.

Firewatch bills itself as a mystery game, and while it does have elements of mystery mixed in, I feel like that's an inadequate description of the content you're going to experience. Firewatch can more appropriately be considered a narrative adventure. What this means is that you will spend a lot of time exploring and interacting with the world you're placed in, and you'll have a lot of dialogue to listen to.

The gameplay itself is intentionally simple, and in many ways plays a bit like Portal. You'll find yourself collecting a reservedly small number of tools, completing tasks given to you by a faceless overseer, and learning about your environment and its past. You'll have plenty of time to sandbox, wander, explore, and so on, but ultimately you're still following a narrative, and the game will gently nudge you along towards your goals.

Unlike in Portal, you'll never encounter complex puzzle mechanics, and interactions with others are limited to, more or less, handheld radio. This is where Firewatch reveals its true colors as an adventure and suspense game rather than as a pure mystery. Firewatch is a pure, old-school adventure game smashed together with the visual novel genre -- just, replace visual with audio.

Much like in the Monkey Island, Ace Attorney, and the vast assortment of, "escape the room," games, you, as the protagonist Henry, will be collecting various objects from within your explorable environments, then using them to interact with the world in meaningful ways. Henry might find some rope and attach it to a climbing anchor, unlocking new passages... or he might find himself in possession of a flashlight to help him see in caves or at night. In this regard, Firewatch more than demonstrates its genius as an adventure narrative.

What you should know going in:
-- The primary focus of the game revolves around Henry and his relationship with his supervisor, Delilah. The nature of this relationship can vary depending on the choices you make during the game, very similar to how Bioware treated dialogue in games like Dragon Age and Mass Effect.
-- This is not an action game. Unlike Portal, you will not be training yourself for a final showdown against a big bad evil guy. This is a narrative adventure game, with a focus on Henry's exploration of both his environment and himself.
-- The ending is foreshadowed early in the game and is pretty much a foregone conclusion, but what's not quite as obvious is how Henry and Delilah will interpret events as they unfold. Remember that this is basically a visual novel game in many ways, and that the point and focus is on the evolving relationship between the characters involved.

Should you buy Firewatch?

Do you like adventure games? Yes.
Do you like suspense games? Yes.
Do you like visual novel games? Yes.
Do you like games that provide heavy immersion? Yes.
Do you like action games? No.
Do you like strategy games or puzzle games? No.
Do you like games with easter eggs or that reward thoroughness? No.
Do you like to gloss over the story of a game in favor of its mechanics? No.

Firewatch isn't for everyone. It is an adventure narrative with elements of suspense and mystery. It plays, start to finish, like an adventure narrative, and its conclusion is extremely similar to how many Hidden Object games (adventure games in their own right) wrap things up.

The pure adventure genre has been predominantly catered towards a female audience for some time, and many female gamers who enjoy such games will likely enjoy the rare male perspective in their otherwise female-driven genre. For male gamers, you'll find yourself able to relate to Henry and sympathize with his isolation. The game is presented well enough that any male players that enjoy it should seriously consider picking up another adventure title and playing as a female protagonist -- many adventure games are just as good from the female perspective, and if you liked Firewatch, then you deserve to give them a chance.

Overall, I rate Firewatch a 9/10. It loses 1 point as I feel as though the disposable camera Henry discovers could have ultimately been put to better use by the developers -- you'll understand once you complete the game.

Great little game unlike anything else I have played.  I was a little hesitant to buy it after reading many reviews criticizing the  length of the game and the ending.  I think those two points are valid to bring up, but I don't necessarily see them as negatives after playing through the game.

The overall visual and audible design of this game is fantastic.  As someone who has spent time in various national forests in the NW corner of the US, the designers really nailed the overall feel of a hot forest in the middle of summer.  The environment of the game becomes another character in the story, and it is dynamic and vibrant.  The homebase of the watchtower was really detailed well, and there always seems to be something to look at.  It didn't feel like a lot of indie games where environments are sparse and minimally populated with objects; it actually feels like a digital snapshot of a real place.  I also enjoyed the "collector" aspect, where if you decide to gather various objects during gameplay, they show up in your tower on subsequent days as though you placed them there.  While the visual aspect of the game is somewhat stylized, somehow it is also very realistic, which I don't quite undertstand how they pulled off.  The voice acting is just about as good as it gets, and the dialogue is really well thought out.

The storyline is where some users have a problem, and I can kind of understand.  I am comfortable with the fact that this game is going for a realistic story as opposed to a fantastic action-packed thrill ride which we are used to in games.  This is not that, it is a well-written mature story.  I don't think the audience for this sort of thing will be as huge as that for a Just Cause or Fallout, but it definitely has a strong place in gaming as the first and second generation gamers find themselves with graying hair and less of an interest in beam weapons and levelling up.  I still love those games, but I also love this one.  This game has its moments of excitement, but don't expect an edge-of-your-seat experience.  It is understated and realistic.  I hate to equate it to "mumblecore" films, as that is a polarizing genre, but I appreciate it in the same way I like some of those films.

The game is short, no doubt about it.  $20 may be a lot for some to spend on a game that can be completed in several sessions.  I will probably not play through the game again, as I took the time to check out everything I could on my first playthrough.  I know there are some things I did not see, and the developers have said that you will not see everything on the first playthrough, but I feel satisfied with my brief journey through this world.  As far as the price, I am alright with dropping a 20 on a game like this as I see it as an investment in both the company that made this, as well as a kind of new branch of gaming that I hope to see expand in the future.  

So, I don't think everyone on Steam will enjoy this game, but I do think it should have a large enough audience to be a viable game, and hopefully a viable genre.

This game has many technical aspects that make it excellent, including immersive environments, good lighting, and a great soundtrack that fades perfectly and never gets boring.

But what makes it really stand out is the delivery of the story. It presents questions that intrigue and involve, but doesn't become weighed down with loose ends. It builds plenty of suspense through plot alone, without having to rely on jump-scares. The story itself is fresh. Most engaging of all is the dialogue that takes place between the protagonist and the other main character of the game.

Some have voiced disappointment over the lack of alternate story paths, and I do agree that a little diversity in player choice would be welcome. While the player can approach events in several different ways, these decisions only really impact the dialogue, and have no real bearing on the development of the plot. This does limit replayability significantly, though, for those who are willing to hunt, there are many rewarding secrets hidden throughout the game.

Another common criticism is that the ending is anticlimactic. I agree that it is disappointing, but I felt that it was absolutely satisfying and was "right". To me, this as a game about the moments and relationships in life that sweep us in, churn our world on its head, and, just as abruptly, come to an end.

And those are the ones worth remembering.

I bought Firewatch fully expecting to play it for half an hour, not get into it, and request a refund. Boy, was I wrong. This game creates a story in a way I've never seen before, with the player character only ever seeing four other humans for the duration of the story, and all of them for less than 30 seconds.

The story is at first told through text-based flashbacks that lay the framework for the story beautifully, even if it is a bit boring. After the exposition is done and over with, the story is told entirely through your radio conversations with Delilah and the things and events you happen upon while hiking around your lookout. This is a kind of storytelling that I have never before seen in a video game, and it works wonderfully. Over the course of the game, you really bond with Delilah as a character and feel as if you perhaps know her personallly, all without ever actually laying eyes on her over the course of the entire game.

The soundtrack fits the mood of the game perfectly, and accents moments of tension and stress. Overall, this game is one of the best I've played in a long time, and even though it is quite short, only 4 hours long, I feel that it is well worth the money, and I'll come back and play it again soon.

Firewatch is a single player, first-person walking simulator. You play as a man named Henry, who due to unexpected circumstances finds himself taking a job as a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness.

While I am recommending this game, before you make the decision to purchase or not please keep in mind that it's very short. It took me 4.5 hours to complete - half an hour longer than most people are reporting. It’s worth playing, but I'd wait and get it at a discount unless you have cash to spare.

Firewatch is an interactive story. You progress by exploring the environment and using a handheld radio to communicate. How you choose to respond to dialogue effects how the person on the other end of the radio responds to you in return.

A lot of love went into this game and it shows. They did a very good job of making everything in a particular setting (music, lighting, background, ambient noise) work towards the mood and general theme of the overarching story. The graphics are outstanding. The voice acting is superb and the dialogue is, in my opinion, probably the strongest part of the game. After spending time on various Telltale products I particularly like the way the controls are set up and the fact that you can save at any point while playing.

The overarching plot isn’t perfect - I’m still not sure how I feel about the twist, but after some consideration I think it fits with what the game was going for. The writing works hard to make you feel increasingly isolated and paranoid while playing, but still manages to keep the beauty of the environment and being out in the wild at the forefront of the story. It feels like walking through a strange, hard section of someones life. The end wasn’t what I was expecting, but I think maybe that’s the point.

Bad (more of that imo): First, the story is really anticlimactic and doesn't make much sense. There's not really any kind of point it tries to make or anything that is actually accomplished at the end of the day. It's comparable to basically a summer adventure that you've made some good memories on but that's about it. Which in itself is not so bad a thing, but is certainly not what you expect from a story-driven game that is praised for provoking thought. It has some good moments and cool ideas, but it fails to develop them well - turns to the kind of "plot twists" that nobody expects because they'd just be a stupid choice. Not all of it was bad, but overall it felt really lackluster, disppointing, unsatisfying and lacking a bigger direction.
While the gameplay was not terrible, it was very frustrating a lot of the time and had a lot of really weird things about it. The way each day/segment ends is always really abrupt an odd,  It also always works against your interest, cuts off when you have some kind of idea of what to do or wanna go somewhere, but almost never lets you skip the hike through the entire forest so you can got to X. Navigating through the forest is also just a massive pain and at first is pretty fun, but towards the end of the game it's really frustrating and annoying. On one hand, you're supposed to feel like you're just in a wild, open forest with no clear paths set out, but then the way it's all actually designed forces you to follow designated, rigid paths which are easy to miss, confusing and tedious. It would be less of a problem if you didn't have to walk everywhere every time, but you do, so you better learn where eery path goes on the first trry.
Also, a rather minor thing, but still a big disappointment - there's not really any fire. You don't really deal with anything important, dangerous or serious. You walk around, find objects and talk on the radio, that's about it. All the fire's in the background and you almost never interact with it. 
Your choices are also supposed to make a difference, but at no point it really ever felt like they mattered at all. Unless it's between the choice of actually talking on the radio or just missing out on the main part of the game on purpose. 

In general, it's just a really disappointing and anticlimactic game with a lot of really odd choices and tedious game design. It's got some really nice things about it, but it's about as impactful of a story game as a generic crime thriller is lifechanging literature. If you just want to play it for the vibes and maybe some fun time, then it's pretty good, but if you're looking for something more this isn't really it.

Firewatch is a wonderful atmospheric adventure game that takes about 3 to 4 hours to complete. The two things that are most outstanding in this game are the graphics style and the voice acting.

The beautiful scenery and amazing colour palette chosen for the Shoshone National Forest makes it wonderful to explore and the hikes through the wilderness to story locations don't feel tedious at all. The variety of flora and rock formations make the terrain easy to memorise without the need for the map.

The voice acting for the two main characters, Henry and Delilah, is fitting and easy to listen to. Listening to the banter over the radio throughout the story means there is never a boring moment. The sound track is pleasant to listen to and adds to the wonderful atmosphere. I encourage players to look up the song "Ol' Shoshone" on YouTube as it is amazing but easy to miss in game.

The story is adequately entertaining and mysterious to hold the players interest. The background of the main character is set up rather quickly, and his story provokes feeling and sets up his personality and relationship background. The moral ambiguity of the character’s actions throughout the story is thought provoking. The plot sets itself up with mystery, and at many points you will find yourself checking behind you when you hear rustles in the bushes as the suspense rises. I found the ending adequate to wrap up the story with no loose endings.

Overall, I recommend buying this game on sale when the price is low enough to justify the 4 hours of gameplay.

Firewatch is a short narrative tale of a man named Henry, who does a stint of time as a fire lookout in a national park to escape from trauma in his personal life. He talks with his supervisor, Delilah, via walkie-talkie throughout the game, who initially gives him simple tasks to attend to as a lookout. After a brief period of time though, strange things start happening around the pair, and they both become wrapped into a mystery that could uncover some hidden secrets of the national park, threatening those who wish to keep those secrets buried for good. Firewatch plays almost entirely as a walking simulator, given a map to loosely traverse the park at your own pace and encountering new hints and secrets regarding the mystery along the way. I felt that the gameplay was simple yet relaxing, and the scenery you walk around is absolutely gorgeous, with some beautiful forests, lakes, and trails to navigate through. The dialogue between the two main characters was charming and felt incredibly organic. The story was mostly intriguing, but if I had to give the game one gripe it's that the ending felt a little flat. There's a pretty big climax build-up for the hour before the end, and then when the resolution occurs it feels kinda...eh? Like I suppose the story is resolved *technically*, but I guess I just expected maybe a little bit more of...something. That being said, I got the game for I think $5 on a sale, and it was absolutely worth $5 for a relaxing and engaging mystery. Even for full price I'd probably still recommend Firewatch, just maybe don't hold your breath for an absolutely amazing ending.

There are many superlatives for this game - first off, it's one of the most visually beautiful ones I've played. I'm not usually one to fuss over graphics much, but Firewatch has a gorgeous pastel-like quality presentation that's winning, and creates a very immersive world to explore. This is also thanks to some lovely sound design, creating a believable forest setting that just begs to be wandered about in and taking in all the sights. Then there's the dialogue, which all feels very realistic and featured some very neat writing. Here, the conversations you have with your supervisor effectively become the main part of the game's story, although the overarching plot is also very effective, even if it doesn't quite tie into your character's backstory in a manner that I would have liked or expected. 

I loved walking and hiking through the wilderness, navigating through the area with the map and compass, and although there's no time limit or anything like that, there were scenes that conveyed a sense of genuine loneliness, and even abject panic. How things that happen in the area seem to conspire against you, or the feeling of being trapped and followed. Firewatch's gameplay may be fairly minimalist - even to the point where it possibly resembles some sort of highly atmospheric interactive story - but crucially you feel as if you're in control of the game and the whole thing feels a lot more meaningful than just a walk through the woods. I loved it.

Firewatch is a great game, but more importantly, has one of the most profound narrative experiences I've had from a game.

Graphically, there's a lot to love, The art style is fantastic. It gives the world such a beautiful, rich and colorful feel. And my goodness, is the world incredible to look at. The lighting effects, the varied scenery in form of trees, grass, water, rock, all gel together to form a beautifully scenic visual experience as a medium to experience the rich narrative of the game. Nothing to complain about the visuals of this game, simply splendid.

As for the gameplay aspects, there really wasn't much in the way of anything interesting. Exploring is enjoyable because of the rich visuals and dialogue, but gameplay is rather uninspired. It mainly takes the form of walking around and button presses to one-dimensionally interact with the environment (such as tap a button to chop a tree, open a supply crate, grab an item, open a door, etc). Simple traversal through areas is really the main form of gameplay. The best thing I can say about the gameplay is how much it evokes the sense of actually experiencing a nature hike, given the beautiful environments and just the organicness of using a compass and map to navigate. That just makes it feel so much more real It's a really immersive exploration experience.

I absolutely loved the character building of Henry and Delilah. One of the most amazing and meaningful developments of characters relationship I've ever seen in a game. The dialogue was fantastic. Fun, witty, extremely well voiced acted (probably the "most real" I've heard in any game I've played), and most importantly incredibly natural and immersive. But even more so than the dialogue, both of these characters simply bled depth and their relationship was given one of the most complex and well thought out stories I've ever experienced. 

It's amazing how well Henry and Delilah complement each other in the story. Both characters are clearly flawed, but more specifically, are shown to be running away from their problems. They are both in the same boat. Henry was unable to handle the situation with his wife (who has dementia) and took a firewatch job to escape the pressure. Likewise, Delilah had left her behind relationship with her boyfriend after his brother died, failing to be there for him and being afraid of facing him. This puts Henry and Delilah in a position to really understand and connect with each other, which can be seen happening as they get very close with each other. The truth is, they've found comfort and solace in each other as they share their past experiences and find out just how similarly they deal with their problems: running away, alcoholism, isolation, and avoidance. Their relationship blossoms because of this, and this makes the dynamic between the characters truly meaningful.

What is interesting as well, is the development of each character differs in how they deal with their problems throughout the story. Delilah is shown to be undoubtedly still running away. She speaks only through a radio with Henry, seemingly reluctant to meet him. She lies about having involvement in the incident with the missing girls in the police report, hoping to avoid the police. Most importantly, she decides not to wait for Henry when evacuating, despite his wishes to see her. She's been avoiding and running away from confrontation her whole life, and it really shows in the progress of the game. Now take Henry, who develops differently. Henry makes an effort to stop running away. He takes the initiative to investigate the strange events occurring around him. He tries to fix his problems. He even seems to stop drinking when he's on the job. The fact that he is the one doing the work really goes to show that unlike Delilah, he's really trying to change himself. Although these two characters come from the same position and grow close because of the connection they share, the difference in how they deal with their problems in the course of Firewatch really shows just how much they contrast each other as well.

In the end, the evacuation really reinforces the idea that both characters are still running away. But this time they are running away together instead of alone, as they've grown to understand and connect with each other. However the difference in how they are conveyed is that Henry is shown to still be trying to tie loose ends, by making an effort to meet with Delilah when they evacuate. It's easy to see that Henry is trying to stop running away. Delilah in contrast however, is unwilling to wait for Henry, and simply wants escape from her responsibilities, instead of looking to face them.

As can be seen, the relationship between Henry and Deliliah is really the centrepiece of the game. It's so much more complex and intricate than what most people who play the game give it credit for. 

I've heard a lot of people call the ending disappointing, because "nothing really happened or was resolved". But I think people give it flak for the ending because they judged the game as a mystery-suspense story. It's not one. It's a drama. The mystery arc was simply a plot device for the development of Henry and Deliliah's story arc. The mystery car was not meant to be resolved because that's not what the game was focused on. People were expecting it to be, and felt empty when it wasn't, which is likely a prime reason for why there was an air of disappointment surrounding the ending. But it's not about the mystery story. It's all about Henry and Delilah and the progression of their stories and characters. It's about showing a bonding between two people, born out of the similarities between who they are how they deal with problems. It's about studying character interactions and development.

If I had a complaint, it would be that the game didn't really seem to fully "complete" Henry and Delilah's character arcs, as they didn't progress as characters all that much and never really "resolved" any of their problems and flaws. But I couldn't honestly expect a full character narrative, given that this game is only $20 and has only 4 hours of gameplay. It was simply meant to *show* character and relationship dynamics and how characters deal with problems and provide a thoughtful perspective on human interaction, thought, and behavior. Definitely a game I enjoyed more when I took the time to really think about it.

Firewatch is a very pretty game. Unfortunately, that's about all there is to it. Whilst some of the dialogue is amusing or involving, most of what you will be doing is selecting which bit of smalltalk you want to say, or you'll be jogging back and forth between waypoints. 

The story starts out well enough, but in the end falls a bit flat. Untimately that's a metaphor for the game as a whole. At the start I was impressed with the beautiful scenery and the attention to detail. From the lighting effects, to the way you can flip a book over in your hand and read the blurb, the designers have put a lot of love into the world of Firewatch. 

But after a while the whole place starts to feel like a tech demo. The forest is devoid of life. There's birdsong, but no birds. It's an illusion. Much like the impression of choice and freedom. What starts out as an interesting way to shape the narrative, talk choices quickly become a little tedious as you realise most of the choices lead back to the same path anyway. The same issue exists in travel. Firewatch looks like a huge forest, full of caves and canyons and rivers. But the game is very much on rails. You can't brush bushes aside. Instead they get in your way. I lost count of the amounts of times I got stuck on rock scenery, or found myself lost inside a forest of tough shrubs. 

This would all be fine were there a way to quick-travel. But you can't. Gone the wrong way? You've got twenty minutes of hiking ahead of you. And whilst I was impressed with the realism of having to look at a map to get your bearings at the start, I actually found having to stop and open up the map (which you can't run with while holding) and then having to put it away every two minutes a very tedious affair.

Like Everybody's Gone to the Rapture, I'm not sure that interactive storytelling is in any way improved, and in fact likely greatly diminished by the removal of most of the gameplay elements. 

5/10

Firewatch is probably one of the best walking simulators ever. The walking is a bit more interactive than in many other games. You have to navigate with a map that doesn't show your direction, and a compass. That alone keeps you kind of busy and makes the walking less boring. I will still say that I started to get a little bored sometimes, when I had to walk great distances to the next destination.

But that was only when there was no voiceover. Because the voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic. The two actors did a really great job. I can't think of any game that had voice acting on that level. The dialogue is very well written. It's funny. It's sad. It's intense when it needs to be. Just awesome. Henry and Delilah are both fantastic characters, and the growing relationship between them is interesting, and not as one-dimensional as stuff like this usually is in games. I liked it a lot.

The ending is at least questionable. I expected something else, to be honest. The game gets more intense as you go, until you really can't wait to get to the conclusion. And when you're finally there - well, I was a little disappointed. It's an interesting idea. But not really what I wanted. This is a personal preference, of course. Some people will like it, others will not.

This is the sort of game that I really wish I could give a middling option to. On one hand, the dialog is well written and expertly performed, and traipsing around the mountain trails is a beautiful and relaxing experience. It's also a very short experience; even multiple playthroughs to hear all the different dialog trees won't take more than a few hours. This could arguably be a negative for some, but given that the game is all dialog and narrative, it doesn't really need more than that to feel complete.

The true negative here is in the narrative itself. An intriguing mystery is established early on and grows bigger and more intense throughout the game, but it completely falls apart at the end. I get the impression that the writer(s) started off with all these different threads and didn't know how to tie them together, and game's conclusion is incredibly weak because of it. It's possible that the blasé explanation for all the events was entirely by design, which is fine in theory, but the execution here makes some elements of it feel outlandish given the grounded mood of the rest of the game.

Tl;dr good atmosphere, great voice work, terrible ending. I don't regret playing it, but it's not something I can give an easy recommendation. If you really feel the need to play this, get it on a steep discount. It's a game at odds with itself in weird ways, and while it seems like it's trying to say something profound with its story focused on middle-aged people dodging responsibility, it never really gets there.
