Firewatch Review:

For those unfamiliar with Firewatch, It’s the first game developed by Campo Santo studios. It was announced in 2014 giving audiences a glimpse at what the game had to offer without disclosing any major concepts behind the game. It was the game that had people asking, “What the f*** is Firewatch?” And with the wait finally over, the game is out and we get a chance to see it in its true colors. I have to admit, I was really excited for this game because it looked like it had so much potential, but it ended up being a dissapointing game.

Gameplay.
Gameplay-wise it is what I feared it would be, a simple and mundane walking simulator. This might be a contreversial opinion to have since some people might catergorize it as an “Adventure” game because it allows you to interact with and collect items, but let me explain myself and where I'm coming from for a sec.  To me, a traditional adventure game enables you to collect random or specific items that generally have a purpose in the grand scheme of things; solving a puzzle, accessing an area, main and minute plot progressions and so on. Whereas Firewatch, the only purpose to interact with items, is for dialogue or commentary reasons between your character and his supervisor. Technically, with the exception of 2 or 3 things, you don't even need to collect said items. All you have to do is highlight them with your cursor to bring up a dialogue option. And yet, aside from plot-related journals, the game gives you an option to take or interact with things for no apparent reason. A bottle of liquor that has no purpose, fireworks that have no purpose, a bar of candy that has no discernable effect. And that's probably 20% of the items you will interact with. The other 80% is nothing short of just admiring things for the sake of admiring things. Sound familiar (See: The Order: 1886)?

This game is also short. Most people could probably finish it in under 3 hrs. Normally, I like to place quality over quantity, but I was hard pressed to find either in Firewatch. And it becomes even harder when you consider that it’s priced at $20.00. As short as the game is on its own merits, it is made even more painfully obvious by the large amount of time spent backtracking through the same areas over and over again. Adding a bit of variety to the gameplay would have gone a long way towards cushioning the repetition. Running into a dangerous wild animal, solving puzzles or having to flee from a wildfire before it engulfs you are just simple examples that could have been implemented without having to compromise the overall essence of the game.

General gameplay aside, I did encounter technical problems, most of which are negligible but The one that stood out to me was the save management mechanic. While the game allows auto saving and manual saving, they unfortunately share the same slot AND, you're allowed  only one save slot per game. This is problematic because if you unknowingly save in a glitched state, you'll have to start your adventure from scratch. I was deep into my first game when I decided to save my progress, only to find out that I was standing on a small tree stump that I could easily step on, but could never alight. The only solution was to start again from the beginning and losing two hours of my progress.... and that was the only time during my entire play-through that I appreciated how short the game is.

Plot/Writing
And for a game that skimps heavily on gameplay, the hope is that it would inundate the player with compelling and robust plot points that engage on several levels. That hope is rightly justified and it is apparent that people behind this game had it at the forefront of their minds. Right from the get go the game entices you with a glimpse of options and consequences using a textual tree of choices that are similar to your standard emotional quotient tests. And as you make your way deeper into the game, you encounter several different plot points that range from simple letters you find in lockboxes to larger geographical areas shrouded in mystery. It’s all thrilling stuff that will keep you cycling through to see how things will unravel...but that's where it starts going downhill. As you slowly approach the conclusion of the game. All potential mysteries and plot points are tossed out and the game relies on a poorly presented discovery that marks an abrupt and unsatisfactory ending that tries to tug at your heartstrings. Which is a HUGE shame because the game really goes out of its way to threaten you with a good time, but never really delivers. It’s tempting to try and justify the nature of this game's plot by analytically approaching it, but When all is said and done, when you sit down and ruminate over your experience from the beginning to the end of the game, the realization that this was mostly an exercise in sarcasm between your character and a disembodied voice will creep in.

Audio
And this is where I can feel comfortable throwing some good points at this game. It has some of the best voice acting I've heard in a long while. That goes a really long way in making the mostly nothing that you do in the game tolerable. The conversations that occur between your character and Delilah, your supervisor, is extremely organic and, although contextual, it's believably adaptive. There are moments where you hold a long conversation with each other, and moments filled with quick, dry remarks when one character gets fed up with the other. And as a testament of how great and well thought-out the conversation are, it’s the moments of silence that really haunt you and make you feel vulnerable.

The game also does sound effects very well. From the sounds of the wind blowing to rustling bushes in the background. There are also several animal noises that are extremely convincing but unfortunately, that's broken by the lack of animals you encounter in the game. I think there were only two animals I saw throughout my entire play-through. A raccoon and an elk. Which, brings me to the visuals:

Visuals
It’s a vast Wyoming wilderness. An “open” world with intertwining paths that will leave you lost or moving in circles if you don't use your provided map and compass. And that's where most of the fun is to be had. Trying to move around and exploring the area by yourself is very fascinating. The design of the map is cleverly done and almost maze-like and every once in a while you run into a historically relevant site or landmark that make you feel like the next big explorer. The geography itself is beautiful and has a lot of breath taking sites like canyons, lakes, rivers and dense forests that lead seamlessly into each other without breaking your immersion.
The map surprisingly gets even more beautiful as the sun begins to set and casts a shed of amber around you. The mornings are often foggy and project a sense of eeriness, and where there is wild fire, the area becomes enveloped in smoke and destructive beauty.

Conclusion
So that's pretty much it for the review. This is probably the shortest review I've done, but I can only work with that the game has to offer, which is not a lot.
And although I've been critical, I don't want you think that this is a horrible game. I just wouldn't recommend it since there's hardly any meat to the bone. There's some fun to be had here, but it quickly wanes at the two hour mark. And for $20.00, unless you’re excited about the prospect of meandering back and forth around a map to no satisfactory end, you're better off waiting for a sale or using your $20.00 on a game that has more to offer.

My take on the first game by developer "Campo Santo" 

Since its initial announcement, I have been pretty stoked about giving "Firewatch" a try. And that is not because of the impressive developer cast behind the game, but because of the idea. After finally getting the chance to step into the hiking shoes of Henry, I was instantaneously blown away by the visuals. The way the Unity Engine is used to simulate the wilderness is something to behold. But don't let the beautiful cartoony exterior of the game fool you! Underneath it you will find well tuned gaming mechanics, which allow you to traverse the Wyoming wildes with ease. So far from a visual and navigational standpoint "Firewatch" is solid, but what about the story? 

The beginning sets a special tone that does not slowly ease you into the life of our protagonist, but on the contrary - it throws you in! While you are still trying to assimilate the predicament Henry is in, you find yourself atop of a watchtower in the middle of nowhere. As the player and the hero take in their new surroundings, the immersion intensifies itself by giving Henry a handheld radio with a voice on the other side - your supervisor Delilah. At this point you learn that not only does she speak, but your character does as well. This initial moment sets up the stage for the upcoming performance by the protagonist and the disembodied voice, as they try to protect the the wilderness from forest fires. This is immersive, because of the incredible voice acting by both actors portraying Henry and Delilah! During their talks the player controls the direction these conversations take and so he shapes Henrys personality, thus turning the player into his own version of the protagonist! 

The developers at "Campo Santo" have fused movement and storytelling mechanics with the visuals excellently, allowing for an immersive and emotional adventure, where you become your own unique Henry, while also forging a unique relationship with Delilah! Sadly we reach the ending quite abruptly, leaving us unsatisfied with the length and the conclusion to the story! 

This is a game that is all about the journey, not the destination! I suggest playing the game more than once, so you can experience different conversations between Henry and Delilah as you make your way through the Wyoming wilderness. During my second playthrough I found new and exciting areas I had missed, and managed to develop an interesting new relationship between our heroes.

In conclusion - I give "Firewatch" a very high recommendation for all fans of interactive storytelling games (or oldschool fans of the choose your own adventure books, like me).

I rate the game Firewatch 4/5. Good, but not a masterpiece.

This is a good first person perspective suspense-thriller personal drama story. Though very linear and relatively short, this was still interesting and humorous enough that I played it through 3 times (mostly to ascertain how much (or how little) freedom this game actually gives you). Ultimately, Firewatch is more of a mildly interactive story than an actual game. Indeed, there are places in the story where this "game" almost seems to play itself out and there are no choices you can make which have any great, ultimate effect on what happens in this game or on how it ends. You, the player, are essentially just along for the ride. It's an interesting (and at times, extremely tense) ride though.

The good:
+Good Graphics throughout, especially outdoors (which is where most of this game takes place. This game has a nice, well thought out cartoony, graphic novel style. One may think this graphical style would be enough to keep the game feeling humorous throughout but surprisingly this game depicts some increasingly tense and suspenseful situations. There are wonderful graphical flourishes throughout and a great attention to detail. Also, when you look down you can see your character's body, unlike many other games. Your character's hands do look a bit too pudgy and odd though.

+Great sound. Perhaps perfect sound actually. The sounds are realistic and excellently detailed. Crickets chirp and birds sing and bushes rattle mysteriously while strange metallic tinkling can barely be heard in the exact places where you should hear it. Every sound is meaningful and intentional. The sounds are vitally important to creating the tense atmosphere of this game and succeed brilliantly. The music works well to increase tension even further but wouldn't make a great soundtrack in itself. Voice acting is outstanding throughout and the script writing is excellent as well with many witty exchanges and jokes.

+The game controls well (it feels like you are playing as an out-of-shape but muscular guy which is exactly what your character is) and the controls mapped very well (and very easily) to my keyboard and mouse using the control settings menu. The controls are also fairly simple making this an ideal game to use if you want to learn how to play a first person perspective game and are uncertain as to how such game's should be controlled or are not yet very good at it. It is a bit odd though that you can make your out-of-shape character sprint around (including up hills) as much as you want to. It was also a bit overly difficult to figure out how to operate the radio and select dialogue choices (Odd considering what a vitally important element of gameplay this is) but I got used to it.

+The environment is big but not so big that things get boring if you enjoy being in the real-life great outdoors. It is big enough to get lost in but small enough that you can easily find your way back again. The environment feels like a fairly realistic outdoor area as well (especially if you were in some sort of state park). It is a bit grandiose for a mere national forest but that's a minor issue which is easy to overlook.

The Mediocre:
+/-This game could have had better pacing. I sometimes felt as though the game was trying to hurry me along through its plot. I particularly wanted there to be more peaceful moments wherein I was not encouraged to hurry but instead encouraged to explore for the sake of exploring. There's lots to see and have your character respond over the radio about but mostly you are busy with some more pressing matter (like trying to make sure someone doesn't set the forest on fire). There's no actual time limit on completing objectives (perhaps there should have been though) but wandering idly along looking at every little thing that catches your interest while someone or other is setting off fireworks in a high-danger fire area seems really strange, particularly after your boss has just told you to hurry (but doing just that kind of thing what you must do in order to get the most character and plot development out of the dialogue in this game's story. The game does give you an opportunity to go exploring on your own before the plot fully winds up but it doesn't seem like its encouraging you to do so at that point.

The Bad:
-It's almost impossible to figure out just how nasty or sarcastic your character is going to be before you select a dialogue choice (if I wanted the character to say anything at all). This encouraged me to want to play through the game again and again in a very frustrating way because, after the game was done the first time, I had yet to really see what would happen if I had responded in a way I wanted to. I had responded to several plot-critical situations with sarcasm or with nasty remarks wholly on ACCIDENT because the game won't tell you whether you are about to say something sarcastic or nasty. It only gives you the first few words of what you might say and nothing more. It's hard to choose one dialogue option over another based just off of that. All Dialogue options should have been labeled with easy to understand emotional labels such as "sarcasm" or "angry" or "depressed" and so forth to give the player a heads-up on what they are about to make the character say before they let the character say it. The dialogue systems in Deus Ex: Human Revolution and in Fallout: New Vegas and Fallout 3 are head and shoulders above the one which this game is built around.

-Regardless of what you say or don't say and regardless of whether you have your character respond at all (even to direct questions being repeatedly screamed at you), the same basic plot occurs and the same basic situations happen each time you play. This game is very linear and (sometimes as sheer luck would apparently have it) nothing you say or do really makes much permanent difference to how the plot develops. This is totally unrealistic. If I refuse to talk to anyone at all, there will be ramifications. If I act insulting on a constant basis, other ramifications will ensue. But in Firewatch? The same thing happens each time. Some of the same dialogue will be spoken NO MATTER WHAT YOU SAY OR DO. Your relationship with the main character will seem different to you but that does not change whether or not the forest burns down and nothing you say or do can change whether or not you prevent it. After playing the game 3 times in a row this inability to affect the game world in any meaningful way left me with a feeling of mild frustration. This game should have been more like a choose-your-own adventure story with multiple different endings. Instead it's like a normal suspense-thriller novel. It's fun the first one or two times but it wears thin far too quickly. 

-I could more easily accept the fact that this is a relatively short game if it had a plethora of potential endings but it doesn't. It has just two endings and they both seem a bit anti-climactic.Despite it's flaws though, I'm still glad I played it once, twice, even thrice (to see and hear everything the game has go offer) but I will not play it a fourth time. Now that I really have seen 90% of what this game has to offer, playing it yet again would just be repetitious and boring.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Overall, this game is a wonderful immersive (1st-person) story-rich experience. Worth the price for me, like a good movie, I would definitely recommend you to play it firsthand, without reading any spoiler beforehand

Here are the breakdowns of my impression;

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Visual Design[/h1]

It’s the first thing you’ll notice - the graphics and art style of this game are [b] gorgeous[/b] . The game is an enjoyment to simply look at, it pleases the eyes, even in the main menu. 

The colours, the nature, the objects and gadgets, the overall atmosphere, all beautifully tuned in to the experience. I particularly like the walkie-talkie and the signal detector, I have a thing for those little electronics

[h1]Story[/h1]

A good but short mystery-driven story. Grounded in realism, the [i]feeling of isolation & paranoia[/i] builds up gradually as you progress through the game. It isn't tagged with the horror genre, but like they say, the true horror is in the unknown anticipation - and in this case: the feeling that you are certain that you are being followed, listened, watched, analysed, and you don't know who and where they are.

[h1]Characters[/h1]

The voice acting in this game is [b]absolutely exceptional[/b] , vivid and convincing that it felt like these are real people, each with their distinct personalities and background past life, in a story that had actually happened. That said, it wasn't difficult for the game to get me emotionally connected to the characters and to the story. 

I fell in love with Delilah as I played. It's her voice, how she swear a lot, and how caring and flirty she is with Henry that got me interested. 
 
in this regard of character depth, this game is far more superior than some big titles.

But now that I have finished and watched some analyses, I think [spoiler]Delilah might have kept something from Henry the entire time, something about the Goodwin, about Brian's death and the research facilities. I had real bad paranoia, but I almost never suspected that she is aware of things and is lying to me - she knew about Ned Goodwin and kept communication with him from the very beginning.[/spoiler]

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Criticism[/h1]

- Ending Disappointment 
It was a disappointment that [spoiler]I can’t meet Delilah at the ending. One can argue that this might be part of the mystery, but given how the relationship between them has developed over months (or hours in playtime), it felt lonely and heartbroken that this person, who has been my only source of human connection for so long, wasn't going to meet me and maybe spend some time together off the radio.[/spoiler] 

- Short in Length
and there isn’t much value for replay either, except for sightseeing. I honestly wish it was longer, it felt like there was something more that was gonna happen to the final revelation of the plot, [b]BUT THERE WASN'T[/b] - and it just ended with the aforementioned disappointment 

- Emptiness of the Wilderness 
I get that loneliness and isolation is part of the intended experience, but wandering around the map, I rarely see wildlife, which, in a more realistic setting, would be ubiquitous in a forest like that in the 80s. The dev team really avoided much of the work lol - [spoiler]no character models, (almost) no wild life models[/spoiler]. Maybe more interactive locations & objects? but that would be dependable on the story

- It's an absurdly short game. It only takes 3-4 hours to complete.
- price, and this is the biggest factor here. The amount of content is simply not worth the asking price (without a sale discount).
- story was a huge letdown. It masterfully built up suspense, but crashed so hard at reveal.
- world is dead, i.e. you visit a section of the map and that's it, you basically never go back to it again.
- It's buggy. I've gotten stuck on fallen trees a number of times. There was a particular shrub-covered passage that I had to go through to progress the story that bugged out on me.

- technical issues - I could not change game resolution no matter how much I've tried. I know this may be a mac specific issue, but other games do not have same problem, so the game was not very well tested on macs. Not the end of the world on its own, but certainly adds to problem pile.

Why do I have to jump over 5 blocking objects in a row, when there is no challenge (or puzzle) and you literally just press a button to do so? How does this contribute to better gameplay or story development? They are just there, because they stretch the gameplay time.

While there are multiple areas which are more or less explorable without any boundaries, the game world is still designed in a very linear fashion and its not that big. You rarely - need - the map or the compass that the game wants you to use. So why using it at all?

There is a single-use camera in the game, which doesnt really have a sense. It is not really a photo mode. A photo mode would be a real benefit in this game, because the game is gorgeous. Instead its just some kind of "toy" with no real usage in the end, despite having an achievement tied to it.

There is some seriously good character development, solely based on dialogues on a Walkie-Talkie. 
I liked that a lot. 
However, the dialogue choices dont affect the game in a noteworthy way, and this kinda makes them bad in the context of a "game". I just dont feel, that this is enough to describe this game as a "masterpiece", which a lot of people do.

While highly appraised, the story doesnt really live up to its expectations. 
The story has indeed a nice pacing, and you get very interested in how it turns out.
But what was good about the pacing in the character development between Henry and Delilah, was completely different for all the other side stories in the game.

The big revelation didnt strike me at all, because there was no attachment at all. (Dont want to spoiler here.) Pacing here was just very bad, as you didnt really got to know the persons part of that plot and therefore you couldnt relate to anything of it.

Seeing Delilah at the end was something I was really looking foward to while playing the game. Not showing her is as big a dissapointment for me, as it was for the games Protagonist Henry. 
A lot of people say, this is why the story is so great. Because the story leaves you with the exact same emotions the protagonist is experiencing. Its a depiction of real life, how we tend to run away from problems, and that not everything has a deep substantial meaning. However I really think this is a bad excuse for not having something to say at all.

In the end there is no message. It started out strong, depicting the struggles of a relationship with alzheimer's. But the games story didnt manage to pick up on that topic at all, actually showing how people might process those problems in the end, or how to overcome those struggles. There are a lot of set-ups in the stories development, and none of them got a concise ending - or any at all. I do like the fan theories. But its just not fair to justify the stories "greatness" based on some theories, that most of the people will never experience or even think about while playing the game.

Firewatch is a primarily narrative driven story game that has you walk around the Wyoming wilderness interacting with varying different points of interest while communicating with another firewatch person via walkie talkie. It’s developed by Campo Santo and published by Panic, alongside of Camp Santo. It released back in Feb 9 of 2016. 

I’m going to be extremely brief with this one. The story and narrative is strong, and this entire experience basically hinges on that because everything else is relatively weak. The pacing is good, and character development can vary slightly dependent on dialogue options that you choose, although overall the outcome will be somewhat the same. The game centers around exploring the wilderness and interacting with different points of interest that often come in the form of stumps or rocks that allow you to traverse different areas that would normally be inaccessible. Controls are fine. There apparently is expanded controller support that was implemented back in December of 2021 on steam, a staggering 5 years after the games release. I never played with a controller, just keyboard and mouse. There is no difficulty to the game nor option for it, just the one fairly linear experience. Visually it’s a well stylized game and it’s aged well at this point. Animations and their details are limited, constrained to what you’ll mostly see by interacting with travel points to get from point a to point b. Music pops up here and there, but doesn’t have much impact. It’s somewhat forgettable. Sound effects for various actions are also limited. The voice acting is strong, which is good given how heavily the game relies on it’s plot and narrative pushing the story forward. Rich Sommer (Henry) and Cissy Jones (Delilah) do a phenomenal job. The dialogue is witty and very human. The direction here was excellent. Environment variety is limited, it’s all forest. Some of it’s burned. Exploration is normally rewarded in the form of additional dialogue or new lore. There’s no endgame content to speak of, and the only reason you would go back and play it again would be to get achievements that you missed, or to experience the games free roam mode within it’s special features on the main menu, unlocked through completing the story at least once. 

Performance wise the game runs well, almost always at a buttery 144fps. I experienced no crashes during my time with it. That being said, the game is riddled with annoying bugs and inconveniences. Henry can become detached from the topology of the floor beneath him when interacting with a traverse point and he will slide in a random direction. This happens frequently. Modeling on rocks are incomplete within a cave. If you interact with a locked cache and then escape out of the interaction during dialogue that is playing on the radio, specifically when you are prompted to provide a response to Delilah, the game will lock you in place. You can look around, but are unable to press escape to bring up the pause menu or press literally any controls to bring up any menu or move away from the cache. This resulted in having to Alt + F4 to restart the game. If Henry is running towards the edge of a large drop off and continues running forward without interacting with it, he can once again become detached from the topology of the floor map and slide down the edge to the floor beneath it. This also happened several times. If Henry pulls up his map during walkie dialogue and is prompted for a response, you will be unable to select a response so long as the map is pulled up, and will have to put it away in order to select an option. Given how quickly some of the response timers expire, it’s entirely possible the player can miss responding, or being able to read the options in time if they bring up their map to check their bearings at the wrong moment. Certain items (such as the turtle) have the chance to not spawn, and these are tied to achievements. The game by default is set to autosave, so unless you know about it, it’s also entirely possible to have a run where an interactable item just doesn’t spawn. 

Achievement hunting in this one is a pain as well. There is no chapter select, so if you miss some achievements during your initial playthrough, you’ll have to play it all the way back through to the point where you can grab whatever you missed. Because of it’s design there’s a lot of sitting around waiting for responses to happen, so it can take a minute to progress through the story if you’re looking for just the one achievement you missed. See also the turtle achievement above. Sometimes it won’t spawn, so you’ll have to reload. Not a huge deal if you have autosaving disabled, but that’s enabled by default. Poor design in my opinion. 

Firewatch’s strongest point is it’s well structured story and superb voice acting direction helping to drive it forward, while it’s weakest points is it being riddled with annoying bugs, poorly designed mechanics and world interaction, achievement items not spawning, and missing quality of life features like chapter select. 

Final verdict is 3/5. I recommend this to players that are largely invested in story telling games with less to none game features and mechanics, but only under the condition that it’s on sale. This is one long interactive movie essentially. I won’t return to this game, but I did enjoy the story the first time around and can appreciate it.

Well, I jumped on the Firewatch hype train instead of buying The Long Dark for myself seeking to get away from MOBAs for an adventure game. There were many parts of the game I enjoyed, but overall, I think it left a lot to be desired. 

Pros:
+ Environment is absolutely beautiful and very well made
+ Voice acting is phenomenal 
+ The intro scene allows you to build your own character's background 
+ Dialougue has so many options- you can build whatever relationship with Delilah you want
+ Story grabs your attention through the first 90% of the game
+ Well-made, enjoyable soundtrack with songs never repeating

Cons:
- Game is very short
- Story's ending is unsatisfying
- Map isn't huge, and there isn't a lot of exploring to do
- Game is extremely linear; no sidequests or satisfying things to do
- Impossible to use the map while you're moving- you can have it out, but you can't see a damn thing
- No option to jump, but rather forces you to vault obstacles stick to the trails
- Very little wildlife- you find a turtle and an elk but that's all

Overall, I did have a very hard time deciding whether or not to recommend Firewatch. There are people out there raving about this and how different it is, and how well-developed the characters are, etc... Don't get me wrong, these statements are true, but those two things don't make a good game. I guess if you want to pretend to have some snobby, high-class appreciation for "something different", this game is for you. If you're looking for a story with some follow-through, this ISN'T the game for you.

One of the most telling things about this game can be discovered by Googling for all the "what if I..." questions that players have asked after completing the game, and the overwhelming response is "It doesn't matter." The game only has ILLUSIONS of choices and possibilities, but nothing actually changes any outcome (aside from a secret ending which isn't really worth anything beyond reading about it on a forum - you'll see why). 

The Firewatch world is full of seemingly-interesting things that seem like they could be collectibles that lead to hidden achievements, or things that could lead to additional intrigue or puzzles, but no, they serve absolutely no purpose except to populate the world so you can pick things up, look at them, and drop them. 

What's that, you say? "Surely, if I collect all of the numbered books and put them onto my bookshelf, that has to unlock something..." Nope, sorry. You've just wasted an hour or two of your time. I'm not particularly crazy about collectible-hunting, but I'd rather not be presented with false possibilities. It seems like the developers wanted to expand the game and they set the stage and maybe ran out of time. But instead of removing these meaningless objects from the world, they just left them so you can pick them up for a few seconds and wonder, "What do I do with this?" (The answer: nothing - drop it and move on).

So this really isn't a "game" per-se. If you're going to get it, better wait for a sale. $20 is WAY too much for this game. It feels like a $5 game with -hints- at greatness that will leave you feeling empty, with nothing resolved.

The shortest way to describe Firewatch is 'what if you got sucked into an old story and you got the freedom to explore', but with a couple of twists. I'm saying an 'old sory' here not so much because you know it by heart, but because the premise and the format are a familiar structure: middle of nowhere, nothing but mother Nature around you, and you only have one person to talk to, a person you can't even see. A
And of course, there's the Mystery. 
While this game is predominantly about storytelling, there is a fine ballance between how the game's design and the plot itself that makes it irresistible to just follow along and see what happens. I think the best part is how well portayed the element of lonesomeness (is that a word? it is now.) is. Sure, you have your radio companion, and you get to talk to them about what happens as the story goes along. But at the end of the day, you're all alone in the middle of the woods - and the mind can go wild when triggered by the smallest thing, or the wrong pop of a branch being broken. 
Last but not least - I've seen some people complain about the ending and I can see the reason why, but I definitely disagree there. The ending is just as good as the rest of the story, because, well, what did you expect to happen?
This game was well worth $25 for the amount of enjoyment I got out of this game. No qualms here, just buy the game and enjoy :)

Absolutely amazing game. Might not be for everyone though. In my opinion you should think of this as not so much a game but more like an interactive first-person movie. The story is excellent, but it's basically a movie designed to make you feel like you're the main character.

There is a bit of walking simulator aspect to it but for me I enjoyed that a lot. A lot of the game is just walking around, exploring, enjoying the scenery. You even get rewarded for exploring with conversation options. It's all meant to get you in the zone of actually being this person you're playing. You're alone in the middle of the wilderness. There's quite a lot of navigating through the forest and moving from point A to point B. But that's part of the charm of the game.

I think if you like the idea of a first-person mystery film in the form of a walking simulator with about a 7-8 hour game-time, you should absolutely buy this game. It was a very cool and well-done experience. Also as other reviewers pointed out, the story was an emotional rollercoaster. There's something about actually being the main character that just gives you the feels.

I can't recommend this game, but I'll mention some pros and cons.  

PROS

[list]
    [*]Nice production quality, good graphics & sound, really makes you feel like you're hiking through parkland wilderness.
    [*]Good acting & well-written dialogue, with a well-paced story
    [*]Intriguing mystery that really makes you think and try to guess what's really happening. 
[/list] 

CONS

[list]
    [*]EXTREMELY linear. You are on rails from the beginning to the end. There are no meaningful "choices" you can make, whether in dialogue or in exploring the world. No matter which of the narrow options available you choose to pick, the game ignores your choice and plows ahead with the predetermined storyline. The game decides who you trust and who you don't, it decides how you respond to danger, etc.
    [*]Characters make really, really dumb choices. Frustrating if you've already figured out the mystery to see them stumbling ahead like idiots while you're powerless to stop them. Example: if you've been attacked by some stalker creep in the middle of nowhere, stop broadcasting where you are and where you're going on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ radio! 
    [*]Very short game. You can finish in a few hours, and the game has zero replay value.
[/list]

As a true adventure game, Firewatch is heavily depended on the narrative. However, the narrative (especially towards the end of the story) seems like a game design course narrative assignment than a finished product. On a personal note I would like the narrative to exploit the background that it sets early on (wife, dementia etc.) without taking everything too literally. You can read the justifications behind the creators' choices here: https://quarterly.camposanto.com/the-end-of-firewatch-8a7d334a9586#.muhqnina2 I would like for the creators to treat the story more like a game narrative and less than a lesson of high value. After all, it is a serious adventure game and games of this kind usually have to be firstly fun and then deep.

The narrative is also linear and the world quite closed, thus the player does not have many choices for real exploration of the game and, ultimately, does not really allow the player to make the choices for the character.

The game also has a very short duration for its price, making it look even more like a course assignment (the project team would score a good grade nevetheless). Most of the game's duration is spent on moving around and try to get from one side of the map to another and not with actually interacting with game elements. 

The music soundtrack is short and the music too generic, it sets the scene nicely but definitely not worth the money as a separate DLC. 

The graphics and the art of the game are very good-looking and colourful. A minor issue: too much emphasis is given on the shadows, thus burdening the performance of the game for some older systems. 

Finally, the game is too overpriced for what it offers but - especially at the beginning - it is a nice experience and sets up a nice mystery story, despite the late disappointment (LOST-like style) and the short duration (appr. 3-4 hours for playing it once-twice, 6 hours for people playing it over many days).

I would recommend the game just for the experience and for you imagining how good it could be with a slightly different narrative. 

PS. I read the news that Firewatch is being made into a movie. It would be interesting to see how the production team will address the narrative issues since it is not going to fit into the Cinema or TV medium with such a mediocre narrative.

What can I say?

Firewatch is a brilliantly made game. It features a fantastically gripping story line with likable characters (although few). The content of the game is short, but in a small space of time it raises questions about morals and personal experiences between Deliah and Henry than most games can in 9 to 10 hours of play. It was compelling throughout and I was (literally) on the edge of my seat while playing. 

Graphics wise, this game is beautiful and surpasses my expectations of what a story driven game would usually have to offer. It tends to keep things simple but shows how the simple "things" can make a vast and eye-opening view. 

The best comparrison I can make to Firewatch is Life is Strange. The art and look of the game gives me the LiS vibe to it, which is an extremely good thing because I was hooked on Life is Strange, even doing a second runthrough. However, the content of the games are similar, except Firewatch's decisions do not impact on the story. As far as I'm aware it all ends in the same outcome, but gives you different ways to approach talking between characters. It is not your story in a sense, but the way that you feel it and react is. 

Overall, I give this game a superb 9/10 because I feel like there could have been more to the ending of the story and that the options you chose impacted the way the story may have been played.

In short I really recommend this game but if you are one of those persons who needs more than an opinion here are some reasons why I find that this game is one of the best I have played in a while:

The story is quite short and it took me around 3 to 4 hours to complete. Despite the story looks fairly simple at the start as you are doing normal things that a fire watcher is expected to do like exploring the forest, locating any persons that could be dangerous to the forest as they are lighting up a fire, there is a 'threat' and a mystery that you as a player is encouraged to uncover and from there you get more information about your fire watcher partner and her experiences as a fire watcher. I found the story interesting as there were quite a lot of twists that I personally wasn't expecting and I found myself sympathising with some of the characters and it had quite a natural flow and it didn't seem like 3 hours of gameplay as I was immersed in the game and the setting and the story of the characters.

The controls are quite simple and they introduce a couple of mechanics as you progress through the story, but they are introduced nicely as it is natural the way that they are implemented. Despite this game was launched in 2016, the visuals and the art hold pretty well up until this day and I really like the settings and the music that went along the tension of the story. It runs really nicely and I didn't experience any lags or bugs which is always a plus. The map is quite big to explore (but heads up, the map is a sandbox) and despite there are limits to the map, it doesn't feel small in the slightest as the story forces you to explore all of it and go from point A to point B.

Overall I will replay the whole game again to collect all the trophies in a couple of weeks and I can't recommend this game enough to someone who wants a cozy adventure, someone who wants to discover a mystery or if you just like the art style and the way that the game looks give it a try!

Firewatch! What an marvelous thing. So beautiful it's impossible you haven't seen an laptop ad without one of the game wallpaper's in the wild, and one such deserves of a review.

[b]Pros[/b]:
-Beautiful, which salutates another of it's strong points:
-Easy to run! I could go on about the wonderful vistas, the excellent crated enviroment or even the dev's PHD on color paletes, but Firewatch just throws at your face on how a game being run even on a potato pc can bring such fidelity to the user's eyes. I mean, just look at Fortnite.
-Immersion, plot and gameplay. Everyone that played the Farcry games remembered on how they couldn't choose between Farcry's 2 "you in the game" thing, with how you had to bring your map on your hand and figure where to go, your character realistically with a health condition - which you had to obligatory progress the game to fix -, OR Farcry's 3 story (With a villain that seemed to come out of a Christoper Nolan movie) - which yes, was that good. Firewatch fixes that!
Not only the game gives you choices to make a background out of your character, since your character gets to comment on almost every interaction of the game, the game lets you choose how said interaction can happen. I'm not talking about the story itself, but the way the game delivers it is amazing. Literally the first 30 second trailer on the steam store page should give you an explanation of it.
What I'm saying is, I'm not particulaly fond of the story, but the way delivers it is amazing. Altough for me a personally not satisfying turn out of events, it still made sense, and the way each element was brought onto the player for the later plot was handled pretty well.

[b]Neutral[/b]: 
-Story: It's one of the love or hate things you do. As I said earlier, the game does a pretty good job at telling it (especially since you have control over almost any interaction of the game), but for me I was not really "ohhhhh" more like "oh." at the end. Some people might like it, some might not, especially considering almost every choice in the game only affects a drawing in the final moments of gameplay, I still got immersed, until the very second, that this was indeed an own unique world.
-Soundtrack: I liked it. Felt kinda weak though
-The style of the game: It's still, at the end of the day, a walking simulator. You won't fight any zombies or save earth from the aliens, but this should be pretty obvious by the very name of the game. You are a guy who works at a Firewatch station, and depending on the type of the player playing, that's where you will like or not. What I think? You should give it a try. Steam refunds exist for a reson.

[b]Cons[/b]:
-No additional plot points: relying heavily on only it's main plot, it doesn't have much forgiving traits if said story is not by the likes of the player. What could have been additional plot points? Hmm, maybe the cabin near the communications wires? You know, I actually wanted some optional backstory on that cabin, would have been cool.
-Runs like ♥♥♥♥ on high-end computers: I don't wanna brag, but Firewatch is a weird game. Playing on ultra on almost 200fps, (I use a stock cooler, but a lot of other players also reported this), the game causes a lot of high temperatures, even if I use vsync. A lot of other games have more dense/heavy graphics than this game and run cooler, especially on very high/ultra settings. It just doesn't make sense to me.
-Certain dialogue choices and the ending: [spoiler]Play the game before reading this. Certain dialogues with your partner can make the protagonist have a different view on his wife, especially the background choices you do at the start. The alternate ending where you wait 2 minutes and the chopper leaves, I presume is a joke from the developers for the "alternate endings" question from a news article. It could have represented on how the protagonist wanna leave his wife behind, or how he acquired some sympathy with Ned (they both have similiar problems). As a redditor said, literally one line of dialogue could have fixed this. Thankfully, the game has a lot of forgiving traits, but it's still pestering on some peoples nerves.

TLDR:the main reason you would play this game is for the story.
Overall it's a slow burn, the game is heavily dialogue & story heavy but I think that serves to the game's strength, but there's still a fair bit of gameplay in light puzzle, parkour, and rock climbing sections.  In addition there's tonnes of little easter eggs (even stuff from other games, movies, & media) there's hidden passages/dialogue options that you don't necessarily have to explore/activate to progress the story but provide alot of incite into the characters' backstories.

If you're still not convinced about the story, i'll give you some non descript examples of what makes it so good: not only do the characters directly tell you stuff, but you can parse information about what kind of person from the way they speak, like small slip-of-the-tongue moments, where characters actually hesitate & choose to withhold information from you tell you alot about the characters and keep your mind occupied trying to connect the dots which makes the characters intriguing and mysterious & keep you begging to learn more, with environmental story telling there's tonnes of objects/trinkets you can pick up & examine which gives alot of clues into what kind of hobbies & personalities certain characters have, (even if you haven't met them directly). sometimes the characters will chat about something earlier in the game, make some promise, etc, and initially you won't think too much of it, but later on, just exploring your watchtower's room, you'll come across an object that confirms the characters went through with their promise, and you can't help but chuckle. And this is done without the game even leading you on to discover it, it's up to you as the player to discover these moments that sometimes even lead to more OPTIONAL dialogue which will make you wonder how many other easter eggs the devs put effort into for stuff 60% of players wont even run into, it's incredibly rewarding to take your time and choose your own path through the forest as that extra time exploring always pays off.

For those interested in a spoil free summary of my essay, firstly it's a bit more subjective, beyond the literal setting of the game, with all the spoilers & plot twists, that I won't get into. For some short context this review was a originally differently worded, I did an indepth analysis of the characters, but I went back and realised I wanted people to actually play the game themselves, and then draw their own opinions about each character rather than take what I say as face value, so everything below is a bit vague and might sounds insane, but the beauty of Firewatch, is that the symbolism isn't shoved in your face, everything i'm about to say is so subtly hinted by the devs, you could finish this game, and never realise any of it, but if you take your time to enjoy the journey, rather than rushing to the end, you'll see.

To me, the game isn't just about being in a forest, it's an analogy that forces the player to question the morality of this concept called "Escapism": running away from your problems if you will. The beauty of it is that the game doesn't present escapism as a black & white topic, Ingame you'll run into and interact with other characters and it becomes obvious they all have unique issues/flaws/traits/guilts, but it's not really your place to judge because the developer's put you in a tough spot on purpose, mostly because of your character own fatal flaw for 'running away' and getting a job out in the Shoshone national park is a certain someone, (who this flaw is gets explained extremely early so it's not much of a spoiler but you'll learn more as you play and get opportunities to fill in the gaps) The developers highlight Isolation in several ways including diegetic sounds, wind, and the symbolic imagery of a forest as not only as place of reflection & recovery, but isolation isn't just used in the literal sense, it's used symbolically, think about it, when you have an argument, a bad take, or controversional opinion, it's often said "You're on your own". Hence why I believe that the forest is the perfect analogy and environment to explain how escapism is neither good or bad. and initially you feel guilty about your character's past (rightfully so), but as the game goes on, you run into other characters with their own problems/commitments they're running from, and you can't help but feel for sorry for some of them, as well as judge other characters (however the devs make you contemplate if it's really your place to judge) One thing I only realised on my second playthrough was the Forest-fire which not only serves as an overarching passive 'antagonist', but the symbolism of the Forest Fire slowly creeping into your character's henry & his coworker's mind slowly realising they cant ignore their responsibilities as a Fire-lookout by just gossiping and having fun all summer, serves as a sort of "symbolic karma" prediction of what ignoring their relationship issues will result in. The ending of the game:
[spoiler] was to many players quite underwhelming with tonnes of the characters' redemption arcs remaining unfulfilled/incomplete, but it honestly serves to the developers' argument as  despite all the fun you had with delilah, +uncovering the truth behind what happened to Brian, whether you think they were in the wrong for running away, in any other situation would be clear cut: wrong, but since you persevered with them and carried the guilt with them, it's not clear, the ending reminds you regardless of what you think of Henry, delilah, and ned, their issues are waiting for them back in the city, & ironically your own issues & commitments in real life are waiting for you when you finish the game, the developers force you accept that the people you hate in real life might have some truth to why they act the way they do.[/spoiler]. 

And again, everything i've just said is like the "B plot" in the symbolism & messaging, there's a whole other can of worms with the literal events of the story in the "A Plot" which I'll let you experience yourself.

Although i'd still have to say that game was amazing, it's a slow burn of mystery & detective-work like conspiracy, it's about the journey not the destination, silly goofy dialogue with milennial humour'ed characters and it shows. 10/10.

I consider myself very lucky as I came into this game completely blind; it sat on my wishlist for a long time pending a sale and free time to invest until just last night when I banged it out in a long continuous session. I didn't even watch any gameplay footage or any in-depth reviews, and it was only on my wishlist because it was lauded as something spectacular when it was released awhile back and occasionally I'll bite when games are universally praised. (I still haven't played Last of Us and I know that's one I should get around to based on it's pedigree).

Well, now that I've digested Firewatch I can say that it does some things splendidly (voice acting, tone, keeping the player on edge who hasn't read spoilers)... and other things rather poorly,  (with the beginning and ending and your in-game choices not effecting the game's conclusion beyond some slight dialogue being the biggest disappointments). To put things in perspective, that last fact alone basically means that unless you desperately want to hear some random radio dialogue about a snail or signpost or stone circle you may have missed off the beaten path somewhere during your first play through, there's no point in replaying the game: you will end up in the SAME EXACT (sullen) PLACE at the game's conclusion. Flirt with Delilah, ignore Delilah... it doesn't matter: she won't wait for you, and will always blow you off during the end sequence. Gather evidence against Ned? Doesn't matter... you can't do a thing about what happened. Even if you piece together the most likely events that happened during the game's story, again... it doesn't matter as you can't act on it while playing the game. It's fairly soul crushing when you realize your fate is sealed the second you hit play with this (well paced and voice acted) game, and I'll never play it again because of that fact.

TL;DR -- I'd say as a Visual Novel (with fairly pointless running + climbing simulations tossed in since you can't die) it's very good, but as a satisfying story it falls rather flat. It truly needed to have multiple endings depending on what you chose as a backstory at the start and how you proceeded, and to give the player choices to make instead of just pushing you along on rails.

[h1] Review: [/h1]
The game looks good and the story is great. The music is wonderful with undertones of different feelings and feel like standalone bangers.

[h1] Story (Spoilers Ahead) [/h1]
The prologue starts with Henry, (The player character) in university meeting with Julia after a bit they become friends and eventually they get married. After a while Julia develops early onset dementia which makes her slowly forget about Henry, after sending her to a full-time care hospital (or taking care of her yourself) Her condition worsens and you see an ad in a paper for a job which you take. This is the job for a Fire Lookout in the Wyoming wilderness. You take a hike to your lookout tower and before going to bed, meet Delilah, your boss. 
After waking up Delilah tells you over radio about what your job is and the equipment around your tower. Before even finishing the last bit of the first lot of equipment she is interrupted by a few teenagers illegally using fireworks. You are sent to go down and take care of them and after almost trashing their camp they run away and you confiscate the fireworks. The way back is blocked so you take another way home, through a cave. Once you make it out a silhouette of a figure shines a flashlight on you before retreating. This is scary because you are supposed to be alone out here. Delilah tells you it's fine because people can come in and out all the time but you still think a bit about it. You make it back to your tower to find it trashed and you think that it could either have been the figure or the girls whose camp you trashed. 
The next 70 days are mostly uneventful (and the game skips over a few days) but one certain day you see a massive fire that you cannot do anything about. Fast forward a few days you go to the lake to fish like normal but something, is... wrong. A clipboard stands upon a tree stump which shows radio conversation transcripts between you and Delilah, after looking around you find a radio which is muffled but a name is made out "Wapiti Station" after picking up the radio you get knocked out. "Wapiti Station" is this a station in Wapiti meadow? The next day you go there finding that your radios have been tapped.  When going to Wapiti Station it is mostly empty other then bios featuring you and Delilah and a device which can track signals. Delilah suggests you burn down the place but you decide against it. You make it out of Wapiti Station right before it blows up, merging its fire with the big fire from a few days ago. Once you make it back to your tower you find a cassette tape which is supposed to suggest that you and Delilah burned down Wapiti Station. 
One day you go caving and are exploring a cave but then you find a body a body of the child that was here before you you find out how to tell Delilah over the radio once you get out. Eventually the fire is too much and you have to escape. Before escaping the device you found starts beeping. You follow the beeping towards a cassette tape, this is from the dad of the dead boy you found in the cave. He says he has been the one who has been spying on you. He says he wants to go deeper into the wilderness and doesn't want anyone to know where he is going. Eventually you make it to Delilah's tower. You don't get to see her, Delilah had left before you in a helicopter. You have one last chat over her radio before going into a helicopter and escaping. That is it. You do not get to see Delilah. Price tags shouldn't [i]really[/i] influence how good a game is, but in this case it does. For example, a AAA title with only 20-30 hours of gameplay (the low end) at $60 is still worth it if the hours are fun (Shadows of Mordor is a good example). In this case, however, I can't seem to justify paying a third of a triple-A title with only one tenth of the gameplay, if that. Something just doesn't feel right.

Anyway, price rant over, here's the actual review, with a warning that some of this may be considered minor spoilers given the nature of a "mystery" game:

Without getting too involved in the plot, the story starts off with an almost text-based choose your own adventure style RPG about the romance, life, and love lost, leading up to your taking a job as fire watchman. You end up wedding a "Julia", and life is good, but some things aren't so good. Eventually, things are pretty bad, and you run off to do manly stuff in the forest. I'm exaggerating points here, but basically no matter how you try to "choose your own adventure", you still end up having to deal with this depressing plot premise. None of the text based intro ends up being relevant to the game except to set the stage for some of the quirky dialog later on. And to tell you what your motivation is. Really? You needed to give me a whole cliché backstory just to justify why I would want to move to Wyoming to be an awesome fire watching person? Oh well, at least we made it to the watch tower! Now we can do fun watch tower stuff with this mysterious radio voice girl!

The game is very linear and story based. It's basically a 3 hour interactive movie. That's not a bad thing, it's actually kind of refreshing, because it's NOT told through ridiculously frustrating cutscenes. Instead, the game is the cutscene, if you will. That said, the story itself is fairly anti-climactic, as others have pointed out. You might have guessed it from the vague trailers and concept, but you're in the wilderness doing one of the most mundane jobs ever. Your expectations should be set around this fact. This is one of those "take joy in the little things" indie type stories that you would see premiered at Sundance. It's [i]Wild[/i], in game form.

As for the artwork, it is nothing short of glorious. The game looks great and that is what sells the game. It's why you will probably buy this game anyway, even after reading this review. And guess what? You can take pictures! And order real life prints of the pictures you took in game! Yay!?

As you may have guessed in the lead up, the thing that bugged me the most about this game is the dialog and character choices. I simply had a hard time empathizing or identifying with any of the characters, and I found the "witty" banter between you and Delilah (your firewatch boss) to be awkward and forced. There were some relatively heartwarming moments, but for the most part, it felt like they were ad libbing half of the conversations, and poorly. The interactions with Delilah did little to advance the plot or relationships in the game except for 2-3 key moments. Everything else I probably could have done without. I get that they were trying to create a Portal-like relationship with this "ominous voice", but I felt like the execution was off. Especially since (major spoiler) [spoiler]she was about a 10 minute hike away but you two never ever meet over the course of 3 months being completely secluded together. And there is one notable "scene" that calls this arrangement completely into question.[/spoiler]

Anyway, moving on. The controls were easy enough to use, so there's really nothing to say about them, though I kind of wish the game had a button to turn off the walkie talkies so Delilah would stop bugging me every 2 minutes. 

To conclude: as a fun little interactive movie to sit through when you're relaxing on a lazy Sunday, this fits the bill perfectly. The selling point is the art style. As a game that's worth $20, it's no barn burner.

[i]Firewatch[/i] will not be for everyone, but I loved it and would recommend it to adult gamers who are interested in good characters and stories. I would also recommend it to people who usually prefer books. Clocking in at about four to five hours of gameplay, [i]Firewatch[/i] is a walking novella and feels a lot like the game equivalent of a [url=http://www.britannica.com/biography/Raymond-Carver]Raymond Carver[/url] short story.

Understand that while there are things to do in this game, it is not a "doing" game. People looking for tons of action and the ability to explore an open world should look elsewhere. It's a "thinking" game—not in a puzzle-heavy sense, but philosophically. It has similarities to other novella-like games, such as [i]Dear Esther[/i] and [i]Gone Home[/i]. (There is even [url=https://twitter.com/iamfantastikate/status/697261856432361472]a nice little [i]Gone Home[/i] Easter egg[/url].) [i]Firewatch[/i] is all about—maybe [i]only[/i] about—the beautiful world and the story within. 

* People who "get" and like literature will appreciate [i]Firewatch[/i] more than those who don't.
* The story is small, almost a [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slice_of_life]slice of life[/url]. It's meant to be. It's not a mistake. 

[h1]Story and Setting[/h1]
It's 1989, and Henry (voiced by [url=http://www.imdb.com/name/nm1360860/]Rich Sommer[/url] of [i]Mad Men[/i] fame) and Delilah ([url=http://www.imdb.com/name/nm4047315/?ref_=fn_al_nm_1]Cissy Jones[/url] from [i]The Walking Dead[/i], [i]The Wolf Among Us[/i], and a host of other games) have taken jobs in Wyoming's Shoshone National Forest as an escape from their individual realities. In the lonely quietude, they find in each other an acceptance that isn't always easy to come by. It helps that they have no real responsibilities to each other outside of their jobs. They don't see each other face-to-face; a radio is their only regular form of communication. In the wilderness, there is no one around to judge them, and they can focus on each other and the tasks at hand. It's a deliciously selfish reprieve from "real life"—much like gaming, actually. And yet their tasks become increasingly unnerving as mysterious things start happening, deep in the forest. 

* The music is great, and I enjoy how it only plays on occasion. It's fun listening to the nature sounds. 
* The world is gorgeous, and the way Campo Santo directs players is clever. [i]Firewatch[/i] is a very closed world, but the wilderness environment makes navigation feel oddly natural and open.
* The opening to the game is a nod to text-based adventure games and sets the literary tone.

[u]A "Mature" Game[/u]
[i]Firewatch[/i] is one of only a few games I would call "adult." (I'm inclined to include games like [i]The Talos Principle[/i] in such a list, but they're of a different gameplay style.) By adult, I don't mean the game has swear words, though it does, or innuendo and nudity, though it has those things, too. I mean that nearly all of the characters mentioned are well over the age of 35 and—without spoiling anything—have dealt with Real Adult Sh^t. 

This makes [i]Firewatch[/i] different from similar games like, say, [i]Gone Home[/i] or [i]Life Is Strange[/i], which have young adult, coming of age stories that adults can certainly relate to, but only, to some degree, by looking back on their past. I don't mean to say adventure games or stories that focus on young adults aren't "deep." They can be. I [i]like[/i] some YA fiction. I just mean they're focused on feelings and conflicts specific to adolescence and early adulthood. They are not often about issues found in adulthood, like relationships between individuals with decades of baggage between them, the difficulties of parenthood, or what to do with a loved one who falls ill. But [i]Firewatch[/i] is such a story, which is refreshing. 

* I suspect people who are 25 and older will appreciate this game a lot more than teens and dorm dwellers. This is okay!
* With regard to the ending: [spoiler]Not every story has to be prettily beribboned with a happily-ever-after or even an unhappily-ever-after. Not every story is here to coddle its readers/players.[/spoiler]

[h1]Sacrificing Replayability and Player Freedom to Create Complex Characters[/h1]
There is probably little to no replayability to [i]Firewatch[/i], but I don't count this against it. Not every game must be replayable. Part of what I really like about this game is that it [i]doesn't[/i] go for the bigger story that might allow for replayability. Some will always want that story—no matter how many times it is (awkwardly) fed to us—and will be upset when they don't get it here. But by choosing the narrative path they do, Campo Santo is able to offer much better characterization for those who are interested in it.

Choices do not make much difference in [i]Firewatch[/i], other than to add some (very) limited personality alterations to dialogue exchanges. The fact that the player doesn't get to tinker with the characterization too much is why the characters are good and, above all, [i]sound natural[/i]. The thing about those bigger, replayable games with more open worlds, harder choices, and additional dialogue options is that it is difficult to control characterization in them. Games like [i]The Walking Dead[/i] do an admirable job of it, but you'd be hard-pressed not to laugh when a dialogue tree doesn't quite go as planned or when a character does something completely contrary to the characterization selections you've previously made. By limiting options and foregoing some or all replayability, games like [i]Firewatch[/i] and [i]Dear Esther[/i] are able to delve more deeply into their themes and characters. To some, that will mean [i]Firewatch[/i] isn't really a game or isn't worth what you pay for it. To others, it will seem like a work of art.

[h1]Price[/h1]
[i]Firewatch[/i] takes about four to five hours to play. In other words, each hour of gameplay costs about $5, give or take a little. It's not a bad deal, so it's sad to see people complaining about it. If anyone wants to know why creatives "starve," it's because some people think they should get hours of entertainment for $5-10, max.

To summarize: a tightly delivered narrative experience that knows exactly what it is -- AND knows who you are.

So, details.

If one of the first questions you're asking about this game is 'what is the gameplay like', then you might be recommended to walk away now. There's exceptionally little in the form of true 'gameplay'. I've often said that while video games are their own type of medium, they can also serve as an evolution of other mediums as well, and Firewatch is best described as an evolution of graphic novels, or even ordinary novels. It's a narrative experience and nothing else. If you're going to ask about controls, aiming, or tactics, then this game isn't for you. Different strokes for different folks.

If, on the other hand, you spent a vast majority of the Elder Scrolls or Mass Effect games simply talking to people, enjoying the dialogue and characters, then you might want to keep reading.

I dislike labelling games as 'Walking Simulators', because that term carries a certain level of stigma with it. I'd rather describe it as an 'interactive narrative experience'. The goal of Firewatch is to tell a story, pure and simple. The great achievement of video games that do this - where they surpass their conventional counterparts, like novels - is in their ability to place you within the story itself. It's not some protagonist walking along the creek, it's YOU. Firewatch stands apart from many other narrative games in taking full advantage of the fact that you are invested and integrated with the game and its story. In fact, it depends entirely upon that very concept.

I would recommend this game for anyone, but I would ESPECIALLY recommend it for seasoned gamers. Why? Because the game knows what you expect. It knows that you've played dozens - maybe hundreds - of games before, and have sort of begun to know what to expect, even from games you've never played before. Sort of like how watching a lot of T.V. makes you able to predict plot twists on brand new television shows - not because the show foreshadowed it, but because you understand how people write shows. Firewatch knows that you understand how people write game narratives, and it's ready for you. It USES that to further its own ends. It's breathtaking in its execution. You can't just drop a gamer down in the middle of an idyllic setting and expect that gamer to actually believe everything is as peaceful as it seems, and Firewatch damn well knows that, and uses it ruthlessly to deliver an atmospheric setting and fascinating story.

I paid $14.73 CDN for the game (Steam summer sale) and it took me four-ish hours to beat it. Some might look at that metric and call it poor. I would contend that four hours of edge-of-your-seat quality storytelling is far superior to eighteen hours of filler side-quests to round out an otherwise empty open-world game. Total playtime is one metric to measure a game, but it's far from the only one. For fifteen bucks I got an extremely enjoyable afternoon. Concerts, movies, sports events... they all cost more and last for roughly as long, or shorter.

The story does a good job of keeping you tense and making you care about the characters ('yourself', the protagonist, and the person you communicate with via radio). The only thing that could disappoint you is the ending. The storyline is definitely a mystery, and clear answers are few and far between until the end. It's easy to imagine all kinds of crazy explanations for the mysterious goings-on, your mind taking you to X-Files and beyond, and when you reach the ending and find it to be quite... mundane, you may be disappointed.

So. The story is excellent. The playtime is short but that's no issue. What about the rest?

The graphics, from a sheer technical perspective, aren't amazing, but that's masked very well by a fantastic art style. The music is gorgeous and used sparingly, to great effect. A couple times I was frustrated by invisible walls even where it seemed like I should be able to walk, but not often.

In summary: a great game if you want to sink yourself into a great narrative experience with fanstatic atmosphere that comes ready-made to play with your expectations, with an ending that could be seen as a bit more mundane than you might be hoping for.

Do yourself a favor and try not to listen to the (largely misguided) criticism for this game.  Sure, to each his/her own and all, and that's perfectly valid.  But above all, this is a game that is most certainly worth experiencing, despite whatever apparent setbacks others have brought to light.  It's difficult to try and review/rate an experience, as opposed to simply commenting on gameplay and playtime and graphics and such, but know that's exactly what you're in for with Firewatch.  It's an experience through and through.  And one that I'd highly recommend - so much so that this is my first review ever posted to Steam.  I finshed the game no more than a few hours ago, and can't stop thinking about the narrative and dialogue and visuals and themes and... well, I can't stop thinking about the game.  It's a perfect example of what a story-driven, deeply personal, gorgeous walking simulator can aspire to be.  It may not be a perfect game, but it's certainly one of my favorite in recent memory.  

Pros
- Incredibly believable, authentic voice acting (conversations feel natural; Delilah and Henry feel real)
- Gorgeous art direction and design 
- Visceral, engaging, (at times) hilarious dialogue
- Story (Many seem to disagree, but I feel the story most certainly pays off. perhaps just not in a way most expected)  
- Atmospheric (This game is a testament to the validity of games as art)

Cons
- Upon completion it may leave you feeling empty, yet somehow full, inside, emotionally drained, and intensely pensive
- Could be the only game you want to play ever again
- There's no sequel immediately available

Bottom Line
This is an experience worth playing.  It's short, yes, but in a way that never overstays its welcome.  Rather than focus on time, embrace the incredible experience and play a game relatively unlike anything else available.  Highly recommended.
