An eight-year-old work, with a very short campaign, but still delivers a lot.

Yes, I spent more time in this game than its campaign actually requires. I have the habit of exploring every detail and breaking down to the fullest the works I engage with, and I feel there’s a lot to say about Firewatch, because it’s much more than it first appears to be.

Two key ideas run through our mind throughout the experience: grief and escapism.

Primarily focused on the narrative, Firewatch has some horror elements, but I want to focus on the drama that drives all the events: the protagonist, Henry. He’s not a very educated, handsome, or delicate man, but he was loved for being authentic and sincere.

''You... you're pretty.''

The weight of his emotional pain and his desire to escape it lead him to isolation. We’re talking about a man destroyed by his wife Julia’s degenerative illness and the guilt of not knowing how to handle the situation. Henry, unable to bear the pain, flees to the solitude of the woods, taking an impulsive job. Yet, even in seclusion, he finds that it’s impossible to escape from himself.

Right from the start, we’re directly and impactfully presented with Henry’s memories: “You meet her at a bar.” Julia is brilliant, humorous, and Henry quickly falls in love. Over time, however, their relationship begins to crumble: “Julia starts forgetting things. Little things, at first.” The decline progresses, eventually destroying everything Henry thought was solid. When asked how to handle it, he hesitates: send her to family in Australia or care for her on his own? Neither option seems enough. So, Julia’s family takes her away from him, while he sinks into drinking, rumination, and self-degeneration.

Weakened and emotionally adrift, Henry becomes vulnerable to the forces acting around him. Delilah, his supervisor and sole human connection, is initially charismatic and helpful but gradually reveals herself to be as ambiguous as the mysteries surrounding the forest.

“Hey, is someone out there?” – A mysterious figure seems to stalk him, amplifying his terror and paranoia. Delilah, in turn, appears concerned, but it’s left implied that she knows something but withholds information, carefully choosing what to share, always guiding Henry in a way that seems convenient to her. The stalker watching him from the shadows intensifies his doubts and vulnerabilities, making him more and more a prisoner of his own mind and the environment surrounding him.

It’s in this stage of mystery and uncertainty that Firewatch’s story unfolds.

Well, all this happens in the first two days of the game. Quite a lot to digest, right? Moving on, I’ll try to be a bit more concise.

The plot develops from here. We have a total of 78 days, not all of which are shown to the player, but even so, we can see that some things happen through the excellent dialogues presented during the days we participate in.

We can notice an increasing closeness between Henry and Delilah as they begin to share more about their lives, interacting more intensely. Their relationship starts to become more like that of partners, which further strengthens their bond but also brings to light the growing divergences throughout the plot. They begin to get to know each other more deeply, revealing traits of their personalities and behaviors, establishing a communication that feels organic and natural, making the dialogues more genuine and loaded with tension. This gradual process of closeness leads to a decisive moment: as their relationship grows, so does their unease. Mysteries accumulate, and the puzzles become denser. The forest, in its solitude, seems to harbor more than just nature. The threats of the stalker’s presence and the questions about what is really happening begin to eat away at Henry, who finds himself increasingly trapped between the desire to find answers and the need to escape it all. The mounting tension leads to moments of uncertainty, constantly manifesting without the game needing to use traditional horror elements or appeals. Here, Firewatch uses a subtle atmosphere where the mystery never stops tormenting the player. In every gesture of Henry, in every word from Delilah, there’s some weight, or a doubt lodged.

As the game moves into its final stages, the closeness between Henry and Delilah evolves. What seemed like a professional and distant relationship begins to transform into something more personal, almost intimate. But this also brings insecurity, with suspicions and some inconsistencies in Delilah’s speech taking over. The stalker, always present in the shadows, seems to feed off the tension between them, adding more layers of confusion and uncertainty. And while all this happens, the forest, with its almost deafening silence, becomes more of a metaphor for Henry’s mind: a maze he doesn’t quite know how to navigate. As the secrets begin to unfold, the story gains new layers. Henry, immersed in his own emotions and solitude, starts uncovering more of what’s behind the events around him. However, things are not easy to decipher. Every clue he finds seems to generate more doubts, as if the truth were a puzzle piece that never quite fits. And in the end, we have the resolution of the mystery and the conclusion of Henry’s journey, which seems to reach its end without him fully understanding what happened. But in Firewatch, the answer isn’t simple, and there is no great revelation of something monumental. It all turns out to be just a local tragedy, people tormented by a past they couldn’t leave behind, just like the stalker, who turned out to be a figure from Delilah’s life, as everything pointed to. The true resolution comes through acceptance. Henry finally confronts his own demons and, in some way, understands that escape is not the answer. He realizes that to find peace, perhaps one must face the pain and grief, not as something to avoid but as something that is part of who he is.

Note: I didn’t do all the possible endings, I don’t know how much things change depending on the decisions you make, but I decided that Henry should return to his wife and face his past, his own reality to be overcome, leaving that forest behind.

Other than that, what else can I add here? I would like to emphasize that the characters are charismatic, have very natural interactions, and this makes you sympathize with them and easily feel their struggles. This helps a lot in guiding the narrative, as good characters contribute to a more engaging plot, not to mention the atmosphere, the sounds of the environment, which have a tangible presence and greatly help in building a reflection of the emotional state of the characters, which is loneliness, isolation. Even the beautiful landscapes, the warm colors of the sunset, and the vibrant tones of some parts of the forest carry a certain melancholy that aligns with the inner suffering of both characters, especially Henry.

And this is my reading of this work. I hope you enjoyed it, until next time.

Firewatch is a beautiful, story-driven adventure with an amazing atmosphere and surprisingly deep characters. The voice acting and dialogue are the highlights, and exploring the wilderness while slowly uncovering the story feels really immersive. It’s not a game focused on action, but if you enjoy short, emotional stories with great writing and mystery, Firewatch is definitely worth playing. **8.5/10**

A lot of reviewers complain about the ending and about the length of the game.

Both of those issues are fair and valid. The game is extremely short, the ending is just disappointing. Despite a very interesting start, good voice acting and great visuals you will be left feeling that you have just wasted your time by the time you finish it, since no of your actions matter at all and the ending is very bland and non-engaging. The closer you get to the end the more disappointed you will be.

TLDR - do not waste time and money on this game, game is a walking simulator and none of your actions matter.

If you want to try to enjoy the story - watch someones "lets play" on youtube, would probably be more entertaing.

It's disappointing that, even as Generation X moves steadily into middle age, the games designed to appeal to the First Video Game Generation are still saddled with the campy, melodramatic conventions of comic books, B movies, and television.

Other than Kentucky Route Zero, Portal and possibly Dear Esther, there isn't much to recommend in the interactive experience category if one is a well-read, well-watched adult with little ingrained patience for complex control schemes and video gamey tropes.

I was really getting into Firewatch. There was some interesting meat there. Two strangers, separated by space, getting to know each other over the radio, possibly the subject of an unethical study, lonely, rough backstories full of mistakes and regret, good characterization, decent voice acting...

And then suddenly there was all this pseudo-thriller drammuh - property destruction, violence, missing teenage girls, a dead kid, a survivalist loner, and a bunch of strained emotive voice acting that sounded like two people trying desperately to overcome constipation.

Why is it that video game audiences demand Big, Dumb Thrill Rides? Firewatch could have been a really interesting, branching, gorgeous love story. Instead, it had to hang on to a rickety scaffold of Dramatic Conflict to sell itself to the perpetually bored, adrenaline junkie crowd and the games reviewers who pander to them.

I found the "thrilling" aspects of Firewatch to be a distracting annoyance from the gorgeous scenery and budding friendship of Henry and Delilah. The title's insistence on inventing stuff for the player to DO, spoiled character building and a setting that should have been allowed to just BE.

In the end, I was just pushing through the actiony, fetchy, double backy bits of the experience in the vain hope that there might be some kind of emotional payoff for the two main characters. There was, kinda.

I'm really don't mean to dog on Firewatch. I asks a fair price for a very polished few hours of time. It pushes the art of the possible further into adult territory for interactive experiences. It's the fact that it comes so close to greatness that makes it a bitter disappointment for those searching for something that isn't shootybang idiocy.

Well, to make a long story short, I enjoyed this game.  I would definitely reccomend it, if only as a view into one of the best examples of storytelling in video games to date.  But, like many other people, I have a few problems.

In many ways, this game lived up to my expectations, but not all of them.  It was gorgeous, with a well-written story and fully realized environment.  I, for one, never expected it to be open world, and it wasn't.  That wasn't a problem for me.  What was a problem for me, however, was that the game seemed a little empty.  At the end, I felt like there was something missing.  Some sort of closure I didn't get.  But, I think that was supposed to be the intention all along.  This game is probably one of the more realistic ones, in terms of story, and for that reason, the ending is similarly realistic.

Now, this isn't to say that I disliked the time I spent with the game.  I most certainly enjoyed my five-ish hours with it.  I wish there was an option where, at the end of the game, I could explore the park at my leisure, but there is not.  Regardless, I'm excited to see what else Campo Santo will do in the future, and while Firewatch may not have been everything I hoped it to be, I do not feel like I wasted money on it.  This is one of the few games I could see myself playing again.

I highly suggest this game and would strongly encourage anyone and everyone to give it a chance. 10/10

I was really looking forward for Firewatch. The trailers they released made me so very hyped for the game. The game looked amazing, the characters looked full of personality, and the story sounded very interesting. A day before the game was released, many websites released their reviews for the game. The reviews were all praising the game for being amazing so, I took their word and took the plunge to buy the game.

I started the game and instantly I saw the slick menu. The options menu is lacking of a FOV slider but I didn't really get too bothered by this but, I know some people who will get bothered with this. I launched the game and it started off with a very well written backstory. Even though this was only about ~10 min long, I really got intrigued to continue  with the story. 

After the starting is over, you start the main part of the game you meet a girl named Delilah. She talks with you through a walkie-talkie. She's a really big part of the story. Hearing the main character, Henry, talk to Delilah is probably one of the best part of the game. The connection they have and the conversations are really fun to hear.

You're probably wondering why I gave this game a "No" after writing all these nice things. Despite all of this, the gameplay is piss poor. The whole game is very linear, you can't take other paths to get to each objective. Places that look like you can go are either blocked by rocks or invisible walls. This whole game is beautiful and all I want to do is explore the forest and take paths my way. I think this game would be better if this could be done. I also find the speed you walk/jog quite slow. 

[b] TL;DR [/b]
Firewatch has a beautiful story, visuals, and very live characters. All of this is hindered due to the fact that the gameplay is just a slow paced and linear walking sim.

[h1] Firewatch [/h1]

Independent developer Campo Santo's first game, Firewatch, tells the story of Henry, who wants to escape from the difficulties in his private life and keep his head for a while. Working as a wildfire watcher in Wyoming's mountainous and wooded area, where Yellowstone National Park is located, Henry's only contact is Delilah, on the other end of the radio. This game, in which the story of two people who do not know each other but who are connected to each other via walkie-talkies in solitude on the mountain will be the main actor, is also embellished with a mystery in the region. Promising a gameplay between Telltale games and Gone Home, let's see if Firewatch has met the expectations.

First of all, it is useful to open up the story and characters a little without spoilers. While entering the game, we experience Henry's meeting with his wife, falling in love, getting married, thinking about having a child, and finally getting sick of his wife by just reading the writings and making a selection with a very beautiful sequence. This marginal story sequence, which is divided by sections of Henry's trip to the desolate nature and his walk to the watchtower, offers a pleasant and powerful experience with a quick return to the elections and reminiscent of 80s text adventures. Thanks to this experience, we can immediately identify and connect with Henry. At times, while the contradictions and stress about his wife, who cannot recognize himself and can no longer take care of him, confuse his mind, Henry seeks the solution. The only person he communicates with in this process is his boss, Delilah. Delilah is as playful as he is mysterious, and in fact a deep character, and indeed, the lead role in the game is the relationship between these two.

There are many choices we can make in the game, but these choices do not affect the end of the game. Instead, it affects our conversations with Delilah, which could be a reason to play the game again. As I said, the main actor in the play is the relationship of this duo and when we make one choice in the conversation, we don't have the chance to make the other. We can also report the sights we see around or what we find to Delilah. However, we have a chance not to report them. So when we play again, the conversation goes on a completely different side. With these, we have the opportunity to deepen and differentiate this relationship by visiting many regions that we do not have to travel to and talking about that region and what we found there. The decisions we make in Firewatch, which we can describe as an "interaction experience", also affect Delilah's reactions to Henry or some common concerns in later chapters. At this point, we should congratulate Campo Santo who managed to present the same story with different experiences.

One of Firewatch's strengths is its visuality, which sometimes resembles a watercolor painting. The fact that they prefer an artistic and even fairy-tale visual instead of a photorealistic visual coincides with the theme of the game. Although it looks like a mystery game, Firewatch is definitely not a mystery game. The mystery in the game is always secondary. It acts as a tool for interaction and character development. This play is about a man's contradictions, escapism, and a woman he unexpectedly finds and connects to in an unexpected place. It can be said to be a literal human drama. Throughout the game, which will vary from 3.5 hours to 5 hours depending on how much you travel and your speed, the most memorable moments that bring different emotions to the top are always the moments of talking with Delilah. For this reason, instead of focusing on the detective direction with realistic images and throwing the characters into the background, they have managed to display a sad and sweet section of the days when the lives of the two characters intersect with artistic visuals. The atmosphere of Firewatch manages to reinforce its emotional and human story with the sounds of the forest, magnificent character voices and beautiful and peaceful music that supports the stage instead of coming to the fore.

Except for the dialogues and our choices at this point, gameplay is entirely based on exploration. We find our way around the map with climbing sequences that do not require skill. In the game, where we can open short paths by tying ropes to the rocks and hanging down, our progress process is based on acquiring items to overcome the obstacles that we cannot overcome. Of course, sometimes it is not enough to investigate in detail and the story needs to move forward. An interesting point about climbing mechanics is that while climbing rocks is automatic, hanging down from rocks with rope is manual. Usually, in such exploration and story-driven games, manual actions are done to increase the interaction with the character and the atmosphere, but here the fact that one of the two similar exploration actions is manual and the other automatic has distorted that feeling. So much so that one of the most important gameplay elements in the game is that unlike automatic climbing, the manual system hits our face.

The most common thing we use when traveling in hills, canyon, river, lake and forest is a map and compass. We are trying to find our way by opening the paper map in our hands. For the sake of convenience on the map, our carcass is marked as if there is a GPS, but the direction it is facing is not shown. We can attribute this to the character's understanding of where he is when he looks around. We understand the direction we are looking at and of course the direction we will go by looking at the compass. Also, the roads are not marked on the map. There are some food chests in the vicinity so that the village guards can be left with materials and communication between them, and there are details of the surrounding map on their covers. When we find these maps, Henry puts marks on his map, and when we look at the map again, we see hand-drawn paths on this physical map. This strengthens the atmosphere and allows us to progress in the game as a gameplay element.

Finally, it is necessary to mention the end of the game. The end of the game split the audiences in two, and the general criticism is that the story did not prepare step by step and then satisfy expectations. While this view is understandable, I disagree because Firewatch is a completely depressive game of human emotions and relationships. Although it makes you smile with a surprising bond that emerged during this process, Henry's experiences, the mystery element in the game, the nature of the story, and Delilah's own contradictions also proceed on the same theme. That's why I think this ending of Firewatch, which is not a mystery game, but a humanitarian interaction and drama game, fits the game completely. Frankly, the end of the game met my expectations.

Firewatch is one of the most successful "experience" games of recent times, a human drama that everyone can find a piece of themselves, and perhaps even not want to. With realistic and deep characters, incredibly natural and successful voices and wonderfully written dialogues, a fabulous conversation that you will want to never end is waiting for you. Campo Santo did such a job that Henry's escape turned into an actor's escape. The real crumbs sprinkled between the pleasant conversations with Delilah and the inability of both Henry and Delilah to escape the truth throughout the story succeeds in keeping the actor constantly on the toes and connected to the facts. In fact, the mystery element in the game can be interpreted as an unconscious escape effort of the characters. These round trips between escape and reality allow us to experience a special blend of emotions. For gamers who are not afraid of emotional experiences and enjoy interactive stories, Firewatch makes a powerful entry into the modern classics. If you like these games, try Firewatch. Have fun!

[h1]❓ What is this[/h1]
Firewatch (2016) is a first-person narrative adventure developed by Campo Santo and published by Panic. It’s a story-driven experience set in the Wyoming wilderness, blending exploration, mystery, and emotional dialogue.

[h1]❔ How I played[/h1]
Completed the story in around 5 hours. Focused on dialogue choices and explored side paths to uncover environmental details and notes. Played on an RTX 4060 with Ryzen 5 5500, where performance was generally smooth but I noticed occasional input lag during movement and camera control.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]🕹️ Gameplay[/h1]
Gameplay revolves around walking, climbing, and interacting with objects, but its real strength lies in the radio dialogue system. Every choice shapes Henry’s relationship with Delilah, making conversations feel alive and natural. The intrigue builds through mysterious occurrences in the forest, giving a sense of paranoia and suspense. Still, the limited mechanics can feel shallow, and technical hiccups like input lag occasionally break immersion.

✅ Pros:
+ Strong, branching dialogue choices that feel human and authentic
+ Immersive exploration with a strong sense of place
+ Gradual mystery that creates tension and unease
+ Smooth controls and clean interface

❌ Cons:
- Minimal interactivity outside of dialogue and exploration
- The buildup of suspense is stronger than its resolution
- Minor issues even on modern hardware

[hr][/hr]
[h1]📖 Story[/h1]
The story explores loneliness, escapism, human vulnerability, and trust. Henry is running from personal struggles, while Delilah uses humor and distance to hide her own. Their relationship, formed entirely through radio conversations, is believable and emotionally layered.

The central intrigue-a sense that something sinister is happening in the forest-keeps tension high but ultimately ends on a grounded, almost anticlimactic note. Personally, the main story felt intriguing but not fully polished, as if the ending was finished in a rush. The emotional weight remains strong, but the lack of refinement leaves a bittersweet impression.

[h1]🎨 Visuals & Sound[/h1]
The painterly art style creates a stunning vision of American national parks-golden sunsets, thick forests, and vast horizons. It captures the feeling of solitude in nature while keeping a warm, stylized look.

The soundtrack by Chris Remo is subtle and atmospheric, leaning on acoustic tones and ambient soundscapes. It’s not bombastic, but it perfectly complements the mood of both calm exploration and quiet unease.

[h1]⚙️ Performance & Replayability[/h1]
Runs well overall on modern systems, but occasional input lag can be noticeable. Replay value comes mainly from experimenting with dialogue paths, though the core story beats remain the same.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]💡 Verdict[/h1]
For me, Firewatch stands out as one of those rare indie games that really nails the feeling of isolation, connection, and mystery. The story pulled me in, even if the ending felt a bit rough and unfinished. Still, the time I spent with Henry and Delilah had weight, and exploring those quiet forests with the soundtrack in the background left a lasting impression.

So let's talk about it. If you're debating whether to get the game or not, you have decide on what is most important to you:

However, if the price doesn't bother you too much, if you're not too keen on ultra-high-tech graphics and textures, if you're prone to getting drawn into a very strong narrative, I'd say pick it up during a sale. Pricepoints should never be a deciding factor on the merit of a game. While it can be used to drive away potential customers (that's entirely on the publishers), reviewers should be critiquing the content of the game and not how much the game itself cost. That's where most of the negative reviews come from. 

The game defines the walking/hiking simulator genre. It's daunting to think that you're in the middle of the vast Wyoming forests and yet there isn't an animal in sight. You seldom every see another living human being. The only saving grace in this vast wilderness is your female companion, Delilah and you're not even sure if she's real. 

It says volumes about gaming nowadays where multiplayer is such a norm and you need interactive interactions every living, breathing moment and yet, Firewatch is able to reduce all of that into nothing but simple textures, beautiful lighting and beautifully crafted banter and dialogue. Now, I don't plan on playing the game again so I wouldn't be able to tell you if the choices you make throughout the game have any effect on the outcomes but what I can tell you is that the responses you get to them feel.. real in a way. It's as if the dialogue was taken from a real-life conversation rather than a scripted one made to make you feel a certain way. It's as if the developers got the voice actors, said "GO!" and they just did their thing. 

It's not all great though. The game does have a few flaws. Not mentioning the price-point, there are some spots in the game where the game and dialogue jitters. It's as if it was loading in the background and couldn't make it in time. That really took away from the immersion. Another thing is the fact that you're in the vast wilderness, and yet there's not a single animal or living being? It's a bit odd and unrealistic to have that sort of expectation or that you'd be so lucky. Although, I can forgive that because the game is isolative in nature so I can understand the dev's making that decision. It's also rather sucky that you can't access any of the contents in your pack. When given the option to fish, I put away my fishing rod thinking I'd be able to bring it back. Nope. No way to access your items. 

This last gripe is a more personal one and might contain the tiniest spoilers. I don't know why the developers decided that they needed to make a shock-value twist in the middle of the story. Why do narratives need to do this? Why does every narrative need a villain? Someone to collectively hate on? It came so out of left field I had a hard time following what the hell was going on. Because of this, the ending seemed... unwrapped? Rushed? Out of place? A bit of a non sequitur? I don't know. I was really hoping to hash things out with Delilah towards the end, sort of get some closure but because of the "twist," everything fell apart. It's like everyone wants to be J. K. Rowling but also wants to be M. Knight Shyamalan. Just.. stop. There's no need. Keep to the original narrative. You're not getting any extra points with the players by shocking us. 

In all, it was a fantastic game with some flaws here and there. Would I refund it if I had the chance? Sure. But I'm happy to say that this is the first game I've perfected and I have absolutely no shame in it.

I'll try to make it short, since I really doubt that anyone will even read my ramblings here.

So first of all, no, I was not following Devs during the development process, neither was I sitting on the edge of my chair in the anticipation of the release. I just noticed that there's a new game on Steam, and I kind of liked the overall synopsis.
Plus, in my region it's only 420 RUB (which is roughly $5), so yeah, I just grabbed it, because why not.

Normally I would not go to Steam forums or read reviews or google the heck out of the game if I am not closely following it. So I just hooked up my controller, launched the game, and crashed on my couch with my headphones.
And tell ya what - it was a great experience playing this little game.

Maybe it is because I was not watching every single teaser, or reading each and every press-release out there - I was not overly demanding at the start. And therefore, for me, it was a struggle of a middle aged man whose rather stable life of habit was just torn from the foundation and sent flying in the nothingness. And, in a way, for me this trip to Wyoming wilderness was exactly what it was for Henry (the protagonist) - a getaway.

Aesthetically, it was a threat. Heck, I even got up from the couch a few times to take some screenshots! Soundtrack was really great (I made sure I have a copy of it). And yes, the voice acting is tremendously great.

As for the gameplay - I honestly can't say that it is bad. I mean, it is basically a novel. You know, saying that gameplay here was mundane, or that it's a simple walking simulator - it's just like saying the The Wolf Among Us was a clicker game. [b]It is a story. Your interaction with it - is merely a mean of advancing it, much like turning the pages in a book. You don't want to solve some finobacchi-sequence puzzle each time you turn the page reading a book, do you?[/b]

And as for the plot - [spoiler]I would say it was quite solid. Because no. This is NOT a detective story (unlike TWAU) it is a story of a man, who spent a good part of his grown-up life with a woman, derailed from the tracks and left shattered. It is a story of him getting away (from the old way of life, from the responsibility, from the pressure). No wonder he bonds with a stranger on the other end of the radio - primarily because Delilah is running as well. But to think that their relationship is what this game is about - is just wrong. In the end, for Henry it was a three months breather. And he has to return to his old life in the end. And this is precisely what you get in the end. For better or worse.[/spoiler]

Can I recommend it though? If you are looking for Shyamalan/Nolan-esque kind of a twist riddled mystery with over 20 hours of gameplay and four possible endings - No. You will be disappointed.
If you have few hours you are willing to spend following a story of loss, guilt, responsibility and other grown-up stuff,  cast among fascinating landscapes, accompanied by a stellar soundtrack, and incredibly good voice acting - Yep, go for it.

If you feel like discussing something above, or asking some questions - go for it and comment.

TLDR version - frustratingly linear non-explore-'em-up.

I'm not really sure why Firewatch rushed to the top of the Steam charts upon release. Maybe everyone was thinking the same as me - this looks different, fun and pretty.

Well, it turns out the game isn't really much different, and the "fun" is quite limited. Firewatch is one of those "experience" games, so maybe I was playing it wrong in expecting there to be more. Perhaps I was supposed to be entranced by the prettiness, and the by the whole idea of being isolated in a remote tower.

I would have loved to start a collection of the things I found, but whilst there are things to find there is no collecting to be done. I was looking forward to exploring the wilderness, but more or less everything was on rails. There isn't even a jump button, and no way to step over even small obstacles unless there is a button prompt allowing you to do so.

The single level contains multiple locations connected by what are effectively corridors, steering the various gameplay tasks in a frustratingly familiar way. Various mechanisms (such as obtaining an axe) allow deeper exploration, but others (such as the torch) seem entirely superfluous.

The game seems to believe it is a work of literature. The story and setting are both quite original for a game, but that only served to remind me why most games are the way they are. The conceptual realism contained within the design was central to the whole idea, and because of that the two main characters are nicely rounded and quite human. But don't we already know what human beings are? Don't we have plenty of media to present that idea to us?

Games should be about what we as players do, giving us choices and changing the outcome.

There are interface problems too. Responding to Delilah on the radio is a timed event, so if you are using the map, or tardy in any way you will lose the chance to respond. But having watched others play I couldn't see any branching caused by dialogue responses. I think everyone is going to get pretty much the same experience.

I found the walk/run toggle to be a bit glitchy. I was using an Xbox 360 pad, and I frequently felt as though I was running through mud. Watching someone play it with M&K they seemed to be getting about a lot faster.

I picked up a whole bunch of notes and letters, but was never able to read them later because the list in the menu would not scroll (again, a controller issue?)

If Firewatch is available in a sale then you might enjoy a couple of hours wandering about in the woods, but if you like a challenge or you enjoy exploring in an open world I'd steer clear even at a knock down price.

Well, where do I start? First of all, the game is about 3 1/2 hours long. Maybe a little longer if you take your time and read every little piece of text you find throughout the game. Also Firewatch isn't a game in the classic sense. I think people might fall into trap to think this is some kind of survival game. You can't die, you won't gather resources and you won't build stuff.

This is more like an interactive experience. And by far the most important part of said experience is the conversation between you, the protagonist, and Delilah, your only real contact to the outside world. Through this conversation you will learn about both of their backstories and thanks to the amazing voice acting you'll most likely enjoy the chemistry between both of them.

The rest of the game is more or less a hiking simulator. That isn't a bad thing though. I found it to be deeply satisfying to wander through the beautifuly crafted world, accompanied by the many dialogue options you'll have when talking to Delilah on the radio. 

The story that ties everything together mostly kept me on the edge of my seat and therefore I found it very easy to finish the whole game in one sitting. Be warned though, even though the game's setting is certainly atmospheric and creepy, this is not a horror game. If walking through the woods alone, being paranoid about noises, is enough to grind your gears, then this will suffice to you.

Overall this is a very well crafted, albeit short, interactive experience with especially great voice acting. The price at about $20 is a bit steep but justifiable. If you're open to alternative storytelling and aren't appalled by the idea of hiking through the woods, this might be for you.

While there were some parts of the game I did not like, I can't not recommend Firewatch.

Before I start, let me just say that if you want any semblance of gameplay outside of the story, go to the options and turn off the tracker on the map. With that off, the game actually does have a challenge in the form of orienteering your character based on landmarks and directions.

When the closest a game comes to a challenge is finding your way to a place where the plot can develop, you know you're playing a walking simulator. But let me say that, for the most part, the rest of the game more than makes up for it.

[b] The Good [/b]

In the game, you play as Henry, a 40-something man who takes a Firewatch job in a national park for the summer to clear his mind after [spoiler] his wife has to live with her family after he's considered unfit to take care of her after she gets dementia [/spoiler]. After making some choices as to some specifics of Henry's past, the player controls him from here on out. The story does a good job of getting across the themes of escape and isolation.

Henry and Delilah are great characters. Their voice actors did incredible work getting the traits across in voice alone, and the dialogue was so well-written that they feel like real people. When Delilah, a character that you never see, has more depth and personality than most main characters in big-name titles (let alone [i] female [/i] main characters), you know a lot of effort was put into making the dialogue between her and Henry believable. And while the player does have a choice in what Henry can say, the choices, along with his delivery, still give him a distinct and consistent personality. No dialogue option feels out of place. The [spoiler] implied relationship Henry and Delilah can develop [/spoiler] feels real despite it being entirely over a radio. You would just be doing yourself a disservice if you decide to stay quiet most of the time, as many dialogue options branch out. The game leaves room for some replayability if you want to hear alternate conversations. Not much replayability in other aspects, but I'll get to that. 

One particularly memorable experience in the game for me was when [spoiler] Henry starts to have a breakdown, thinking he also developed dementia, and that everything from Day 1, including the conspiracy to spy on him and Delilah, is just some elaborate punishment he made in his own head for abandoning his wife because of her illness. Listening to Delilah trying her best to calm him down was one of the most touching moments I've heard in a game, and almost made me tear up. [/spoiler]

Also, the game looks gorgeous. The stylized forest is beautiful, and seeing the varied environment at all times of day just enhances the hiking experience. I was able to recreate most of the screenshots you see on the store page. I know some people didn't like the acoustic guitar that comes out of nowhere at times while you're walking, but I'm a sucker for ambient music, so I liked it. If you let yourself get lost in the game (metaphorically and literally), it feels like an experience.

[b] The Bad [/b]

Aside from the orienteering, there's not much in the way of gameplay. Most of what you do is go to a place and interact with something. This game is firmly a walking simulator, and anyone even slightly outside of the circle of people that enjoy that genre is going to get bored fast. 

Since the gameplay is more of a framework to hang the dialogue and story on, the game has to really bring it when it comes to those two things. And for most of the game, it does. Henry and Delilah's relationship gets developed on a steady pace, there's a lot of things to see and have them talk about, and there's an air of tension over the first few days. And what's essentially a montage in the middle of the game gets across the passing of time over a few months. And let me just say, for me, the game provides one of the biggest letdowns I've ever experienced in a game's story.

On the tail end of the summer, they discover [spoiler] some conspiracy to spy on them when Henry finds a clipboard containing highlights of their radio conversations. The last few days bring the tension right back up when the two of them try to figure out what's going on with the very small amount of information they have.

Do not get your hopes up that the big conspiracy has any kind of substantial payoff, because it doesn't. It essentially amounts to a facade of conspiracy that gets taken away in the form of a minute-long tape that you listen to while you get to the conspirator's hideout. One major hint at the conspiracy (a fenced off area with a research station in it) turns out to be something mundane, and should be common knowledge to a person in Delilah's position, but isn't for seemingly no reason other than to add to the mystique.

The relationship gets no payoff, either, since the two never meet, and essentially go their separate ways regardless. The circumstances also mean that both of them sound so down at the end of it all. I can see what the game's going for: trying to escape your life to find some new excitement only results in something equally sad or mundane in a different way. But I wish the game didn't reveal its key theme at the very end. Maybe a series of connected mysteries with mundane solutions over the course of the game would have worked instead of this. [/spoiler]

All I can say is that how the story is resolved seems both rushed and disappointing.

[b] Summary [/b]

If you're interested in beautiful stylized scenery, great dialogue, as well as a game centered around the interaction between two characters with great chemistry over the summer, then you'll love Firewatch. If, however, you want involved and action-filled gameplay, or the dramatic tension and conspiracy is all that drew you in to the game, don't get it. Firewatch feels very human and has well written dialogue and is, overall a good experience. But it should be bought [i] just [/i] for that experience, and not for the complexity it alludes to.
An adult game that deals with serious adult issues. It is among the very best of the first-person narrative genre, and it reminds us what video game storytelling is capable of in the right hands.

Firewatch is a narrative driven game that put you into the shoes of a newly hired fire lookout in a Wyoming state park.  A brief prologue before the events of Firewatch kick off sets the backstory of our main protagonist Henry and his motivations for taking this job out in the middle of nowhere.  Once the game starts, you are let loose into the wilderness and your journey really begins.

The initial reaction I had when receiving my map of the wilderness was how big the world was, but it became apparent after the first couple of days that the world is far more linear than it seems at the outset.  However, the world never felt small and was structured in such a way to keep the story moving at a fair pace and to avoid confusing the player with a large world that would otherwise serve no purpose to the narrative.  Eventually, you'll begin to recognize paths and trails but when the game sends you to someplace new, you'll likely need to make good use of your map and compass to navigate.  The actions and tasks I was assigned with never felt repetitive and while it does make you pass previously explored areas, you're often sent to a new area that you likely haven't explored yet.

The main hook of this game is the narrative and it is convey almost entirely through a two-way radio you get soon after you arrive at your watch tower.  Your boss, Delilah, speaks to you through it at key points and initiates a dialogue that you can choose responses to.  Outside of the scripted dialogue, there are tons of opportunities for you to initiate them just by exploring and examining things.  I've only played through once, but it's clear your responses have an effect on shaping the developing story.  The story obviously being the main purpose of this game, is not only very well written, it's voice actors are also perfect for the roles.

The story is very carefully crafted and well written.  It has a lot of different emotions that it dips into with seemingly effortless command and it works very well to create the changing atmosphere as the game progresses.  One day it can be lighthearted banter and simple 'getting to know you' type dialogue, to serious and more depressing chats, to seriously creepy and distributing dialogue.  At one point, I was legitimately feeling scared being out in the dark wilderness by myself, constantly looking over my shoulder.  This game focuses directly on the narrative and doesn't try to be anything more than that.  It effortlessly pulls you into its world and its two characters while continuously pushing you forward to not only discover whats coming next, but to get a chance to further your relationship with Delilah.

The game world itself is a beautiful piece of work and its attention to the detail of the world itself as well as its keen eye for atmosphere and color really sets the perfect backdrop for the narrative to unfold.  This is also where my only real complaint comes in, and it's more of a technical one than anything else.  For some reason, the frame-rate jumps around while out exploring and sometimes while standing still.  I don't know if it's streaming in data or has other background functions that are causing the drop, but it just seemed random with no real correlation with what was happening on screen.  It happened often enough that I was slightly annoyed towards the end but it ultimately wasn't a deal breaker.  Still, it would be nice if such an issue could be fixed because it can pull you out of the experience momentarily.

I've seen a lot of polarizing views on this games ending and while I won't spoil anything, I feel that both views are valid.  I would say that this game is more about the journey than it is the destination but to some, that's not acceptable and that's fair.  Narrative games like this take a risk because while it's a great story, it has to end and the writers have a very specific ending in mind.  That ending may be wildly off base with any given players expectation of how they feel it should end.  While I feel the ending was the logical conclusion to the story, that won't be the same sentiments from everyone who plays.  What I think is the real treat here is examining the story after the credits roll.  Much like similar narrative based games, there is a deeper narrative than what one would think if just taken at face value.  When you really start to examine the dialogue, the timing of it, and the events that unfold, it opens various avenues that just beg for a replay to truly discover what is happening.  However, it should be noted that this game and the subjects it deals with lend itself to many various interpretations and I think that's the hallmark of a great story.  Some may see a story with a deeper mystery that needs deeper examination while others may see a story dealing with grief and depression.  It's because of this that I believe the ending can be polarizing because depending on what your personal experience with the story is, your expectations of the ending will vary.  If this is at all concerning to you, then waiting for a sale might be the way to go.

The technical issues with frame-rate aside, I think this game is a great piece of work.  It's short, sweet, and a must buy for anyone interested in narrative based/driven games.  It's choice driven narrative and underlying mysteries offers enough to net some replay value and I can see myself coming back to this game from time to time, just to enjoy the story again.

It had a lot of good moments especially in the first half, and set up a strong immersive mood and interesting narrative mechanics that I was excited about. But then it developed a red herring story that uses up the rest of the runtime of the game. It was so close to being good, but they focused on side characters that don't matter and don't connect to the main characters. The voice acting is wonderful, and along with the visuals, carries the game. The dialog writing is odd, the way they speak is 2010s not 1970s, but I accepted it. The narrative is awful: the big reveal is disappointing, then the main relationship ends abruptly. It feels like a movie that ran out of budget and couldn't film a real ending. Looking back on the plot now that I know the mystery's big reveal, a lot of events in the game don't make plausible sense. Like other weak mystery stories, the buildup is great but then the reveal ruins it and make you feel you wasted your time.

Dementia is a key part of the narrative, and the writers have put zero work into learning about it. They have a heartless view of the difficulty and complexity of being a caretaker for someone with that illness. The writers are trying to tell a story about the futility of running from your problems, but ironically they don't engage with what it would actually be like to be in the main character's situation. In the end, they moralize about him needing to go home and face it. But he already has faced it, and there isn't necessarily anything further to do besides process his grief. They similarly use the "crazy PTSD veteran" trope in a shallow and unconvincing way. It's just bad writing.

I had been making dialog choices assuming my choices would matter somehow, but your picks only affect the immediate responses you get. There were a handful of things that seemed like clues to reward players who thoroughly explored the world, but they were just flavor and didn't expand the story, it feels like a waste of time to have called in every item.

Also as a walking simulator, the walking is glitchy. You often get stuck on things, and at one point whenever I tried to interact with objects like the yellow cache boxes or the gate, it made me sprint backwards(?) instead of interacting. The only reason this wasn't a game breaking bug was that I found that mashing R2 would interact and break the backwards sprint. Also if you have vsync disabled, walking breaks entirely!

Firewatch is a wonderful experience.  I'm not quite sure how to classify it, though. It's a bit of a walking simulator, adventure, and suspense game, with some humor thrown in there.  You play as Henry, who is working as a lookout for wilderness fires over a summer season.  His only human contact is via walkie-talkie, to his boss.  Henry is trying to escape his life's difficulties, which I'm sure many of us can empathize with. The graphics are charming for a 9 year old game, the voice acting is excellent, and the near-solitary immersion is very well done.   You go through a lot of emotions playing the game as you work through some background plot stories.

The controls are simple and easy to understand/use, since you don't have to worry about things like entering an inventory to use items, etc. This lets you focus on the environment and the tasks at hand, which are also not overly complex.  This is a good game to play when you just want to appreciate the environment and plot without too much other complexities interfering.  The soundtrack also helps to set the mood and is great to listen to.

If I had any criticism with this game, it has to do with the ending.  No spoilers, but since I was emotionally tied to the game by the time I reached the ending, I personally found it to be a bit anti-climactic.  That said, while I subjectively didn't love the ending, I do understand why the developers chose to end the game the way they did.  Their ending has its own meaning which I can appreciate, despite it seeming superficially anti-climactic.  For information's sake, your choices throughout the game are somewhat limited and ultimately don't change the outcome or path of the plot.  That said, this is not marketed as a "choices matter" game, so that did not bother me, but it seemed to annoy some previous players.

If this game is on sale, it's a no-brainer.  Buy it.

The story itself features some of the best voice acting in games altogether in my opinion. The soundtrack is beautiful, and extremely atmospheric. The sound design is brilliant and fits the theme perfectly.

One of the prettiest games available, based off a concept by Olly Moss, a well-known artist. The scenery and setting is beautifully created, and is extremely engaging and immersive to explore.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The most criticised piece of the game, but I cannot agree with the people saying they are disappointed. If you don’t rush the game, and enjoy engaging novels this is still a brilliant game. The voice acting and depth of narrative well makes up for the ending, which i still believe is great.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Extremely good game with some of the best visuals and sound design available. If you are into game design, or just love action or crime novels definitely give it a go. Look at the Campo Santo YouTube for more information on the brilliant devs, and also check out their GDC talks which are also amazingly in depth.

Firewatch is an aesthetically pleasing game, with good voice acting and dialogue to boot. However, its hampered by a vague plot and an underwhelming ending that is filled with a lot of monotonous walking which takes place in an environment where very little happens. 

The game starts off with a lengthy exposition where you get to decide some of the back-end story of the protagonist, Henry. This is only serves to provide additional dialogue options further on in the game which really don’t have any bearing on the game. Once you start out, you will be initially impressed by the beautifully designed landscape. The first day on watch you are indirectly taught how to use your compass, or rappel down slopes, and so on. You use your radio to talk with the only other person you can, Delilah. The conversations can be as amusing as you like, and add something to do on the walks. There aren’t any other gameplay mechanics to the game. Firewatch would have greatly benefited from adding 1 or 2 game mechanics to help fill the boring treks back and forth between places. Even as a 'walking' simulator it can get frustrating. Navigation is unintuitive and forces you to pull out a map and look at your compass. An optional HUD compass would have been a great addition to help ease navigation and reduce wasted time back tracking. Additionally, it seems counter-intuitive for a walking simulator to have a lot of invisible walls while in a forest. I appreciated that they include some side areas to explore, and you were rewarded with tapes and other interesting items, but they felt more like dead ends. During your walks you will also come across Firewatch caches which contain extra details of the area that the protagonist will add to his map. The locks on these caches are all the same, 1234, which makes me ask why even include a password if its all the same for every box, just give the character a key to open them. There was potential here to add something interesting. Finally, there was a lot to be desired from the sites you get to visit. As for the music, I never really noticed it until it starting playing ‘mid-walk’ for no particular reason at all. 

The story wasn’t really fantastic. Yes, my interests were raised by some strange and spooky happenings in the forest, and an interesting discovery towards the mid game had so much more potential. There just wasn’t enough rising action. By the end the climax just fizzles out and I was left confused if this was a story about Henry the protagonist or a certain character which was really not the focus of the story for about 95% of the game. After the climax, there was one final boring trek and some more chit chatting on a radio which by this point just felt unnecessary.

While Firewatch is beautifully stylized and the banter between Henry and Delilah is amusing, the game is let down by tedious treks in the forest, a lacklustre story.

Final Score: 2/5 Uninspiring
Pros: Beautifully stylized scenery, excellent voice acting and dialogue
Cons: Little to no gameplay, underwhelming story, monotonous travel

Finally the bad. The games physics and it's use of invisible walls makes things feel so constricted at times. I wanna feel like I'm in a forest, not locked in a mime's sex dungeon. It also breaks immersion too. I mean I've seen Henry traverse rough terrain and cliff faces but he can't jump over a foot tall boulder cause 'oh uh yeah, invisible wall...' Really? Also I brought this game on sale not even realising its original price was $30. I recommend waiting for a sale, as a $30 game should NOT have the following issues...

Achievements bugs. One achievement requires encountering an animal. If you encounter the animal but have alt-tab'd at any point during your playthrough then tough luck cause now the achievement won't trigger. I went in almost totally blind and played through the game in a single sitting because it was impossible to put down.

Firewatch is the walking simulator that actually deserves the praise that was lavished upon Gone Home. It is richly detailed, thoughtfully designed, the narrative is creative and well executed, and it has probably the best voiceover work that has ever been done in a video game. Seriously, the banter, writing, and delivery in Firewatch is some of the most enjoyable I've ever experienced.

It is a mystery game, and fairly linear. Probably the best way to think of it is like an old point and click adventure game or the modern Telltale games, except with a gameplay engine that has you hiking through the beautiful territory of Wyoming in between plot points. The gameplay is very slim, in service to the story. It explores themes of grief, regret, responsibility, and isolation. I found the story to be deeply engaging and did not have the problems with it that I am seeing come up as common complaints looking at reactions around the web.

The total amount of gameplay is between 4 and 6 hours, which I think is fine, but has earned some backlash from the plebeian internet masses who don't understand the difference between a tight, short narrative experience and a complete failure of design like The Order 1886. Portal is about 4 hours long and linear, and it is a classic of game design. Firewatch is a similar experience that I cannot imagine having been better if it had a branching story or multiple endings or collectibles.

Bottom line: definitely recommended if what I just said about it sounds interesting. Definitely check it out sooner rather than later, avoiding as much discussion about it as you can. It is a mystery so the less you know going in, the more effective the story will be.

There are other reviews that say it better, and go into deeper detail, but I find myself a bit too deflated to dwell on it too much.  When I saw previews for this game months ago, I kept it on my radar because it looked FANTASTIC.  The premise of a story-drive narrative in a gorgeous world really drew me in.  And it did deliver, on some parts.  I think the game looks amazing, though frame hiccups were prevelant and slightly annoying, and the voice acting between Hank and Delilah was top-notch, with great witty dialogue.  However there's not really much dialogue, not much of anything at all to be frank.  There are a few cute diversions, such as digging through ranger bins or finding a turtle or a burned shack ( which literally nothing is said about...no back story, no point at all from what I could tell )...but by the end, all these little nuances that I had been filing away for the end to see how they measured up instead began to give me a stark, depressing realization...they had no point whatsoever.

What should have been factoids that added to the overall story instead, at the end of my 3.5 hour journey ( I paused and took an hour for dinner ), felt like just enough added weight to hold me over the 2-hour refund limit.  No, I'm not being overly dramatic...I honestly think most of the extras in this game are just there to make sure you cannot get your money back.  The story climaxes in a very oddball, unoriginal way with a paltry plot point and an abysmal ending that just sorta...happens and leaves you there with nothing to show for it.  I paid 20 dollars for a 3.5 hour game that gave me nothing in return, not even a good wrap-up of the meager story I had invested in.  

So no, I would not recommend this game at all.  You can literally go onto youtube and watch a full playthrough of it that ends at somewhere short of the 3-hour mark and get all the story, all the ambiance, and miss absolutely NOTHING in the process except a 20 dollar bill...I hate sounding petty, but I am reporting this to Steam and petitioning for a refund.

Although this game has been regarded as a "walking simulator", it's not that bad considering you can jog and the map is not that long (10 minutes jogging to get from West to East). Most of the gameplay is free-roam, meaning you can progress the story when you feel like it, as long as you have the equipment to do so (rope for climbing, axe for spiky bushes).
Without going too deep into the story, you take on the role of Henry, a married man that decided to take a job listing to (NOT) go sit in a tower all day and look out for smoke, and the only one to keep him company through a walkie-talkie is Delilah, his boss, to whom he has to report anything he finds. Things start easy, put out fires, watch out for smoke, ward off drunk teens, but then you start suspecting that this forest has more secrets than people oughta know about...
That's it, no more spoilers, go play it yourself. I'm sure you'll enjoy it!

Now, for the achievements:
5 are story-related.
2 are obtainable as soon as Day 2:
 - Use up all the film in the disposable camera you find with the rope backpack;
 - Find the Turtle in the SouthWest lush forest and adopt it.
3 are obtainable as soon as Day 77:
 - Go to the burned down cabin that you found when hiking for the wires in Day 2 and open the stove;
 - Head West from the cabin and use your axe to find a chair and a tape;
 - Head to the fenced area, open the gate and check the inbox to find a bee.

At this stage in my life, I am interested in games for the story and the experience.  I like being able to explore an environment at my leisure without the fear of dying or missing something critical to the game experience.  Firewatch was able to deliver on all of these points.

The theme of hiking initially pulled me into this game.  Firewatch was able to create a wonderful facsimile of exploring the great outdoors.  Sure a couple of things do look artificial here and there (like every climbable ledge has the exact same rock patterns), but the views you get are stunning.  Also, its great not worrying about getting ticks or falling to my death.

I found the prompts in the opening scene a great way to flesh out your character in a somewhat personalized way.  While this doesn’t change the outcome of the game, it does create more variety in how people will interpret the story based on who their protagonist is.  In a YouTube video discussing the ending of the game, the presenter talked about how [spoiler]the DUI that his character had[/spoiler] impacted how he viewed the ending.  In the comments, people talked about the different backgrounds their character had and how it affected the story meant to them.

Some of the criticism for Firewatch revolves around the ending.  There was amazing tension building throughout the entire game as the two protagonists tried to figure out what was happening.  Instead of a big reveal at the end, I can see how many people could feel the conclusion of this game was anticlimactic.  For me, however, the ending was bittersweet.  [spoiler]Our characters did survive, but there is still a lot of emotional pain that they will have to work through as they leave the wilderness.[/spoiler]

The only thing that irked me once in awhile was trying to figure out where I can and cannot go.  For the most part the its pretty clear where I need to be heading, but once and awhile I was trying to walk up a hill or a rock that looked like it was traversable.

If you are looking for a low stress, beautiful game, that tells a compelling and emotional story, than Firewatch for you.

Firewatch isn't just a game—it's an emotional work of art that demonstrates how much depth, feeling, and atmosphere an interactive experience can have. From the very first minute, the atmospheric world of the Wyoming forest captivates you—with its vibrant sunsets, rustling treetops, and the impressive expanse of nature. It's as if you're actually standing there.

The strength of Firewatch lies not in its action or complex gameplay, but in its calm, profound narrative. You play Henry, a man grappling with his past while working as a fire watcher in the wilderness. The only human voice you hear is that of your superior, Delilah—and this is where the game unfolds its true magic.

The dialogues between Henry and Delilah are incredibly realistic, funny, sometimes sad, and always touching. It doesn't feel like a game, but rather like a real conversation you're having—full of emotion and humanity.  The decisions you make may seem small at first glance, but they shape your personal path through the story and make the experience unique.

What also makes Firewatch so perfect is the fantastic sound design. Every footstep on dry leaves, every distant rumble of thunder, every musical note is perfectly placed. The soundtrack is minimalist, but that's precisely what makes it so effective—it hits you in the heart at exactly the right moment.

The graphics are also beautiful. They're stylized, almost like a painting, and create an atmosphere you won't forget. You'd want to walk through these woods forever, watch the sunset, and listen to the wind.

Firewatch is a quiet but powerful game. It's a meditation on loneliness, memory, closeness, and loss—and that's precisely what makes it so perfect. Anyone who thinks video games are just shooting games or puzzles will be proven wrong here.

Conclusion:
Firewatch isn't a typical game—it's an experience you feel. A perfect blend of story, atmosphere, dialogue, and art.  If you haven't played it yet, you're missing out on one of the most beautiful, human games of all time.

I've seen many people calling Firewatch an exploration game, a survival game, a "puzzle/mystery" game (similar to Outer Wilds), etc ...

Firewatch is none of the above. It is a story-driven, linear adventure game. There are no puzzles to solve, there's no survival aspect, and there's no "proper" exploration (since the game is, again, linear). This isn't to say that you can't enjoy the atmosphere of the game and its world, but it is definitely not focused around you exploring the map freely.

If anything, i'd say Firewatch is closer to a mystery novel, or movie. There's not much interaction required from the player. You go from point A to point B, recover new clues, watch the story unfold, and repeat these steps until the end.

That said, the narration of the story is quite good and the pacing makes the whole experience very enjoyable.

Firewatch gives you three hours of gameplay, roughly. A basic rundown of it would be;

• Walking around a small open world investigating disturbances as a forest lookout.

• Following instructions via the women who speaks to you throughout the story. Which leads to such things as collecting materials from item caches and updating your hand drawn map. 

• Investigating a mystery surrounding you both. 

Believe me, the intrigue of the world rubs off within 20 minutes as almost all in-game assets look the same, but interestingly enough the creators do try their very best to disguise this by -admittedly- deploying beautiful varying lighting across the world. Be that as it may, do not go into this expecting a huge world of wonder with much to discover and fawn over. There isn't. Much of it looks the same, and this isn't aided by the lack of 'gaming' you can do. Mechanics are limited to 'interact' (opening boxes and climbing ropes) and 'sprint'. 

Ultimately, from a content point of view this doesn't hit high marks. So, what about the story? The characters? Well...

They aren't really characters. The dialogue between them is fun and engaging, but their 'backstory' which is shoved down our throats from the offset isn't relevant to the story whatsoever and I sat there scratching my head at the end wondering why I needed to know any of it.

Imagine you go to a cafe and ordered a coffee. The person who brings you it then goes on to tell you the origin story of said coffee. You'd just sit there with your mouth open wondering, how does this make me enjoy it further? Stop! Stop!

Sadly the creators didn't think about that, so friviously throughout the game they drag up the dregs of the characters past to add 'interest' to the game. Why? Because Firewatch is so bare bones that they have to try everything they can to keep players engaged. This game is worth perhaps £3, certainly not £14.99 that it's marked as currently. What were they thinking?

The mystery holding the game together has some of the widest gaps I've recently witnessed, unexplained red herrings are treated as main selling points to this game and we are expected to swallow them all as a part of this supposedly 'emotional' experience. 

The ending, as most have highlighted, is not good. It. Just. Ends. Like. This. Review.

SPOILERS ensue. To the business of the ending.

I'm not going to go on a giant tirade about this. I want to make a very specific point. This ending of this game, to me, is a beautiful example of how our imaginations can exert such powerful control over our thoughts. I assume anyone playing this game had their imagination running wild with all sorts of possible explanations at some point or another. This may be why some people were disspointed with the ending. 

 The fact that the boogeyman just turned out to be a mentally unstable ex-firewatch father who may or may not have caused the death of a bright and emotionally isolated young child, his own son, makes the wild fantasies my imagination spun that much more beautiful. My mind really explored a wild and wide variety of explanations for what I was experiencing.

 John Keats once accused Isaac Newton of destroying the poetry of the rainbow by describing how it exists and why it appears to us the way it does us using a physics and maths-based explanation. I submit that the beautiful nature of the rainbow and the wild stirrings of my imagintion are that much more interesting and powerful considering that they have a more mundane explanation than some people are willing to bare.

And now, the reason I'm even leaving this review is I was trying to open a lock box, but I needed to respond to Delilah, and for some reason a game where someone is constantly talking to you, and you don't know if you need to respond or not until a timer comes up. A poignant, dialog rich game in which you play the down-to-earth, educated Henry. To put his head on, lose it altogether, or just remember which way is up-  even he hasn't figured it out, and you're there to maybe help that, and experience the revelation with him.

You discover the stories of the Firewatchmen that came before, guided and connecting with the Firewatch supervisor Dililah through witty banter and the confines of being two people who might as well be on an island as they are so isolated.  That isolation presents obvious risks that you could be hurt and no one would know for days, and you'll soon learn that you are not alone. 

Every second of this game is enjoyably thought provoking and keeps those thoughts lingering even when you're done playing.  This game is not for the people who are into hyper games, or enjoy being flighty.  Its slow, steady and rich.  This game is not for people who only play games to experience what you couldn't do in real life.  You can do this in real life.  But it will take you to a different state of mind, put a different emotional filter on your thoughts that you would hope you or your family would never have to look through. First off, let's get it out of the way and say that yes, the game is extremely short. It took me about three hours to play all the way through the story. With no incentive to replay it, the game might not be worth the asking price for many people who read this review. If you don't want to pay $20 for a 3 hour experience, then that is fine, and respectable.

However, the experience that you're buying here is something unlike other games you've played. Firewatch, no matter what all the naysayers believe, is a very groundbreaking game. It did something no other game has ever done for me: make me feel like I was talking to an actual human being when I had conversations with Delilah as Henry. The connection you build with her is something unlike anything you'll see in another game. It just feels so... real. She feels like a real person. I believe that the feeling is amplified by the fact that you never really see a physical representation of Delilah in the game. You only ever speak to her through your handy walkie-talkie, which means the only thing I ever associated her with, was with a real, breathing human.

The story that Firewatch tells is also an extremely believable, heart-wrenching, and yet heart-warming one. I'll not go into details or spoilers, but let's just say that the story is a very human mystery, and has a few twists that leave you pondering every single thing you ever did in the game, and wondering how it was all connected. The story wasn't something that will completely blow your mind and make you rethink your life, but it is just that hint of subtlety that makes it so enjoyable. It just feels so real, man.

I believe that the price tag on Firewatch is worthwhile. The beauty of the landscape in which the game is set isn't really comparable to very many other games. The world is exquisitely detailed, and the art style does a lot for the overall atmosphere the game is going for. Photorealism wasn't something that the developers were going for, as the art has a very cartoonish, animated feeling - and yet all of the finer details in the world are still there, such as print on the back of some of the books found in the game that can actually be read. The environment will immerse you in your surroundings, and if not for your map and compass and Delilah's guidance, it would be quite easy to get lost in the extensive wilderness in which the game is set. On top of that, the voice acting in the game is probably some of the best you'll ever hear. For such a small title, it is astonishing how well voice acted it was. The voice acting certainly helped to add to the immersion of the world, but it also helps justify the price of the title, as quality like that can't come cheap.

In the end, if you're looking for a quick, hearty game that you want to make you feel something, then this game is definitely worth your time, and your money. If you don't have the cash to fork out for a game you'll probably only ever play once, then I don't think this title is for you.

A character-driven narrative game disguised as a hiking simulator, Firewatch tells a story that is compelling until it attempts to resolve itself. While the plot's climax may subtly relate to the game's stellar (and deeply sad) intro, it can't support the weight of the events leading up to it.

Firewatch is beautiful, the art style is striking, the voice acting is superb. A few rough edges are present, but forgivable. It can be completed in four hours or so. There are no challenges or traditional gameplay to speak of: your choices are entirely narrative in nature. Time advances as dictated by the story. Exploration is rarely rewarded.

Sadly, through no fault of its own, the game's narrative is shackled by the near-total absence of animated human beings. Being a small studio, it seems Campo Santo determined that they didn't have the budget for animated people, and designed Firewatch around this restriction. While their attempt should be lauded, the character-centric story they are telling ultimately suffers from it.

I'd recommend this to people that like narrativist gaming or are craving a survival-free first-person adventure game experience... but I'm still mad about the ending, so this gets a red thumb from me.
