[h3][b][u]Short Answer:[/u][/b][/h3] A really good narrative-driven game, often considered one of the best "walking simulators" for good reason. Artistic direction is stellar, the story is engaging, and the characters are the highlight of the whole experience; with only some mild pacing issues and a few minor glitches to complain about in my playthrough. Can be beaten in roughly 4 hours, and even as someone who typically dislikes walking simulators, I'd still say it's worth giving it a shot.

[h3][b][u]Long Answer:[/u][/b][/h3] [i]Firewatch[/i] is a narrative-driven mystery game that has you take on the role of Henry, who seeks to escape his tumultuous life by applying as a fire lookout, tasked to sit in a tower in the middle of the Wyoming wilderness and watch for signs of wildfires. Your only contact with the outside world is your supervisor Delilah on the other end of a handheld radio, and it's up to the two of you and your watchful eyes to keep the wilderness safe--but as you'll quickly come to discover, wildfires are not the only thing you need to watch out for. It's considered one of the best in the "walking simulator" genre; and after finally getting a chance to play it myself, I can see why it's so highly regarded.

Much like other walking sims, [b]gameplay isn't too complex[/b]: a lot of walking from one story-dependent location to the next interspersed with "dialogue tree" conversations over the radio about anything of interest you find along the way; but it's made a bit more interesting thanks to a light "open-world exploration" element. When tasked to visit a new location, you're not always given clear instructions on how to get there, often being told to just start walking in a cardinal direction or find things based on nearby landmarks. The idea is to regularly consult your map and compass while traveling to determine how to reach your destination, much like you would if you were actually hiking in the wilderness. [b]The most interesting part of the game to me, oddly enough, was the way the game uses your map.[/b] You don't get a traditional minimap, but rather a physical paper map--which you must equip like an item in order to read--that will keep track of your position as you travel (though you can turn this function off for a more immersive experience). It gives you the basic lay of the land, but supply cache boxes scattered around the park hold annotated pieces of the same map, which can then be recorded onto your copy to reveal available walking paths nearby; any story-related points of interest you discover will be automatically added in the same manner. The sense of freedom you get when you first view the sheer size of the map quickly fades once this process reveals how constrained travel can be; but the thrill of exploration can still be found in finding new shortcuts, the occasional secrets not marked on your map, and really anything and everything that will trigger new dialogue between Henry and Delilah.

Speaking of which, [b]the dynamic between the two main characters was fantastic[/b]. You can relay information to Delilah over the radio about nearly everything you find, and these are often accompanied with a dialogue tree to change up how you respond to her remarks. You can't change the outcome of the story through your choices, but they can affect Henry's background/personality and the relationship he has with Delilah in meaningful ways. Finding new things to trigger these conversations and learn more about these characters was a huge incentive for me to thoroughly explore whenever I could, and not just do the bare minimum to push the story along. Much of this is thanks to solid writing, but the high-quality voice acting helps turn the interactions between Henry (Rich Sommer) and Delilah (Cissy Jones) from "good" to "great". This relationship is only one half of the game's overarching narrative, the other half focusing on a series of events that coalesce into a big mystery story. [b]I don't really want to say much about the mystery story for obvious reasons, though I can say that I liked it overall.[/b] I've heard some say that the ending was underwhelming, but I honestly didn't mind it. [spoiler]Multiple times I was concerned that it would jump the shark in some regards, but it managed to ground itself in the end and make something that feels fitting given how true to real life (sometimes uncomfortably so) the story and characters can be.[/spoiler]

[b]It goes without saying how gorgeous the game looks, but I wish I had more chances to stop and take it all in[/b]. Each time you get the opportunity to go somewhere new, there's always this element of urgency that pushes you to go there. It makes sense from a narrative standpoint that things need to keep happening to drive the plot forward, but the only downtime you'd get were in brief scenes that had you locked into one location right before unceremoniously jump-cutting you into the next scene. I constantly felt like I was being rushed through to the end of the game, and I would've liked more opportunities to explore without needing to be as concerned with time management. You do get a "Free Roam" mode you can play with in a special settings menu, but unless you're looking to unlock some missing achievements, you don't have as much incentive to use it after you've already beaten the game; and since you're unable to talk to Delilah in this mode, using it before you beat the game robs you of what I feel is a valuable part of the "first-time player" experience.

Final side note, [b]you may run into some minor glitches during your playthrough[/b]. A couple times when trying to interact with something while still running up to it, my character would suddenly run backwards a few steps without my input, only to give me back control a few seconds later. One time I had triggered an event that was supposed to unlock an achievement but didn't, and I had to reload the game and try again for it to work--something I've seen people struggle with on several of the optional achievements in both normal and free roam mode. It's nothing serious, but it felt like something worth noting.

[b]It took about four hours to beat[/b], and I spent another hour getting the last few achievements I missed in my main playthrough. I went into this almost completely blind, not even realizing it was a mystery game before playing, and I'm glad I finally got the chance to experience it. I'll admit, I've been quick to dismiss this genre of game in the past, but coming out the other side of this one, I'm interested in trying some of the others I've seen put on a similar pedestal. [b][u][i]Firewatch[/i] is a quality experience, one whose presentation and story can even appeal to those that aren't typically interested in the walking simulator genre.[/u][/b]

It's a fun, albeit *extremely* short story. It's pretty straight forward, there aren't multiple endings, thus not much replayability except to see a few variations of conversations between the two characters and minor fluctuations in their relationship, played out via walkie-talkie. The voice acting is top notch, and beautifully done by Cissy Jones and Rich Sommer as Delilah ("D") and Henry, respectively.

This is good, because this game lives and dies on its story as it unfolds between these two characters - some people find the ending to be subpar or anticlimatic; which is a fair critique - it's not for everybody.

BUT

That said, personally, I felt it fit the atmosphere just fine. Overall, the game does a good job of getting in your head and letting you spin in the mystery along with D and Henry, and it does it in a very short span of time. It reminded me of the movie 'Blood Simple' (Coen Brothers, ~1985) Not in content, of course, just in terms of story telling methods. If you know what that means, then you might want to give it a try.

I really wanted to like Firewatch. It has beautiful visuals and the voice acting is pretty well done. But the gameplay is completely uninspiring. It's technically open-world, and should be considering you're in the wilderness, but you feel like you're "on rails" ... like that scene in Jurassic Park. You approach every part of the storyline the exact way the developers intend it; no sneaking, no clever alternative approach. You have to lead your character into dumb/obvious traps for the story to progress. No 'choice' (eg. dialogue) seems consequential as it all weaves back to spilling the same information. To be brutally honest, I kinda felt dumber for playing this game.
Well, what can I say... the game makes you think.

Firewatch is not your usual type of game. I've read some of the negative reviews, and I believe they stem from people who just would never like this type of game. It's not a game for everyone, but that doesn't make it a bad game. In fact, I loved the game so much my wife and I played it for 7 hours straight just to see what happens with the story!


This game is very narrative driven. You won't be ambushed by 50 people trying to rip your throat out. You won't be speeding through a busy city with 100 cops chasing you with sirens ablaze. No, instead you will have a suspenseful story that gets more and more on the edge of your seat the longer you play. It can get genuinely creepy at times. It can also get very emotional.

As far as plot and voice acting goes, it is phenomenal. I would easily give the game an 8/10 for story and a perfect 10 for voice acting and dialogue. The ending of the game is a little bit of a let down, which is why I can't give it a better rating than 8, but it's still a very good plot and I really enjoyed the experience.

The graphics take some getting used to as well. They aren't super realistic. In fact, they aren't realistic at all. They are more water color like, similar to Borderlands. While certainly not a style for everyone, I liked it.

Overall I would give this game an 8/10. As much as I enjoyed the game, I don't see a lot of replay value, and I was a bit disappointed with the ending. That said, I'm good for a good second playthrough, maybe a third. The game is only 20 dollars, so it's affordable, and provides a very memorable experience.

Would I recommend this game to everyone? Hell no, but if you don't have to be having someone try to kill you every 5 second or decapitating something every minute to have fun with a game (which is honestly where a lot of the negative reviews comes from), then you should give this game a try.

First, let's talk about what this game isn't.

This game isn't challenging, difficult, fast-paced, or action-packed. You don't fight, solve puzzles, and you can't die. In fact, you never come face-to-face with another soul throughout the entire game. A cynical or easily bored person could dismiss this game as being simply "push button to make story happen." 

And really, it is. But that's not at all a bad thing. This game is immersive, suspenseful, and overwhelmingly beautiful. As the game progresses, you explore the beautiful park, unravel your character's backstory, uncover a decade-old mystery, and develop a friendship with another lonely ranger whose face you never see. This isn't a movie that requires the occassional press of a button; you become fully immersed in the story and are quite free to encounter the story on your time, taking breaks to explore the forests and cliffs. Oh, and take some great pictures. Don't neglect that camera, you'll kick yourself if you do.

I've only played maybe one first person game on a flat screen in the past ten years, so it could just be that, but the controls in this felt very.. off. I used a dual shock style controller. For some reason you can't re-bind the buttons. And the default config never clicked for me throughout my playthrough. It didn't help that there seemed to be way more buttons than even necessary for a game that consists of walking and talking. All in all, Firewatch just feels janky.

It doesn't help that the world is absolutely full of invisible walls. These walls funnel you through the extremely linear path that you're supposed to take. I understand why they did that, but you get hung on on all kinds of invisible objects at every turn. I've gotten stuck on rocks, trees and at a few points started floating backwards.

And this leads to why I'm not recommending this. There really is no actual game here. You have zero choices to make in regards to anything. Sure there are some dialog picks but they have no real effect on anything. Maybe they mention the type of dog you owned or something but it's all meaningless. You have no problems to solve, no real directions to choose, nothing meaningful to collect (maybe there's an achievement for picking up books?).. this really could have been an animated short. You could watch someone else play through this on youtube and get the exact same experience. Actually that would be better since you wouldn't be the one getting frustrated. All you do is walk the path, which triggers story elements, which are almost entirely sound bytes. Occasionally you have to press A to do an animation to get over a log or something. That's it, that's the "game".

You play as Henry a guy trying to escape his pretty bad life problems for a summer. You take a job as a "firewatch" park ranger. Throughout the game your only company is Delialah another ranger and your boss who you talk to through the radio given to you. Things start off simple enough, running some drunk teenagers off a lake but things quickly begin to take a darker turn. Things go from odd to seriously strange and you set off discovering just what is happening in the woods.

Its a neat little mystery and while the payoff was something I wasn't quite expecting its still a very nice little story with a good beginning middle and end to it. Its not going to win game of the year or anything but its really nice to see something like this that is just about immersion and trying to tell a story. How the story unfolds and your relationship with Delialah is based entirely upon the conversational choices you make. 

If you got a good 4-6 hours and want to fill it with a good little story I suggest picking it up. I enjoyed it and I hope these guys put out something else like it in the future.

Firewatch is the debut title from Campo Santo, a recently founded game studio. I'm glad to say that Firewatch proves to be an excellent debut from them.

The initial most striking thing about Firewatch was the way that the game looks and sounds (I guess the overall aesthetic package). The game has a sort of cel-shaded feel to it graphically, but with really beautiful lighting that casts shadows on the ground in front of you and peeks through the trees as you wander throughout the wilderness. There are plenty of moments in the game where I found myself take screenshots (both using the hotkey and the in game camera), just because of how incredible it looked. The games music is provided by the same composer who did the music for Gone Home, and it shows: the music is kind of droney/ambient, but it fits really well with the general melancholic mood at points in the game itself.

The narrative of Firewatch is relatively simple: the player assumes the role of Henry, a man who decides to take up a job watching for forests (and ultimately other happenings) in a forest preserve. He does this not only for monetary reasons, but also to search for himself (think Walden or any Thoreau, I guess). Things quickly become more complicated as the player sorts out Henry's various emotions. If you'd care to read more about that, my review above goes into more spoiler-y detail regarding the games actual plot.

I can't recommend Firewatch enough. It's a game that does an outstanding job on all fronts and makes me incredibly excited for what Campo Santo has in store next.

Each of the two clearly are not perfect people and have their own varying vices which are dealt with in different ways. It's very human and very, very well executed.

Environment wise, yuuuup, that looks like a forest, alright. My only criticism as far as the design goes, is that it sometimes feels very easy to get 'stuck' on a particular piece of geometry (rocks, mostly) and you need to wiggle yourself out of them, but even then, that's just a minor complaint. The only thing I felt overall, outside of minor nitpicks, is that the conclusion and wrapping up of the narrative was a little unsatisfying. To say the game’s masterful story telling got me to care and shed a tear about a character I had only been introduced to minutes previous shows how well the game has been crafted.

I am going to start by saying that the experience of playing Firewatch is one of the best things I have played in recent memory. I am going to give a few spoilers for the early part of the game so if you do not wish to see these please do not venture any further.

The start of the game sees you advance a story through our main protagonist Henry’s life from meeting his future wife in a bar and through the rest of their relationship. Needless to say everything did not go quite according to plan and the game starts proper as you find yourself in the middle of nowhere having taken a job as a Fire look-out in Wyoming Woods to get away from everything.

This opening sequence is amazingly moving and really gets you invested in Henry as a character moving forward.

The game then takes place over the course of a summer with different days being treated as different chapters in the story. The location you are in is beautifully realised and an absolute joy to move around. But the main standout in Firewatch are the 2 voice-over leads. Henry is a heart-warming character who is relatable and you instantly feel for. Delilah who is Henry’s boss and must guide him through the summer is equally as well realised and pretty soon you care so much about these 2 characters in fact pretty much more than I have felt about 2 video game characters in recent memory. I will go out on a limb and say that the script in Firewatch is the best I have ever encountered and this game has as much in common with a fantastic written short story as a video game and could easily be converted to that.

For a man who is supposed to sit in his lookout and watch out for fires he doesn’t generally seem to do a lot of that. The game starts with you going to investigate some drunken teens setting off Fireworks and this sets the rest of the game’s narrative into motion. As well as the sublime voice acting the score in the game is also exceptional. The tension mixed with humour is beautifully brought to life by the excellent soundtrack.

While Firewatch falls into the walking simulator genre this is way more involved than most and you hardly notice the lack of certain types of conventional gameplay as you navigate the world and advance the story. As you travel around the area you often can pick up items that later appear in your Firewatch station. The game also has a little bit of Metroidvania in it by cordoning off certain areas until you pick up a certain tool to advance.

Another very cool moment is the disposable Camera that you pick up early in the game. As you play the game you can take up to 15 pictures and what is very cool is that once the game is finished for $15 you can actually get these photos developed and sent to you. I wish I had known this before I finished the game and I might have been more thoughtful on wasting them but I may very well play through the game again just to make and order a cool set of $15 prints.

The game is not absolute perfect. Navigating was often a little tricky using the map and compass and while I didn’t want a minimap or a big arrow pointing my way you at the very least could have let me still run while holding the map.

You probably have already heard by now that most people’s issue with the game is the ending… and while I will be the first to admit the ending was not my favourite part of the game It could have been worse. I guess it just wasn’t the ending or the big reveal I had expected or hoped for but this did not damped one of the purest and most enjoyable narrative gaming experience I have ever experienced.

Firewatch is the best story driven game I have ever played. I cared more about the characters in the 4-5 hours of gameplay in Firewatch than I have done in many TV shows I have seen for countless hours. The game approaches adult themes in a sensible adult way and weaves in an unforgettable story that I will definitely play again (and that’s something I almost never do)

Firewatch is an interactive story where you play Henry, a man who’s trying to escape his current
life by becoming a Fire Watcher out in the Rocky Mountains. During the course of the game you
make friends with Delilah, a fellow Firewatcher who keeps you company throughout the game.
The gameplay mostly consists of exploring the forest and talking with Delilah as the story
unfolds and you unlock tools to help you explore more of the forest.

The scenery is beautiful, there are several sprawling landscapes and areas to explore in the
forest. The interactions between Henry and Delilah are very charming and I really enjoyed their
chemistry together. The story has a strong beginning and I quickly became invested in the
characters and the story. However, the second half of the game really fell apart for me. I feel like
they tried doing too much at once as more story threads began appearing and I felt like the
writers were trying to do too much with the story. The major climax of the story was lackluster as
it feels like all the plot threads get quickly wrapped up in a short time and leave an unsatisfying
conclusion. However, I really did like how the story concluded with Delilah and Henry, as it
wasn't something I was expecting, but felt like the best way to end their story.

Overall I liked this game, the world was beautiful, I liked the characters and even though the
climax of the story wasn’t my favorite, I liked several parts of the story. If you’re a fan of
interactive stories I’d give this one a try.

Firewatch was all over the internet years ago, and I never really bothered to play it till recently. And I can certainly say that it is a game. 

Gameplay is basically a walking simulator. Which while boring at times, works well enough. You sometimes have to press the contextual key to do stuff, such as rappel or move stuff around. Only other gameplay I can really say is there, are some VN style dialogue choices that I am 90% sure don't actually change anything related to the story. 

The story, which is what mostly everyone played it for, starts out well and interesting. You take a job for the park service to watch out for fires (OH HEY THE TITLE) and occasionally chastise idiotic teens for being drunk. Some weird Alex Jones level conspiracy stuff starts happening and you gotta figure out whats going on. This is where the game hooked me. The game had me questioning everything I saw, and even questioning the only other voiced character in the game who is supposed to be on your side. It was set up as the grand mystery, only for it fall completely on its face for the grand reveal.

Aside from the story, the game is "Go to point A, do the thing, then go home". Thats basically it. You get new equipment that will let you into areas you couldnt go, but you are forced to go there anyway for the story to progress. You are effectively railroaded. There is no point in exploring as almost all collectibles are found easily throughout the story.

Firewatch in my opinion is an alright game. Had some good ideas, but couldnt flesh them out. I suspect that writers thought they were clever with the ending, but it did more damage than good. I was annoyed and disappointed at the end.  I finished the story in less than 4 hours so its good if you are looking to kill a few hours, but dont expect anything grand. I really cant recommend it unless its got at least a 50% off sale.

Firewatch is a story-focused game that takes you into the beautiful Wyoming wilderness. You play as Henry, a man working as a fire lookout to get away from his problems. Your only human contact is Delilah, another lookout in a nearby tower, and you talk to her through a radio.

The story is emotional and full of mystery. At first, you’re just doing normal lookout work, but soon strange things start happening. The conversations between Henry and Delilah are the best part of the game—they feel real, and the voice acting is excellent.

The graphics are amazing, with colorful sunsets, quiet forests, and a feeling of being alone in nature. The music fits perfectly, making the world feel peaceful but also a little mysterious.

The gameplay is simple—you walk around, explore, and use a map and compass. There’s not a lot of action, but it fits the game’s focus on the story. The game is also pretty short, which might disappoint some players.

Overall, Firewatch is a game that tells a great story and makes you think about connection and loneliness. If you like games with strong stories, this one is worth playing.

One of my most anticipated releases of 2016, and sadly I bet it'll end up as one of my biggest disappointments. 

Firewatch focuses on a very grounded and human story, about a man named Henry who's just trying to get away from life and get some perspective on things. As the story develops you as the player get to choose what kind of man you want him to be, through the conversations you have with your watch partner Delilah. This is where the game shines the brightest and it was pretty much the only thing keeping me interested throughout the game. The dialog is well thought out with great voice acting to boot. There were moments I found myself grinning like a complete idiot because of the friendly banter between the characters, and there were also the heavier darker moments which made me genuinely feel for them as well. Add to this a beautiful woodland setting and a great soundtrack and you've got yourself one heck of an immersive experience.

This is pretty much the only good I have to say about this game though, sadly. When it comes to mechanics it falls short in pretty much every department. The hiking around is teadious and I found myself having to bring up my map way more often than I'd like just to see that I hadn't gotten turned around. And while we're on the subject, there really isn't any point to exploring becuase most of the areas are locked away until the game tells you it's ok to progress down the storyline. Most of the areas you explore are just big empty spaces anyway (albeit pretty spaces, but vast and devoid of content nonetheless), so in the end I just found myself plowing through the story just so I could get to the next section of dialog.

And to adress the elephant in the room: this game is short. As you can tell by my game time I beat it in two sittings at around the 4 hour mark. For a 17 pound game this is not ok, no matter how great your characters are.

At the end of the day though, I advice you to get this game, just not at full price. And I genuinely wish the devs the best of luck. Its been a long time since I felt so invested in the relationship between two videogame characters and I'm eager to see what Campo Santo can cook up in the future.

I enjoyed Firewatch, and would recommend it to those who enjoy narrative experiences, but it isn't a game without its flaws.  It does have some very pretty art, and it's writing and voice acting are excellent, however I did feel a certain disconnect with the characters in the game due to an odd sense of 'illusion of choice' I experienced from the very start.

Without wanting to spoil too much, you start the game off with a short text adventure sequence where you get to make a series of decisions about the nature of your character's relationship with their wife.  It is ultimately of no consequence, as the outcomes of your choices all account to the same final conclusion.  This is where the disconnect happened for me; I am not choosing my character, I am playing Henry, and I am just piloting him around.  I expect it was intended to get us invested in his character, to give us a sense of him as a person so we could really play the role of Henry.  Instead I felt like the character I created, and the Henry we play as were two different people entirely, and it was a feeling I couldn't shake for the rest of the game.

Across the course of the game, we're only with Henry for a short period of time, chronologically speaking.  He keeps being Henry whenever we're not with him, and the world responds to him as that Henry, not the one you choose to be whenever you're in control.  It reminded me somehow of the film [i]Being John Malkovich[/i]; being inside someone's head, but never really being them.

[b]Major narrative spoilers follow:[/b] [spoiler]It could easily be argued that the whole narrative arc is about the illusion of choice, and how in running away from their problems the characters haven't actually chosen to do anything, merely delayed the decision to a later point.  The plot repeatedly asks us to make decisions that ultimately don't matter, as the course of the plot remains unaltered whatever we choose to do. This reinforces the idea that these decisions are not why we're here, we're merely avoiding making the one choice that actually matters.  However, I feel this message could have been much more effectively communicated if I felt like I was the character I was supposed to be playing as, not just some foreign observer existing in his head, at odds with the character presented to me.[/spoiler]

So, overall a fun game, but not as satisfying or cohesive as it could have been.

Firewatch is a touching narrative-driven game with an appealing art style and superb voice acting.  

You experience the Wyoming wilderness as Henry, a man whose life circumstances drove him to accept a summer job that requires living in total isolation -- except for his manager Delilah on the other end of a walkie-talkie.  The gameplay is minimal, simply walking from point A to B, and serves mostly as a vehicle for the interactions between Henry and Delilah.  These interactions are where one really "plays" Firewatch.  You choose how Henry responds to Delilah and watch their relationship develop.  

Music is sparse and impactful when present.  Most of the time, you're listening to sounds of the wilderness and chirps from your radio.  The voice acting is convincing and really helps sell the experience (it better be on-point since it's front and center in this game).

Firewatch is a first person interactive story, featuring Henry, a man in his late 30s who, following his wife's diagnosis with early-onset dementia, finds himself working as a fire lookout in Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming, seeking to get away from the stress of dealing with his wife's condition.

As Henry, you experience the day-to-day tasks of working as a lookout, from telling partying teens that they can't set off fireworks in the park, to cleaning up trash, to maintaining utilities of the wider park. Throughout the game, Henry's boss, Delilah, communicates with Henry via radio, and serves as the deuteragonist of the game. The game's missions are represented through days, with each in game day being forwarded with a titlecard that lists the day's number, with days becoming more sporadically denoted as the game goes on.

Gameplay consists primarily of moving around the map, using ropes to scale cliffs, using a map and compass to navigate the forest, all the while communicating with Delilah, her relationship with Henry being forged and determined through however much you decide to reply to her, if at all.

I won't get too in depth as to the goings-on of the plot for Firewatch, but it's an incredibly effective narrative, relying on in-game cues to create an atmosphere of unease and anxiety that, for me at least, translates to the player's anxieties, strengthening the message and ethos of the title. If you enjoy story-driven titles, Firewatch is up your alley.

Pros:
- Amazing graphics, the art style with the lighting and everything else makes for a unique and beautiful world.
- The landscape itself feels real in the sense that it doesn't feel like the map is built around you and instead you are exploring this world put before you. (If that makes any sense)
- FPS was stable and performing well, no drops or underperformance. This game has been optimized well.
- The ambient sound and the soundtrack itself fit the game perfectly and none of them feel out of the place or forced.
- The voice acting is believable and it feels like the protagonist and other characters are actually talking to eachother and not reading lines off some paper. Feels very organic and that helps build to the emotion of the game.
- The story for the most part is well told and realistic and gets the player very invested in the lives of the main two characters, making choices a thing of importance. There is plenty of backstory and mystery embedded into it as well.
- The game mechanics are simple and easy to use, can very easily pick up this game and just play. 

Cons:
- I have finished the game and done most things inside of it you can do, and only racked up 5 hours. With little replayability this means for a $20 price tag I might get 9 hours out of it overall. In my opinion this game is worth around $10 and I advice any cautious buyers to wait until this game is down to around that price.
- Like I said a majority of the story is actually really well told and intriguing but it starts to fall short near the end. I was disappointed as they could have done so much more with this, it's not completely terrible but in comparison to the excellent story previously displayed it didn't match the same caliber. 
- There are still a few bugs around as any game does, but I did encounter a few more annoying ones such as world not loading walking on nothing to being stuck on top of objects that are difficult to get down from because there is no jump mechanic.
- There is a lot of walking in this game, a majority of this game is just walking from location to location. Now this is a minor con because the world is stunning and just walking through is fun, also the person on the radio is usually talking to you and there is story being unfolded so you get distracted, but in some points in the game it can get repetitive and I was just groaning at the fact I had to trek so far through already explored parts of the map. Also for some missions it will just make you backtrack the exact path you took to go back somewhere, where in other missions it would just fast forward time for you and put you there or close to there to save time and I just wish they had put more of those in.

TL;DR: Graphics and atmosphere are amazing, story is gripping but lacks at the end and there is only 5 hours max of gameplay per playthrough.

The game is pretty good. It takes between 4 and 5 hours to beat the game, based on how much you explore the forrest. You might replay the game with the developper's commentary and then add another 4-5hs for a total of around 10.
For that reason, I wouldn't advise buying the game full price. I got it for 5 bucks on Steam during a Sale but the game is otherwise around 25€, which is a bit much. 

Other than that though, the game's awesome. It's a classic Walking and Talking simulator. 
So let's tackle the walking first: it's good! It's amusing to see 40 years old Henry having unlimited stamina, as well as arms, kneecaps and ankles made of titanium. The man casually climbs stuff to get up and then yeets himself off ledges to go down, he jumps above gaps with ease but will take his time to vault over a wooden log, it's great. That being said, his legs when walking can be pretty meh, you will get stuck on the tiniest rock regularly because the game's like "no".
It's not that big of a deal however.

Now, for the talking part, that's when it gets awesome. Henry and Delilah are a great pair and their banter is very endearing. 
They tease and make fun of each other when the mood is light, talk seriously When the mood isn't for jokes. And there's this flirty mood between the two even though they both know they shouldn't. 
Which is something I really like in gaming. Both Henry and Delilah are their own characters, sure you can select the answers Henry gives (or chose to say nothing) but every choice possible is something that Henry could "realistically" say in the moment.

That's something I really enjoy and that I believe too many games get wrong. A silent/placeholder character in games is usually boring unless given many opportunities to express themselves in meaningful ways. 
Instead, here, Henry is a guy and you're going along his ride. He's riding the bike and you're in the Side-Car with the map telling him where to go, but you're not driving, and it's great.

But Henry isn't alone in this Ride, so is Delilah, and just like Henry, she's not a placeholder waifu, she's a person with a believable personality and reactions. 

All of this is helped with a fantastic voice acting from both Henry and Delilah. They're delightful to listen to. 

As a whole, the game's amazing. I was hooked on instantly with the characters and the story and was as invested as I could with Henry and Delilah. Sharing their happiness and their fear, their banter and their anxiety as adults that can sometimes be nothing but relatable.

This game is so well constructed that it's really disappointing to have to say that I do not recommend it. The voice acting is great, the script is great, the art is stylized, unique and beautiful and the atmosphere is convincing and complete.

The problems arise in the gameplay department. At first you feel like you're actually making decisions and figuring things out, but after the first few missions you begin to realize that there is no fail state and the stakes have never been lower. I kept thinking the early missions were just setting the stage. I thought that after one of them, something big would happen and the game proper would begin. But after every plot point, the game just kept going on as before and I was left observing and not really acting. The "missions" all follow the same formula:
1) Walk to the thing.
2) Have a conversation about the thing.
3) Walk back from the thing.

Sometimes you don't even get the third step and it just skips you to the next day.

At one point in the game, for example you are tasked with finding a way through a locked gate. However, rather than an involved search or any kind of a puzzle, you simply walk to where you are told the solution is, find the solution sitting in plain sight, and then go home. By this point in the game however, I was on to the formula and didn't expect anything else.

All of this is not to say I wasn't invested in the story or characters. As I said off the hop, the voice acting and script are top notch. I just want a little more "game" in my games. Give me some agency and present me with some consequences.

Also, as others have said, $20 is way too much for a game of this length. Particularly a mystery game as now that I know what is actually going on, the game intrinsically has no replay value.

If you really want to play it, at least wait for it to be on sale.

Your choices don't matter in the game and you are shoehorned into the same story even when it doesn't make sense. I think I would have enjoyed the game more if it either didn't present options that it will ignore anyways or if the game expanded to work with (rather than against) your choices.

For example, [spoiler] if you refuse to set the surveillance camp on fire, then Ned just sets it on fire anyways...which doesn't make sense because Ned would either die from the wildfire or be found out when help arrives to deal with the wildfire.[/spoiler] Also, [spoiler]I didn't flirt with Delilah, so it's not a big deal that she left me behind at the end,[/spoiler] so I didn't feel any emotional impact from the story. Since this game is a walking sim, if the story dialog choices don't matter, then I don't see the point in playing this game vs watching a video. 

Lastly, I experienced bugs that required me to restart the day to progress. I always stayed to the linear story, so I imagine there are a more bugs for players that explore around the map or delay doing the immediate goal.

I paid full price for the game which I do not recommend. At $5 or below, I would recommend the game if you're okay that Firewatch will tell you a specific story, rather than tailor the story to the dialog options you chose.

Anyhow, in a nutshell: definitely give Firewatch a buy&try if you love interactive stories and amazing environments, you won't regret it!

Firewatch is a forest-strolling conversation video game. There's a few racoons in it. It's very pretty. And while the few trailers will successfully get you wrapped up in its mystery and escape to the world of the game quickly, the real heart of the story is in why you get wrapped up in said mystery, as well as the main characters. If you are observant, and take your time, you will realize that this is a stunning game about some very well written characters given a real world to live in and experience. You'll probably feel like it's not long enough, you'll probably feel like the mystery plot is sub-par to what was possible, and you'll probably feel like the developers could have spent some more time polishing the game (I've noticed some oddities and areas of the game the devs didn't think the player would look). And yet, the important things in this game really do outweigh the bad. Not enough games are about the subject matter in this game, which I won't spoil for you. Life is Strange [i]could[/i] have been a game about the the complexities of time travel and the impact of changing the known "should be's" of the time travel continuum. Instead Life is Strange is about the strength of friendship using time travel and confronting life scenarios with the ability to undo mistakes you don't like.

Firewatch, in that manner, is similar to Life is Strange. It's not about the mystery.

And that doesn't hold the game back from greatness, in fact it helps push Firewatch towards it.

I'm in two minds about this walking simulator and whether I could recommend it to friends.

All of the books and objects around the place you can interact with have no real actual meaning. You can read the various letters, but why even bother - they are flavour items only and can be totally skipped without impacting the game play.

Speaking of game play, there is none. There are no puzzles to solve, no mini-games, interactive sections - nothing that would be considered game play.

I completed the game in 3-4 hours. So, could I recommend it? That's a soft maybe. The story, which was so promising in the start fizzles before the end and the environment has a ton of invisible walls. Navigation is made slower and more painful by being funneled through coriadors which make each journey longer then needed. Plus, the map was flat out broke for me, so seeing where I was meant to go was overly difficult.

Still, I enjoyed playing it and I was aware of the short play length before buying it. The game has some shortcomings, but is almost certainly worth a few bucks when it's on sale and a few hours of your day - if only for the voice acting and lovely environment.

At first, I thought this was a game where your duty is to just stay in your tower or roam around the forest to prevent any fire disaster that will burn down the forest. I was dead wrong.

This is why I love games with story line rather than multiplayer games. The atmosphere is addicting. You get the feel. You get the emotion. You get attached to the characters. You're enthralled in the story. You feel like you're in the movie where you are the protagonist. But this is the character's story and we are just the silent observers. But most stories has a protagonist and an antagonist character at the very least. Firewatch? It doesn't have one. All you're facing with is just a human problem. A person who wanting to get out of his problem just to relax for a moment but ended up facing a new one. Makes him realize that no matter how hard he's trying to escape, his problem will always be in front of him until he work it out. And the characters? Don't get me started, the conversation is what you expect from any other people doing their daily activities in any other day. You get a rocky start at first, but then you realize how important you are to each other and that makes your bond grew stronger and stronger you wished it wouldn't last. You worked together to solve a mystery that somehow happened shortly after your arrival.

Firewatch is amazing; especially the ending. You don't get the happy-go-lucky ending kind of way. One word, bittersweet. I feel that most people that have played this game don't get what they expected; even myself. But we know that the characters here will go continue on with their lives, and it was sealed in the last conversation in Thorofare Lookout.

It is easily one of the most memorable experience I had in games. And I don't regret every single second of it. Thank you, Firewatch.

[b]Spoilers for the story below[/b]

Having watched some pre-release footage, I went into this game expecting a pretty-looking mystery with an interesting premise and setting backed by some snappy dialogue writing, with the vague hope that it might be something that could come close to the phenomenal PS4 game Until Dawn. 

Upon starting a new game, however, you are immediately greeted by an absolutely vile text-only intro written in a second person narrative style that is equal parts superfluous and pretentious. It immediately confirms that yes, Firewatch was indeed spat out from the infernal orifice that is the San Franscisco indie developer scene. The game *clearly* wants us to focus on the story by omitting silly things like, I dunno, gameplay and other archaic concepts like that.

Once it gets going, the dialogue writing is actually charming for the most part. The voice acting is competent, but for a game that essentially foregoes any semblance of gameplay, the story just isn't good enough to hold it up. It goes through a lot of buildup and dangles several red herring plot threads in front of the player that are never followed up on. For a moment, there is even some immersion and a sense of tension, as the mysteries seem to ramp up towards the climax. It all soils the bed very quickly at that point, however. The 'twist' is literally that nothing out of the ordinary actually happens during the game.
 
It doesn't matter whether the writers were out to prove a point about how isolation drives people to start imagining things out of paranoia and how it's a reflection on our collective existential ennui or whatever interpretative drivel you can come up with. It's essentially a glorified "it was all a dream" type resolution. And hell, if the writers thought this twist was clever, original, or even a remotely good idea, doesn't that make that worse than if they had written it like this out of ignorance?

The visuals, although probably one of the games' strongest aspects, lose their luster pretty quickly too once you realize that the map actually consists of a series of prettified corridors rather than an actual open world as one might be tempted to assume given the setting. Outside of the chubby protagonists' body, character models are conspicuously absent. I'm sure that was a deliberate choice as well in order to underline the protagonists' isolation and not just cheaping out on animators and 3D modellers.

The sad thing about this game is that it could have been so much more. The potential for gameplay is absolutely there. There could have been more adventure elements, or a greater focus on day to day survival. Even simple menial tasks would have worked. But nope, you just walk around and listen to people talk.

Stay away, even if you like games with a strong narrative focus. Get something by Telltale instead or hell, get a PS4 with Until Dawn.

I sat here for a while after finishing my first and possibly only playthrough of this game trying to figure out whether I recommend it or not.  I will say what I liked about it first: the opening was extremely powerful.  Without spoiling anything, I will say that due to family history, I have a deep fear of what happens to one of the characters happening to me in a few years.  The storytelling was compelling and due to that person connection I have with the subject matter, I was in tears right at the start.  The game is also visually very beautiful and I enjoyed the dialogue back and forth between the two characters who have the most interaction in the game.  The music and sound design of the game was also very good at setting the tone and immersing me.

So onto the negatives -- I wasn't as let down by the ending as a lot of people were because by that point I didn't care anymore.  I just wanted it to be over after about the first 2.5 hours.  For someone like me, accessibility options needed to be much more expansive.  The first person view was nice for taking in the scenery, but it make me extremely motion sick.  I wanted to play the game in one sitting since it's relatively short, but had to keep taking breaks to try and settle the churning.  I also have a massive headache from all the camera motion from climbing up and down and up and down.  Oof.  The other major downside this game had for me was navigation.  If you took out all the time I spent wandering in the wrong direction, often straight into bushes and rocks, while trying to figure out how to go the direction the game said I needed to go, I'd probably only have 4 hours in the game instead of nearly 6.  It was so damn frustrating.  There should be some type of accessibility option that allows you to either fast travel to particular points or put up a minimap on your screen or lets you mark where you've left ropes, just SOMETHING so I didn't have to get so frustrated.  There were a couple of times I even had to turn to online guides to figure out how to get around in game, which is not really something such a simple story + walking simulator should have required.

As someone who gets easily attached to a story, Firewatch was short and sweet. However, it also possessed it's own moments of sadness. The story was, as I said, short in length; but even with only a few hours of game play, it still managed me to encapsulate me, and this still stands as one of my favorite games.

There are many twists and mysterious plots that build up the suspense as you continue to play. As well as an unfolding relation between characters involved; and characters you have yet to meet. The environment you travel in is comical or cartoon-ish in style, but I find that the beauty shines through; as if you're looking at a beautiful landscape painting. 

If you are an achievement hunter and are interested in a game that is easy to 100% complete within just a few hours, I would say Firewatch is a good choice for you. You can easily obtain each achievement in a single run, especially with the help of an achievement guide.

Unfortunately, if you're looking for exciting game play or a highly evolved combat system, I would genuinely say that this game is not for you. Others have described Firewatch as a nature-walk simulator, which I can wholeheartedly agree with. Unless you are willing to spend a few hours purely for it's story telling, then I cannot recommend this to you.

This game is a solid 10/10 from me. If you are interested enough to start watching a playthrough of the game to see if it's worth your time, I highly recommend you just buy the game for yourself instead. I made the mistake of having the story spoiled for me and I can only imagine how much better my experience would have been if I hadn't watched a playthrough first. That being said, playing the game somehow made the story feel [b][i]more[/i][/b] captivating and relatable than it was when watching the playthrough and experiencing the story that way.

[b]Story and Storytelling: [/b]This is the reason anyone would want to play this game in the first place... Firewatch's story is perfect, or at least nearly perfect. It feels believable and it's told in a way that makes it feel relatable so much so that I teared up a bit by the end of the game. (This is a commendable feat as I rarely get emotionally attached to characters in fiction so I almost never really cry at books, films, games, and other forms of media)

[b]Gameplay: [/b]There isn't much to Firewatch when it comes to gameplay, but that's a good thing. Having minimal gameplay means that you can focus more on the story, which is the entire selling-point of the game. So, even though all you're doing is pressing W or using the joystick to move forwards (with a few other things occasionally), there really isn't more that's needed.

[b]Music: [/b]Remo did an absolutely FANTASTIC job with the soundtrack for Firewatch. The acoustic guitar and twangy, telecaster-ish sounding (I think?) electric guitar gave the soundscape an outdoorsy feel and matched the setting perfectly. The synthesizers give some of the tracks a sort of Minecraft feel and also provides a welcome contrast to the brightness of the guitar parts. An interesting thing I noticed about the soundtrack is that it seems to ramp up in intensity at a slightly slower pace than the story itself which provides this moment where the music is calm and serene but the story is starting to get a little bit more suspenseful and tense. The calmness of the soundtrack made me feel even more tense and anxious to see what would happen next. Remo's song "Ol' Shoshone" was written perfectly for this game; it gives a sort of '70s vibe which matches the fact that Firewatch takes place in '89, and its theme syncs up perfectly too. Every moment of the soundtrack is nearly perfect and easily puts it on par with the works of Kelly Bailey, Mike Morasky, Mick Gordon and Joel Nielson.

[b]Graphics: [/b] The art style of this game is beautiful, so much so that I found myself actually saving film in the camera just in case there was an even more amazing landscape that I might find later in the game. The game looks absolutely lovely.

Not every time you need to save the kingdom, rescue the princess or slay the dragon. Not every time you must overthrow the galactic empire or defeat primordial evil. Not every story is an epic tale about heroic battles and cosmic struggles. Sometimes all you need is just a simple walk through a wild forest and talk to a fellow human.  

If I could describe Firewatch in one word, it would be — mundane. This is a game about regular activities that you, me and everyone could perform every day. About stories of normal people living their normal lives and having oh not-so-epic problems, failures and successes. You will not experience grand talks and deep thoughts and yet this game is far away from being simple. Imagine dealing with subtlety and minimalism when playing but at the same time focusing more on this vague feel of being…. watched?

Our protagonist is Henry — a middle-aged man with a difficult, yet not tragic past. His wife got early dementia, and was forced to be with her family because the dude cannot handle taking care of her by himself. Then he later stumbled on a job advertisement about a Ranger gig in Shoshone National Park. He took the job and met — only through radio tho — a woman named Delilah, a fellow Ranger and his supervisor, with whom later he created a friendly bond. And then things get a little darker, but it mostly smokes and mirrors, because the story itself is focusing more about human relations than surviving in the wild and other mysterious shenanigans. The game teases us with something extraordinary, but due to not being long (5hrs max with doing all achievements) it quickly discards that kind of narrative, funneling to “big” reveals and explanations. To be honest I expected something more after two first in-game days, but then the plot started literally galloping forwards.

From the gameplay perspective this game is nothing more than a walking simulator. Don’t be fooled by the game world being an open wildlife area, it is mostly composed from little places connected by corridors surrounded by invisible walls, like to hills too steep to climb, bushes or cliffs accompanied by Henry’s inability to jump on his own. There are some tasks you need to do every day but mostly they are connected to the story and you don’t need to rush to complete them. So for the majority of time you will be walking from place to place, picking items needed to progress (ropes, axe) checking supply caches and listening to dialogues between characters. They are dynamic by the way — you need to initiate conversation and then respond within a limited time window, so pay attention to it.

The game shines when focusing on Henry’s and Delilah dynamic. Both of them are middle-aged, both had hard times in the past, both are more grounded and realistic in approach to reality and lack this youthful naivety. They know they are in Shoshane for a moment, so aside from a little flirting and teasing each other from time to time they do not try to establish some deeper connection. And yet they do not shy from opening more about their past experiences, struggles and life in general. Overall, I think the main theme of Firewatch is about the human inability of creating deeper human connection. We sail through the surface but are too afraid to dive deeper because we don’t want to get hurt when exposing our true self to another person.

Now. It's over. Go home or something.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Firewatch is a first-person adventure / walking simulator game and is the debut title from development studio, Campo Santo. It's getting a bit old now, having been first released in 2016, but it's been on my Steam wishlist for a long time. I picked it up on deep discount in a recent Steam sale and I am really glad I did.

You play Henry, a Colorado man fond of booze and tuxedoes (sorry; in-game joke). The game begins with a brief text introduction presenting Henry's adult past, setting the scene for his arrival at Two Forks firewatch station, around which the core of the story takes place. I won't spoil the backstory, as I found it very moving, immediately filling me with empathy for Henry and his situation. You're able to make some either-or choices through the introductory text, but -- as with the rest of the choices in the game -- the outcomes are really only skin deep; you can't change any of the major plot points.

The game proper begins with Day 1 of Henry's time at Two Forks, where he is introduced (via radio) to his new boss, Delilah.

[h1]Presentation[/h1]
Initially I was unimpressed with Firewatch's portrayal of nature. Many of the rocks and rock formations look far too blocky and I thought there was too much repetition of them -- though actually it turns out these repeated objects indicate places that you can climb, jump, or rappel up or down. But there's also very little animal life and flora doesn't seem as abundant and varied as I thought it should be; everything just seems a bit too sterile. The lake is rather bland, too.

After playing for a short time, though, I came to appreciate the unique aspects of each distinct area in the game world, from the lovely aspen grove to the burned-out fire break, or the rocky slopes near Beartooth Point. The excellent lighting effects that clearly indicate time of day and progress of any nearby fires, and the smoke and wind effects, too, add significantly to the ambiance, making the world and particularly the trees come to life. Though I still miss the dynamism of life I'd expect to see in a wilderness area such as that portrayed in Firewatch, by the time I'd played for an hour or two I'd come to appreciate what was here, too.

The game is fully spoken and the voice acting from the two main characters -- Henry and Delilah -- is brilliant. It's some of the best voice acting I've heard in a game. The excellent script doesn't hurt, of course, but these two actors really bring their characters to life, evoking a sense of understanding and empathy the likes of which I haven't felt since my time with Elika and the Prince in Prince of Persia (2008).

Music is sparse, but very well chosen and applied. You'll spend much of the game with only the sounds of nature, your footfalls and breathing, and Henry and Delilah's conversation. But particular moments of beauty, realisation, or suspense are expertly enhanced with some wonderful and non-invasive tracks that fit the events perfectly. 

Performance with everything turned up to maximum is mostly fine on my GTX1070-based laptop. The game does have a few hitches or pauses, though; I assume that's while it's loading in a new area. It's a bit distracting, but not too bad.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
On arrival at Two Forks you pick up a radio and you'll use this everywhere to stay in touch with Delilah, your boss, who also happens to reside at the nearby Thorofare tower. Your job, according to Delilah, is whatever she says it is. On Day 1 that involves finding out who's illegally letting off fireworks, but essentially you're there to keep an eye out for fires and monitor them when they break out. Other than your radio, you have a map and compass and, if you keep an eye out as you explore, you'll quickly find a flashlight, too. You update your map with notes as you progress through the story; "♥♥♥♥♥♥ Boss is Going to get Me Killed Hill" is probably my favourite landmark.

You control Henry using typical first-person controls: WASD for movement, space to jump, and the mouse to control which way Henry is looking and to interact with the game world. This isn't a shooter or action game, though; the core gameplay involves walking around the big, but not huge, Two Forks area of the national park, using your map and compass for navigation, and following Delilah's instructions over the radio. The basic gameplay loop has you hiking to different areas on the map, looking around or picking up or using something, talking a bit with Delilah, and then hiking to the next area or back to your tower. As with any most other walking simulators, the experience isn't the game play, exactly, but rather it's the story the developers tell you along the way.

The game necessarily has a fair bit of backtracking and covering familiar ground, as your only mode of transport is hiking and Henry spends every night in Two Forks watchtower. The developers have managed to reduce this in a few cases, though, such as by having you start a day already on your way to a spot of fishing at the lake, or sitting watching the sunset from a rock, or even in the middle of a conversation with Delilah, hiking towards some new mission goal. Though the story has Henry spending almost three months at Two Forks, the game itself is played only over a dozen days or so, spread across the Summer.

Ultimately, though you're free to wander the map and ignore Delilah's instructions and advice, the story will only advance when you go where you know you need to, and do what she's telling you, which makes the game feel a lot like an interactive movie. Your conversations with Delilah can usually take a few different twists and turns, but in the end the story goes where the developers intended; any choices you make only give you a few altered lines of dialogue here and there.

If the story weren't so well written and the characters so well realised, Firewatch would fall flat on its face. As it is, though, everything comes together just so, to make one of the best story-based games I've played in a while. It would be really well suited to seated VR play, too, but I don't know if that's ever likely to be an option.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
Pros:
+ Superb voice acting
+ Great script
+ Interesting and believable characters
+ Pretty graphics
+ Great music

Cons:
- Short (3-4 hours)
- Choices are only superficial
- A bit too much backtracking in places

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Firewatch is good: very good. Some might say that its main drawback is that it's short, and thus doesn't offer a whole lot of bang for your buck. But I think it's just long enough to tell the story the developers wanted it to tell without overstaying its welcome. It has a good story with a well-written script, believable characters that you can actually care about, and some of the best voice acting I've heard, alongside mostly pretty graphics. It's a shame the choices you make in the game are only superficial -- I'd love to have been able to see different endings that depended on my decisions -- and I did get ever so slightly sick of covering the same ground over and over again, but for the most part the interaction between Henry and Delilah kept my interest even in these parts.

If you appreciate a good story told in an interesting setting, then I recommend you take a look at Firewatch. The relatively short story may just haunt you for longer than you expect.

Note: I should probably mention there's quite a lot of swearing in the game. It doesn't feel out of place to me, but I suppose some people may be offended by it.

It's hard to explain why you may like this game or not without spoiling the surprises of it has, because, while many compare it to Gone Home, I'd say it's more like The Stanley Parable or The Beginner's Guide in that it plays with your expectations but it does so in a more subvertive way.

So I'll give it a try and tell you first [b]what Firewatch IS NOT:[/b]
[list]
[*]It's not a fully open world adventure game
[*]It's not full of action
[*]The story is more akin to a Jon Kazenbach thriller than to a J.J. Abrahams or Stehen King fiction-fantasy novel (take that as you will)
[*]It's a slow burn semi-thriller (despite what the trailers may led you to believe)
[/list]

Firewatch doesn't give you a lot room to bend or shape the story. The characters are pretty well stablished and know what they want and who they are. You sort of help them pick reactions to some stuff but you're mostly a passanger in this unfolding story. You've been warned.

[b]What Firewatch is is...[/b]
[list]
[*]A very human story
[*]A self contained story with an open-ended ending
[*]A game that let's you explore in the same way Mafia II does: You can deviate from the path and see what you can find, but the story pushes you in a very specific direction
[/list]
All in all, Firewatch is a very unique game, one you can honestly love if you know what you're getting into and let yourself be indulged by its mesmerizing views and involving script. But, like some of those cozy books one reads under the sheets in a cold and lonely winter, it is a game you need to go into in the right mood.

Having seen the artwork months ago I had been eagerly awaiting this title. The environment looked amazing and the premise and user experience seemed top notch from the trailers.

The story of Firewatch sees the player as a new employee of the Parks and Wildlife service. You are alone in your watch tower with no communication with the outside world except from your two way radio.  On the other end of the radio is Delilah, an experienced firewatch ranger in another far away tower. Through this radio you recieve tasks from her while engaging in frequent banter. The developers of Firewatch have tried to incorporate the same 'time' based response as made popular by Telltale games. However they don't pretend that any of the decisions you make really matter. And unlike in Telltale games it seems dialog does't really affect much in the short term either. I ended up find this mechanic a bit annoying as there was no real purpose for being rushed and just instead it became an inconvenience.

The core gameplay revolves around 'walking'. The idea of hiking around the wilderness sounded appealing and really tingled my sense of adventure. However, Instead of wandering  around the environment and finding cool secret areas or perhaps spotting wildlife, the player is instead stuck on fairly linear paths. I spent a lot of time trying to find my own path but  would end up being blocked by a small rock. This really destroys the illusion of the game and makes it feel claustrophobic. Additionally as you spend most of the game walking, the linear paths make the  mechanic of walking feel like a chore. It brings back the horrible memories of "shooters" where you would trapse across half the map to get a key, then have to find your way back again. I found myself wishing for a teleport option. Of course if they did that this game could be completed in twenty minutes.

The tasks the player is issueed is fairly standard fare and follow a "go and investigate over at X" which requires bring up the in game map and compass to navigate the paths. As the player progresses mysterious events occur that creates an intriging atmosphere. [POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD]

It was a nice game. People complain about the plot but really, sometimes the greatest mystery isn't about the unrealistic things that's going on around you, or that could be going on around you. Sometimes the greatest mystery is people. Why they do the things they do. Why can't everything just be normal and peaceful. 

Delilah is a gal that lives in the moment (or so I believe). Henry is a guy who's trying to figure out what the hell he's to do now. Ned is a mental case that got his familial life taken away from him by his own mistake. And I think that's the mystery of the game: who these people are, why they're here in the middle of nowhere instead of being wherever living their life and what are they gonna do next in their boring, mundane lives. In other words, people.

People are a real mystery. And life too, consequently. It's not as exciting as conspiracies maybe but nonetheless interesting. Every minute of your life could be your last. Someone may break into your house to kill you, or just run up to you on the street and plunge a knife in your throat (and who's to say that in a few years a certain chain of events won't transpire that'd turn you into such a person?). Or your brain could suddenly pop a vein and you'll die from bloodloss in the middle of the night. Your friends and family, if you have them, would react differently too. Some would accept your sudden death, some may find it weird and decide to investigate, some would have no strong feelings, etc. And that, I think, is our grand mystery.

Why these things happen. Why you were destined to die, and whether your death was destined in the first place whether it's via the actions of a person or your own body deciding it's just time for you to go. And why people act the way they act and do the things they do. The thing is, your death may not be even random. Many cases of abuse happen between family members, who's to say a relative of yours wouldn't decide to murder you one day? Or someone you've never seen before but who's been seeing you almost every day. It's not like these things can't happen to you.

I had a really great time with Firewatch. For a studio's first game, it feels expertly crafted - the setting, tone, and style all fit together perfectly to tell its story, with riveting twists and turns that kept me guessing from start to finish. I really loved how the story plays with your expectations, setting up narrative threads that could resolve in any number of ways, really pulling you into the sense of paranoia that Henry develops over the course of his summer in the wilderness, with nothing but a distant voice over the radio for company. The walking simulator part of the game controls excellently, which is truly essential for a game like this where there's very little proper gameplay outside of the traversal and dialogue options, and I really appreciated that even the map was a physical object that you had to manipulate to read properly. Even with its rather short four-hour length, I feel like you really get some bang for your buck with Firewatch (though I'd suggest waiting for a sale because it routinely gets deep discounts), and if you have any interest at all in narrative-driven walking sims like this, I'm not sure there's a better one to experience. All the more reason that it's a shame the developers were gobbled up by Valve to do approximately nothing at all...
