[h1]Into the Shoshone[/h1]
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1241247199
Walking simulator. In gaming as we know it today that term has a rather negative connotation stuck to it, normally associating the game with three things: that it’s going to be short, extremely linear, and almost entirely narratively reliant. The genre used to deserve this connotation, with the majority of its games containing extremely poor stories and relying wholly on their perception as “art”. As it stands though, I fully believe that the title of walking simulator is now as valid a genre as any other, and that it’s finally outgrown the previous negativity surrounding it. Now, in stark contrast to previous associations, recent walking simulators have more positive implications: that they’re going to have exemplary stories, gorgeous worlds, and some of the greatest characters and dialogue possible. Firewatch perfectly compounds all of that, and really is symbolic of these new walking simulators that focus on actually trying to create an unforgettable experience instead of seemingly playing the “games as art” card to excuse their mistakes. Firewatch wastes no time creating said experience and right from the get go you start forming attractions to the two, arguably three, main characters. First off is Henry, a gruff boyfriend-turned-husband with an extraordinary personality who you’re going to be playing as all throughout your journey. Second comes Julia, not a main character but included anyways since she plays an important part in the story as Henry’s wife. Sadly, before the game begins you find Julia is beginning to show symptoms of early-onset dementia, slowly killing her and stressing Henry out to the point he takes on a job as a Forest Fire Lookout in the Shoshone to get a break. Lastly comes my favorite character Delilah, your supervisory lookout who you never actually see, but can visualize better than any other. Again, there’s really only two main characters, as Julia is more of an idea used to push the game forward than an actual character, which might seem a problem but instead is a unique way to focus attention on character development. When you only have two real characters, it’s a lot easier to flesh out their dialogue and make every conversation have value. I appreciate that they didn’t become too ambitious and try to have a full cast, because there’s something indescribably serene about interacting exclusively with Delilah for something of four hours. It’s intimate. It’s personal. It’s Firewatch. 

[h1]A Trek to Remember[/h1]
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1241224067
I'd argue that Firewatch’s two strongest features are the exceptional artwork and the absolutely unparalleled character development/dialogue, though not the only two strong features, these two were just the ones that stood out from my first playthrough. Artwork is one of the most critical aspects to a game’s success, though plenty of people would love to claim otherwise, and is intertwined with many other gameplay elements. For example, environment design and immersion are both nigh impossible with poor graphics, and if there’s no immersion or decent environment design then gameplay suffers, causing a catastrophic chain reaction. While there may be other games that have to worry about sub-par artwork, Firewatch is absolutely not one of them, having the most unique and attractive aesthetic I’ve ever seen. Artwork is an important part of building atmosphere and can heavily influence how you feel about the game, and I think Firewatch’s serene and peaceful air is built heavily on the fact that its art is so calming and beautiful. While this may have just been me, I found the game about an hour longer than expected, and I feel that can be attributed to me taking my time and genuinely wanting to just enjoy the scenery. I’ve never experienced anything like that before, Firewatch wholly immersed me in Henry’s character, as if I’m actually living in the Shoshone, with my only link to civilization being a small orange walkie-talkie. Looking back at my experience with Firewatch feels more like reminiscing on the past than it does playing a game, and I think that's caused by the various gameplay mechanics that pile even more immersion on top of what’s already there. My favorite one is the disposable camera you find about halfway through the game, allowing you to take pictures of the various parts of the environment. While that would be pretty neat on its own, the ability to upload your pictures online and to purchase high quality prints of them on the Firewatch website takes the feature from being neat to being unforgettable. What’s more, this literally gives you a physical way to remember and reminisce on your playthrough, an innovative idea that works well with how walking simulators tend to feel closer to experiences than games. I appreciate that, the small things put into the game to add detail and make this feel like a genuine world, I really do. 

[h1]All Adventures Have an End[/h1]
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1241250035
Now story quality is irrelevant if you can’t experience it due to horrible gameplay decisions obstructing the narrative with pointless or poorly designed mechanics. Firewatch has none of this and maintains a simple method of interaction with your environment, really only requiring you to press a button to interact with whatever you’re looking at. I enjoy this simplicity because more often than not complex game design, especially in walking simulators, tends to focus attention on the mechanic instead of the atmosphere, shattering your immersion with mechanics that seem out of place. Firewatch however has an extremely minimalistic UI that borders on pretty much none, only really showing up when you interact with the world or talk to Delilah on the radio. The gameplay is simple enough to where it’s not like you’d really need any UI at all, it isn’t particularly hard to just go around pressing E on different things you find in the environment after all. I am however glad that they didn’t make this entirely devoid of gameplay because it gives you something to do, even if that something is just pressing E on a door or radio, it still makes you feel involved without breaking immersion. Gameplay isn’t really what you’re playing Firewatch for though and ,while it’s extremely well implemented, it isn’t the game’s main focus, that would be the story. Firewatch has a story unlike most others that I’ve seen, because it tries to avoid telling a story of aliens, heroes, or what else could have been, and instead focuses on being real. Firewatch has a story that, to me, feels like a retelling of a friends vacation, all believable and real, but with a few minor details embellished or twisted to sound better and build suspense. Many people have a problem with the game's ending and honestly I’m torn: on one hand, they really built the ending up in a direction it clearly never had any intention of going, but on the other it’s a story of Henry and Delilah’s real suspense, and real mystery. It’s not the satisfying conclusion that I was hoping for, but it’s symbolic of the whole journey, it may not be the greatest ending in the world, but I think that it still has significant merit to it and ties in well with the themes all throughout Firewatch.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Firewatch has the most intimately personal dialogue of any game I’ve ever played, with characters to match, and provided a beautiful, if short, experience I’ll never forget.

Clocking in for me at a little over 5 hours, Firewatch packs a lot of emotions into a small, beautifully crafted, package. Firewatch differs from most video games as it lacks any sort of combat mechanic, this is more refreshing than you might think. I truly enjoyed just walking around the wilderness, talking on my radio, and enjoying the occasional reminders of humanity in the form of discarded beer cans. I made it a point to collect every piece of garbage I came across, as far as I could tell this didn’t have any impact on the game, but it felt like what Teddy Roosevelt would have done in the same situation. I also channeled my inner Smokey the Bear by ensuring that I stomped out every smoldering campfire I encountered. 

The game has been designed in a way that effortlessly guides you through the story, while rewarding those who prefer to take the road less traveled with scenic vistas and an opportunity for reflection that is usually reserved for great literature or film. If the game was nothing more than an opportunity to walk around and explore while doing your best to prevent forest fires, that would have been enough; However, Campo Santo studios has more ambitious plans for their debut title than simply walking around collecting garbage. Firewatch does a great job of lulling you into a sense of complacency with just enough excitement sprinkled throughout the first half of the game to keep you focused on your main goal of keeping watch for fires. The game’s second half takes a sharp turn and plunges you headfirst into a very thrilling mystery set against the backdrop of the ever expanding June fire.

There is an immediate and obvious chemistry between Henry and Delilah, they very quickly cling to one another, as if they are both running from their own lives but are afraid to go it alone; Henry needs Delilah just as she needs him. Firewatch explores loneliness from multiple angles and forces you to confront complicated emotions. Henry is a man running from his past and Campo Santo has done a fantastic job of making you feel that it’s up to you to use this time in Henry’s life to influence the course of his future. The dialog choices available feel like what someone might actually say when put in a similar situation, I didn’t have any trouble trying to find the choice that would best reflect my actual feelings at that exact moment. 

Firewatch is not so much played as it is experienced, It doesn’t feature any difficult platforming or puzzle solving elements and much of the conflict presented is internal. The ending left me with more questions than it answered, but I think I prefer it that way; the player is left to make their own interpretation as to what happens next.

Dive in: there are few experiences available right now that challenge your emotional fortitude in the way that Firewatch does. It’s visuals are stunning and the voice acting and writing are superb.  

FULL DISCLOSURE: My Firewatch experience may have been influenced by the delicious notes of pine and citrus that were present in the Dogfish Head 90 Minute IPA that I was enjoying during the second half of my playthrough.

This is the game equivalent of one of those films that you don't feel the need to watch ever again, but which still move you ages after you saw them. It is sad and at the same time very life-affirming.
[list]
[*] The voice acting and character building is great. Without this, I have the feeling that Firewatch would be nothing.
[*] The character and object animations are solid and authentic.
[*] The map is beautiful. It's also large enough to make certain tasks feel authentically like a trek, but not so large that it becomes frustrating.
[*] The balance between tension and relaxation is carefully maintained. While the threat and mystery ramps up towards the end, you are allowed time to be alone with your thoughts and admire the views even as[spoiler]you're running to escape the wildfire.[/spoiler]
[*] While the opening is a bit slow, the plot progression is generally well paced. Fast-forwarding through days at certain points is a nice trick which adds temporal and emotional scale.
[*] The way dialogue works feels very natural. Your character's isolation combined with the walkie-talkie device really makes you weigh your responses in a way that you might not otherwise. Silence sometimes feels like the right choice, not a missed opportunity.
[*] I genuinely had to steel myself before some of the mystery scenes. The soundtrack does a good job of making the usually benign environment seem host to malevolent forces.
[*] You're never sure who, or what evidence, to trust. Even when you're sure something is a red herring, there are enough loose ends and allusions to withheld knowledge to keep you paranoid.
[*] The end credits really got me. Especially because[spoiler]at the beginning I used the camera to capture pretty landscapes, but as the story progressed, I increasingly used it to document evidence I thought I'd need to solve the crime. When the contents of the reel were revealed, going back through my own loss of innocence to the "before" scenes of the tragedy was very affecting.[/spoiler]
[*]I was also moved by[spoiler]seeing the contents of Delilah's watchtower[/spoiler]and felt that[spoiler]never meeting her[/spoiler]was a fitting conclusion to the story.
[*] A walk in the sunshine while listening to [i]Ol' Shoshone[/i] is one of those rare game experiences that has to be good for the soul.
[/list]

If you're looking for a fully story driven game where it requires you to walk from Point A to B to progress, then you've found the right game. If you require something more to keep your attention, don't even bother reading the rest of the review yet alone buying the game.

Plot: 
You are Henry, a middle aged husband whose wife got sick and was moved away for her health. Now all alone, he takes up a summer job as a fire lookout for a national forest in Colorado. A solitary job with only his supervisor, Delilah, to give him jobs and company via walkie talkey, they tackle a mystery involved with the forest and it's connection to an approaching out of control fire.

Gameplay: 
As I said, this is a walking simulator. Which there's little else to do but go to the designated spot on your in game map and follow the story. And this is not a bad thing as it forces you to soak in the nature of the world of game. The lighting is pretty spot on too. There was a point during approaching sunset that was so bright it literally almost obscured my map (you're going to be pulling that thing out often). There's no inventory wheel and the map is brought up in real time to keep you in the experience. I love this mechanic in games and wish it would be implemented more in non stressful environments of course. Dialogue choices are present as you talk to Delilah on the radio. To me the best part of the game was the Dialogue and two top notch actors are probably the only people who couldve pulled it off.

Characters: 
The characters of Henry and Delilah are practically the only characters in the game and thankfully their likeable. Henry is weary and tired from his wife's illness and Delilah is likeable, yet quirky. Their dynamic is the highlight of the game and other than the main mystery is what kept me playing.

Conclusion:
This is a game you should not pass up, sale or no sale. Everyone's finances are different but in my opinion 20 dollars is a more than fair price for this game.

Firewatch is a beautifully written game with a remarkable sense of place. Its warm lighting, rich colour palette and finely detailed environments bring the Wyoming wilderness to life, and the unhurried pace invites you to linger in it rather than rush through. The voice acting is the standout. Henry and Delilah's radio exchanges feel natural and believable, and the dialogue choices let you shape a relationship that feels like your own. The gameplay is deliberately modest, built around exploration, navigation and interaction. That restraint is its strength, because nothing competes with the characters or the mystery that slowly unfolds around them. The blend of exploration, conversation and slow-burning storytelling held my attention from start to finish. For anyone seeking a short, emotional and memorable experience, I wholeheartedly recommend it.

Firewatch was one of these games where I've visited the store page for the very first time, watched some trailers and ranked the game to number 1 on my wishlist. Literally it was love from the first sight. Short summary of a long text: This game is amazing, it even exceeded my expectations and will maybe forever have a special place in my heart.

People complain about many things: The game is way too short, it is a stupid walking simulator, there is no real open world, dialogues are boring, the story is too linear, the ending is bad. I don't want to argue too much, everybody has his own opinions, I just want to share some of my impressions. 

The main reason why Firewatch got my first attention was the graphics. I don't care too much about texture quality, shaders etc. What matters for me is that this game is by far the most beautiful game I've ever played. Firewatch has an awesome graphic style, colors and illuminations create an outstanding atmosphere in a very well designed environment with lots of little details to discover. While it is possible to do this in 3 hours, personally I've never understood why people buy and play games in order to rush through them. This is a wonderful exploration game, so take your time, pace yourself and enjoy. I visited many places, watched the sunset, took many screenshots, looked at the books and information pieces lying around and had fun for around 10 hours. If you have an eye for details 5-6 hours should be viable at least. People are right when they say that Firewatch is some kind of walking simulator with simple interactions. You don't need skill to play this game, there is no challenge, no puzzles, everybody can play through it. And this is great. Because It is so chillfull and allows you to focus on the real package: the nature, your map, your compass, your walkie talkie and you. If you disable the location marker on the map it feels even more realistic. Yes, there are borders limiting your open-world experience, I did not care about, everything else was just so good. Voiceacting is the best I've ever heard in any game, no exaggeration, and the music is also very immersive. Boring small talk? C'mon, this 'boring small talk' is absolutely fantastic and one of the reasons why this game is so authentic and emotional. This is what makes you feel like being a part of the game and not just being the audience of a hollywood blockbuster. It is about small and ordinary things, things we like because we are familiar with them. Do you like french movies? Maybe you know what I mean. While the story builds up tension during progress you should not expect and action-packed survival game, expect heart-touching dialogues and an adult story about people dealing with their feelings and problems instead. Firewatch is unusual mature and honest for a game and for me it did far more than just scratching the surface. I also can't think of a better ending, in my opinion it is perfect because it is refreshing realistic and consistent. Everything is said, there's nothing more to explain.

Seriously, nothing has been really negative for me. Sometimes I've wished there would be a bit less talking, a bit more silence. Also there could be more animals. Often you hear but don't see them, for example at the lake. I have not seen the turtle however, another reason why I need to play the game at least once again. Possibilites for hiding the HUD or crouching for better screenshots would be sweet. Regarding the price it can be reasonable to say that there are cheaper games out there in relation to the pure playtime. But that depends on your viewpoint. For me this gaming experience was really revolutionary and I don't regret a single cent I've spent.

I think there should not be a question if Firewatch is good, because it undoubtedly is, there is just the question if this is a game you would like to play. If you are not totally scared by walking simulators in general and the game appeals to you, you should give Firewatch a go. For me it was certainly one of the best games I've ever played.

  -The music is solid. I couldn't stop myself from buying the soundtrack. 
  -The game is surprisingly well polished bug-wise. There are only a couple bugs that I noticed and they weren't exactly game breaking.

Campo Santo did a wonderful job, especially when you consider that their team had maybe a dozen people at the time of making this game. However, the story must be set. Think of it as the Prologue to a new adventure and possibly a new life, well, for Henry of course.

Since folks fancy having things broken down into pros and cons, here we go:
Pros:
Immersive Story
Beautiful world
Witty and believable voice acting
Characters were realistic 
What the characters said directly related to what you were looking at/holding.

Cons:
Short (for $20, I expected something longer than 5 hours of gameplay)
Story fell flat at the end
Henry's inability to navigate over a simple chain-link fence. (play it, you'll see)


If you're looking for action, adventure, romance, puzzles, running from scary axe-wielding maniacs with a flare for hockey, Firewatch isn't for you. The term “walking simulator” gets tossed around quite a bit, and it's technically correct. Henry (the character you play) just basically strolls from one part of the map to another while talking over the radio to his boss. There's no puzzles to sort out and no bears to wrassle. You just do a lot of walking, climbing, jumping down from rocks, and more walking.
However, that being said, the experience was far from boring. In fact, it was wonderful. It wasn't until I finished the game that I realized just how little I had actually done, and I was okay with that. It was a story that kept me gripped and entertained the whole ride.
Henry's conversations with Delilah were witty, well thought out, a ripe with emotion. The voice acting was stellar and it was hard not to get drawn into the story. The developers took a great deal of time and care when it came to designing the conversations between Henry and Delilah. And while it has no impact on the plot, what you're looking at, holding, and interacting with will change the words and responses between the two. That's some awesome game developing, in my opinion. I'm extremely curious what a longer, more in-depth game would be like with this style of character interaction. How immersive would it be if the world and its characters could react to everything your character is doing – such as holding a random poo-shovel for way longer than a normal human would? Little things like that which make the game draw you in like a trap. I'm excited to see more, I'll say the least.
Back on topic, though, Firewatch wasn't perfect. My first run-though took just under 5 hours – which is short for a $20 game – so snag Firewatch when its on sale. The ending also left a little to be desired. Without going into detail, Henry and Delilah are sorting out a big mystery, and it's stocked full of suspense, confusion, and high-strung emotion. And just as it's starting to hit the peak, when some answers might be given – WHAM – out comes a curve ball and you're left going “wait, what?”. The developers do tie it all in, but it left me feeling as though this impressive story they were designing fell flat in the end.
The biggest flaw was with the chain-link fence. No barbed wire – no electric current – just a simple fence with a padlock. How, oh, how will Henry get around this obstacle? Henry decides not to climb the fence (who knows, he might rip his shorts) and decides not to use the terrain to get a boost over (there's a rock next to the fence that ran up the fence to the point where all he had to do was step over and drop down) but instead comes to the conclusion that he will hike a bazillion miles to see if he can find a tool to smash the padlock. In the end, this was more humorous than game-ending, but a flaw nonetheless.
Despite anything wrong with the game, I enjoyed it and I recommend Firewatch for anyone who wants to get drawn into a beautiful game with a nice story. Grab it on sale and take a long evening enjoying it.

So I've finally found the opportunity to play through this indie darling of 2016. And let me start by saying that I thoroughly enjoyed it.
A short but sweet one-and-done type of a game. Its brief playtime (4-5 hours) doesn't take anything away from the impact Firewatch has. I'd actually call it a strength, as anything significantly longer would potentially detract from the final experience by making it feel unnecesarily padded out and risk that the player would start to feel dissatisfied with the lack of deeper game mechanics.
Propelled forward by a strong story with incredible voice acting performances in the spotlight, Firewatch with its beautifully stylized wilderness really immerses you in its world and creates atmosphere that's simultaneously relaxing and cozy, yet unnerving and tense. The groundedness and mundanity not only making it way more relatable than the standard "go save the world" hero's journey you'd find in most games, but also significantly scarier than most survival horror games, despite Firewatch definitely not being what you'd call a horror game.
Go play it, preferrably with as little prior information about it as possible. It's touching and sweet, melancholic, yet funny, scary, yet beautiful, all in the span of 4 hours. It's a game that values your time and I appreciate that.
One small gripe. I'd love it if there was an option in the menu that would disable the player position showing on the map to make the experience even more analog and the navigation bit more challenging.

I don't mind a "game-that-is-not-a-game". I don't mind a very short playtime. But I like my walking simulators to actually bring a provoking story or setting to the table. And Firewatch simply did not deliver for me in the end. It failed to deliver the main thing I was looking for... (just like Gone Home btw).

*SPOILERS*





I really liked that the story in the end wasn't about a big conspiracy, but two (three) flawed characters and simple human tragedy. However, the story being grounded in reality is no excuse for delivering such a muted ending. The setup for an amazing catharsis for both Henry and Delilah was there: however, we ended with some more walking, an empty lookout and a helicopter. I don't really know what I would've wanted instead... but perhaps a bit more resolution and closure. A proper epilogue, I don't know. I get that it's one of the things the game is selling: that real life is not (always) an exiting adventure and that you can't always get what you want. However, I this is also a story, and I am experiencing stories to be moved, to get a different view or to be inspired. Firewatch, in the end, just gave me a really beautiful journey. But to me it's the end that matters.

Pros:
-Beautiful scenery and art direction, even on lowest settings
-Outstanding voice acting
-Very good writing
-Compelling, complex characters
-A unique approach to setting and narrative
-Thought-provoking ending
-Actually engrossing story
-Good pacing for most of the game
-Fantastic level design (Subtle yet effective)

Cons:
-Only 4 hrs gameplay for $20
-Very thin illusion of choice
-Feels like you're on rails while the game is trying to convince you you're not
-Little benefit to exploring in between quests
-No replay value
-A little slow-paced at some points

All in all, I'd recommend this game to people who enjoy short, emotionally engrossing, plot-and-dialog-focused games. But if you were expecting a game where you could wander around in the wilderness for days and find hidden goodies Bethesda style, or a game that is choice-heavy and episodic ala Telltale, you'll be disappointed. Highly recommended. This game was my first step into the "walking simulator" genre, but for those of you who haven't yet tried something like this, it is so much more than what it sounds like. Firewatch was a unique gameplay experience for me, one where you step into the life of your character and sympathize with him even if you don't relate. The game starts off with a surprising amount of backstory, and throughout the game you are able to look at your character's journal and find information about others in the world, but much of it is extra. They're not collectibles; they're purely there to add to the atmosphere and to enhance your immersion. The story is the same for everybody who plays, but there can be differences that may end up adding to your experience. My friend and I played through the game around the same time, and he managed to find a little treat that I missed, that being a pet turtle that he kept through the end of the game. I found myself being rather disappointed that I didn't poke around more. Games like these are not about action, they're more interactive stories than they are games. You are offered small choices, and whether or not these choices make a difference, they feel personal. The strong points in the game are the story, the characters (namely your character and the voice on the radio), the immersion, and the setting. The game won't take you a long time to complete, but it will be a rewarding experience.

[h1] Firewatch is NOT a GAME	[/h1]
When it comes to playing games I don't really have a lot of criteria. I want my experience to be enjoyable, or thought provoking, or I want my game to offer some sort of interesting design or feature. Firewatch does none of these things.
The Firewatch Devs had a story, they wanted to convey what they thought was a "deep" or "relatable" story. And it fell flat on it's ass.

[h1] "Gameplay"	[/h1]
As a game it has absolutely nothing to offer, choosing to rely on it's story to get you through, but here's the thing, if you're planning to make a "game" you've got to offer something for the player to actually do to connect all of the setpieces that the story includes. So what do you do in Firewatch? You walk. A lot. That is the only actual "game" part of Firewatch. Along with some contextual button presses. 

[h1] The World	[/h1]
Being set in the wilderness of Wynoming the devs had every oppurtunity to make the wilderness somewhat pretty to look at? Maybe have some varied wildlife or flora? Nah. You're gonna be seeing a lot of stones and trees. And you better get used to them, because in such a tiny map a lot of your journey is going to be back tracking and getting lost. With nothing but a compass and a map, and with every area of the game looking identical, it's a safe bet you're going to get lost. A lot.

[h1] The Story and the Illusion of Choice	[/h1]
Firewatch's biggest selling point is it's story, it's a narrative based game. And boy oh boy does it suck ass. Donkey ass. You start by making "choices" to decide your character Henry's past. You'd think something like that would impact the story? Does it ♥♥♥♥. The choices you make in dialogue have no bearing on the story what so ever. You may think that you may be making progress with the only other character you speak to, Delilah but the story's ending is a suckerpunch to the ballsack. It commits the sin of making the character think you're making an impact on the events of the game but you're not. Dialogue effects Dialogue and that's it. The actual story is a anti-climactic piece of trash that wouldn't pass for an 8 year old's school project. Without going into too much details or spoilers, you discover someone is listening in to your radio, and you have to discover who it is and what their motives are.

[h1] What it Gets Right	[/h1]
There are a few things that Firewatch gets right, mainly the performance of the two voice actors for Henry and Delilah, they make the characters believable and real, and their respective performances deserve nothing but praise. 
They're are a few moments that set a nice or tense atmosphere using meloncholic music which was a nice touch, however if you linger during any of these moments you'll discover the music loops.

[h1] Final Thoughts.	[/h1]
This game is poor. It presents a faux interesting story that would only appeal to hipsters or people lying to themselves. It isn't fun, it isn't pretty, your choices don't matter and the story sucks balls. This is the only game to ever inspire me to write a full fledged bad review.

tl:dr
The games ♥♥♥♥. Avoid it like the plague.

Mind you that I was playing on all high and I have i7 4790k @4Ghz and gtx 970. 

Sure the story was interesting and the voice acting was great, not to mention that the character's emotions were brought up well, but the fact that most of the plot, such as the boy being found dead, were really predictable, so not really a "WOW I didn't think that would happen"  type of experience. 

Without a doubt the ending was the most annoying thing about the game. You never got to see the Delilah (the person who you communicate with the walkie-talkie throughout the game), Ned (The dude who was creeping on us) or the girls (who vandalized the place). In conclusion, this game is really a one and done type of game, and for 8.99€  I don't see it being worth it.

Firewatch is a beautiful game, but not for everyone. It is said, that it is a walking simulator, but in my opinion this the walking is only used as a trigger for the dialog between you (as Henry) and your supervisor Delilah. Both of you are about 40 years old and have some serious personal problems. And that the reason why this game is not for everyone. You should be of same age and experience in life (at best you are in some relationship) to understand the feelings and thoughts of Henry and Delilah.

The story of the game evolves very fast to something that seems to be a great conspiracy, but in the end, all is very normal, no aliens, no conspiracy, nothing special or unusual at all. You can think of it as a boring end, because your expectations gets quiet high on the secret you think you will find, but this story is so normal that it can real happen, perhaps some aspects of the story are not fiction.

The game mechanic is very simple, not much to learn about it, but you sometimes must decide very quickly your dialog answers. Also it was not easy for me (as non-native speaker) to fully understand some lines. The game give you goals to reach, but the map has more than these goals and if you do not leave the paths you will miss some beautiful places and their story (told you by Delilah). As far as I experienced there is no pressure to reach the goals in a specific time, even if there is a fire burning in the woods. So take your time playing the game and do not rush through it.

It is not a cheap game, but the money was invested in two very good speakers and one or more very good dialog writers. And it was totally worth the money.

I really liked this game, but I am going to have to give it a downvote.

On the plus side, the art and world is beautiful, and it was almost completely bug and typo free. The characters a lovingly created and seem real... even making real, heartbreaking mistakes. The story was engaging and you cared about the characters. As I went along, I grew more engrossed in the mystery - how did the [Spoiler] two "murdered" girls [/spoiler] fit into the plot? Why were they [spoiler] murdered and their camp destroyed? [/spoiler]. Was it some sort of framing job? What were the [spoiler] scientists studying? [/spoiler]. Why wasn't delilah told about the [spoiler] giant fenced off area? [/spoiler]. Basically, who was behind what was [spoiler] an obvious consipiricy? [/spoiler]

But the downsides are vast. I got lost, sidetracked, checked out the view... and the entire story took 3 hours total. This is the length of a long movie :/ The world is also almost completely lifeless - a few very rare wildlife enounters in an area that should be teaming with rodents and birds. The game's short duration also left me with the chance to reflect on the story. Which does not make a lot of sense the more you think about it, as you unravel the "mysteries" above. Specifically, there are a number of serious plot problems:  

First,  [spoiler] the scientist camp springs up out of nowhere, very close to the characters fire tower. And yet Henry doesn't notice and Delilah isn't informed about it and can't get any information about it. Is it really a secret hush-hush government experiment? From what we see, it is a research project relating to earthquakes, or weather, or elk tracking. So WTF is the secrecy about and why can't Delilah get any info? Even if, somehow, Delilah was not informed, then surely she would find out the instant she called in to HQ. Also, again, how TF did someone put up a mile of chain link fence without the character ever noticing? [/spoiler]

Second, [spoiler] why did the sad dad mess with the lady hikers? There was no reason for him to do this, and every reason for him NOT to do this. Consider if a specific area of the forest suddenly has a problem where a mysterious force is regularly attacking campers and hikers. Maybe this would cause an investigation, no? Of course, in the story, it becomes a plot point that Delilah doesn't report this and it looks bad because the kids are missing, and you think they maybe died because their camp is messed up... which really ratchets up the tension. But really the two girls are just in jail?!? If so, all the worry was for nothing, and the sad dad's attack on their campsite only revealed to everyone that there was a mysterious force operating in the park. For. No. Reason. Whatsoever. Man, I really really wanted to like this game. The gameplay I saw of it prior to playing it myself, the dialogue options, the potential for really great character development due to that dialogue... But now after playing it, I'm split down the middle. The dialogue IS great and the voice acting is very good in my opinion, I wasn't let down by that aspect at all. But is that enough to carry the whole game? After having just finished it in 4 hours, I'm at a crossroads in my mind. There were certainly enjoyable moments to it, the banter between your character and Delilah is very charming at times, and fun to listen to. The feeling of seclusion is very real also, and the graphics are definitely above average.
But the MEAT of the game... it's just not there, sadly. The "story" of the game seems a little hamfisted, like it's supposed to be this huge mystery to what's going on, but it turns out to be quite normal in the end. Is it a comedy on how we always perceive things to be different than what they really are? Is it an artistic depiction of impending dread that we are supposed to feel throughout the game, that something truly bizarre is going to be the endgame?
I don't think so. 
The end result we get, is some huge opportunity for character development and friendship through dialogue during many many days of seemingly mundane responsibilities, that is ultimately cut short. The game misleads you into thinking every day will be as long as the first and second, before rapidly fast forwarding a week or two for one dialogue exchange, before then fast forwarding another few weeks. It feels forced and a bit lazy. Instead of actually getting to experience how these characters end up talking in the way they do, we are forced to ASSUME what happened. This would be fine in a sort of "non story centric" game, but in this one, where this is the main attraction; it falls flat, sadly.
I don't feel like I wasted my money, however. The quality of what IS there is very good, and the work behind it is evident. It's just the sum of all the parts that doesn't quite come together in the way you want it to. I'm not going to bash the people behind the game, as what is here is certainly competent. It's just not the "greatness" the critic reviews would have you believe.
I definitely hope this developer learns from this experience and makes more games like this in the future, though. There is a ton of potential here, but my ultimate feeling from playing the game is that that potential was not fully realized.

Firewatch is a really good game. It's on the short side, sure, but it's a great piece of storytelling, world-building, and character design, and it looks and sounds gorgeous to boot. Some people have said the ending is a bit unsatisfying, but I think they're missing the point. It's a really unique story that not a lot of games would try to tell, and although I don't want to use industry buzzwords like "immersive", it really does make you wish you could never leave the world it creates. Oh, and the voice acting is simply spectacular.

Firewatch is a beautiful game, with a compelling story that keeps you hooked until the end. While the game is fairly short, it is in the "walking simulator" genre of story-driven games, so its short length doesn't feel like you've been cheated. It has some of the most unique visuals of any game I have ever played, and I am certain most of you will have seen ingame screenshots from the game across many wallpaper websites. The lack of a HUD simply make the numerous vistas throughout the game, look amazing and compelling. It is one of the most complete game experiences I have had the pleasure to play through, and the only downside I can find with this game, is that sometimes the movement can feel a little clunky and awkward, but this is a problem that typically  plagues walking simulators, so it's  not a serious complaint.  I highly recommend this game to anyone who just wants a short, but moving story to be completely immersed in for a few hours.

Pros:
- Beautiful scenery and art. 
- Very fluid animations for climbing, vaulting, jumping, picking things up, etc. that really help add to the immersion.
- As stated before, voice acting is superb.
- Character development is indepth and leaves you feeling like you personally know each character.
- While short, the story is exceptionally well written.
- Dev's truely care and believe in this game, yet are respectful of people who (respectfully) feel otherwise. That alone is something we don't see too often anymore. 

Cons:
- Short story. 
- May cause motion sickness - I have played hundreds of games, and have only had issues with motion sickness on one game (Dead Island), yet this game left me feeling sweaty, nauseous, and sore after playing for only 15 minutes or so. Luckily for me, I just had to disable head-bob and I was good to go, but some people may also get motion sickness from the unusually low FOV (55-degrees). While this can be adjusted manually in the regedit, you would expect an fov-slider in any modern game. Also, adjusting the FOV to anything wider will cause the animations to clip and will take away from the immersion immensly. 
- I wasn't really satisfied with the ending entirely. SPOILER: [spoiler] I wish you would have the option to be with Delilah and move on from your ill wife, OR stay with your wife. Also, I kinda wished it ended similar to it began, with the text on screen saying what happened to Henry and Delilah after they went their separate ways. [/spoiler]

Over all, For the $10 I spent when it was on sale, I would recommend this to any friend in a heartbeat. For the usual $20 asking price, I would probably only recommend it to a friend whom I know will be able to take it slow, and enjoy every aspect of the game instead of just rushing through the story.  9/10 for me.

But at last I must also point out the ending is kind of anticlimactic (In my views). But still the game is too much fun to miss out.

我取下了布莱恩的照片，我想带给你。我知道你会很难过，但我不希望布兰恩没有留下任何东西在这世上。

灼灼山火鼓起灰蒙的烟雾，我一次次迷失在路上，我以为你会在无线电的另一头 像往常一样鼓励我、陪着我。
我只是始料未及，你说你想先走了，你无法面对我。我很失落，其实我并不担心直升机不会回来，只是有些话还说不出口。
在我可怜兮兮的请求下，你说你可以等等我，让我加快速度。我急得一直在奔跑，我心里喊着，你等等我，我想和你一起离开，一起在直升机上聊聊这两个月的点滴，一起看六月之火最后一眼..
我把照相机带来了呢，我还想跟你合照呢，还有小木桶，它很可爱。
我一边跑，一边想，这就是你天天走的地方啊。

终于到了缆车这里，对面就是你的瞭望塔了，我习惯性地跟你报告着，“Delilah?...”没有回应，好吧，或许你在和救援者聊天呢..

第一次来到你的瞭望塔下，高兴又平静地拾级而上，既熟悉又陌生，就像你一样..
扭开门把手，你不在里面。我很少拍照，但这次一进来就先拍了两张你小屋的全貌。我想了解你，我一样一样，慢慢地翻看着你的东西。瞧，你真的给我画了画像，还贴在了窗户上，可是没我本人帅气呢。
红白灰相间的床单、挂在墙上的白净的衬衫、纯白的碗碟整整齐齐地摞成一叠，很像你的风格呀。
床边有两本填字游戏，就是上次我想抓小浣熊却被你吓走的时候的帮凶吧。
海报上挂着个牌子，写着猪肉水塘，哈哈，看来你真的很喜欢这个名字。

碟子上有切好的苹果，我想你是特地为我准备的，很好吃。
我坐了下来，戴上那副耳机
“Hello，Delilah...”
你说我们可以给对方做未来的选择，我鼓起勇气追求你，我说你应该来我身边，你却劝我回去看看妻子。
我的妻子已经傻了，我一个人很累。你勉强同意来年路过我家时会来看看我。
飞机来了，我们的通话该结束了。平静地走出你的房间，下楼梯....
我看见你的木椅，在房间外，上面还有一副望远镜，当时你就是坐在这偷偷看我的吗？
下了瞭望台，我忍不住打开了你的户外厕所，里面还放着鲜花。

我真的很想和你在这过一辈子，我想和你一起喝着冰镇威士忌，陪你做数独，天气好时爬爬山，我钓鱼回来你做给我吃。
本以为我们还会在一起很久，没想到就这样断了联系。
我对你的感情，或许就像“六月之火”一样，白天只是一缕缕若隐若现的烟雾，到了晚上，却无视忽视。

To start with my only complaint- having played this game so soon after the release of The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, it was difficult not to feel trapped by the trails of Firewatch's Shoshone National Forest. I never once was lost in the woods, and with only a scribbled-on paper map and compass in hand to guide me, that felt like a detriment. A little more time spent creating an open, messy world would have furthered the theme this game seemed to be all about - life isn't tidy.

In that regard, Firewatch's plot was successful from beginning to end. That seems to be a break in the general consensus, but I found the narrative about two people connecting in a strange place in their lives to be cathartic and resonant. A gorgeously crafted soundscape, thorough and flexible script, and two spectacular voice actors allow the player to experience grief, loneliness, fear, distrust, annoyance, amusement, wonder, and genuine interpersonal connection. All in a rather short game! Delilah's performance is particularly effective. Despite most of your few hours together being spent chatting about mundane actions or whatever happens to be in your hand, the actor has brought to life a character you can fall in love with and be pained to leave. I definitely recommend this game to anyone interested in unique or emotional gaming experiences.

I feel that Firewatch isn’t a game for most people. There’s a lot of people and friends I would not recommend this game to but if you’re already looking to buy it, this review is for you. I’ll prewar that this is almost less of a review and more of a love letter. I think all parts of this game are great and as you play through it fully wraps itself up nice and complete. Every little detail in this game was handcrafted to the story they wanted to tell. From the moment I started the game til the moment I finished it, I viewed myself as Henry the entire time.

[h1] Characters [/h1]
There are two main characters: Henry and Delilah. Henry is the main character, you make his decisions and you talk for him. The person you talk to is Delilah. There’s a lot that can be said about Delilah and it’s hard not to say I grew an attachment for her. As a character she was sweet with just enough sass that you could enjoy. She seemed like the kind of woman to take no ♥♥♥♥ but when she was scared it made sense. She was clearly written with a distinct idea in mind and her flaws are probably what made her a good character. I felt that the voice acting only made the characters come out stronger. They had good emotional range and it never felt like I was talking to someone putting on a voice unless of course they were.

[h1] Story and Script [/h1]
The most important aspect of the game and personally the reason why there’s nothing in this game I would change. Every little exchange you have with Delilah adds to the story bit my bit and as you play, you can clearly see the characters feeling for each other. Everything about the interactions is fantastically realistic and I found myself drawn into every moment and every word. From the relaxed banter to the panicked mutters, it was all so real which was only aided by the fantastic voice actors. Each time Henry and Delilah would sass each other I could feel myself giggle and when they were scared I was too. Their emotions easily influenced me and I can honestly say that this is the type of writing one aspires to do. I haven’t really mentioned the story so far and I think it’s better to just play the game with no idea of what’s to come. I honestly could have sat there and talked to Delilah for the entire game but I’m glad they decided to have a story that really drew me in. It’s a bit more on the realistic side and I feel that a lot of gamers won’t really appreciate it but as an avid reader, it was really refreshing for a game’s story.

[h1] Environment [/h1]
This is a beautiful game. Living in Australia this isn’t the type of landscape I can see or explore. Being able to walk through the game as Henry and every so often stopping to take photos, I feel was a great experience. It feels like all the little details in the game are really lovely. Even though each area looked distinct enough, I did find myself getting lost and walking the wrong way but I strongly feel that, that’s a me thing. I think that the most spectacular part though was how they used the environment to section off areas for you to unlock later. It was a brilliant use of design and made perfect sense. I feel all in all that the environment, the trees, streams and canyon areas, really tie the game and story together.

 [h1] Soundtrack [/h1]
I will be listening to this soundtrack for the rest of my life. I think every song is perfectly atmospheric and add to the mystery that slowly amounts through the game. Each song made with the sole intention to truly sink the feelings you’re currently having in. They beautifully reflect what is happening or about to happen. All of the really peaceful songs set in as you walk into an area for the first time and it just makes my heart sing. You could almost say they use silence in this game far more then they use sound but when they do, they do it perfectly. I’d also like to make a little note that the choice of credit song was fantastic. While I’m pretty sure it was picked based on the idea that the people playing this game are on the older side, I still loved it. I grew up with this song and it really, for me, tied the game up perfectly.

[H1] What Makes it Special? 100/100 [/h1]
There’s not a single thing I would change about this game and sure there’s a lot of you who would disagree but this game was so well written. I loved every moment of it. I craved to play the game when I couldn’t and if I could go through again with fresh eyes it would be a fantastic experience. As I have stated again and again through this review every little thing was handcrafted. Each feature and idea they put their all into. This was a game made with love and while I was playing it, I felt that love. If you do like walking simulator type games, this is a must buy.

It is more of an interactive movie than some other games. I’d expect play times to really vary from about 2-5 hours. 

I’ve seen some reviews complain about the duration of the game. I think it is a complete narrative without a lot of filler content. The game could have been padded with some more non-plot content: you could have had to report fires or use the fire finder in some mini-game or go out and do maintenance work. But they would have simply been padding and it wasn’t at all really needed. 

The story continuously moves forward and is engaging to the end. If you think about the game in terms of something like a movie, TV show or book and less like a typical game, I think you would be satisfied. Though, much like with a book, there is limited “immediate” re-play potential. 

The writing and story were outstanding. The opening series of scenes left me heart-broken and the end also hit me hard. The mystery and suspense were definitely very intense and exciting. The ending felt a little weaker after the intensity of the middle acts, but was not a disappointment. 

I’d recommend Firewatch to many of my friends who are into narrative-driven content, whether games, books or TV. I don’t think I’d recommend it to younger friends or friends who just want to blow stuff up.

It's been called a "walking simulator" but in all honesty I'm not sure if I can even call this a game.  See to me a game has to provide some kind of obsticle to challenge the player to be called a game,  

While video games often resort to obsticles trying to kill you, a game certainly doesn't need violence to challenge a player, but it needs something.  This game really doesn't really have much in the way of such obsticles.  You pick things up and look at them, you talk to your supervisor, and you walk around, and if you come to what looks like a dead end, your supervisor will point you in the right direction.  So I'm not sure I can call this a game, though it makes for an interesting interactive experiance.  

The world is colorful, There are choices to be made in how Henry responds to Delilah that can effect their relationship.  Henry and Delilah feel like actual people and not caricatures.   

Furthermore the game does a better job making tragedy believable in the first 5 minutes of play using simple text, then most AAA games do  with visually dramatic opening sequences.  Even those who have never watched a family member go through Dementia will find it hard to fight the feels that the opening gives you just by text alone.  

Some who have played this find the ending anticlimatic, but then such is the way of life, and I think that's what the dev's were going for, real people facing situations in a realistic manner.  

In closing If your looking for a game to challenge you, you might want to look elsewhere.  But if you're looking for an well thought out and put together interactive experiance that won't make you want to smash your keyboard, you may want to give this a try.

Like a lot of the other reviews for this game, I really wanted to love this game. The atmosphere and scenery were really well done. It reminded me a lot of that isolated feeling you get when playing something like The Long Dark, and I appreciate the consideration that went into trying to create an immersive experience like that. The voice acting was well done, but Henry could have had a little more life to him. Delilah was the one character that was well established, even if there were a lot of unanswered plot holes about her past. I'm not sure why certain things like her sister, her boyfriend, etc... were brought up very briefly and then never explored again. Then it takes a turn for the weird with how attached she is to a certain character, and how the game goes from Henry struggling with his past to all eyes on Delilah. The ending was just abrupt, and the story seems like it was done by two writers; someone started, and someone else finished.

I even feel a little cheated by the intensity that the game starts with, like it was used to drawn me in quickly and get me emotionally attached, and then the sincerity and severity of the first 5 minutes are just discarded for booze jokes and sudden paranoia. 

And I was really aggravated by the way things ended with Delilah. This woman starts their relationship by prying, and almost relentlessly probing Henry's past. She draws him. She starts building this relationship with him very aggressively, even pushing romantic notes, and then at the end, Henry is made to feel like he's crossing the line and she treats him so coldly? Very poorly done.

Firewatch isn’t loud about anything. The air is quiet, the colours soft, and the loneliness feels familiar in a way that stirs something old inside you. It doesn’t shove grief in your face or hold your hand through resolution. It just lets you walk, slowly, through the kind of quiet that says more than words ever could, long enough for you to hear the things you’ve been trying not to say.

You play as Henry, who takes a job watching for wildfires in the Wyoming wilderness after his wife’s illness and their unravelling life leave him emotionally stranded. He doesn’t fight. He doesn’t try to fix. He just… leaves. And the story never punishes him for the urge to retreat, for finding comfort in emptiness, for choosing the peace of doing a job no one sees or thanks him for.

But solitude doesn’t mean isolation. Over a radio, you meet Delilah. And slowly, you open up to each other. It’s messy, funny, intimate, and vulnerable. You speak into a radio and hope the voice on the other end stays. You hold your breath, waiting for the next reply, pretending it’s enough.
It isn’t. You know it isn’t. But some of us only speak our truth when we think nothing will come of it, when we’re safe behind the distance.

Firewatch is warm, aching, quiet. It’s a beautifully lonely piece of storytelling.
If you’ve ever needed space before you could speak, if you’ve ever left something unfinished but not forgotten, this one will stay with you.

If this is meant to be a hiding place, it fails, gracefully. Because even in the wilderness, you’re eventually asked to come back. To choose. To do.

And maybe that’s the quiet message we are meant to see in it: Some doors don’t close when you leave. They remain open, just enough, for you to come back and try again.

I have a complicated relationship with this game, having pirated it way back when it came out and really disliking it back then. I was also young back then and went into it with a sour disposition for the same reason I didn't pay for it - half-writing it off under the oft-thrown-about label of "Walking Simulator". Recently, I played a couple other National Park horror/mystery games (namely [i]Radiolight[/i] and [i]Fears to Fathom: Ironbark Lookout[/i]), which took a lot of DNA from Firewatch to mixed effect and made me somewhat nostalgic for a game I didn't like very much. I thought that now, as a more mature and experienced person, I would give it another try in the hopes that I would get more out of it. It's happened before, it could happen again. Besides, it was like five bucks in the winter sale.

But nah. [i]Firewatch[/i], I still hate you so much. 

I don't hate this game because it's bad, mind you. I actually find the majority of this game to be pretty good. There's not much in terms of proper gameplay outside of walking around and reporting stuff over the radio, but the conversations that result (more on that later) are often charming enough to make it somewhat engaging to look for things around the park to talk about. The art style is also gorgeous to this day, and there's some truly beautiful sights to see around the park, especially at sunset, and the soundtrack - while not something I would casually listen to - is a great backdrop for wandering this chunk of wilderness. It's relaxing to just walk around and explore, seeing the sights, idly chatting over the radio, and there's even a camera to snap a couple pictures of vistas you particularly enjoyed. Good stuff. 

So, this is all pretty positive so far, I'll admit - but this is one of the fundamental problems with [i]Firewatch[/i]. 

All of this is in service of a story that left me scratching my head and wondering what the point was. Ostensibly, this is supposed to be a mystery game, and that aspect is actually not bad, if a little haphazard with its introduction to the story, kind of just popping into the narrative at a certain point. The resolution isn't entirely logical, and there's many logical leaps in the actions of the antagonist, but a lot of this can be attributed to that antagonist's characterization, so I don't entirely mind.  I didn't like this resolution much when it came out, but now I think its fine. Had everything else wrapped up in a satisfactory fashion, I'd probably be flipping this to a recommend and not writing this right now, but here we are. 

You play as Henry, a man whose wife contracted early-onset dementia, leaving him alone, sad, and looking to get away from it all, hence why he takes up the position of a fire lookout. She doesn't remember who he is, her family snatched her away and hates his guts, and so here we are. Your only company is your supervisor Delilah, who you speak to over the radio and report things to. Their relationship is meant to be the real crux of the game, and their voice acting and dialogue tends to be great and one of the best aspects of the game. They're characters with defined personalities, but this relationship that the game hinges on is awkward paced and with a resolution that makes the mystery plotline seem like a work of absolute art in comparison. The progression of their attachment to each other is very strange and the game skips over vast swathes of time that really could have been used to further develop their relationship in a way that would resolve almost all of these issues. 

The resolution of their relationship at the end of the game is just deeply unsatisfying. This is intentional to a degree, but in combination with the resolution of the mystery, it really just leaves you sitting there wondering what the point of playing any of this was. Maybe that feeling is the point, but it doesn't mean I like it. Maybe the game is a character study of these two people, but the more I ruminate on it, the more I feel like neither of these characters actually has much depth to them outside of Henry and his wife's whole deal - which is something I also don't like because the game throws a lot of really bizarre messaging out there and seems to really want him to not move on and live his life outside the shadow she cast. Odd. 

The game seems to want you to get really invested in this relationship, but I just wasn't having it. I liked the dialogue, I liked the banter, but I didn't find much of their closeness believable at all and Delilah in particular is charming but a real piece of work when you get down to it and really think about her after the fact. Again, probably the point. Your mileage may vary. 

The other problem actually is with the gameplay, and that's that while walking around is fun, there's not much firewatching you get to do. You check out smoke plumes a couple times, and other times you go around hunting for tools, but there's entire implied mechanics like the Osbourne Fire Finder that actually aren't mechanics and never utilized. I actually really wanted to just have Henry do his damn job, but the game never allows for that to happen outside of a few spots. It's also pretty buggy, which is something I didn't remember. I had to restart the game twice (thank god it's short) because Henry got his ass clipped on top of the climbing tope tie-off rocks and stumps and I couldn't get down no matter how much I spastically jiggled him around.

Anyway, yeah. [i]Firewatch[/i]. I give it a "Don't Recommend" almost entirely because Steam doesn't allow for any nuance with this kind of thing, but it might still be worth picking up on a deep sale just to wander the national park and take photos. Just don't expect to get anything rewarding out of it.

Firewatch is a walking simulator that evolves into a mystery in its final stages before it all fades away. This game explores themes of isolation and delves into feelings of solitude and sadness. It is a game about grief.

As I mentioned earlier, this game primarily functions as a walking simulator. Thus, the gameplay isn't particularly exciting; however, exploring the forest can be quite soothing. It encourages a sense of calm; there isn't much to do except hike around, fix things, and discover your surroundings, along with experiencing getting stung by a bee, being startled by a raccoon, adopting a turtle, and occasionally getting hit in the head.

The beginning of Firewatch features a poignant story. As you hike up the mountain, you receive flashbacks of the past, learning how Henry met his wife, how they fell in love, how they spent their time together, and how everything changed once Julia developed Alzheimer’s. This makes for an emotionally charged experience. Henry struggles to escape his sadness, trying to forget that his beloved wife is forgetting him, while a father copes with the death of his son, creating a powerful emotional journey. That said, the ending of Firewatch was disappointing, yet it also felt fitting. Although there was no grand conspiracy, twist, or perhaps a happy ending, the conclusion felt like a true ending—an end to evading the real world, an end to trying to forget your grief, and an end to both summer and the job you took. It's hard to express in words, but the ending is crafted in a way that leaves everything open to your interpretation. Did Henry reunite with his wife? Did he leave? Did he and Delilah ever meet? It’s up to you to decide, which, in my view, was a wise choice. This makes the game more memorable than others because the ending prompts you to ask questions and encourages you to fill in the narrative with your own imagination.

Before a few days ago, I was caught between wanting to immediately play Firewatch and waiting until I had a decent enough computer to run it without immersion-breaking frame drops while also having enough funds to actually buy the game. After waiting for so long, I had of course heard that it was a very short game but nonetheless good, and with this I wholeheartedly agree. 

Firewatch is a grounded game that does more exploration of human mentality than it does exploration of nature. Even as you play through the game and strange things start happening, it all eventually circles back to a grounded telling of the characters involved, and explains away odd happenings with desperation and denial. 

With a game being beautiful on both the visual and mental side of things, I can do nothing but recommend a game that, on the surface, appears to be naught more than a 4-hour walking simulator, but opens up to an amazing storytelling experience.

This is one of the most beautiful, emotional, and immersive stories I've walked through in a very long while. Where as Gone Home was a story from an outsiders standpoint, reading about what was going on in the home while you were gone. FireWatch is a story where you play as a character, experiencing what it's like to be him while facing a difficult trial in his life, in a time where he felt the need to escape the life he had for a summer. 

You get placed into a very beautiful forest (yellowstone?) and your story unfolds as you learn about the life you're escaping from along with the life of the person on the radio and the former watchers that stayed in your tower before you. Meanwhile learning about the mysterious events that seem to be following you. There are also a myriad of things to find and collect along with a Disposable camera that at the end of the game you can get the photos you took in game developed and mailed to you IRL.

Although the game is short, very short (Too short for most peoples tastes. But as my grand-pappy always said, "it's not the size of the ship but the motion of the ocean" and this story, although short has a lot of motion.). It's important to note that this isn't a "game" as much as it is an interactive short story. [u][b]Anyone who wants to buy this game thinking it's going to be fast pace, rush through, full of action, heroism, valor, etc. Should probably turn away and not buy this.[/b][/u] However if you're going to take this game slowly, explore and let yourself be immersed in the character and his surroundings and truely experience the world that Cammpo Santo create, if you want some time to spend on a story that will have you ponder life choices, give you many hard feels and leave you shocked, then this is a game I reccomend. (Basically if you liked games like Dear Esher, Gone Home, Lifeless Planet, Stanley Parable - to an extent -, The Beginner's Guide, or Dream you'll enjoy this. However if you didn't like that style don't get it, you'll dislike it.) 

[h1]In Conclusion[/h1]
This story is potentially going to be one of the best interactive story "games" that will come out this year (and perhaps for the next few years). Also is quite possibly my favorite of these interactive stories to be released yet. [b]Though I cannot emphasize this enough because I can definitely see this happening; [u]if you're going to buy it, do it knowing it's a short story. One of the best story-driven experiences ever. [b]Firewatch[/b] has this crazy way of sucking you in with its charming characters and narrative, making it almost impossible to put down. 

It's a first person linear-open world experience with a big focus on story following a broken man named Henry and the relationship he has with his cohort, Delilah. Players will experience a really well-written script between these two characters through radio communications as part of the Wyoming wilderness firewatch.  

The core gameplay is simple and streamlined with the main focus centering on dialogue choices and how the player advances the relationship between the characters. This ends up being the game's strong point however, seeing as the voice acting and writing offered here is superb. 

The main issue [b]Firewatch[/b] struggles with has to do with its length. While shorter narrative experiences can be every bit as impactful as longer titles, [b]Firewatch[/b] ends up faltering because there's just not enough time for the characters to fully open up and develop. 

When essential character development starts to take place the game already reaches its end, making a lot of the dialogue feel like filler - seeing as most of topics discussed between Henry & Delilah are never revisted. 

Other than that, [b]Firewatch[/b] still offers an excellent experience, giving players with a beautiful game world to roam around and explore in coupled with a really touching story line. 

[h1]Verdict:[/h1] 

Offers a story that will definitely tug at your heartstrings and will leave you dying for a sequel. Despite its short length it's still more than worth your time if you enjoy story-driven games.

This game opens up, I think, better than any story I've ever heard. It puts you into a scenario, and tells you that you experience certain things. Of those certain things, you can decide certain outcomes to determine future narrative in the story. And honestly, that part, the connection that the beginning had with me personally, was great. The scenario described is something I've had a certain deep lingering fear in the back of my mind as if, what if this were to ever happen to me, to my family. It scares me. It honestly does; indeed, I could even imagine myself taking similar courses of action as to those which are in the game. However, as far as that segment of the story goes, that's it. I mean, it will be brought up in conversations, sure, but the entire purpose of the story from that point on, is how disconnected you can get from that. The beginning of the game is by far the most emotional point of the entire game, which traditionally, is kind of odd.

My real pet peeve in regards to this game, is that the climax comes almost out of nowhere, and then it's gone. There was no real rising action leading up to it either. All of a sudden, there's something going on, there's more stuff going on, there's a bunch of even weirder stuff, both that you find, and are told about. And then, in the end, half of all that you found out, half of all that had peaked your interest, and really made you question what was going on, is seemingly completely and totally irrelevant. What?

All of that being said, I still for the most part, like the game. It has excellent voice acting; excellent, interesting visuals; and at times, but like I said but, mostly the beginning, was very emotionally touching. I won't defend some holes in the story that honestly could have been far better. All I'm saying, is that there could have been a far deeper, more exhilarating ending, if there had been just a little more effort involved, in my opinion; but like I said, I enjoyed it. 

Whether or not it's worth $20, I will leave purely up to you, though.

A very pretty game that very, very narrowly gets a recommendation.  I wanted to like this game, but it's not entirely what I expected.  Despite being set in the Wyoming wilderness, there's no real exploration to be done.  All the locations feel close together, and are arbritarily walled off by story, hamfisted item progression, or invisible walls.  Despite this, due to the game keeping you almost always on the low ground, navigation is almost impossible without the map.

All of these are minor compared to the story mechanics.  The time limited chance to respond to radio messages is crippled by disallowing radio responses while the map is up or the player is examining some items.  Since responses drive the story, this was a pretty huge oversight by the development team.  To their credit, the characters seem well enough written, and they have reasonable backgrounds.  Unfortunately, the story amounts to: even out in the Wyoming Wilderness, with mysterious events transpiring, the human condition shows up to miserably wipe all that away and substitute it with "yeah, people suck."

A huge question remains up in the air.  Or, possibly, I missed the chance to have the characters discuss it correctly (possibly due to the bad story response mechanic), and the writing down that particular path ignored the elephant in the room for the rest of the game.  [spoiler] Even after the story turns to Ned monitoring radio communications to cover up the fact his son died, there is no good reason for the Wapiti Station documentation to exist.  Are we really supposed to believe Ned created and filled out forms that included the susceptibility of Henry and Delaila to manipulation and discovered history they hadn't even discussed on the radio???  In my game, once it was revealed that Ned had been stalking the player, concerned about Henry making a discovery at the cave, this subject never comes up again between the protagonists.  It seems like the writer forgot what they wanted to do with this information, and it just got swept under the run.[/spoiler]

It could be that I wasn't able to progress the story or make a discovery that brings this into better focus.  Perhaps the main characters were both misled in my game, but the fact neither of them brings it up ever again, even questioningly, feels sloppy.

Also I took photos expecting I would need them to back up the story the characters would have to present at the end of the game.  Instead, they're just fluff for the gallery, so you may as well take just the prettiest pictures you can, or better yet take more and better ones by pressing F12, because this game is on Steam.  Sheesh.

So, why even call this game a positive experience?  I like the visuals, I like the characters, the voice acting is really good, the gameplay does mostly what it needs to (I only experienced one bug, falling through a log crossing), and for a few minutes there things were pretty tense.  It's just unfortunate that the main storyline leaves the player feeling "damn, that sucks" rather than "Whoa!  Mystery solved!"

It's like watching a movie, only you're part of the movie and have a dominant hand in how the characters develop. About five hours of playthrough content, and I HIGHLY recommend you just play through it all at once. 10/10, would eagerly play any sequel.

Gameplay 
The gameplay is simple, basically just navigating the map, walking/climbing and making dialogue choices based on the conversation and your surroundings. This is very much a narrative driven game.

Note - The beginning of the game has you reading a through the back story of your character, this does not continue throughout the game. 

Story
Obviously I will not be giving any spoilers, but I feel that this is definitely a game worth playing. It’s not ground-breaking, but the writing & performance of the characters are done really well. I can say, without hyperbole, that Firewatch is one of the best games I have played in years. It looks gorgeous, it has a rich story, and it has more humane and relatable characters than any game I have ever played. The first five minutes is Pixar style merciless emotional gut punching. By the end, you are reduced to a tinfoil hat wearing paranoiac. In between, there is constant stream of big laughs. In just five hours, I experienced a more complete story than a hundred of Skyrim.

Some people will moan about "walking simulators", and dismiss these kinds of games as though they need a challenge to be wroth investing in. Firewatch has a lot of walking, but it isn't as if there is no game here. The only difference is that the gameplay takes place in your head, rather than on the keyboard. Did you find a weird out of place clue? Did someone not answer your question quick enough? You are constantly cross-examining and second-guessing every little detail you pick up, as the story funnels you into an ever expanding intrigue plot. A lot of that is down to the lack of face to face human interaction; with only a walky talky to communicate, you find yourself incredibly suspicious of any ambiguity in conversations, and tactically trying to craft the best response. This isn't a walking simulator, it is a talking, thinking, walking, flirting, lying, mystery, thriller, adventure game. Don't cheat yourself out of it.
