[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Firewatch is a short and charming game. A lot of people know it as the average walking simulator that is great for wallpapers, but I think it’s much more than that. The game is a beautiful walking simulator with great voice acting and writing. It is worth a playthrough, but not at the price of $20.

[h1]✅ Quick Pros and Cons List ❎[/h1]
[b][u]Pros[/u][/b]
[list]
[*] Great setting complimented by simplistic but beautiful graphics that give the game a unique pastel style.
[*] Surprisingly great voice acting for the first indie game by a small indie game studio
[*] Story keeps you on the edge of your seat, and makes the peaceful wilderness into a place of mystery and even horror.
[/list]

[b][u]Cons[/u][/b]
[list]
[*] Despite the great story, its ending falls a bit flat.
[*] The story goes by very fast, and the game is very short. You could easily finish it in one sitting.
[/list]

[h1]🕹️ In-Depth Review[/h1]
Firewatch is a very simple game, with not a lot of people you talk to as a firewatcher in the lonely Wyoming wilderness. The only person you talk to in the game is your supervisor: Delilah. The world is absolutely beautiful and the voice and writing is great, but the game just goes by too fast. It doesn’t help that there isn’t a lot to the game outside of hiking, climbing, rappelling, investigating, and chitchatting with Delilah.

[b][u]Gameplay[/u][/b]
The gameplay of Firewatch is simple. The game is notorious for being a walking simulator, which get a bad rep as barely being a “video game.” Despite this, I still think the gameplay was a nice change of pace from most games I play. Hiking, climbing, and rappelling through the beautiful Wyoming wilderness was relaxing and jaw dropping in the right lighting. There even is an option to explore the open world without the story. The exploration you’ll be doing is complimented by the game’s superb audio design. The calming wind, rustling of leaves, and the sound of displacing grass and dirt as you walk through it is spot on. There is also some pretty amazing music in this game. While there isn’t a lot of it, it always seems to come in at the perfect time during your adventures among the medium-sized open wilderness you explore during your time in the game.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2028813072
My main problem with the gameplay is that Campo Santo didn’t take more advantage of the atmosphere. There isn’t much beside hiking, climbing, and rappelling, and there’s not more to do outside of the linear story besides finding some extra dialogue. There’s almost no animals and no other activities you can do, like camping or fishing. The story just encapsulates the game too much, when there could have been much more to the game that could have taken advantage of the wonderful world and atmosphere Campo Santo has developed.

[b][u]Story and Writing[/u][/b]
The story is the game’s biggest strength. The protagonist you play as is Henry, a man who decided to take his break from his stressful life by becoming a firewatcher in the Shoshone National Forest in Wyoming in 1989. You quickly meet and connect with Delilah, the supervisor of all the firewatchers in the forest, who you can romance or simply befriend through your dialogue choices. As the game seems calm at first, it quickly takes some crazy, wacky, and terrifying turns. It also touches on some heavy topics, like the paranoia that can come from the isolation of being a firewatcher, PTSD, and being framed by someone you’ve never known or met.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2028808191
Despite loving the story, I thought it went by way too fast. I preferred the lighthearted and calm first hours of the game against the dark and intense later hours of the game. I wish the slow start of the game was longer, with more moments of lighthearted banter between Henry and Delilah before the story ramped up, so we had more time to see their natural chemistry. Campo Santo got me attached to them and had me wanting more in 3-4 short hours. Imagine what they could’ve done with 10+ hours of high-quality story and voice acting, with more balance between calm and intensity. I dare to say it would’ve been one of the best indie games ever made. The ending was also a bit underwhelming. I expected a big payoff at the end, but there was mainly some dialogue that wrapped up the story and some neat things that you discover. I think it felt underwhelming because the game was simply so short, which didn’t leave a lot of time to build up to a climax. 

[h1]🖥️ Technical Overview[/h1]
[b]PC Specs: i5 8600k, 16GB RAM, GTX 980ti
Played at 1440p[/b]
Even though this game is about 4 years old as of the writing of this review, the graphics have aged very well. They give the world a great cartoon-y and pastel feeling, and make the world look like a painting in the right view. Lighting, shadows, fog, and physics are perfect. I ran the game at 1440p with the settings maxed out, and stayed around 100-120 FPS, which is more than enough for this type of game. I ran into the occasional stutter when the game was loading the world during gameplay, but other than that, the game ran butter smooth.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2028809520

[h1]💳 Content-to-Price Ratio[/h1]
As of the writing of this review, the game retails at $19.99, and it can drop under $10 on sale. Despite all the positivity I’ve just spouted about this game, I think it’s not worth the retail price, because it’s simply too short with a lot of untapped potential and relatively low replay value. However, it’s definitely worth it on sale because it is worth a playthrough.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Firewatch is a small, charming, and beautiful game. This is the only game by Campo Santo as of the writing of this review, and I can’t wait to see what else they brew up in the future, because there is some serious talent behind this game. In fact, there is a Steam store listing for a game called [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/687440/In_The_Valley_of_Gods/]In the Valley of Gods[/url] that is being developed and published by Campo Santo, with no release date planned yet. I’m excited to see what’s next for this small indie studio!

I'll be honest, this is a very good game. Much more mechanically rich than its peers such as Gone Home, Dear Esther, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, the Witness, et cetera. As in you actually do things and work to unravel an actual mystery.

However, the game is short, and the devs fail to deliver on promises they made about the game.

Someone who takes their time and doesn't spring everywhere will finish the game in three hours. Three. That's it, that is all it takes to go from start to finish. Someone intentionally speedrunning could probably finish the game in less than an hour. The developers had promised a six hour game if one were to rush. That is most certainly not delivered on. Additionally, the game's story is decent at best and raises more questions than it actually answers - the only way the story could be worse was if it hinted at a sequel.

At $18.00 USD, $20.00 when off-sale, I can't reccomend this game. Maybe if it gets 50% or 75% off during a spring sale will it be worth it, but not at this price.

[h1] My Honest Reaction to [b] Firewatch.  (9/10) [/b] [/h1]
I didn't know how a game as beautiful and naturally 'human' as it is, could instil in me so much terror.

[i] Minor spoilers as this is something to play firsthand with no context. [/i]

At first, I was expecting a chill game and space out to a significantly gorgeous nature simulator, having to set out and accomplish minor tasks as a forest lookout volunteer. 
Then finding out I'm not so alone in these woods, did something to my gut that made me feel a ounce of fear than any other intentional horror game I've played (I usually never get vocally scared, but this game did slightly widened my eyes and increase my heart-rate by a smidge). 
I also want to give props to the realistic back and forth between Henry and Delilah's dialogue, whose realistic banter has only captivated my attention and intrigue for how this story will progress and what becomes of these lonely forest lookouts.

I totally resonate how fragile and vulnerable Firewatch portrays the experience of life through the glimpses and utters of Henry's life leading up to his job as a lookout. The specks of his downsides has sculpted what can only be described as a sympathetic human figure and I appreciate the game introduces our main character and plot's catalyst in the form of a stripped-down visual novel format establishes Henry's character to immediately feel sorry for and relate to (since we are playing him).
I also appreciate that the game [spoiler] doesn't lead to a happy ending, but instead leaves the player with a salty & bitter taste in their mouth; that they didn't uncover the conspiracy or save the forest from a ravaging wildfire, [/spoiler] whose entire summer job was not an escape, but a place to reflect how life's complications need to be fixed rather than reminisce on how to prevent it, which is what Henry probably needed to take from this journey.
The game's minimal provision of controls (running, interacting, compass etc.) only heightened the level of vulnerability that the player must've felt, reinforcing the fact that you are not an invincible, combat-proficient sleeper agent... but just [i] some guy [/i], which made the adventure so much more enticing.

[h3] TL;DR [/h3]
[b] Firewatch [/b] is a magnificently alluring outdoors simulator masquerading as an intriguing and life-resonating mystery thriller experience. [b] 9/10 [/b]

The first two hours of Firewatch were very excellent. Then it kind of slowly and awkwardly slides its way off-stage with one of the most unsatisfying endings I've ever played.

It's a shame that a game so laugh-out-loud funny, so emotional, and so well-crafted has to end with such a sad whimper of an ending. Why. 

Imagine if you were playing Uncharted or something and you're being hit with the usual story flags: hints at the ancient civilation, signs of a curse, and then Drake discovers that it was all some elaborate prank some dude pulled off. Everyone packs their stuff up and goes home. The game ends.

What I'm getting at is that Firewatch has incredibly minimal payoff for everything it expertly builds up, Reflecting on it now, there's a defining moment in the game [spoiler] Finding Wapiti Station and you start second guessing everything that has happened to you	[/spoiler] where the story begins its gradual descent from everything it worked towards. 

Is the point of the story that [spoiler] sometimes there doesn't always have to be crazy conspiracy experiment going on? 	[/spoiler] Maybe so. But this could easily be told in a way that doesn't make you feel like you've just wasted four hours.

Here's another wonderful kicker. None of your choices matter.

Firewatch is an amazing experience at the start. There is a great setup, tremendous innuendo that hints at a great mystery, and a world that quickly sucks you into the story. The problem is that the game cannot sustain this for the final act. And the grand reveal is - unfortunatly - underwhelming. 

The game spends a long time setting up conflicts that are never actually explored. And at the end, i was quite convinced that  i hadn`t seen the "true" ending, because all of the conflict and mystery i was invested in was tossed aside.

I wont spoil the story. When I read reviews that complain about story i often find that super subjective. If anything, i take statements like these as challenges to see the story myself. And if you are a skeptic like me and do play it, i think you will agree the setup is amazing. You wanna see the end of the mystery, There are these weird unexplained events, and the things you say trap you in the unwraveling mystery. But i warn you, the ending does not do the story justice. There are plot holes everywhere at the end. 

And its such a shame! The VO work is great, and the walkie talkie mechanic really grounds the characters. There are tons of little treats to be examined everywhere you look, and its such a pleasure that they feed into the mystery and suspense of Firewatch. The world is beautiful, and the exploring mechanics - especially early on - fire off all of the good brain chemicals.

But i cannot stress this enough: the ending takes all of the goodwill the game builds up for three hours and betrays it. It doesn`t accomplish it by making the characters do something without choice (a la Mass Effect 3 forcing you into a set of choices) or by an ending that disregards the players choices (a la bioshock infinite). Its not a cliche or even a nonsensical twist.

The ending is just deeply dissapointing. 

Play it yourself and see. If there turns out to be a true ending, i would be totally willing to reconsider. But for now, its a character study that portrays itself as a mystery. The ending is not bad in a subjective way, i think. Its bad in how it sets up the characters and our relationship with them in a way that is deliberatly manipulative.

I want to firstly say I have mixed feelings on this game, and that I recommend getting it on sale.

Technically speaking, the game is weak. Its kind of just a walking simulator that breaks up walking with animations. And even the few interactables in the world tend to have some issues. Animations ending too early, dropping you at the wrong point, or causing your to just straight up move in an unintended direction with no way to break out. Softlocked me once or twice in my playtime, had to load a previous save and try again. This seems like something that should have popped up in playtesting and been fixed for the amount of times it had occurred to me. Story's ending is kind of weak if you didn't find all the bonus things that aren't required for the story, too many loose threads (which does encourage a second playthrough). Even with all the information, there's no real moral to the story, or even a solid conclusion. You kind of just experience it, which I suppose is fine for most. You arrive, you participate, you leave. The mysteries get solved and you get sad. The side objectives are pretty few and far between, mostly tied down to your exploration. And it feels like some of these systems could have been fleshed out just a little bit more. For instance, collecting all the books doesn't really have any benefit other than being able to fill your bookshelf. But the game never even tells you its possible, and you can't 'save' them the way you can with papers. You have to lug each one by hand back to your watchtower. Last bad thing, the choices in the stories dialogue change so very little. I enjoyed hearing differing voicelines on the second playthrough, but the only 'choices' that really affect the outcome of anything are what you choose in the text section at the beginning. It really feels like this game was created the way it was to avoid having to animate other people besides yourself, but a lot of the core moments in the story are sort of distant from the player as a result. You really have to roleplay the role you've been given, rather than experiencing the player's background. And your choices don't really matter anyways.

There is good in this game though, hence the recommended status. It's pretty, the music is great, and the character dialogue is very well written too. There's not a line or delivery that feels out of place in the whole runtime. If you're here for story, the games got it. Like walking in the woods? This may not be a one-for-one, but it's pretty darn good. It's cool to go exploring, to talk with Delilah (the voice on the radio), to solve the mystery at hand. The game genuinely had me deeply interested throughout, even if the ending was a little weak. For such a short game, you get real connection with these characters the same way you would with any novel. I think the mild obsession with books in the game tells a little about the world-builders in a non-straightforward way, because its evident they know how to write. Anyways, I can't say much more without forwarding a game playthrough. If you don't mind a little jank and enjoy e-novella type games, this is absolutely something you should take a look at. Being an outdoorsman myself I have quite a bit of appreciation for the content, but I think anyone willing to enjoy some scenery will enjoy the game.

[h1]Firewatch Review[/h1]
[i]**Spoiler Free**[/i]

[u]Quick Review:[/u] Firewatch is an atmospheric exploration game that’s light on gameplay mechanics but delivers a fantastic experience. The story and voice acting are top notch, and the atmosphere is inviting with its stylized art.  This game might be about walking through the woods, but it can be as intense and thrilling as it is peaceful and beautiful. I highly recommend you give this game a shot. Walking around in the woods can be much more interesting than you think. 

[u]Gameplay:[/u] As I said before, the gameplay is a simple atmospheric exploration game. There is no combat, no health, no platforming, and no upgrading.  Your actions essentially revolve around walking around this gorgeous stylized environment, interacting with items that you find, and using the radio to talk to your colleague, which gives you basic dialogue options when replying. You’ll also be taking out your map and compass often to orient yourself and figure out where you need to go.

With this sort of bare-bones gameplay, you might expect this to be a rather boring game. But to the contrary, this is one of the most interesting and engrossing games out there. That’s because it is heavily story-based, and heavily based on your relationship with your colleague. In fact, the simple gameplay mechanics actually [i]help[/i] to deliver that great experience because it allows you to focus on what the game does so well instead of distracting you with abilities, events or side quests.  This game can be really tense at moments, more so than other games I’ve played where combat and quick reactions are needed to survive.  

The gameplay is simple. The game is fantastic. 

However, this is where your own preference in gaming will have a big affect. If you want an RPG, open world, platformer, or whatever and don’t care about story and dialogue, then this game is going to sound like a turn off for you.  But even if that’s the case, I’d recommend trying out this game. It’s not that long and you might find that a good story can keep you hooked.

[u]User interface:[/u] The interface is simple and effective. Menus are easy to navigate and intuitive. The HUD is minimalistic, which I felt it was appropriate for this kind of game.   If you want to look at a Map or a Compass, you have to actually pull it out and observe it.  Mechanics like this, along with a lack of visual clutter, really helps to immerse you into the environment and story. 

The control scheme on a DualShock 4 is a little odd. You use the back triggers often, for actions like picking up items and using the radio.  I figured some of these actions would be mapped to buttons like the square button.

Instead, square is reserved for a toggle for running, which is pretty annoying. I’m not sure why running needed to be a toggle and couldn’t have just been implemented into pushing the joystick in a direction.  It’s annoying because every time you stop moving, it defaults back to walking. So you’re constantly having to toggle running on.  For an explorative game in the wilderness with wide open spaces and no need for stealth mechanics, I’m not sure why this decision was made. It’s a relatively small annoyance, but it’s there. 

 Overall the interface is straightforward, solid, and doesn’t get in the way. 

[u]Atmosphere:[/u] This is certainly an atmospheric game.  It’s how it’s advertised and it does not disappoint. The stylized environment can make for some very relaxing and serene visual moments. The level design often gives you opportunities to look out over vistas onto the background environment, which is a nice subtle artistic touch in encouraging you to appreciate your natural surroundings.

The sound adds wonders to the atmosphere too. Just the natural sounds of trees blowing in the wind, or birds chirping, or water running is enough to help you feel at ease during some of those long walks. The voice acting is top notch too,  and in my opinion is the true outstanding achievement of this game. It may be a peaceful wilderness, but the emotions, tones, and story that takes place between you and Delilah over the radio completely colors your emotional experience and investment in this world.  The verbal story progression, along with some haunting music, can turn the serene outdoors into a very tense thriller.  Honestly, it feels like the whole game is there to support the sound, and comes together in a fantastic experience. The sound is that good. 

This games atmosphere is so strong and so intertwined with the story that I promise you're going to get invested in this world.

[u]Accessibility:[/u] This game supports multiple inputs, which I greatly appreciated. You can change the controls to four different configurations: keyboard, gamepad, DualShock 4, steam controller. (FYI, changing the layout in settings doesn’t just show you what the control scheme is for that input, but [i]actually[/i] changes the type of input you are using. This is not made clear. So if you’re checking out a certain control scheme, and then your controls are all weird, that’s why)

For some reason the triggers on my DualShock 4 controller were not being registered by Firewatch. I ended up re-mapping the trigger functions to keyboard/mouse commands (right trigger = left mouse click, left trigger = Left Shift). It was annoying at first, and it’s possible I was not using the correct settings under controller figuration in Steam, but because of the multi input capability, you can see it was not a problem.

I was able to play this game using a DualShock 4 controller, voice attack, and a 3DRudder (keyboard or joystick modes)

[u]Conclusion:[/u]  I definitely recommend you play this game.  The gameplay, atmosphere, story, voice acting...just all of it comes together for a really great experience. It’s not super long, and priced reasonably so. Take some time and have some fun running through this stylized Woodland. You’ll be glad you did.

This whole game serves as an allegory for why you shouldn't run away from your problems. The setting and the characters all play their part in driving this narrative, and it does so incredibly.

Life isn't about wallowing in the bleak moments, or trying your best to escape from them, life is about salvaging meaning from those same bleak moments. Life is always going to be full of hardships, and running away from them doesn't solve anything. This game is a beautiful example of that.

There's nothing wrong with enjoying the occasional distractions from our everyday lives, but you also shouldn't lose sight of what's important. You can take a new job far away, drink lots of alcohol or play video games all you want, but all that does is delay the inevitable. When life gets rough, it's up to you to make the correct decisions to better your situation, and losing yourself in temporary bids of escapism will only make the challenges ahead more difficult to face.

Firewatch is a beautiful, highly immersive mystery/'walking simulator' with an engaging narrative and imaginative storyline.  If there were somehow an episode II, I'd play it in an instant!

The good:

- PLOT was fantastic, obviously the primary focus of the game, not just an afterthought for superficial depth.  It was like reading a good book as opposed to racing through a script in search of something interesting.

- VISUALS, while not photorealistic, have a pleasant, surrealistic quality to them and even near the end of the game I was still stopping to look around at the scenery, which is something I don't tend to do even in those 'AAA' games that are always praised for their gorgeous graphics.  The game is a little heavy on the saturation at times, but I really didn't mind all at much.

- MUSIC was excellent!  Nothing fancy, just soft and atmospheric.  I'm listening to it now, and will be adding the tracks to my music library.

The bad:

ORIENTATION was difficult.  With VR I imagine it would have been perfect.  I was excited about the option to turn off the locator icon on the map and rely solely on gameworld features and my map/compass, but although I'm great at finding my way in the real world I've always had trouble in computer games...such as this one.  Luckily, the entire world is designed from scratch with plenty of unique objects in the landscape.  Beware, though:  getting around is a HUGE part of this game, so pay VERY close attention to your surroundings.

INTRODUCTION, although well-done in terms of story, felt a little thrown-together.

Features:
- Not a 'fighting' game
- Plays out in 'days' (like chapters); there are plenty of good stopping points so you can get to bed.
- Semi open-world, organized in a somewhat maze-like fashion (picture a huge network of tunnels and chambers, like an ant nest.)
- Engaging storyline
- Mainly for guys:  The main character is a guy, and the dialogue plays out with respect to that (G-rated, from my experience).
- Timed, multiple-choice responses to dialogue; I'm not sure yet if they affect the storyline or mood.

TLDR: [i][b]*NOT A GAME ALARM BLARING*[/b][/i]


[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]


Once again I find myself producing a slightly odd review. Once again I find myself looking at the boundary of ‘what it means to be a game’. Once again I find myself asking, ‘How much of why you play games is to appreciate them as a story telling platform, and how much is to master a set of mechanics and overcome obstacles based on those mechanics?’.

Firewatch is not a game, it’s a walking simulator. So I guess if you don’t like walking simulators you have everything you need right there. Firewatch is, however, better than pretty much any other walking simulator I’ve ‘played’.
You find yourself in the shoes of Henry, a man who’s life and love have unravelled in his hands (in a tell it yourself type background story), and so he has taken a job in a remote forest to, as the title very clearly states, watch for fires. (I am also happy to report that there are, in fact, fires to watch.) 
The main arc is one of the development of the relationship between Henry and Delilah, Henry’s boss, who is only interacted with through the radio Henry carries to report with. 
There are mysteries to unravel, as strange occurrences pepper Henry’s time at the outpost, all while he finds old notes and abandoned hats. Is he alone, or are there shenanigans afoot?

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Atmospheric. Incredibly so. The feeling of isolation, the vistas, the fear of that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ grizzly, scratching at the back of your mind. It all feeds in nicely to making the story extremely immersive. 
[*] The game had me guessing to the end. I hadn’t completely bought into the drama, but it [i]is[/i] set in America, and if anywhere, then there. I really wasn’t sure which side it was going to fall on, but I’m glad it went where it did. 
[*] The characters are fun to be with. They are well written, have a good dynamic, and are voice acted well.
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The game is just tedious. Esp in the earliest portions where there is no investment. There is no hook, no reason to keep playing beyond ‘I paid for it so I’ll damn well play it’, and it’s just eye rolling. The entire game is in the development of those things, you have to want to get invested before it starts. 
[*] The responses you can give to Delilah do not always get reflected in the text provided, or are given with a very different tone to the one anticipated, making some of the dialogue feel out of character or out of place.  
[*] Lack of closure. I won’t spoil how it ends, which is natural and decent. But I will spoil that it criminally doesn’t tell you what happens after the story ends. I want to know what consequences my actions spawned, I want to know where the characters go and what they do next, I want there to be some kind of meaning to it all. And there just isn’t. It’s very disappointing. 
[*] There doesn’t feel like there would be any replayability. Having spoken with a couple of friends who played it, we all took different routes and ended up with the same ending… So I guess it’s a one and done.
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
 [list][*] This game would be massively improved if you could put stuff in your backpack to decorate the cabin with. It would also bring a little personalisation to the game.
[*] I want an Easter egg for bringing all those damned books back with me. Imagine my disappointment when my outpost is full of them and nothing happens?
[*] A debrief/what happens next thing after the game ends. What, if anything, is reported? Where do the characters go, what do they do with their lives? Closure, man!
[/list]


[b][u]Overall Recommendation:[/u][/b]


If you don’t like walking sims, it’s a hard no. If interpersonal drama isn’t your thing, it’s a hard no. If you’re not interested in atmospheric mysteries, again, hard no. 
It’s actually harder to say who Firewatch is for, other than folks who are just in it for a story…
Firewatch just isn’t a game. It’s an interactive story, and one done incredibly well. I thoroughly enjoyed it… but it isn’t a game. There are no challenges to overcome, no puzzles to solve, no enemies to defeat, no resources to manage. Just choices. I don’t think there is even a way to lose… so it may as well be a TV show. 
It also isn’t great value for money, though I bought it on sale when it was reasonably priced.
Ultimately, I can’t recommend this. It isn’t a game, it isn’t replayable, your choices don’t matter, and you don’t get to find out what the summation of your experiences were. If steam had an ‘it’s alright’ button, I’d have hit that, but it doesn’t, so it’s a no from me.

it is really hard for me to give a lengthy description of something that didn't last longer than 4 hours, so I will just give my personal sorta "bullet points" of what Firewatch came to be in the end:

- story will become personal to you, and in the end you might will not want to share it with anyone else.
- sometimes you would want to stand in one place for minutes and gaze over all that beauty that Campo Santo team has managed to create. the world is beautiful.
- it creeped the hell out of me at certain moments, I was literally sweating- being "alone" in the forest will do that to you.
- game had a satisfying conclusion, not the one that will blow you mind away, but the one that will still be stuck in your head for a while, just like good movies tend to do. 
- at some point story starts to develop way too fast and it might be an immersion breaker, I don't know why they did it so- budget cuts may be?
- I wish there were even more dialogue between two main charachters, because at times it felt like I needed to say something, but I couldn't, because the only way to reach the other end of the radio is to "report" something, like a fire or an occasionally found toilet paper, but you can't really report your feelings, can you?

To sum up, I think you should treat Firewatch like this- it is a good 3-5 hour movie where you can choose what to say and how to respond, and, as a good movie should, it leaves you with something to sleep on. If it succeeds in that, then it's certanly worth your money.

This is a walking simulator and you must know that going in -  so don't expect to be firing guns, starting fires, and taking cover, because none of that is here.  

What is here is hands down the best walking simulator that has ever been made to date. It tells an incredibly intricate story about love and loss, faith and hope. 

The premise is that you Henry are a 39 year old man married to a woman named Julia who is in her very early 40s. You live in Boulder Colorado. Julia is suffering with severe dementia and has to be taken in by her family in Austrailia for 24 hour home health. You, Henry decided to take a job in Shoshone National Forest Wyoming as a Park Ranger from an ad you saw in the paper. You wanted to escape your life - your problems. And that's where this story begins.

You meet Delilah, your boss, and the two of you communicate over walkie-talkies for the next 79 days. You will have some of the most intimate organic communication I've ever seen in a video game. The conversations feel extremely real and extremely natural, and that is the highlight of the game. The dialogue is unmatched by any other title out there, and it will hit you incredibly hard. 

The writing here is outstanding, and the developers have paid attention to every single small little detail. 

For example: [spoiler] When you finally make your way to Delilah's tower at the very end of the game, look around very closely. She has many things in there that relate directly to conversations you've had over the course of the 79 day journey. And if you pay close enough attention, you'll smile so big. [/spoiler]

The world is absolutely beautiful, I took over 50 screenshots depending on the weather, the time of day, fire statuses, etc. It's very rewarding to explore the world as there are many great sights to take in. 

The gameplay is fantastic too! Outside of just walking you have to use your map and compass to navigate the world, as well as repelling gear to climb up and down terrain. You recieve an in-game camera to take pictures as well, and all of those images will be displayed in the credits, which was also very fun. 

Once you've beaten the game there is an option to play again with developer commentary, play sandbox free roam, as well as the ability to upload all of your in-game pictures to your email and have them developed in real life! 

All in all this game is 100% worth the $20 and you shouldn't think twice about it. If you get it on sale then all the better, but this game is worth its asking price, and provides an experience you will never forget!

It's definitely a neat game, don't get me wrong, but $20? It has less than 10 hours of content for even the most extreme easter egg hunter. If you follow the plot, expect about 3 hours of gameplay. It's certainly not a bad story, and it makes you think, but the resolves are not satisfying, including the ending.

It's definitely not a waste of time to play, but I would put this in the $10 range for what you will get out of it. Almost all the gameplay is simply walking from point to point staring at a map. You don't collect anything, really, so there isn't much to do except follow the linear plot. You choose dialogue, but there are no branching paths, just different dialogue. Really the only thing you can do except follow the short plot is to find the few easter eggs spread around the world, but it's not much. The map seems big at first, but then you realize that you've seen almost all of it over the course of walking through it in only 2 hours.

As a side note, I also had some technical issues with the game. Every 20 or 30 minutes, the whole game video would freeze, although the game was still playing (the audio still worked, and I could tell my inputs still worked since I could hear myself walking around and I could hear when I entered the pause menu, etc), and this forced me to restart the game and load from a save several times which was frustrating. It would also be nice if this game supported SLI, although that's a lesser point, but still kind of disapointed that it didn't.

TL;DR
Not a bad game, but not worth $20, if you could get it on sale for $10, I might recommend it, as I did enjoy the game, but nothing groundbreaking.

[h1] Firewatch is absolutely an experience I would recommend to anyone. [/h1]

You play as Henry, a man who retreats to the Shoshone National Forest to get away from his life back in civilization (you get to decide the important events of your life in the moments before the game properly starts). Your role is to be a fire lookout at the Two Forks tower for a summer. You quickly meet your supervisor over the radio, a woman named Delilah, who will guide you through the span of the game. 

At first, you are tasked with menial things but then you notice fireworks going off not too far from your lookout, and Delilah sends you down to investigate. This is where the story really starts. I wont share any further details of the story at risk of spoiling the game, but the story gets quite intense at times. The sheer amount of paranoia or uneasiness it can make you feel will push you to want to know more and more of the story and how things will turn out. 

The graphical quality is superb, yet manageable even on computers with lower specs. The art style however is a matter of preference, some people love it, some people not so much. The true charm of this game however is the voice acting. The interactions between Delilah and Henry over the radio are masterfully done and voiced, and I truly wish more games would put the effort into voice acting as Firewatch has.

Is it worth $20 however? Maybe, it depends if you feel 4-5 hours of play time is worth $20. I will note that I have played through the game 3 times over the past couple of years and the replay value is great, with each experience being just as memorable as the past with several options being available in ways to progress with Delilah.
The game does go on sale for cheap and it can be found at other places for less than $10 as well. For that price, it is absolutely something worth picking up.

Firewatch is an exploration adventure game set in the wilderness of Wyoming.  As the protagonist, Henry, you chose to become a firewatch ranger to get away from your life and be in solitude.  During your adventure you meet, via radio only, Delilah who is another ranger at another watch tower.  During the course of the game you will deal with campers, wildlife, and fires.  The true highlight of this game is the dialogue between the two characters.

The graphics for this game remind of The Witness, but with more animation making it much more alive.  The different times of day are beautiful as the lighting really paints a masterpiece especially as the light goes through leaves and branches of the trees.  The only drawback on the graphics that I had was that the motion of the camera made me nauseous.  I had to mess with the FOV and it was better, but the motion of the camera really follows the players head and motion which can be a bit more than you are used to.  The only other game that made me feel this way was 3D Sonic, other than that I'm not weak when it comes to motion.  I was able to overcome it with settings though and was able to complete the game.

The sounds are great.  Nature sound like what nature should sound like, there's music in areas where mystery or suspense is occurring, but again the true highlight is the dialogue.  The voice acting is spot on and the conversation that you engage in are very real and natural.  The person who wrote the script for this game should be handling movie scripts because this was beyond what most games offer and beyond what most movies offer as well.

Between the graphics, sounds and the dialogue this game truly immerses you in an atmosphere most games just can't create.  The backstory evolves, the characters evolve, and it's just a really good mixture of all of the above for the making of a great game.

The game is short, which is great because it is afterall just an exploration game where you are hiking around the mountains and through the trees.  But the storyline and gameplay last just long enough where it doesn't feel drawn out where it overstays its welcome and you are able to truly enjoy the whole game rather than feel like you are doing meaningless tasks just to add more time to the game.

While I wouldn't buy this for the full price, I think that it is a pleasant experience to have so check it out for sure if it's half price or even less.

[i]Firewatch[/i] has brief brushes with greatness but never quite blossoms due to its over-tight scripting. This single-track journey is overlayed with a poignant walkie-talkie dialogue between the protagonist and his supervisor that [i]does[/i] offer some differing conversational forks, but this too never manages to feel entirely consequential. Midway through the game it is revealed that persons-unknown are eavesdropping on the walkie-talkie conversation, which suggests that the conversational forks [i]should[/i] effect the physical story, but such expectations are for naught.

Despite the rigidity, [i]Firewatch[/i] is rich with atmosphere, and exploring the rugged terrain is fundametally satisfiying. Rich Sommer's voicework as the protagonist is particularly effective and goes a long way to rounding-out what might otherwise be a flat experience.

Put them together and you have a legitimately funny yet poignant conversation that basically continues for the entire length of the game. The same story without them would've been a shadow of itself.

The graphics are simple but well executed and consistently styled. The music, on the other hand, is amazing. Some of my favorite moments in the game would have been boring walks through the woods without the music. Each track managed to transform idle time into something serene and precious.

The mechanics are largely like any other "walking simulator." I've had such good experiences with that moniker that even though I know it started as an insult I'm beginning to think developers should take it as a complement. The single biggest problem with Firewatch's particular implementation is that there is a minimum distance to interact with objects. Watching someone struggle with trying to climb a rope they are right next to is painful. "No you need to back up. You need to be farther away from the rope to climb it." That's advice anyone playing this game should take to heart, but it's stupid that it has to be given in the first place. There's also a bizarre bug where the reticle can be partially on an object, but then pressing shift to bring up the radio moves the reticle off the object. Talk about frustrating and unintuitive. Though other than those complaints the game plays like you would expect.

If you're looking for a game where the focus is on the journey instead of the destination then you should pick up Firewatch. The ending is truly disappointing compared to what it could have been. It's almost like the developers had less of an imagination than the people playing their game. I'm holding out hoping for some alternate, apocryphal interpretations to gain traction. Until then, the journey alone is well worth the price.

UPDATE: I've been meaning to add an addendum to this review for a while. The game must've received a massive update between when I first played it and about a year later in mid-2017. I re-installed because I was missing a few new achievements and was in for a big surprise.

They cleaned up the controls a little, but the biggest difference was the graphics. They're much, much better now, primarily due to an overhaul of the lighting system. It's much more dynamic. The world feels less flat, like it has more depth, and a lot of the scenes are more visually stunning than they were before.

Which is all to say I thoroughly enjoyed a second playthrough. Firewatch is an even more memorable journey now.

Walking Simulator + Feel good/bad Simulator

10/10

[b]Overview:[/b] [i]Conversation simulator, but in a good way -- really well-done interactions, writing, and voice acting. Having a Wallpaper Generator like this makes it worth the $20. Runs well on low-end computers.[/i]  

If you enjoy Life Is Strange or Telltale games but hated how restricted gameplay felt, Firewatch is a good bet for you. 

The gameplay is more liberal though still linear, in the sense that the game gives you [b]a lot of breathing room to let you do things[/b] between plot points. [b]You're allowed to explore,[/b] and look around, and take everything in. The game's not going to let you jump off a cliff and die (or at least I avoided it well enough), but you can see some cool stuff if you wander around. 

Wandering around is definitely worth it. You can have some [b]pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gorgeous views[/b] -- even on low graphics. And they set the atmosphere really well. The way they use nature to frame each day/night's events is brilliant. 

Speaking of graphics, this game has a [b]nicely low threshold in terms of computer requirements,[/b] which is wonderful for low-end gamers like myself. [b]Everything loads gorgeously regardless of graphics settings,[/b], but if you have the privilege of being able to load it in Ultra settings, you're in for a treat. The game even lets you take a limited number of photos -- limited likely because they store it in an online server, which lets you share with friends and buy prints if you're feeling up for it. 

I have to say, though, while the physical gameplay of the game is solid, as are the graphics, [b]the plot-related gameplay centers around your conversation with another ranger,[/b] who describes herself as a veteran and talks you through the ropes. It's pleasant conversation, really. The writing's great in that sense. 

What really got me was [b]how naturally your conversations are integrated into the context of the game.[/b] In other games, the "jolt" of reaction from the game is usually more obvious, or they'll exaggerate it: "Riningear will remember this." "This action will have consequences." Part of what makes Firewatch so great, though, is how subtly the game itself will pick up what you've said. Sometimes it'll point out things that your character observes in terms of reactions, but mostly obvious things. When you return to replay or watch the game through someone else's perspective, though, sometimes the unique dialogue makes it feel like you're playing a completely different game.

[b]The voice acting and writing really make the game, though.[/b] The two characters, Henry and Delilah, make hilarious, entertaining banter that doesn't shy away from their characters and situation. When they need to be serious, they're serious. And mixed with the way the game is designed to react to you, it's all absolutely persuasive.  

I do agree that the ending left a bit to be asked for. I personally don't think it's a [i]bad[/i] ending. Bittersweet, maybe, and a little awkward. But it's realistic, in my honest opinion, and I don't dislike it that strongly for that reason. 

[b][i]Is Firewatch worth it?[/i][/b] To put it into perspective, a movie is about $9, and that's about 100 minutes. It took me about 3.5 hours to get through this game. And I personally liked this game. [b]So yes, I'd say it's worth it.[/b] $20 is a good price for this neat experience.

Damn fine game.  Great aesthetics, great banter.  If you're a patient gamer, someone who enjoys watching a story unfold but won't be too disappointed by a more literary than fantastical ending, I highly recommend this game.  Only complaints I really have are that the game could take advantage of the "walking" element more, i.e. there could be more to explore, more places to walk and less restrictiveness.  

As far as the story is concerned, I generally disagree with the boys at IGN or whatever review comes up on youtube first.  They got all hot and bothered by the ending.  Let me try to describe it without spoiling anything: I think this game would make an excellent book, one that would involve vivid descriptions of Shoshone National Park with its lonely beauty, piercing that peacefulness with the lives and conversations of the two main characters.  You have to be open to what the author, in this case authors, want to tell.  While video games are different from books in that they place the reader/viewer in the action, games sometimes ask us to step back and examine a tragic situation much akin to the catharsis of Greek tragedy.  While we often wish to be the agents of the action, sometimes it's just as interesting to be a pawn or someone who is unaware of what is happening.  I think some reviewers missed the cerebral nature of those who play games like this one.  It's not always about the finale, but how resolution is achieved and this game does it masterfully, evoking a number of feelings in the player while challenging us to simply view something that happened before we even arrived for a summer of fire lookout duty, to view it and have a response, rather than create that response ourselves.  The game makes the viewing great, though.

I got this game because I love adventure games, am crazy for exploration & atmosphere, and even like walking simulators that other people are bored by. I do recommend this game but with some caveats.

First things first: Firewatch is an absolutely [i]beautiful[/i] game. It's a pleasure to look at from beginning to end. The scenery is top-notch. Likewise, the atmosphere is wonderfully done. There were moments where I simply walked around and enjoyed the wonder of it- I always wanted to see what my exploration would turn up next. This part of the game is so well done that, as the climax of the game approached, I felt a genuine sense of dread about what was happening.

So, if you're a gamer who lives for the "mood and feel" of a game, you will like this aspect of it.

Now for the area where I feel conflicted: the story. A "walking simulator", of course, lives and dies by its story and how well that story is crafted and presented. I feel that the story had a lot of promise, but ultimately disappointed. You come to truly feel for Henry and Julie (however, I found the character of Delilah more obnoxious than anything). But... there's something lacking. I don't know how to say it any better. The story feels empty on the inside, and not in an intentional way that reflects Henry's personal problems! There are too many instances where it's obvious the developers didn't want to make too strong of a decision regarding the direction the story took. Everything is open to the point of feeling unrealistic. Henry's decisions are vague, his friendship with Delilah is vague, the ending... is vague.

After playing the game for almost 8 hours (I took longer than necessary cause I wanted to go everywhere and look at everything!) I felt a bit cheated. It was sort of like reading a long novel that ends in the middle of a chapter. I realize that life isn't always neat and tidy, but in fiction having your characters go through too little character development comes across as poor writing. In a game genre that [b]needs[/b] an excellent story, this one left me feeling like the characters wasted my time.

Oh, and a minor nitpick: there's a bunch of anachronisms in Firewatch. If you're old enough the mistakes will stand out like crazy. Like, no one used the word "burn" to mean "insult" in 1975. Also, there were no Victoria's Secret supermodels in 1981. There's some other dialogue options that do not fit in the '80s as well as they should. Not a dealbreaker but it pulled me out of the game for a moment, and again- a walking simulator needs to avoid that at all costs.

So yeah. Play this- it's beautiful, it's something different, and it will scratch an adventure gaming itch if you're into those sorts of games. But don't expect to get too much out of the story except some 'feels', I guess.

Despite the myriad accolades and overwhelmingly positive reviews surrounding [b]Firewatch[/b], I managed to remain unspoiled about the game's narrative. Initially uncertain about my affinity for this style of storytelling, [b]Firewatch[/b] astounded me completely. The game exhibits a remarkable pacing, a distinctive art style, and introduces an utterly relatable and likable everyman – a character many of us can easily resonate with, as I certainly did.

Beyond the abundant acclaim the game has received, [b]Firewatch[/b] stands as a poignant ode to self-discovery, addressing themes of grief, shame, self-worth, and somehow the harsh truth over life's formidable challenges. Sometimes, all it takes to unravel one's thoughts is an unfamiliar yet sharply sarcastic guide leading you through the mundane aspects of daily life, offering purpose when you're unsure of where to begin.

It unfolds as a captivating journey, an adventure amidst lush forests and windswept mountains that characterize the arc of an audacious summer. [b]Firewatch[/b] fills your days with a blend of curiosity, courage, fear, comedy, and tragedy. I wholeheartedly recommend experiencing it, as it promises a journey that leaves you awestruck, perhaps prompting contemplation on the simple choices in life.

While I've noted that some individuals expressed dissatisfaction with the ending, I believe such sentiments reveal more about those players than the protagonist. The narrative, crafted with brilliance from start to finish, serves as a testament to the game's exceptional writing.

Firewatch is a damn good game. It is the first game where I made sure I had gotten everything else I needed to do finished before I began so I could play with not interruptions. Firewatch kept me enthralled the entire way though; had me laughing, frightened, even verbally exclaiming at my monitor when something happened, which is a rare thing from me in a narrative-driven game. The story is very well presented and wrapped up in a nice package so you're left feeling satisfied if you made sure to go out of your way to find secrets. Olly Moss and Jane Ng deserve a massive shoutout as well for creating a unique and beautiful aesthetic for the game. I often found myself simply exploring the wilderness and taking pictures with a camera I had picked up along the way, and then found myself taking screenshots once I had run out of film. The soundtrack is sparse, yet beautiful and adds appropriate mood to the game throughout. My only complaint about the Firewatch, if I had to make one, is that I wish there was more of it! The big twist at the end seemed like a bit of a copout (I was hoping for aliens) and the ending was lackluster and left me scratching my head until I replayed it and chose some different options which led to a far more satisfying conclusion. My advice to people who didn't like the ending: Consider your options as much as you can with every dialogue choice. How you two interact most definitely affects the nature of the ending. I will be keeping a very close eye on any projects from Campo Santo in the future. If this is any indication of the quality of their work, it'll be the next game up on my favorites list; right next to this one.

Boy was I wrong. After thinking about this for several weeks, I've come to realize that this is a fantastic game, twists and all. At its core, this is a game about running away from your problems, and depending on how you play the game will determine how you perceive the ending. I was anticipating a relationship with Delilah that never came, and was disappointed as a result. However, after thinking about it, I realize now that Delilah was an unhealthy influence on Henry. Her overreactions throughout the game caused Henry and her to concoct this fantasy of them being spied on and there being some massive conspiracy against them. Really, it was all in their heads, mostly caused by Delilah convincing Henry that there was something more than there really was. In the end, Ned was running away from what happened with him and his son, Delilah is running away from her problems of a lost lover, and Henry was running away from a terrible situation at home with him and his wife, leading him to go into the wilderness for an unforgettable summer. After going back home, presumably back to his wife after a failed attempt to convince Delilah to come back home with him, I felt disappointed. Now I see that Henry had to go home and face his problems, lest he never fully come to terms with them, like Delilah and Ned never did. This game is perfect for what it is, and if you're okay with sitting down afterwards to think about the open endings this game offers, then it is a must own.

The year is 1989. You are Henry, an ordinary guy whose wife got very sick recently, so he decides to accept a job in the middle of nowhere to get away from the everyday pressure of life. You arrive in the Shoshone National Forest in the beginning of summer, eager to get started on your new job. Aside from the forest critters, your only company will be your boss Delilah, with whom you'll be talking using a walkie-talkie. A watch tower in the valley will be your home for the remainder of the summer season, while Delilah is holed up in the command center at the top of the hill. Everything seems rather idyllic at first, but you'll soon realize that you got more than you bargained for when you signed up for this job.
Firewatch is basically a walking simulator with elements of psychological thriller. The gameplay follows a pretty unique concept consisting of walking, hiking and communicating with your boss. You’ll be responsible for monitoring an open-world perimeter while taking direction from Delilah and reporting your findings to her. Communication between you and Delilah is very realistic and highly interactive, often presenting choices that can influence the direction of the story. 
Firewatch surrounds you with a quiet sense of solitude and isolation, lulling you into relaxation before shifting into moments of unexpected suspense. The graphics are simple and yet beautiful at the same time, presenting the wild nature in an artistic manner. Sadly, the game world is limited in size and seems rather empty. More on that note, the whole game is pretty short and the story feels a little unfinished. Still, in this case, quality definitely outweighs quantity.

Firewatch is short, but memorable. In fact, I’ve never encountered a game quite like it before. If you enjoy games that focus on exploration or conversation, this one is absolutely worth a go.

[h1] A Unique, Emotional Human Experience [/h1]
On its own, [i] Firewatch [/i] seems like just another indie game with decent graphics and a decent story, but after playing it, I'm finding out about just how beautiful this game is at its core. I first noticed this game back when it first released back in 2016, at the height of the PS4/Xbox One era, but nothing ever compelled me to pick it up until I found it on-sale and decided to see what the fuss was about years later. 

What I discovered was a game that grips you to your core in terms of storytelling. You play as Henry, a 39 year old married man who, in order to escape the reality of personal turmoil, becomes a lookout at Shoshone National Forest in 1989. There, he meets his supervisor, Delilah, who lives in a neighboring lookout tower north of where Henry is posted. Delilah becomes the sole voice that Henry communicates with the most throughout the story and through the player's own choices - can forge a new relationship with her. 

All the while, as Henry and Delilah work together and get to know one another more, a mystery brews in the background of the story. Like a forest fire, the embers grow with each passing day until the mystery envelopes every aspect of the story. Paranoia seeps in and you're left wondering what's going on, who's watching you in the forest, and if all of this is just a bad dream come alive. 

At its core, I feel that [i] Firewatch [/i] is a real human story - one that reflects over love, life, family - the problems that we face as human beings, and the resolve needed in order to overcome them. Sometimes we get the outcome we want - but the reality we often face is that we don't. This game is a rollercoaster of a story that envelopes you into feelings of peace, of happiness, and all the while intrigues you with the mystery that besets Henry and Delilah and how you both work to figure it out together. 

It's not a perfect game, but a game absolutely worth experiencing. 

[hr][/hr]
[h2] The Things I Liked [/h2]
[h3] Simple Gameplay Mechanics [/h3]
The mechanics are very simple. You can run, walk, and use an action button to traverse crevices, jump, rappel, and so on. There are no combat mechanics, the game keeps it simple in that regard. You can pick up items, examine them, keep an eye on your dynamic map (that updates as you walk across so that way you know where you are at all times), and explore new areas around the map. The game doesn't make itself so complex in this regard, so the simplicity of the controls is something I really enjoyed. 

[h3] Well-Written Dialogue & Voice Acting [/h3]
Dialogue is one of the more consistent mechanics, where you can communicate often with Delilah on your walkie-talkie. You can report to her observations that unlock new dialog tree options or can choose to stay quiet, which can lead to a more reserved conversation. In my playthrough, I decided to be more flirtatious, romantic with Delilah, and that unlocked wonderful new conversations with her. 

With that in mind, I've got to say that Cissy Jones and Rich Sommer absolutely rocked in their voice roles as Delilah and Henry respectively. There was unmatched chemistry in the way they interacted with one another and it felt like a [b] real [/b] and believable conversation between two people in that situation. For a game where you lack facial animations, the voice work more than compensates for it. Outstanding. 

[h3] Maximized Graphics with Low Resources [/h3]
The graphics are very good for 2016 and for the type of game being played. It sort of reminds me of a much more refined [i] The Long Dark [/i] style of animation. It's cartoonish with a blend of realism but the game seems to use its resources well to depict the landscape as beautiful as it does for such a small storage space. 

[h3] Musical Score [/h3]
The soundtrack was one of the best parts of the game. There was something serene about it - so connected with the story and vibe of the environment. My favorite tracks are "Canyon Sunset" and "Calm After the Storm".  

[hr][/hr]
[h2] The Things I Didn't Like [/h2]
[h3] Controversial Ending [/h3]
Without spoiling too much more than I already have, I'm still pretty conflicted about the ending. It's something of a bittersweet ending. The game will play out as you see fit for the story, so you may arrive to a different conclusion than I did, but I sort of wanted more in the end - actual closure - which eludes the Henry I played. Although, the game sticks true to its theme in the way it portrays itself - we often do not get closure in real life - and the game doesn't shy away from reminding you of that fact. 

...and that's pretty much it. There wasn't really much I didn't like about the game at all. I really enjoyed it. I'm not sure about how high the replay value is, but it's certainly a title worth replaying to show your friends who've never played it before. 

[hr][/hr]
[h2] All in all, I'd give it a 9.5/10 [/h2]
Even a decade later, [i] Firewatch [/i] holds its own against the blazing and unpredictable wildfire of time. It's a story that a lot of adults can relate to as it touches on mature themes like family, death, marriage, and the meaning of life. We can all relate to Henry's plight in some way, as well as relate to Delilah too. The two of them create such an amazing duo that sets the foundation to the rest of the story. While the ending isn't what I expected [i] or preferred [/i], it's still an ending that reminds us of the reality of life and how we should all enjoy the moments we have for we never know what tomorrow might bring and what new wildfire we may have to endure.

Non-Spoiler Review: This game is another potentially fantastic walking simulator that is limited by the all-too common issue within this genre of the lazy unwillingness to animate faces. 

There, I said it.

You have this whole experience drawn up for you, full of possibility, but about 1/4 of the way or less through, you realize you will not see another human's face in the game. Every single experience is then defined and limited by this realization. Your entire outlook of possibility is completely deflated, and any intentionally minor encounter that you do have with a human, is ruined by this obviously convenient limit of not showing you the other person in any form, save for the odd silhouette or well-timed disappearence. 

This game was honestly a disappointment, hence why I've put off buying it until the current sale. If I had spent $20 on this game, this review would have been more anger, less disappointment.




Spoiler Review: ( I MEAN IT, THE FOLLOWING PARAGRAPHS WILL SPOIL THE STORY FOR YOU, YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED )


The prologue is extremely depressing. You cowardly take a job in the remote wilderness after your sick wife is relinquished from your care by her parents, due to your inability to maintain the exhaustive practice of caring for her, or whatever sort of path you chose.

You start hiking toward this fire tower, and once you arrive, you "meet" Delilah, your ever-physically distant supervisor via radio.

Having played various walking simulators in the past, this game has the typical cutesy doodles or hand-drawn character photos to give you an idea of who you are, and what you look like, but then the slow but then sudden realization hits you that you will not see a single human face in the actual game. You realize that you will never actually meet Delilah, the mysterious figure, or any of the scouts, rangers, firefighters, what have you. In the end, you are rescued by a firefighter who is wearing a reflective mask, and you never see his face.

The voice-acting is absolutely incredible, don't get me wrong, but this at-times hot and heavy distant verbal relationship with Delilah loses it's draw at the consistently convenient avoidances and Delilah's uncharacteristic unwillingness to meet with you in any physical capacity. She even leaves things in places for you, but this scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ woman won't even come to your tower to try and decide what to do with the only person she can trust? It's cheap, and lazy. This incredible story is so obviously limited by the inability to spend the time on in-person character interactions, that numerous decisions are made to prevent them entirely, where they would normally be appropriate or expected.

Overall, I enjoyed the story to a point, but was constantly drawn out of immersion by the lack of obviously appropriate interactions and reactions. Everything that happened in the last half of the game became predictable and not mysterious in any way.

As for the divisive ending, while I won't provide spoilers, I will just offer that I personally was not underwhelmed in the slightest—I would even go so far as to say I loved it.

It's an okayish game. It plays like a visual novel and not so much like a game, which really isn't my cup of tea. I don't think it lives up to the hype it got post-release. I do admit that the game's scenery can be quite pretty, although I wasn't expecting it to be poly graphics.

As other people have already said, it's more of a hiking simulator than a tower watching experience, and it's very story-focused. The dialogue adds a lot of flavor to the game, but everything else you do is pretty much all predetermined.

My biggest specific gripes are:

1. The camera panning. As someone who's prone to experiencing motion sickness, most of the game isn't that bad once you get used to it, but I dislike the way that the camera pans around whenever you interact with environmental obstacles. For example, I really hope that in real life I don't swing my line-of-sight around and stare at my boots every time I hop over a log when hiking, or that I don't tilt my head sideways 90 degrees and swing it around wildly every time I use a hammer. This game does that; it's stupid. It just feels like those forced object interactions to jump and climb don't increase the realism that much and are distracting when in the middle of hiking .

2. Lack of free choice. As far as I can tell, the events in the game are predetermined. You don't choose to take an alternate route, because the game is designed so that there's often only one way you can take. 
It feels like there's no point in wandering off and exploring anywhere besides where the game objective is, because either you won't be able to get there, or you'll be forced to go back there later on anyway for a game objective. It really takes the fun out of exploring.

3. Somewhat cumbersome travel mechanics. When hiking, it's easy to get lost sometimes. Checking the map helps prevent this, but it's a bit annoying to repeatedly pull up and zoom in on the map and compass. You kinda have to put the map down afterwards because you can't run and hold the map at the same time. Running makes you go a bit too fast, but walking feels too slow sometimes, there's not a happy medium. Luckily the world you move around in is actually pretty small, so it's manageable. I wish you could jump or travel over rocks, but unfortunately you can't.

People aren't kidding when they rave about Firewatch being a sort of masterpiece. I came into the game expecting a walking simulator with pretty scenery, maybe with a bit of park ranger action on the side... Needless to say, when the main storyline started to take shape, I was just as ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up over it as the protagonist was.

You don't need me to tell you that this game is beautiful, with functional (although sometimes clumsy) gameplay and great sound design that gets you fully immersed in minutes. You also probably don't need me to tell you that the story is one of the most unexpected and gripping narratives you can find in a simple game like Firewatch. Although a bit hectic, I appreciated that the plot managed to keep both feet in reality from start to finish. Plus, although the story is linear, dialogue trees and free-roam give you just enough wiggle room to prevent it from feeling constricting.

Though the map is reasonably sized and designed brilliantly to encourage you along certain routes, it can be easy to get lost, and switching between the map and scenery can be nauseating. Additionally, I was faced with a handful of freezes that forced me to load previous saves - quicksaving frequently should spare you from some of my pain.

Really, this game gets its praise from its stunning creativity, chilling story, and all-around impressive air. I would love to leave this review glowing, but the longer I think about it... the more I think that it's not worth the price. With next to nothing interesting or exciting to offer in terms of gameplay, no diverging story, and zero replay value outside of achievement hunting, Firewatch is seriously more of a movie than it is a video game - and who the hell spends 20+ dollars on a movie this day in age? I bought it on sale, and would consider it a near scam to buy it at full price for the whopping four hours of gameplay it offers.

This game is beautiful, and wonderful, and gripping, and I loved almost every minute I spent playing Firewatch, but I seriously think it would have been a better deal if I'd just watched someone play it on YouTube; It would have been functionally the same experience, and I'd be a few dollars richer. For this reason, I'll give it a 3.5/10. While I don't think it's a waste of time, Firewatch is unfortunately not worth more than ten dollars at the very most. Watch a silent playthrough or something and you'll be just fine.

Considering how I had picked this game up on little more than a whim after having heard it mentioned on a podcast that I frequent, I've gotta say that this was quite the fascinating and interesting experience. 

First of all, this game is very pretty. Its mix of stylized realism (as well as the gorgeous lighting) made it quite the pleasant experience to explore the world and consume the story. 
Perhaps, the most notable note is the voice acting. While I struggle to find the words to describe how it is so, this game has one of (if not the) most realistic and natural voice acting delivery that I've come across. 
The music is quite nice, too. While I didn't have any particular piece get stuck in my head, it did enhance the atmosphere quite well without ever becoming grating. In short, it did its job quite well. 
While the game's mechanics are simplistic and can be cynically described as a mere hiking simulator, that's not the insult that it may appear to be. In my opinion, the game’s delivery of its story is just fine as it is and would likely be hampered by more complex mechanics. 
Finally, we have the run button. It's always so nice to have the run option (Unlike some other games). Yes, there were times when times were tense and I preferred to walk. And then, there were times when I walked up the wrong path and it was even nicer to run back and not have the game waste my time. 

Those positives aside, I do have a couple of quibbles. Amusingly, they are all consequences of the game's phenomenal visuals. 
One, the game, sometimes, doesn't do a fantastic job of telling you just where it intends you to go at times. For instance, there was one point where I had spent several minutes circling an area, just because I was told to go to a creek, but the next set of instructions wouldn't trigger until I had arrived in a particular place. 
And two, despite the art style's suggestion of open and free world design, the game is actually quite linear and chock-full of invisible walls. Now, as I said, I did find the world to be very pleasant to explore, but... At times, it did get quite annoying when I'd be trying to enter an area that looks easily accessible and be unable to step over a fallen log or continue going up a large rock. 

Edit: So, I've talked to a friend about this game and realized there's a ton of stuff that I missed that I couldn't have seen in a single playthrough. 
Here's the thing. If you didn't like the game because you didn't like the story or the characters, keep going as you were. However, if you didn't like the game because of length, you're overlooking quite a bit. For instance. Go back and play through the game and try not responding to Delilah a single time. I guarantee you'll be surprised at how different the experience is. And, that's just one example.

At the time of this review I have completed the entirety of Firewatch in 22 hours, I held off writing a review until I completed it in its entirety including the "Free Roam" and "Audio Tour". I couldn't just write a simple review saying something tacky like "Oh I love this game" because I feel it deserves more, so I'm going to try and review a couple aspects of this game in separate sections.

[b]Set the stage[/b]

Firewatch is a game set in Shoshone National Forest in the state of Wyoming and takes place in the year 1989!

[b]Main Playthrough[/b]

The main playthrough was gorgeous! The graphics were stunning, I couldn't get enough of it! I took full advantage of my ability to screenshot so I could keep those beautiful photos forever. The dialogue was hyper-realistic, I could see this actually happening in real life. The game also includes many options for dialogue with thousands and thousands of different outcomes making your experience in the game truly personal as you develop emotional bonds with the dynamic characters. The controls can be a little strange at first but you get used to them relatively quickly, the game is mostly an adventure style type game with a world roaming aspect, with a bunch of little secrets for you to find on your own! The music (composed by Chris Remo) goes great with the locations and situations they go with. Chris did an amazing job on the OST and I thank him for these beautiful pieces.

[b]Free Roam[/b]

The free roam is unlocked after you have completed the main playthrough at least once, its not much other than what it says with having full access to the world. The main purpose of the free roam is to discover places you may not have checked during the main playthrough. However, in the free roam you have what seems to be a Sony Walkman that starts off with 1 cassette tape with 4 of the songs from the games OST, you can accumulate more cassettes by roaming around the world searching for them with there being a total of 20 songs and I believe 5 cassettes. Other than that there's not much to do in free roam.

[b]Audio Tour[/b]

Finally we arrive on the Firewatch audio tour which is a developer commentary version of the main playthrough with little booths scattered throughout the game as you progress through it with cool facts for how they made the game, came up with ideas, as well as little parts of the map with added props where you can test cool features. I highly recommend you do the audio tour if you plan on purchasing this game, it would be a huge waste to not include this in your playthrough of the game.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Thank you for reading through my review, I hope I convinced you to either purchase this game or bring attention to some parts of the game that you previously did not know about and might wanna go back and check! Once again thanks for reading my review, I really appreciate it!!

I will start by saying, that this is not a game for kids, maybe even not a game for teenagers. That's not to say that is deals with excessive adult content or anything like that, but it is very much mature in nature. Anyone looking for a straight horror game or some one-note action adventure is not going to be satisfied by this game.

The game is a walking simulator to its core, all the while focused on a developing relationship between two middle aged people, stuck out in the middle of nowhere. It's steeped in midlife issues, dealing in themes such as mental illness, paranoia and isolation. It's not one great, black cloud however, and there are a lot of genuinely funny moments throughout. It's a slow burn throughout (no pun intended) and there are a number of twists and turns that slowly unravel over the course of five hours. Without wanting to spoil anything, things often boil down to character's imaginations getting away from them. There is however one sinister plot element hanging over the whole thing which in my opinion makes this worth playing.

Firewatch really impressed me with its art style. It’s not going for hardcore realism, but that’s exactly why it works so well. The visuals are clean, atmospheric, and genuinely beautiful without trying too hard.
The story is very engaging, especially the prologue, which immediately pulls you in emotionally. It sets the tone perfectly and makes you care about what’s going on from the start. The characters are another strong point. Their chemistry feels natural, and I really liked how the game explains things through dialogue instead of throwing obvious tutorials at you. It feels organic and immersive.
What holds the game back from a higher score are the bugs. There are several moments where you randomly glitch around, and some animations look straight-up broken, like the game briefly forgot how it’s supposed to work. It doesn’t completely ruin the experience, but it does break immersion more than it should.
Overall, Firewatch is a strong narrative-driven experience with great atmosphere and characters. Technically a bit rough in places, but still absolutely worth playing if you value story and mood over perfect polish.
