I got Firewatch on sale, and played based on the large number of positive reviews.  I played it through and enjoyed the story, finishing just today.  I won't spoil anything (alright SOME of my critique is a tad spoiler-ish.  You've been warned) but I will say that I left the game wanting a little... more.  I wish it was a bit richer - in just about every aspect.  

The world and effects are quite pretty and stylized in a cartoon-ish way.  The previews give you a glimpse of that, and it's pretty easy on the eyes.  It's relaxing and slow paced.  The controls are easy, and there were just a few glitches and screen stutters.  There was one Supply Box that just shoved me away about 6 paces when I tried to open it.  Never got that one open.

The world navigation is pretty linear.  Not open world.  There are definite boundaries that direct you in the game.  Some things where you are thinking "man I should be able to walk over that" you just get stopped.  Eventually you come to understand where you can and can't go.

The dialogue with Delilah is interesting... but ultimately sort of shallow.  Wish it could have gone a little deeper.

The choices in dialogue you get to make... they felt inconsequential.  Like the game wouldn't change much based on how you chose.  I might play again and choose completely different choices just to see.

The mystery was fun ... until it wasn't a mystery anymore and it was sort of just ... meh.

I wish the stakes had been a little higher.

I was not prepared for the salty language used throughout the game.  Is this how all games are these days?  (yes I have been away from gaming for a while).  I wish there was a way to "turn off" the profanity.  It's definitely R rated.  I am an adult - so I can handle it.  But I wouldn't recommend the game to kids or family members based on this alone.  Give me a way to make it PG and I would.

Ultimately, I got what I feel I paid for - (Winter Mid Week sale).  A quick diversion that was fun.

What this game and its makers really have is POTENTIAL.  This could easily have a far superior sequel.  Firewatch could be just the prologue in a far deeper and interesting story.  Devs could take this in any number of directions.  My biggest wants?  Not in order of importance... 

1.  Clean up or give option to play a profanity free game.
2.  Make it a truly open world.  I understand some barriers need keys and quests.  Make them real barriers - not something it looks like I should be able to walk or jump over.  Anyplace I think I can walk, I should be able to walk.
3.  Increase the peril.  I would have enjoyed a little more respect for the heights or hazards in the game.  Falling to your death is impossible in this game as it is, despite the high vistas.
4.  Increase the stakes.
5.  Make the threat to our protagonists more... of a threat.
6.  Make the relationship more meaningful.
7.  Give our protagonists the option for closure given certain choices.
8.  Make the choices you make in dialogue more meaningful, even if it means having the story go a completely different direction.

Overall - I am glad I played.  Maybe I thought it was something more ... but that's ok.  Overall a cool game.

If there's another one that promises more of... all of it... I'm in.

Firewatch places you in the role of Henry, a man trying to reconscile his past choices, to process regret, failure, and the uncertainties of life. Henry takes a job manning a fire tower in an wonderfully crafted rendering of the Rockies, with the player guiding him through sun-dappled aspen groves and steep canyons. The visual style and quality are immersive, and I was quickly drawn into the setting and narrative.

Henry is alone in his job, save for a handheld radio linking him to Delilah, his supervisor. The story unfolds in large part through conversations with Delilah. A simple but clever game mechanic of placing dialog choices on a timer mean ther are both more tense and flow more naturally; just as you can't pause indefinately to consider every implication when speaking to someone in real life, if you wait too long to select a dialog option Delilah will interpret your silence accordingly. The voice acting is extremely well done throughout, and the limited music in the game also serves the story well.

Firewatch is certainly an adult narrative -- not in the sense of violence or sex, but rather of emotional maturity and the ambiguities of life, where we all make difficult choices, doing the best we can. It gave me many things to think about, and also made me want to hug my family at the end. Players looking to feel clever by unraveling a mystery or be entertained by a twist or scare may be disappointed. Those looking for thoughtful, engaging storytelling will find Firewatch a great piece of interactive fiction.

This game is f---in' awesome.  If that kind of language offends you, then this is not the game for you, as it primarily involves two adults engaged in adult conversations and using adult language.  If your fine with that sort of thing, keep reading.


*MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD*


Before you get to even get to really see anything you are presented with a series of emotional choices - several of them are HARD choices - that set up your character and his personality.  Whatever you choose, you, as an average joe named Henry, are made to spend 14 years watching your relationship with a beautiful and intelligent Aussie woman named Julia grow, flourish, and then die in the most horrible of ways.

Then it is May of 1989.  Julia has been taken away from your care.  Your dog has died.  You take a summer job as a firespotter lookout with the National Forest Service, and wind up hiking to your post in the beautifully recreated wilderness of the Shoshone National Forerst, just east of Yellowstone, in Wyoming.  You are tasked with watching for fires, dealing with campers causing fire hazards and whatever else your supervisor, Delilah, tells you to do.

Delilah has been doing the job for ten years.  She's an alcoholic.  She has issues.  She sees you as a potential friend, or maybe more?  The choices you make in your talks with her will determine how far that friendship goes.  You can be standoffish and cold or open an engaging, but the more you open up to her, the more she opens up to you.  This can have consequences as you work together and unravel the mysteries of the Shoshone.

(These chats, by the way, are all done over a walkie-talkie, you don't see her face-to-face, since her lookout tower is six miles away across an impassible ravine.  And your reaction time with answering her questions may end up determining your answer, or if you answer her at all.  If you screw up with an untinded response you may have to reload your last save point to get it right. Or just run with it and see what happens.)


*PROS*
 - Gorgeous scenery:  I can not gush over this enough.  Every every tree, branch, leaf, and blade of grass sways with the wind in a perfectly natural way.  The canyons and rock formations all look like they were carved out by God himself, rather than a graphic artist.  Hiking and climbing your way through this landscape - something you have to do a lot of - never feels like a chore.

 - Deeply immersive and emotional story:  By the time the forest starts to burn (the game's not called Firewatch for nothing) and your view of the wilderness is blocked by smoke and ash, it doesn't seem to matter, because by then the story has ramped up the tension enough to keep you hiking toward your goals without the need for scenic distractions.  Delilah's voice on the radio, alternating between skepticism, whimsy, paranoia and near-panic, is ample distraction on its own.

 - Great voice acting:  Every conversation comes across as completely natural.  Nothing sounds phoned-in.  Both main character's voice actors are alumni of succesful television shows, one of which is the same show the game's writer worked on.  They don't treat this like a step down in their careers.  They are completely on-point with every piece of sharp, witty, poignant and frantic dialog.

 - Simple, intuitive controls and interface:  What do you need to navigate in the backwoods country?  A well-marked map, a compass, and nothing else.  So that's what you get, aside from a helpful "you are here" marker and the last hundred yards or so of whatever path you walked to get there traced out for you, to help you backtrack and find the trail if you get yourself lost.  Basic WASD-Mouse controls and a few reconfigurable command keys in mostly easy reach complete the deal.  I remap R and LCtrl to Radio, LShift to Jog, Map and Compass from M and N to X and Z, and assign MsWhlUp/Dn to be alternate dialog selection controls so I don't have to use the arrow keys.  This brings all the controls under my left hand or onto my mouse.

- Replayability:  As mentioned, your dialog choices can completely change your relationship with Delilah and even some minor plot points.  You can be a complete jerk to her the first time through, then the next time you can form an open and trusting friendship.  Then you can play around with different answers and see how they affect the dynamic and the game, or discover new things out in the Forest, which prompt new discussions with Delilah.  Or just hike around and find new and interesting vistas to photograph with your camera, which you can upload to twitter or facebook and people will be convinced they're pictures of the real world.  I've played the game through twice now back-to-back.  I'm trying other games now but I'll be back soon, if for nothing else than to pay another visit to the beautiful woods and canyons of the Shoshone.


*CONS*

 - The game is too short:  It's taken me about seven hours on each of my playthroughs, but others (who obviously are not big into exploring) have done it in four or five hours.  It seems to me that there could be a lot more for the player to do before things start to go bad; build a fishing dock on the lake, clear brush in advance of the fire, round up campers and help them evacuate, etc,  And then the mystery story felt like it could get drawn out further too.  My gameplay time could have easily been doubled, and to a lot of people, paying $20 for a game that wraps in five hours - even a game as good as this - feels like a rip-off.

 - I honestly can't think of anything else.


*BOTTOM LINE*

If your the kind of gamer who just mindlessly completes tasks and asks "okay, what's next?" kindly move along, this game is not for you.  But if your the sort who can take the time to explore this world and the relationship with Delilah and appreciates the intricacies and attention to detail, the payoff cannot be measured nor expressed.

The voice acting is superb, the buildup of the story was engrossing, the mystery in your head, you dont know whats going on, it felt epic. Then if fell right on its face just like Lost did. A clean wrap-up ("Oh it was that all along!" Hmm..."). The story ends and you realize everything that happened to Henry and Delilah was completely inconsequential. You realize all youve been doing for the past 3 hours was walking through a linear story. Nothing you chose to say to Delilah mattered. Nothing you did really mattered.

Basically a 3 hours movie for 20 bucks.

Can't recommend it. You will just be let down.
